title: Trading in Currencies
q: Bank A faxes Bank B an offer to sell currency, valid for 24 hours. Bank B faxes its acceptance after 10 hours. When is the exchange contract complete?
options: At the moment Bank A transmits its offer
When the 24-hour offer period expires
As soon as Bank B's acceptance is transmitted to Bank A
When both parties take possession of the countervalues
explanation: Per 2/8/2, the contract is not completed until acceptance by the offeree and possession (actual or constructive) of the countervalues by both parties.

title: Trading in Currencies
q: Ahmad holds EUR in his account at Bank A and buys USD from the Bank in a spot contract; the USD is credited to his account. Has possession occurred?
options: Yes, the credit entry is constructive possession
No, possession requires physical handing over of the notes
No, he must first withdraw the USD in cash from the Bank
No, unless the Bank also issues him a cheque
explanation: Per 2/6/5(a)(2), a spot purchase of currency against another currency already in the customer's account, credited to it, is constructive possession.

title: Trading in Currencies
q: In a Mudarabah dealing in currencies, the Mudarib offers to guarantee the Rabb al-Mal against currency risk. Is this allowed?
options: Yes, since the Mudarib bears no capital loss anyway
No, one partner may not guarantee the other's currency risk
Yes, if the guarantee is written into the Mudarabah contract
Yes, if it covers only half of any currency loss
explanation: Per 2/9/3, a partner in Musharakah or Mudarabah may not be a guarantor for the other partner against the risks of dealing in currencies.

title: Trading in Currencies
q: Ahmad and Bakr conclude a currency exchange and appoint agents only to take possession. Whose departure before possession invalidates the exchange?
options: The departure of either agent from the place of the contract
No departure matters once agents are appointed
The departure of both principals from the contract place
The departure of the buyer's agent alone
explanation: Per the Basis, where agency is for possession only, the rule relates to both principals leaving before possession is taken, not to the agents doing so.

title: Trading in Currencies
q: A customer gives Bank A a cheque as the countervalue in a currency exchange. When does receiving the cheque count as constructive possession?
options: When the balance is available in its currency and blocked
Only when the cheque is endorsed to a third party
When the cheque is post-dated by no more than a week
Whenever the drawer is a known and trusted customer of the Bank
explanation: Per 2/6/5(b), receipt of a cheque is constructive possession if the balance is available in the issuer's account in the cheque's currency and blocked for payment.

title: Trading in Currencies
q: Bank A offers credit facilities letting a customer trade currencies in amounts exceeding the funds he owns. What is the ruling?
options: Permitted if the Bank caps the leverage ratio
Permitted if the customer pledges his balance
Not permitted under the standard
Permitted if every trade is settled spot
explanation: Per 2/12/1, it is not permitted for a customer to trade currencies beyond what he owns using credit facilities from the Institution handling the trading.

title: Trading in Currencies
q: A merchant receives a voucher signed by a credit card holder for a purchase. When is this constructive possession of the voucher amount?
options: When the merchant deposits it within the grace period
When the voucher amount is within the card's limit
When the cardholder settles with the issuer at month end
When the card issuer pays the merchant without deferment
explanation: Per 2/6/5(c), a signed voucher is constructive possession provided the card issuing Institution pays the amount to the merchant without deferment.

title: Trading in Currencies
q: A compliance officer at Bank A asks whether the standard on trading in currencies governs the discounting of bills of exchange. What is the position?
options: It is covered as a deferred exchange of currencies
It is expressly excluded from the standard's scope
It is covered only when two currencies are involved
It is covered as a form of al-Muqassah (set-off)
explanation: Per the Scope (1), the standard does not cover the discounting of bills of exchange, nor debt transfers without currency exchange or goldsmithery.

title: Trading in Currencies
q: Bank A buys USD from Bank B on condition that Bank B buys EUR from it in a second exchange, with no delivery of the currencies. What is the ruling?
options: Not permissible, as a parallel purchase and sale
Permissible, as the two exchanges offset each other
Permissible if the net amount is settled at maturity
Permissible if each exchange is in a separate document
explanation: Per 2/9/2, parallel purchase and sale of currencies is not permissible: no delivery, one exchange conditional on another, or a binding bilateral promise.

title: Trading in Currencies
q: In the Hadith of Ibn Umar about selling camels for dinars and taking dirhams, which condition did the Prophet (pbuh) set?
options: Delivery within one day of the camel's sale
The rate fixed on the day the camel was sold
Equal amounts, as dinars and dirhams are one kind
Price of the day, leaving no debt owing between them
explanation: Per the Basis, the Prophet allowed taking the other currency at the price of the day, provided they did not part with anything remaining owed as a debt.

title: Trading in Currencies
q: A customer owes Murabahah instalments in USD. When settling an instalment, he and the Institution agree he will pay in local currency. Which rate applies?
options: A rate fixed in advance in the Murabahah contract
The spot exchange rate on the day of payment
The rate prevailing on the Murabahah contract date
The average rate over the whole instalment period
explanation: Per 2/5, at settlement of instalments the parties may agree on payment in another currency, applying the spot exchange rate on the day of payment.

title: Trading in Currencies
q: Bank A in Dubai and Bank B in London conclude a spot currency exchange by electronic messaging, each in its own office. How is the contract treated?
options: As binding only after courier confirmation is received
As void, since the parties are not in one session
As if concluded in one place, with the same consequences
As a forward contract owing to the distance involved
explanation: Per 2/8/1, contracting between remote parties by modern means of communication has the same juristic consequences as a contract made in one place.

title: Trading in Currencies
q: In a sale of 10,000 currency units, the parties complete possession of the countervalue for only 6,000 units before dispersing. What is the result?
options: Valid in full, since part was possessed at closing
Valid for the 6,000 possessed; invalid for the rest
Void in full, since possession was not complete
Valid in full if the rest is delivered within two days
explanation: Per 2/6/2, partial possession is valid only for the part fully possessed; the remaining part of the transaction remains invalid.

title: Trading in Currencies
q: Bank A argues that a binding bilateral promise to exchange currencies later is not itself a contract. Why do most jurists still prohibit it?
options: It is equivalent to a contract without immediate possession
It breaches the rule of equality between countervalues
It involves an interest-bearing loan between the two parties
It always leads to a monopoly in the currency market
explanation: Per the Basis, binding bilateral promises equal a contract, and they are not immediately followed by possession of the countervalues.

title: Trading in Currencies
q: Bank A converts a customer's funds and transfers them to a payee abroad; per market practice the transfer takes two days. May the payee dispose of the funds meanwhile?
options: No, and the exchange is void because of the delay
Yes, constructive possession occurred at the order
Yes, provided Bank A guarantees the transfer
No, not until the transfer takes effect
explanation: Per 2/6/5(a), a customary delay in transfer is allowed, but the payee may not dispose of the currency until the transfer takes effect.

title: Trading in Currencies
q: Ahmad gives Bank A local currency and asks it to remit the equivalent in USD abroad. Bank A converts the money and charges a fee. What is the ruling?
options: Not permissible, as exchange and transfer are combined
Permissible, but no fee may be charged for the transfer
Permissible, and a fee may be charged for the transfer
Permissible only if the remittance is in local currency
explanation: Per 2/11, a money transfer in a currency different from that presented is permissible (exchange then transfer), and the Institution may charge a fee.

title: Trading in Currencies
q: Ahmad exchanges USD 100 spot for an unequal amount of Indian rupees. What is the Shari'ah basis for allowing the inequality?
options: Only coins, not paper notes, must be exchanged equally
Each country's currency is a separate kind, like gold and silver
Paper money is outside the rules applied to gold and silver
Inequality is allowed in any exchange the parties agree to
explanation: Per the Basis, scholars likened paper money to gold and silver; each country's currency is a different kind, so amounts may differ if possession is mutual.

title: Trading in Currencies
q: A customer wants Bank A to finance his currency trading. Per the Shari'ah basis, which arrangement is the permissible alternative?
options: A facility repaid with a fixed increase over the principal amount
A facility letting him sell amounts he does not own
A loan so he deals in amounts he owns, without conditions
A loan on condition he trades only through Bank A
explanation: Per the Basis, the Institution may lend so the customer deals in amounts he owns; requiring him to trade with the lender combines loan and exchange.

title: Trading in Currencies
q: Ahmad appoints an agent to carry out a currency exchange for him. On what basis does the standard permit agency in currency exchange?
options: Agency is allowed in any act the principal may do himself
Agency turns the exchange into a transfer of debt
Agents are exempt from the possession requirement
Agency is allowed only for possession, not contracting
explanation: Per the Basis, agency is permissible for an activity the principal could undertake personally; possession must still occur by the parties or their agents.

title: Trading in Currencies
q: Bank A lends a customer money interest-free on condition that he conducts his currency trades only with Bank A. What is the ruling?
options: Permitted, since the loan itself is interest-free
Not permitted, as any loan for currency trading is barred
Permitted if the Bank's rates are competitive
Not permitted, because of the trading condition
explanation: Per 2/12/2, lending on condition that currency dealing be done with the lender is not permitted; without such a condition there is no prohibition.

title: Trading in Currencies
q: Company X owes Company Y 1,000 dinars and Company Y owes Company X 5,000 dirhams. They agree a rate to extinguish both debts. What is this?
options: A prohibited sale of a debt for a debt
A permissible set-off (al-Muqassah) of the two debts
Permissible only at the exchange rate when the debts arose
Permissible only if the debts share one currency
explanation: Per 2/10/1, parties owing debts in dinar and dirham may agree a rate to extinguish the debts wholly or partially; this is al-Muqassah (set-off).

title: Concession Contracts
q: A licensee managing a public water utility wishes to rescind its fixed-term management concession. Under what condition may it do so?
options: It may never rescind a fixed-term contract
The State has breached a condition first
It takes measures ensuring services to the public continue
It pays the State a set penalty for early exit from the contract
explanation: Per 10/3, the licensee may rescind on condition that it takes measures that ascertain the provision of services to the public.

title: Waqf
q: A real estate Waqf is to be exchanged, and there is no risk of misuse. How may the exchange be done?
options: Sell for cash held by the judiciary until real estate is bought
Exchange it for listed shares of equal market value
Sell it and distribute the cash among the beneficiaries
Sell and invest the cash in Mudarabah on a permanent basis, not in real estate
explanation: Per 9/3/5, real estate Waqf is exchanged for real estate; where no risk of misuse, it can be sold for cash kept with the judiciary until a new real estate is bought.

title: Sharikah (Musharakah) and Modern Corporations
q: A creditor of a joint-liability company claims his whole debt directly from one partner, without first claiming from the company. Is he entitled?
options: No, he may claim only each partner's pro rata part
Yes, but only from the managing partner
No, he must first claim from the company
Yes, he may claim from any partner as he deems fit
explanation: Per 4/2/2/1, a creditor may demand fulfilment of all or part of his rights from any partner; he is not obliged to claim from the company first.

title: Ijarah and Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek
q: Along with an Ijarah, Bank A and the lessee sign a sale contract of the asset that will become effective at the end of the lease. What is the ruling?
options: Permitted in Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek contracts
Permitted, as the sale takes effect only at the end
Not permitted as a means of transferring ownership
Permitted, if the price is only a token amount
explanation: Per 8/7, transfer of ownership cannot be made by executing, along with the Ijarah, a sale contract that will become effective on a future date.

title: Commercial Papers
q: Ahmad issues an account payee cheque to Bilal. Bilal asks the payee bank to cash it over the counter. What must the bank do?
options: Return it to Ahmad for a new cheque
Cash it, since the cheque is payable at sight
Cash it if Bilal shows his identity card
Credit the amount to the beneficiary's account
explanation: Per 3/3(d), an account payee cheque binds the payee bank to fulfil its conditions by crediting the amount of the cheque to the beneficiary's account.

title: Sale of Debt
q: Bank A uses a monetary debt owed to it by Company X as the capital of a Salam with Company Y for future wheat. What is the ruling?
options: Not permitted, as the wheat is deferred
Permitted, if the wheat is precisely described
Permitted, if Company X consents
Permitted, as Salam allows deferred delivery
explanation: Per 5/2, a monetary debt may not be sold for a commodity with deferred delivery, e.g., making a third party's debt the Salam capital.

title: Islamic Reinsurance
q: Islamic Insurance Company X uses a traditional reinsurer under necessity. What limit applies to the size of such reinsurance?
options: It may cover all risks once necessity exists
Kept to the minimum, with Shari'ah Board follow-up
It may cover up to half of all risks
It is limited only by the reinsurer's capacity
explanation: Per 6/5, Islamic insurers should stick to the minimum size of reinsurance with traditional reinsurers, and Shari'ah Boards should follow up.

title: Waqf
q: A cash Waqf is held in a foreign currency exposed to exchange-rate fluctuations. What does the standard direct?
options: Use any market hedging tool available, whether or not Shari'ah compliant
Leave it unhedged, as a Waqf bears its own exchange-rate risk
Convert the whole Waqf into real estate
Use Shari'ah compliant hedging to protect the principal
explanation: Per 2/4/13/5, Shari'ah compliant hedging should be followed to protect the cash Waqf principal and hedge currency fluctuation risk (see SS 45).

title: Zakah
q: Ahmad rents farmland from Company Y and grows wheat on it. Who pays the Zakah on the wheat?
options: Both equally
Ahmad, the tenant
Neither, as the land is rented
Company Y, the landowner
explanation: Per 5/4/9, Zakah on produce of rented land is paid by the tenant; in Muzara'ah or Musaqat it is paid by the two parties proportionately.

title: Sale of Debt
q: In a Salam, the agreed substitute asset is worth more than the Salam subject at delivery. Why does the standard's basis bar this?
options: The substitute was stipulated in the contract
The substitute must be of the same kind and quality as the subject
The creditor would profit from what he bore no risk of
Salam may never be substituted after maturity under any rule
explanation: Per the Basis for 4/1/1/3, it would let the creditor profit without assuming risk and could become a loan yielding benefit.

title: Istisna’a and Parallel Istisna’a
q: A government grants a builder the right to operate a toll road for 25 years as the price for building it under Istisna'a (BOT). Is this a valid price?
options: Yes, usufruct of the subject-matter may be the price
No, usufruct can be paid only from another unrelated asset
No, the Istisna'a price must always be paid in cash
Yes, but only if a cash amount is also added to it
explanation: Per 3/2/1, the price may be cash, goods or usufruct for a period, including usufruct of the subject-matter itself, as in Build Operate Transfer (BOT).

title: Ijarah and Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek
q: Bank A's lease stipulates that the lessee shall carry out, at his own cost, the major maintenance needed to keep the asset able to provide the contractual benefits. What is the ruling?
options: Permitted in Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek contracts only
Permitted if the rent is lowered by a matching amount
Not permitted; it may be delegated at the Bank's cost
Permitted, as the lessee is the one who uses the asset
explanation: Per 5/1/7, the lessor may not stipulate that the lessee undertake major maintenance; it may delegate the task at the lessor's cost. Ordinary maintenance is the lessee's.

title: Sharikah (Musharakah) and Modern Corporations
q: Company G owns Partner P and offers to guarantee P's capital in a Sharikah. Per the Shari'ah basis, why is such ownership a problem?
options: It is in substance a partner guaranteeing a partner's capital
Company G would become a sleeping partner in the Sharikah with no right to manage
The guarantee would then be given for consideration paid out of the profit
The guarantee would amount to contributing debts as capital of the Sharikah
explanation: Per the basis, the guarantor must not own the guaranteed or vice versa, since ownership makes it in substance a guarantee by a partner of another partner's capital.

title: Waqf
q: Ahmad bought land with an option for himself to cancel the purchase. During the option period he declares the land a Waqf. What is the effect?
options: The Waqf is valid only after the option lapses
The Waqf is valid and his option is cancelled
The Waqf is valid and the option continues
The Waqf is void while the option exists
explanation: Per 3/4/1(c), if the Waqif himself has the option of disposing of the property, the Waqf becomes valid and the option is spontaneously cancelled.

title: Combination of Contracts
q: Two parties agree beforehand to combine Salam with Ju'alah for the same contract value. What is the ruling on this Muwata`ah?
options: Permissible, as each contract is lawful when concluded alone
Permissible, if the Ju'alah is subsidiary
Prohibited only if the Salam price is deferred
Prohibited, as the contracts contradict each other
explanation: Per 6/3/4 and 4/4, Muwata`ah to combine contradictory contracts, such as Salam with Ju'alah for the same value, is prohibited.

title: Revocation of Contracts by Exercise of a Cooling-Off Option
q: A buyer holds a cooling-off option. After delivery, the sold item is destroyed by a natural disaster, and the buyer then tries to revoke within the option period. Can he?
options: No, unless the seller agrees to share the loss
No, destruction after delivery is an impediment
Yes, since the option period has not yet expired
Yes, since he did not cause the destruction
explanation: Per 7/1, destruction of the sale item by a natural disaster after delivery is an impediment to revocation.

title: Options to Revoke Contracts Due to Incomplete Performance
q: Ahmad's contract specifies a red car; the seller delivers an identical white one. Ahmad decides to keep it. What price does he pay?
options: The market price of a white car
Half the difference in market values
The full price, with no compensation
The full price less a colour discount
explanation: Per 4/1 and 4/3/1, if the item fails the description, the buyer may return it or accept it for its full price without any entitlement to compensation.

title: Loan (Qard)
q: Why does the Basis distinguish interest-free overdraft arrangements between correspondent banks from 'You give me a loan and I will give you a loan'?
options: General need, and the benefit is mutual, not the lender's alone
The overdraft is a Mudarabah between the banks
Banks are exempt from the rules of Qard when dealing with each other
Overdrafts are always repaid on the same day
explanation: Per the Basis, such overdrafts rest on general need; the benefit is mutual, not specific to the lender, and it is a step for dealing with one's counterpart.

title: Waqf
q: In a Waqf for his children, Ahmad gives a larger share to his divorced daughter and his son with special needs. Is this permitted?
options: No, all children must receive equal shares
Only with the consent of his other children
Only if done through a bequest of one-third
Yes, as there is a valid reason for the increase
explanation: Per 2/4/4/5, the Waqif may single out some children or increase their shares for a valid reason, e.g., divorcees or people with special needs.

title: ’Arboun (Earnest Money)
q: A customer concludes a Salam contract with Bank A and wants to pay 10% of the capital of Salam as 'Arboun, settling the rest within a week. What is the ruling?
options: Not permissible: 'Arboun may not be paid in Salam
Permissible, as Salam involves deferred delivery
Permissible if the 'Arboun is refundable on revocation
Permissible if the option period is fixed by custom
explanation: Per 3/2, payment of 'Arboun is not permissible in Salam and currency exchange contracts.

title: Credit Agreement
q: Bank A issues a letter of guarantee and also acts as agent in a documentary credit for a client. What may it charge?
options: A return on both the guarantee and the agency
Actual expenses for the guarantee, and a return for the agency
A return on the guarantee, and only actual expenses for the agency
A percentage of the guaranteed amount for each service
explanation: Per 5/3/2/3, no returns on guarantee in DCs, letters of guarantee and suretyship except actual expenses, but returns may be obtained for agency in DCs.

title: Competitions and Prizes
q: Bank A announces a prize of SR 50,000 for every SR 1 million placed in its investment accounts. What is the ruling?
options: Permissible, if the prize is announced in advance
Permissible, if paid from shareholders' funds
Impermissible, as it guarantees part of the capital
Permissible, as all holders have a chance to win
explanation: Per 3/5/2/2, prizes must not lead to guaranteeing invested capital or part of it, as with SR 50,000 for every SR 1 million.

title: Payment Cards
q: Bank A plans to raise its card fee in return for a feature giving 2% cash back on all purchases. What is the ruling?
options: Permitted, as cash back is a gift
Permitted, if the fee rise is disclosed
Permitted if the cash back is capped
Not permitted
explanation: Per 5/6/2, it is not permitted to increase card fees in return for cash back, a price reduction, a usage-contingent feature or one with no known limit.

title: Indices
q: Bank A agrees to sell shares to a customer, the sale to take effect only when a market index reaches 5,000. What is the ruling?
options: Permissible, as the index is publicly known and cannot be manipulated
Permissible, as with an agent's instructions
Prohibited: a sale may not be suspended on an index
Permissible, if the price is fixed now
explanation: Per 6/4, it is prohibited to link a contract that should not be suspended, like selling, to a specific index.

title: Mudarabah
q: Which Qur'anic verse does the Shari'ah basis cite for the permissibility of Mudarabah?
options: 'Allah has permitted trading and forbidden Riba'
'O you who believe! Fulfil your contracts and promises'
'And, verily, many partners oppress one another, except those who believe and do good'
'Others travelling through the land, seeking of Allah's bounty'
explanation: The basis cites the verse on those travelling through the land seeking Allah's bounty, interpreted as those who travel to trade and seek permissible income.

title: ’Arboun (Earnest Money)
q: Which narration does the standard cite as the basis for the permissibility of 'Arboun?
options: The Hadith "Al-Kharaj Bi al-Daman"
Nafi' Ibn Abdul-Harith's purchase of a Mecca building from Safwan
The Hadith on paying in advance for dates by known measure
Ibn Umar's question on selling camels in Baqi' for dinars and taking dirhams
explanation: The Basis cites Nafi' buying a building in Mecca from Safwan Ibn Umayyah: if Umar approved, the sale held; if not, Safwan kept 400 dinars.

title: Zakah
q: Bank A calculates Zakah on its cash and trade assets using the solar year instead of the lunar year. Which rate applies in a normal (non-leap) year?
explanation: Per 3/2/4, the Zakah year for cash and commercial assets is lunar (354 days); if the solar year is adopted, the rate becomes 2.577%.

title: Mudarabah
q: Contrary to the Mudarabah terms, the Mudarib invests the funds in a sector the capital provider excluded, and a loss results. What is the Mudarib's liability?
options: He loses his profit share but owes no capital, as the provider bears the loss
He is liable only for half of the resulting loss, the rest falling on the provider
He is not liable at all, since he remains a trustee despite the violation
He becomes liable for the amount of the Mudarabah capital
explanation: Per 4/4, breach of the terms of the Mudarabah contract is a breach of trust making the Mudarib liable for the amount of the Mudarabah capital.

title: Indices
q: An analyst at Bank A plans to base investment decisions on one stock index alone, ignoring other analysis. What does the standard indicate about using indices?
options: Indices are used alongside other analysis and experience
Indices may be used only for Consumer Price data
Indices should never inform investment decisions
A single well-designed index is enough for investment decisions
explanation: Per 2/2, due to inconsistency between indices, they are used besides other analytical methods and experience of market situations.

title: Arbitration
q: After an arbitration decision is issued, Company X says it does not consent to it. Is the decision binding on Company X?
options: No; the decision needs the consent of both parties after it is issued
Yes, but only once Company X signs it
Yes, unless revoked as contrary to Shari'ah or public order
No, until it is registered with a court
explanation: Per 11/12, the decision need not meet the parties' consent; it is binding on them unless revoked for being counter to Shari'ah or public order.

title: Istisna’a and Parallel Istisna’a
q: A contractor cannot finish a building on the purchaser's land. Why may the land owner not take the structure without paying, per the Shari'ah basis?
options: The structure is a gift to the owner
Built at his request, which is stronger than permission
The owner must pay the full contract price for the structure
The contractor has become the owner of the land under it
explanation: The basis: construction was started by the builder at the purchaser's request, which is stronger than a mere permission to build on his land.

title: Investment Sukuk
q: In Mugharasah Sukuk, the holders are workers rather than owners of the land. Subscription has closed, certificates are allotted and activity has commenced. May they trade?
options: No, only land-owning holders may trade, not those who are workers
Yes, but only under the rules for the trading of debts
No, not before the maturity of the trees planted on the land
Yes, whether holders own the land or are workers
explanation: Per 5/2/18, Mugharasah certificates may be traded after closing, allotment and commencement of activity, whether holders are landowners or workers.

title: Zakah
q: A bakery making bread for sale holds year-end stocks of flour and of cleaning materials and fuel. Which are Zakatable?
options: The fuel and cleaning materials only, as consumables used up in the business
Neither, as they are not finished goods
The flour, at market value before manufacturing
Both, at their cost
explanation: Per 5/2/8, raw materials that remain components of goods made for trade are valued at market value; supporting materials such as fuel and cleaning materials are not.

title: Rules for Calculating Profit in Financial Transactions
q: Bank A uses an agreed benchmark to set Murabahah profit at the promise stage, and the contract makes later instalments vary with the benchmark's movement. Is this valid?
options: No; the total price and instalments must not vary with the benchmark
Yes, provided that the benchmark used is a well-established one
Yes, since the benchmark was mutually agreed by both parties
No; benchmarks may never be referred to at all in Murabahah
explanation: Per 6/2, a benchmark may be used at the Wa'd or contracting stage, but the total price and instalments must be stipulated and must not vary with the benchmark.

title: Settlement of Debt by Set-Off
q: Ahmad, owed a debt now due, forgoes that privilege and demands set-off against his deferred debt to Bank B. Why does Shari'ah not object, per the basis?
options: The creditor of the lesser debt always consents to the set-off
The creditor of the superior debt has forgone his advantage
Debts set off on demand are deemed equal
A court approves every set-off on demand
explanation: Per the Basis, set-off on demand is permissible because the person entitled to the superior debt agreed to forgo its advantage; Shari'ah does not object.

title: Islamic Insurance
q: A participant claims indemnity but disputes who must prove the loss. Per the basis, on whom does the burden of evidence lie?
options: On the Shari'ah Supervisory Board
On the reinsurer of the fund
On the participant, as the claimant
On the company, as the agent
explanation: The basis: responsibility of providing evidence lies with the participant, per the general rule that evidence should be established by the claimant.

title: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
q: Bank A wants to distribute profit without converting all Mudarabah assets into cash. Which method of liquidation may it use?
options: Estimation based on the expected rate of return
Constructive liquidation, with expert valuation of assets and debts
Valuation of all assets by the Bank's own board at their book value
None; actual liquidation into cash is always required
explanation: Per 3/1/2/1, liquidation may be constructive: noncash assets are valued by experts, debts valued for collectability, with allocations for bad debts.

title: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
q: Bank A buys aluminium on spot in an organized market. The seller provides documents proving the metal exists, is owned by him and is distinguished from other metal. Are the conditions met?
options: Yes, but only if the price is deferred
No; Bank A must physically inspect the aluminium in the warehouse
No; the aluminium must first be moved to Bank A
Yes; such documents are sufficient proof of these conditions
explanation: Per 3/1/1-3/1/2, the commodity must exist, be owned and ascertained; documents establishing existence, ownership and distinction are sufficient proof.

title: Waqf
q: A Waqf has income held during the waiting period before its beneficiaries are identified. May the superintendent invest it, and how?
options: Yes, in permissible low-risk modes such as Mudarabah
Only with the Waqif's written condition
No; Waqf income may never be invested in any mode
Yes, in any investment offering the highest return
explanation: Per 7/1, Waqf income may be invested per the Waqif's condition, during the waiting period, or from excess income, through permissible low-risk methods.

title: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
q: Ahmad holds a cooling-off option on a purchase and wants to sell this option to Karim for a fee. Is this permissible?
options: Yes, at a fair market price agreed between Ahmad and Karim
Yes, if the seller consents in writing within the option period
Yes, within the option period
No; options to reconsider may not be sold
explanation: Per 5/1, it is not permissible to sell or transfer options to reconsider.

title: Zakah
q: Company X paid 'Arboun to a seller. How is the 'Arboun treated in the Zakah of each party?
options: Deducted by the buyer; Zakatable for the seller
Not Zakatable for either party
Zakatable for both parties
Zakatable for the buyer; deducted by the seller
explanation: Per 5/1/5/4, 'Arboun is deducted from the buyer's Zakatable assets, while the seller pays Zakah on it, since he gets it whether or not the contract is concluded.

title: Hawalah
q: Ahmad asks Bank A to transfer USD 1,000 from his USD current account to his creditor Bakr; the Bank charges a fee. How is the fee viewed?
options: As Riba over the amount transferred
As consideration for delivering the money
As a discount on the transferred debt
As a guarantee fee for the transfer
explanation: Per 12/6, a same-currency remittance to the applicant's creditor is a transfer of debt; the fee is consideration for delivery, not an excess over the amount.

title: Irrigation Partnership (Musaqat)
q: A Musaqat worker waters the trees but refuses to pollinate, prune or control pests, saying only irrigation is his job. Is he right?
options: No, but the owner must pay for the pesticides
Yes, unless the owner pays him an extra wage
No; husbandry includes pollinating, pruning and pest control
Yes; his duty is limited to watering the trees, as that is what the contract names
explanation: Per 6/1/1, the worker carries out plant husbandry: watering, pollinating, fertilising, weeding, pruning, controlling pests, harvesting and seasonal work.

title: Settlement of Debt by Set-Off
q: Ahmad owes Bank A 1,000 due now; Bank A owes Ahmad 1,000 due in a year. Who may trigger a set-off on demand?
options: Ahmad, by forgoing his deferred maturity
Either party, but only with the other party's consent
Neither, because the maturities differ
Bank A, by forgoing the privilege of its due debt
explanation: Per 2/1/3-2/1/4, the creditor of the superior debt (here the one now due) may demand set-off by forgoing his privilege, whether or not the other consents.

title: Sharikah (Musharakah) and Modern Corporations
q: An investor sells shares he does not own, relying on his broker's promise to lend him the shares by delivery date. What is the ruling?
options: Permitted if the investor pays no interest to the broker
Not permitted: the promise is not ownership or possession
Permitted if delivery is made on the settlement date
Permitted if the broker is licensed by the authorities
explanation: Per 4/1/2/7, one may not sell shares he does not own; a broker's promise to lend shares at delivery does not constitute ownership or possession.

title: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
q: Goods held by Bank A as agent for a customer are destroyed in a fire. The Bank was not negligent and did not breach the contract. Who bears the loss?
options: The Bank, as the goods were in its possession when they were destroyed
The Bank and the customer share the loss equally, as both gained from the agency
The customer, as the Bank holds the goods as a trustee
The Bank, if it received a fee for the agency, as a paid agent guarantees
explanation: Per 5/2, the agent is a trustee and is liable only for damage from his misconduct, negligence or breach of the contract terms.

title: Buyback
q: Bank A promised to sell an asset to Ahmad for 100 but repudiates. On the performance date Ahmad has to buy the asset elsewhere for 108. What may Ahmad claim?
options: 8: the purchase price minus the promised price
Nothing, as a promise to sell never binds
100: the full promised price
The profit he expected from reselling it
explanation: Per 5/1/7, for a promise to sell, actual damage is the purchase price on the performance date minus the promised price.

title: Credit Agreement
q: A client buys a commodity from Bank A in a transaction where both the price and the commodity are delivered instantly. Is this a credit facility?
options: Yes, as an incidental facility owed by the Institution
Yes; every sale by an Institution to a client is a credit facility
No; transactions with instant delivery of both objects are excluded
Yes, as a cash facility in the form of an asset
explanation: Per 2/3, transactions that entail instant delivery of the transacted objects are not considered part of credit facilities.

title: Sale of Debt
q: A scholar argues that the creditor should first collect the debt, then sell it back to the same debtor. How does the standard's basis view such a requirement?
options: As a meaningless contriving formality
As needed to avoid riba al-nasi'ah
As needed for the transfer of risk
As a valid form of set-off (muqassa)
explanation: Per the Basis, requiring the creditor to take possession of the debt and then sell it to the same debtor would be a meaningless contriving formality.

title: Documentary Credit
q: After a credit is opened, a court declares the underlying sale contract null and void. How is the credit to be executed?
options: It is executed at half its amount, the other half being refunded
It lapses automatically and the buyer keeps the goods
It is executed as originally issued, because the credit is independent of the sale
Its execution becomes subject to a new agreement
explanation: Per 3/1/4, if the contract concluded before the credit is nullified by a court decision, execution of the credit is subject to a new agreement.

title: Ju’alah
q: A worker not required to work personally hires helpers to finish a Ju'alah task. On what basis does the Shari'ah basis allow this?
options: Ju'alah is a partnership in which all those present may work together
Ju'alah is similar to agency, where seeking help is valid
Ju'alah creates a binding Ijarah on the helpers
Ju'alah is a sale of the worker's own labour, so he may sub-contract it
explanation: Per the basis, the worker may seek others' help when personal service is not stipulated because Ju'alah is similar to agency, in which seeking help is valid.

title: Concession Contracts
q: A licensee holds a concession area for years without working it. Which precedent underlies requiring continuity of utilization?
options: Umar's ruling on wasteland left undeveloped for three years
The hadith 'Muslims shall honor their obligations'
The rule that the secondary is subservient
The hadith on not selling food that was bought before measuring it
explanation: Per the Basis, continuity derives from the ruling on retained, undeveloped wasteland: Umar said land left undeveloped three years becomes the developer's.

title: Commercial Papers
q: Bank A pays a client's cheque without a balance but charges interest along with the cheque value. Per the Shari'ah basis, what is the ruling on writing and dealing in such a cheque?
options: Permitted, as an agency for borrowing
Permitted, as a form of absolute Hawalah
Prohibited, since it includes Riba-bearing profits
Permitted if the client consents to the charge
explanation: Per the basis, a no-balance cheque is valid as absolute Hawalah or agency for borrowing, but if it includes Riba-bearing profits, writing and dealing in it is prohibited.

title: Sharikah (Musharakah) and Modern Corporations
q: Bank A's Shari'ah board explains why partnership with conventional banks can be permitted despite a hadith restricting partnership with non-Muslims. What reason is given?
options: The conventional bank's funds are purified once they are mixed with Islamic funds
The feared Riba is absent where Shari'ah compliance is guaranteed
Necessity always overrides the hadith, since banking cannot operate without them
The hadith applies only to individuals, not to banks or other juristic persons
explanation: Per the basis, the cause of the prohibition is fear of interest or impermissible contracts, which is absent when there are guarantees to apply Shari'ah rulings.

title: Islamic Insurance
q: At year end, the insurance account of Islamic Insurance Company T shows a surplus. The company proposes to take 20% of it. What is the ruling?
options: Allowed, if it does not exceed the agency fee
Allowed, if the policyholders approve it
Allowed, as its reward for managing the fund and bearing its risks
Not allowed: the company has no share in the surplus
explanation: Per 5/5, the surplus may go to reserves, reduced contributions, charity or distribution to participants; the managing company is not entitled to any share.

title: Murabahah
q: Which precedent does the Shari'ah basis cite for the permissibility of taking 'Arboun (Earnest Money)?
options: The practice of Umar Ibn Al-Khattab
The case of Hibban Ibn Munqidh
The case of Ubay Ibn Ka'b
The Prophet's purchase from Abu Bakr
explanation: The basis cites the practice of Umar Ibn Al-Khattab in the presence of Companions, permitted by Imam Ahmad, and a Fiqh Academy resolution.

title: Istisna’a and Parallel Istisna’a
q: An Istisna'a customer pays early. Bank A wants to give him a rebate, which was not stipulated in the contract. What is the ruling?
options: Not permissible, as it resembles Riba
Permissible, as it was not stipulated at conclusion
Not permissible; the full price is due
Permissible only if stipulated in the contract
explanation: Per 4/1/3, a rebate for pre-payment is permissible provided it is not stipulated at the conclusion of the contract.

title: Ijarah and Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek
q: Which Qur'anic command does the Shari'ah basis cite for the binding nature of an Ijarah contract?
options: 'O my father engage him on wages'
'Allah has permitted trade'
'Help you one another in Al-Birr and At-Taqwa'
'Fulfil (your) obligations'
explanation: The basis: Ijarah transfers ownership by exchange of counter-values, and such contracts are binding per the verse 'Fulfil (your) obligations'.

title: Waqf
q: Ahmad, who has no grandchildren yet, creates a Waqf for his future grandchildren. What is the ruling?
options: Valid only if it is converted into a Charitable Waqf at once
Valid only once the first grandchild is born
Valid; a beneficiary need not exist at creation
Void, since the beneficiaries do not yet exist at the time of creation
explanation: Per 2/4/4/4, it is not required that a Waqf beneficiary exists at the time of creation of the Waqf.

title: Hawalah
q: Ahmad paid Bank A for a travellers' cheque and later endorses it in favour of his creditor Bakr. How is this endorsement classified?
options: A restricted transfer of debt against Bank A
A sale of the cheque to Bakr at a discount
An agency for collection by Bakr from Bank A
An unrestricted transfer of debt owed by Ahmad
explanation: Per 12/3, the holder is Bank A's creditor; endorsing the cheque to his creditor is a restricted transfer of debt for the value the Institution received.

title: Sale of Debt
q: The tangible assets of a listed Sukuk entity fall to 25% of its asset value. What follows under the standard?
options: Only new issuances of the Sukuk are restricted
The Institution must buy back the Sukuk at par from all holders
Trading continues at market price while the ratio is restored
They trade only under debt rules and are delisted
explanation: Per 8/2/3, below 33%, holders are notified that Sukuk are negotiable only under debt trading rules; listed Sukuk must be delisted.

title: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
q: A spot commodity contract contains a condition preventing the buyer from taking delivery and obliging him to accept a set-off for value. What is the ruling on such a condition?
options: It is permitted if the market rules require it
It is not permitted in a spot contract
It is permitted if the buyer is an institution
It is permitted if the price is paid on a spot basis
explanation: Per 3/1/3, a spot contract must not include a condition that prevents the buyer from taking delivery and obliges him to accept a set-off for value.

title: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
q: Bank A's agent, without asking the Bank, appoints another firm as sub-agent to complete the task. What is the ruling?
options: He may, if the sub-agent is paid from his own fee
He may, as long as the task is completed on time
He has no right to do so without the Bank's permission
He may, since he remains liable for the sub-agent
explanation: Per 6/4, the agent has no right to appoint a sub-agent except with the permission of the principal.

title: Documentary Credit
q: Bank A issues a credit under which payment to the project owner is due only if the contractor fails to perform. Which type of credit does this resemble?
options: A red clause credit paid in advance
A standby credit, resembling a letter of guarantee
A revolving credit for repeat operations
A transferable credit for other beneficiaries
explanation: Per 2/3/3, a standby (guarantee) credit resembles letters of guarantee, with payment conditional upon the beneficiary's (contractor's) failure to perform.

title: Hiring of Persons
q: Company X hires a shared employee to print brochures, giving the work's type and specifications but no deadline. When must the work be done?
options: Within one month by default
Whenever the employee chooses, without limit
Within the period set by normal practice
The contract is void for lack of a period
explanation: Per 4/4, the shared employee is informed of the work, its type and specifications; when no period is stated, resort is to normal practice.

title: Procrastinating Debtor
q: Per the Shari'ah basis, why may a penalty clause apply to late construction work but not to a debtor's late payment?
options: Contractors are presumed solvent under the standard
Construction contracts are not binding contracts
Debts are always secured by a mortgaged asset
Penalty clauses suit only non-financial obligations
explanation: Per the Basis, penalty clauses are valid in construction, Istisna'a and supply contracts, but are permissible only for non-financial obligations; a debt increase is Riba.

title: Al-Wakalah Bi Al-Istithmar (Investment Agency)
q: The principal told Bank A to sell an asset at 100. Bank A, in breach of this instruction, sold it at 120. What is the position?
options: Bank A is not liable; the gain belongs to the principal
Bank A is liable for breach and must undo the sale
Bank A keeps the extra 20 as its own profit
Bank A loses its right to any performance incentive
explanation: Per 7/1 and 7/2, a breach advantageous to the principal does not make the agent liable; the gain belongs to the principal without affecting the agent's incentive.

title: Options to Revoke Contracts Due to Incomplete Performance
q: Heirs of a buyer claim his option to revoke for breach of description. Per the Shari'ah basis, why does this option pass to heirs?
options: All options pass to heirs without exception, being part of the deceased's estate
The seller consented to it in the contract
It is a personal right of the deceased buyer
It falls within ownership of a physical asset ('Ayn)
explanation: Per the basis, the option for breach of description transfers on death to heirs, general or special, because it falls in the category of physical asset ('Ayn) ownership.

title: Hiring of Persons
q: Six months into a two-year hiring contract, Company X wants to end it simply because it found a cheaper provider. The employee objects. What is the ruling?
options: It may terminate with one month's notice to the employee
It may not terminate without the other party's consent
It may terminate since hiring is non-binding
It may terminate if it pays a penalty
explanation: Per 4/7, hiring of persons is binding; neither party can terminate or amend it without the other's consent, except for breach, emergent excuse or inevitable circumstances.

title: Islamic Reinsurance
q: Per the basis, what is the capacity of the company in an Islamic reinsurance contract, compared to commercial reinsurance?
options: It is an agent of the reinsurance account, not a principal
It is a guarantor of the reinsurance account
It is a principal party that contracts in its own name for its own account
It is the owner of the contributions received
explanation: Per the basis (b), the Islamic reinsurance company is an agent of the reinsurance account, whereas in commercial reinsurance the company is a principal in its own name.

title: Murabahah
q: After concluding an 'Arboun-based Murabahah, the customer revokes the contract. What is preferable for Bank A to do with the 'Arboun?
options: Keep the full 'Arboun as its right
Keep the 'Arboun and also claim the lost mark-up
Refund the remainder after deducting actual damage
Refund the 'Arboun in full without deduction
explanation: Per 2/5/6, it is preferable that the Institution deducts actual damage (cost minus third-party price) and refunds the rest of the 'Arboun.

title: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
q: Bank A enters a Salam contract and wants to stipulate an option to revoke if the buyer fails to pay. Is this allowed?
options: Yes, in all deferred contracts
No; it is not permissible in Salam
Yes, if the period is specified
Yes, if expressly stipulated
explanation: Per 3/2, options to revoke for non-payment are permissible in contracts not requiring spot payment, but not in Salam and currency exchange contracts.

title: Possession (Qabd)
q: Why does the depositor bear the costs of deposit and withdrawal in a Wadi'ah, per the Basis?
options: Custom always places costs on the weaker party
The depositor is deemed the borrower of the depositary
The depositary is a trustee and therefore cannot bear any cost at all
Gains are based on the bearing of costs, and the benefit is his alone
explanation: Per the Basis, the burden of possession falls on the one who benefits from it ('Gains are based on the bearing of costs'); the benefit in deposit is the depositor's.

title: Ijarah and Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek
q: In the first lease period, Ahmad pays rent of 100 on a spot basis and leases the same asset back to its owner for 120, also on a spot basis. What is the ruling?
options: Permissible, as both rentals are paid on spot basis
Permissible only if the second rent is lower
Not permissible, as lease-back to the owner is barred
Not permissible, as the second rent is higher
explanation: Per 3/4, the lessee may lease the asset back to its owner for a lower, same or higher rent if both rentals are paid on a spot basis.

title: Documentary Credit
q: Bank A wants security for a credit it opens for a client. Which of the following may it accept as cover?
options: Interest-based receivables owed to the client
Interest-based bonds held by the client
Withholding the credit documents that stand for the goods
Shares in companies dealing in prohibited activities
explanation: Per 3/4/1-2, cover may include cash, frozen permissible accounts and withholding the credit documents; interest-based bonds and receivables are not allowed.

title: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
q: Bank B cannot legally avoid paying interest on an old loan without facing penalties. Per the Shari'ah basis, why may it pay?
options: Necessity, as acts done under compulsion are forgiven
Interest is a valid debt that must always be honoured
Paying interest is allowed if the amount is donated later
The loan was taken before the conversion decision was made
explanation: Per the Basis, interest is not a valid debt, but necessity allows payment where avoidance lacks legal protection; Allah forgave acts done under compulsion.

title: Ijarah and Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek
q: An Ijarah allows Bank A to accelerate remaining instalments if the lessee delays without valid reason after due notice. What must the Bank still provide?
options: A new lease at a reduced rental
Nothing, as the lease ends on acceleration
The asset for use for the remaining period
A refund of all accelerated rentals at once
explanation: Per 6/2, acceleration may be stipulated provided the asset is made available for the remaining period; accelerated rent is settled at the end or termination.

title: Payment Cards
q: Bank A finds Ahmad using its card for gambling transactions. What does the standard provide?
options: Bank A must report but keep the card active
Bank A has no right to intervene
Bank A may only charge a penalty fee
Bank A may cancel the card, as it bars such use
explanation: Per 5/9/2, the issuer must stipulate that the card not be used in prohibited transactions and has the right to cancel it in such a case.

title: Financial Paper (Shares and Bonds)
q: Company X issues new shares to increase its capital while the old shares' value is well above nominal value. At what price may the new shares be issued?
options: At any price chosen freely by the board of directors of the company
At the value of the old shares, by expert valuation or market value
Only at the original nominal value of the old shares
Only at a premium fixed at 10% above the nominal value
explanation: Per 2/3, new shares may be issued at a price equivalent to the value of the old shares, by expert valuation of assets or market value, at a premium or discount.

title: Online Financial Dealings
q: Why is an online contract valid once acceptance is given, even before the offeror learns of it, per the basis?
options: Contracts are valid only after they are registered online
Possession takes place at the moment of acceptance
The offeror is deemed to know everything that is sent to his website
A contract is the concordance of two wills, achieved on acceptance
explanation: Per the basis, scholars define a contract as 'the concordance of two wills'; once the acceptor declares consent, concordance occurs and the contract is valid.

title: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
q: An item that is 60% gold mixed with substances other than silver is sold for a commodity that is not gold, silver or currency. Is spot exchange required?
options: No, spot exchange is not required in this case
Yes, any item over 50% gold needs spot exchange
Yes, unless the item is below 21K
Yes, for the gold portion of the item
explanation: Per 3/3/1/1 (second form, first type, c), when sold for substances other than silver or currencies, spot exchange is not required.

title: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
q: In one financial period, one Mudarabah operation of Bank A lost 50 while others earned 200. How is the loss treated?
options: It is borne by the Bank as Mudarib, since it managed the operation that lost money
It is covered from the profits of the other operations
It is carried forward to next period's profits
It is charged to the capital before the profits
explanation: Per 3/2/1, a loss in one operation may be covered from the profits of other operations; if it exceeds them, from capital. The final liquidation result matters.

title: Istisna’a and Parallel Istisna’a
q: Bank A agrees to complete a customer's project left unfinished by the previous contractor. Who bears the cost of assessing the project's existing status?
options: The previous contractor
Bank A
The customer
Bank A and the customer equally
explanation: Per 4/2/2, the project is assessed on its existing status at the customer's cost; debts from the incomplete Istisna'a are the customer's personal responsibility.

title: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
q: Ahmad appointed Bank A as agent to sell his car, then sold the car himself before the Bank found a buyer. What is the status of the agency?
options: It continues until the Bank is formally notified
It expires, as the principal no longer owns the asset
It continues for any similar car Ahmad buys later
It becomes binding on Ahmad for the agreed term
explanation: Per 7/1/3-7/1/4, agency expires when the principal performs the task himself or no longer owns the asset in question.

title: Debit Card, Charge Card and Credit Card
q: Bank A requires a charge card applicant to deposit 1,000 as a guarantee, which he cannot use while he holds the card. What must the Bank make clear?
options: It pays a fixed annual return on the deposit
It keeps all profit on the deposit as a card fee
It holds the deposit idle as an interest-free loan to the Bank
It invests the deposit by Mudarabah and shares the profit
explanation: Per 3/2/2, an unusable guarantee deposit must be invested for the cardholder on a Mudarabah basis, with profit shared at a specified percentage.

title: Al-Wakalah Bi Al-Istithmar (Investment Agency)
q: With the principal's permission, Bank A buys goods for him with its own money before receiving his funds, then asks for an extra 2% for the advance. Is this allowed?
options: No; the advance is an interest-free loan bringing it no benefit
Yes, as fair compensation for Bank A's own cost of funds
No, since an agent may never start investing before funding
Yes, if the principal agreed to the extra charge in advance
explanation: Per 6/3 and 6/4, the agent may start with permission by advancing a loan, but it is an interest-free loan that may bring no benefit to the agent.

title: Financial Paper (Shares and Bonds)
q: Ahmad held shares of a mixed company for most of the year but sold them all before the end of the financial period. Must he eliminate the prohibited income?
options: No; elimination is only due on distributed dividends
Yes, in proportion to the number of days during which he held them
No; elimination falls on the owner at the end of the period
Yes, the full year's prohibited income per share
explanation: Per 3/4/6/1, elimination is obligatory on the share owner at the end of the financial period; it is not obligatory for one who sells before then.

title: Islamic Reinsurance
q: Islamic Reinsurer R applies the Shari'ah controls set for Islamic insurance companies. Who are treated as the participants in R's scheme?
options: The insurance companies
The individual policyholders of each insurer
The shareholders of the reinsurer
The traditional reinsurers it deals with
explanation: Per 8/1, Islamic reinsurers observe the controls of the Islamic insurance standard, considering that the participants in this case are the insurance companies.

title: Ju’alah
q: A client questions whether a bank, as a juristic person, can be the worker or offeror in a Ju'alah. What basis does the Shari'ah basis give for allowing it?
options: Banks are agents of the state in all contracts they conclude with clients
Ju'alah is a banking product by its nature, so only banks may use it
Natural and juristic persons have equal capacity for Ju'alah
Juristic persons act only through Mudarabah, not through Ju'alah or Ijarah
explanation: Per the basis, an Institution may undertake Ju'alah as worker or offeror because natural persons and juristic persons have the same legal capacity for it.

title: Mudarabah
q: A Mudarib wants to distribute profit while the Mudarabah capital is impaired. Which hadith does the Shari'ah basis cite against this?
options: Umar giving an orphan's funds for Mudarabah trade in Iraq, the profit being shared
The Musali likened to a trader profiting only when capital is safe
Al-Sa'ib Al-Makhzumi, the business partner of the Prophet before his mission
The co-owner who frees his part of a jointly owned slave and must value the rest
explanation: The basis cites the hadith likening a Musali to a businessperson who secures no profit unless the capital is secured; profit before capital recovery is invalid.

title: Combination of Contracts
q: During preparatory negotiations, the intentions of Bank A and a customer coincide on a Murabahah to be signed later. What meaning of Muwata`ah does this reflect?
options: A condition added after the contract is signed
Agreement to contract with a third party
Intention to use a trick for practicing Riba
Coincidence of intentions at the negotiation stage
explanation: Per 6/1/3, one meaning of Muwata`ah is the coincidence of the intentions of the parties at the stage of preparatory negotiations before signing.

title: Hiring of Persons
q: Per the Shari'ah basis, to which contract is hiring for a service delivered in the future compared?
options: Salam
Mudarabah
Wakalah
Murabahah
explanation: The basis states a hiring contract for a future service is judged by analogy to Salam, as it does not lead to dispute; Shafi'is and Hanbalis do not require advance pay.

title: Sale of Debt
q: After a Salam matures, the parties agree, with no prior stipulation, to substitute the Salam commodity (gas) with oil. Which condition applies?
options: The substitution must have been stipulated in the original Salam contract
The substitute must be of the same kind as the gas and of equal quality
The oil's value must exceed the gas's market value at the time of delivery
Oil must be fit as Salam subject for the capital; value not above the gas
explanation: Per 4/1/1/3, after maturity the Salam subject may be substituted, same or other kind, if fit as Salam subject for the capital and not above its market value.

title: Waqf
q: A Waqf beneficiary owes an amount to the Waqf and delays payment. The overseer purports to waive it. Per the Shari'ah basis, whose debtor is the beneficiary?
options: No one's, as beneficiaries owe nothing
The Waqif's, so only he may waive it, and not the overseer
The Waqf's, so the overseer cannot discharge him
The overseer's, so he may waive it at his own discretion
explanation: Basis 2/4/2: the beneficiary is the Waqf's debtor, not the overseer's, as the overseer cannot discharge the debtor from the debt.

title: Financial Paper (Shares and Bonds)
q: Company X wants to issue its share certificates to bearer rather than in the shareholders' names. What is the ruling?
options: Permissible only for shares that are fully paid up by the subscribers
Permissible: it may be in the name, to order or to bearer
Not permissible, as bearer documents involve Gharar
Not permissible: it must be in the owner's name
explanation: Per 2/8, the share certificate is evidence of the shareholder's undivided share in company assets and may be in the owner's name, to his order or for bearer.

title: Ju’alah
q: Per the Shari'ah basis, why is Ju'alah not binding on the offeror before work starts?
options: The worker is unknown to him, as in a gift made to the public
The work is fully certain, as in a sale where both counter-values are known
Compensation is contingent on a condition, like a bequest
The compensation is a debt on the offeror, as in a loan he has taken
explanation: Per the basis, accrual of the compensation is contingent upon a condition, so it resembles a bequest, which is not binding; for the worker, it resembles Mudarabah.

title: Revocation of Contracts by Exercise of a Cooling-Off Option
q: Ahmad buys a car with a cooling-off option and, within the option period, gifts it to his brother, who takes ownership. Ahmad then wishes to revoke. What applies?
options: He may revoke but the gift remains valid
Revocation is barred since a third party gained ownership
He may revoke if he recovers the car from his brother
He may revoke, since the option period is still running
explanation: Per 7/3, conduct that transfers ownership and creates third-party rights, such as selling or gifting the item, is an impediment to revocation.

title: Hawalah
q: A trainee at Bank A describes Hawalah as a sale of one debt for another. Is this correct under the standard?
options: No, it is an independent courtesy contract, not a sale
No, it is a form of personal guarantee
Yes, it is a sale of a debt at a discount to its face value
Yes, it is a sale of a debt for a debt
explanation: Per 3/1, Hawalah is a legitimate, independent contract made out of courtesy, not a contract of sale, permitted to facilitate payments and recovery.

title: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
q: In computing distributable profit, at what stage is the reserve for investment risks deducted?
options: Only from shareholders' funds
From gross profit, before the Mudarib's share
From the capital of the investment accounts
After deducting the Mudarib's share
explanation: Per 3/1/2/3, allocations for bad debts and the reserve for rate of return are deducted from gross profit, while the reserve for investment risks is deducted after the Mudarib's share.

title: Islamic Insurance
q: Islamic Insurance Company T is setting up its Shari'ah governance. What does the standard require?
options: A Shari'ah audit carried out only once at incorporation
A board with binding Fatawa plus internal Shari'ah audit
A Shari'ah board consulted only on the fund's investments
An external Shari'ah adviser whose views are only optional
explanation: Per 5/9, a Shari'ah Supervisory Board issues Fatawa binding on the company, and an internal unit for Shari'ah monitoring and auditing is set up.

title: Istisna’a and Parallel Istisna’a
q: Bank A, as ultimate purchaser, pays 'Arboun to a manufacturer. The Bank then rescinds the Istisna'a. What is preferable regarding the 'Arboun?
options: Limit the forfeiture to the actual damage
Refund the 'Arboun in full to the Bank, whatever the damage
Forfeit it and add a penalty for the rescission
Treat it as part of the price of a new contract
explanation: Per 3/3/1, 'Arboun becomes part of the price if fulfilled or is forfeited on rescission, but it is preferable to limit forfeiture to the actual damage.

title: Waqf
q: A person whose legal competence is restricted for irrationality declares his land a Waqf for a school. What is the ruling?
options: Valid if his guardian later approves the Waqf
Valid if it is made as a temporary Waqf only
Valid, as Waqf is a good deed open to everyone, even the incompetent
Invalid, unless he makes the Waqf for himself while alive
explanation: Per 3/2/3, the Waqf of a person restricted for irrationality is invalid, except when he declares his property as Waqf for himself as long as he is alive.

title: Waqf
q: Ahmad dedicates cash as Waqf to be developed by turnover on commercial grounds, aiming at the Waqf's sustainability through its assets or their substitutes. Which type is this?
options: Private or Dynasty Waqf
Joint Waqf
Investment Waqf
Specific Waqf Assets
explanation: Per 2/2/2/2, Investment Waqfs aim at development by turnover on commercial considerations, e.g., cash Waqf and Waqf companies.

title: Hawalah
q: Bank C, the payer in a Hawalah, is declared bankrupt by a court order before paying the transferee. What may the transferee do?
options: Claim from Bank C's depositors
Only claim pro rata in Bank C's bankruptcy
Nothing, as the transferor is discharged
Have recourse against the transferor
explanation: Per 7/2, the transferee has recourse to the transferor where the payer Institution is declared bankrupt by court order, or liquidated in bankruptcy before payment.

title: Payment Cards
q: Why does the standard bar waiving card fees exclusively for current account cards?
options: It discriminates against investment depositors, who bear more risk
It breaches the card network's pricing rules for issuers
Current accounts are loans, so it is a loan with benefit
It is gharar in the card fee, as the waiver is uncertain
explanation: Basis 4/1/2: current accounts are characterized as a loan, and singling them out by waiver or discount turns them into a loan against interest.

title: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
q: Per the basis, which Hadith grounds the right of Tahjir and rights established by first use?
options: The best amongst you is the one who is best in settlement of his obligations
Anyone who first uses what no Muslim used is more entitled to it
No harm and no reciprocal harm
People share in three things: water, pasturage and fire
explanation: Per the basis, Ibn Qudamah cites: 'Anyone who first uses what no other Muslim has previously used is more entitled to it'.

title: Waqf
q: Per the Shari'ah basis, why is a Waqf superintendent barred from leasing the Waqf to himself or his son without the legal authorities?
options: To guard against favoritism and neglect of the Waqf
Because such a lease is a form of Riba
Because he is not allowed to collect rent
Because relatives cannot be tenants of any Waqf property
explanation: The basis: the prohibition stems from fear of favoritism, part of human nature, and minimizes the chance of neglecting the interest of the Waqf.

title: Zakah
q: Company X holds statutory and voluntary reserves that appear under liabilities. How are they treated under the net assets method?
options: Deducted, as they appear under liabilities in the balance sheet of the company
Deducted only if required by law
Not deducted; they are Zakatable as owned by the company
Only voluntary reserves are deducted
explanation: Per 8/2/1, both statutory and voluntary reserves are not debts in Shari'ah and are not deducted; being owned, they are Zakatable under the net assets method.

title: Ijarah and Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek
q: Why does the Shari'ah basis say that ownership in Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek cannot be passed by a sale effective on a future date?
options: The price cannot be known so far in advance
The lessee may die before that future date arrives
Future sales always involve Riba and Gharar together
A sale's effect, transfer of ownership, is immediate
explanation: The basis: a sale contract cannot depend on a future date, since 'sale' means its effect, transfer of ownership, takes place immediately.

title: Documentary Credit
q: Per the Shari'ah basis, on which valid contracts does the permissibility of documentary credit rest?
options: Kafalah, Wakalah and Qard
Murabahah, Ijarah and Salam
Hawalah, Bay' al-Dayn and Qard
Mudarabah, Musharakah and Wakalah
explanation: The basis states documentary credit relies upon contracts valid in the Shari'ah, such as Kafalah (personal guarantee), Wakalah (agency) and Qard (loan).

title: Islamic Insurance
q: An Islamic insurance company records its own capital and the policyholders' contributions in a single account. What does the standard require?
options: Separate accounts only when there is a deficit
Two separate accounts: company and policyholders
One account is acceptable if it is audited annually by an external auditor
Separate accounts only for the investment returns
explanation: Per 5/2, the company should maintain two separate accounts: one for its own rights and liabilities and one for those of the policyholders.

title: Salam and Parallel Salam
q: Bank A's Salam contract stipulates at signing that the seller may deliver olive oil instead of the agreed wheat. What is the problem?
options: Replacement may not be stipulated in the contract
Replacement is never permitted in Salam, even afterwards
Oil and wheat are of the same genus under Riba rules
Oil cannot be sold by Salam as it is a processed good
explanation: Per 4/2, exchange for other goods is allowed after the due date only as long as such substitution was not stipulated in the contract.

title: Sale of Debt
q: A company whose assets consist entirely of debts, with no other assets, sells shares. Which rules govern the sale?
options: The rules for Mudaraba-based Sukuk
The rules of the sale of debt
The rules for sale of tangible assets
No restrictions, as the debts are ancillary
explanation: Per 8/1, the exemption for ongoing entities applies provided the entity is not entirely composed of debt; otherwise sale of debt rules apply.

title: Indices
q: Bank A is offered a call option contract on a stock market index. What is the ruling?
options: Permissible, if used to hedge a share portfolio
Permissible, if the premium is paid in advance
Permissible, if the index is Shari'ah-screened
Prohibited, as options on indices are not allowed
explanation: Per 6/2, it is prohibited to conclude option contracts on indices.

title: Salam and Parallel Salam
q: Bank A signs a contract with a factory to manufacture machines to order. Does the Salam and Parallel Salam standard govern this contract?
options: Yes, as it is a sale for deferred delivery
Only if the machines are fungible goods
No, Istisna'a is covered by a separate standard
Yes, if the Bank pays the price in advance
explanation: Per clause 1, the standard covers Salam, Parallel Salam and Salam Sukuk, but not Istisna'a (manufacturing contract), which has a separate standard.

title: Irrigation Partnership (Musaqat)
q: The orchard needs a major new well drilled, work customarily beyond an irrigator's duties. How may the Musaqat worker arrange it?
options: He may hire others on the account of the partnership
He must hire others at his own sole expense
He may not arrange it; only the owner can
He must drill it himself at no extra cost, as it forms part of his husbandry duties
explanation: Per 8/3, the worker may hire others, on the account of the Irrigation Partnership, to perform work customarily beyond the scope of his duties.

title: Online Financial Dealings
q: Company X's website shows a product and states it may withdraw even after a customer accepts. A customer clicks to accept. What is the status?
options: The contract is concluded, but Company X keeps an option to cancel it later
The contract is concluded once the customer clicks to accept
The contract is void, since withdrawal conditions are prohibited
It was only an invitation; offer and acceptance must still take place
explanation: Per 5/3, retaining the right of withdrawal even if accepted makes the message an announcement or invitation for contracting, not an offer.

title: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
q: Bank A sells a gold ingot for currency and gives the buyer a certificate. Which certificate gives the buyer constructive possession?
options: One for a specified ingot, issued two days after the sale (T+2)
One for an ingot allocated by serial number, issued at T+0
One that gives no right to physical delivery
One for an unallocated quantity of ingots, issued at T+0 on the sale date
explanation: Per 3/4, the certificate must represent a distinguishable (allocated) ingot, be issued on T+0 by recognized agencies, and allow physical delivery on request.

title: Waqf
q: Why does the standard require relevant authority approval for substituting tangible Waqf assets?
options: Because overseers lack legal personality
Because the state owns the legal title of all tangible Waqf assets
To protect the Waqf under the state's public guardianship
To allow the state to tax the substitution and collect a fee
explanation: Basis 10/1/5/5: authority permission protects the Waqf, supports its interest, and establishes the public guardianship of the state on Waqfs.

title: Istisna’a and Parallel Istisna’a
q: After an Istisna'a is signed, the authorities impose new safety requirements that add costs not borne by the manufacturer under the contract or by law. The contract has a clause for this. Who pays?
options: The ultimate purchaser
The Institution's Shari'ah Board
The manufacturer
The two parties equally
explanation: Per 4/2/5, a clause may provide that extra expenses from later directives of the authorities, not borne by the manufacturer, are borne by the ultimate purchaser.

title: Monetization (Tawarruq)
q: A customer buys a commodity from Bank A for Monetization and asks the Bank to sell it on his behalf. Local regulations allow him to sell it himself. What should the Bank do?
options: Accept the delegation once the customer has received the commodity
Accept the delegation if no fee is charged for the agency
Accept the delegation, since agency is a separate contract
Refuse; the customer sells it himself or through another agent
explanation: Per 4/7 and 4/9, the client shall not delegate the Institution to sell a commodity he bought from it, and the Institution shall not accept such delegation.

title: Irrigation Partnership (Musaqat)
q: Midway through a Musaqat, it transpires the trees actually belong to a third party, not the contracting owner. Who gets the crop, and what does the worker get?
options: The contracting party; the worker gets his share
The third party; the worker gets a market wage up to his share
The worker and contracting party share it as agreed, since the worker acted in good faith
The third party; the worker gets nothing
explanation: Per 11/1, the crop belongs to the third party; the worker gets a market wage from the other party, not exceeding what his share would have been.

title: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
q: An orchard owner sells Company X the fruits his trees will yield over the next five years. What is the ruling on this Mu'awamah sale?
options: Permissible if the price is paid yearly as the fruits ripen
Permissible, as a form of Salam with the price paid in advance
Impermissible, as the fruits' future existence is not ensured
Permissible because fruits are a corollary of trees
explanation: Per 5/7, it is impermissible to sell a commodity that neither exists now nor whose future existence is ensured; Mu'awamah sale is an example.

title: Protection of Capital and Investments
q: An investment agent invests strictly within his mandate. A market downturn reduces the capital by 20%, with no misconduct, negligence or breach on his part. Who bears the loss?
options: The agent and investor, equally
The agent, as he holds the funds in trust
The agent, for any loss above 10%
The investor; the agent is not liable
explanation: Per 3/4, the investment manager acts in a fiduciary capacity and is not liable for loss of capital except for wilful misconduct, negligence or breach of contract.

title: Unilateral and Bilateral Promise
q: Relying solely on Ahmad's resolute promise to buy, Bank A buys a car for 50,000. Ahmad refuses to buy, and Bank A sells it to another buyer for 46,000. What must Ahmad pay?
options: 4,000 plus the profit Bank A expected to earn
Nothing, since a promise is only a moral duty
4,000, the actual loss suffered by Bank A
50,000, the full cost, in exchange for the car
explanation: Per 3/4, a promisor who caused the promisee to incur liability must indemnify actual loss: the difference between cost and price obtained; actual loss excludes opportunity cost.

title: Online Financial Dealings
q: Why is an e-mail that does not state all the rights and commitments of a contract not treated as an offer, per the basis?
options: An offer must always include a period for its validity
An offer must be categorically obvious and bear no other meaning
E-mail cannot carry an offer under the rules of message contracting
An offer is valid only if made in the presence of both parties
explanation: Per the basis, such a message is not an offer because, from a Shari'ah point of view, an offer should be categorically obvious and cannot bear any other meaning.

title: Financial Paper (Shares and Bonds)
q: Bank A agrees to subscribe at nominal value to any shares of a new corporation left unsubscribed, and asks a fee in return for this undertaking. What is the ruling?
options: Underwriting is allowed, but not compensation for it
The fee is allowed as it is a market practice among underwriters
Underwriting itself is not permissible, whether or not a fee is taken
