options: As soon as he offers the property for sale
Only when the option period expires
Only once a sale to a third party is completed
Once a third party makes a firm offer
explanation: Per 2/4/4, the option owner may offer the item to third parties, and the option does not lapse until the sale is completed.

title: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
q: Bank A announced an expected rate of return of 7% based on a feasibility study, but actual realized profit is 5%. What is distributed?
options: 7%, as the announced rate is binding
The actual realized profit after liquidation
7%, with the Bank covering the shortfall
6%, the average of expected and actual
explanation: Per 5/2, an expected rate of return is not binding if not achieved; final distribution is based on profit realized after actual or constructive liquidation.

title: Settlement of Debt by Set-Off
q: Bank A discharges a customer's liability by waiving the obligation. Is this discharge governed by the standard on settlement of debt by set-off?
options: No, waiving of obligation is covered by another standard
Yes, if the waived debt equals another debt between the parties
Yes, as a form of compulsory set-off
Yes, as a form of contractual set-off
explanation: Per the Scope (1), the standard does not apply to discharge by transfer, waiving of obligation, composition or bilateral cancellation; other standards cover them.

title: Zakah
q: Bank A is not legally committed to pay Zakah, so Zakah is the responsibility of its shareholders and investment account holders. What must the Bank do?
options: Nothing, as Zakah is a private matter
Deduct the Zakah from dividends without any disclosure to holders
Pay the Zakah anyway from retained profits
Indicate the Zakah payable per share or per account balance
explanation: Per 2/2/5, when Zakah is the shareholders' and account holders' responsibility, the Institution has to indicate the amount payable per share or per investment account balance.

title: Hawalah
q: Bakr accepted a Hawalah on condition that Zaid, the payer, is solvent. Zaid proves to be insolvent. What is Bakr's position?
options: He loses his claim entirely
He may claim only from Zaid's guarantor
He has recourse to the transferor
He must wait until Zaid becomes solvent
explanation: Per 7/1, if acceptance was conditional on the payer's solvency, the transferee has a right of recourse to the transferor if the payer is not solvent.

title: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
q: Bank A buys 1,000 tonnes of wheat and wants a cooling-off option on only part of the deal. What must the contract specify?
options: The percentage of the wheat to which the option relates
The identity of the eventual end-buyer
Nothing; the option may cover any part chosen later by the buyer
The specific bags to which the option relates, identified by number
explanation: Per 2/8/3, an option may relate to part of a deal; for differing items they must be specified, and for fungibles like wheat the percentage must be specified.

title: Murabahah
q: Bank A's Murabahah contract mentions only the total selling price, without stating the cost or the profit. Is this sufficient?
options: No, the Bank's staff costs must also be shown
Yes, if the customer accepts the total
No, the profit mark-up must be known
Yes, a known total price is enough
explanation: Per 4/7, the Institution's profit mark-up must be known; the mere mention of the total selling price is not sufficient.

title: Documentary Credit
q: Before paying under a credit, Bank A obtains proof that the bill of lading presented by the beneficiary is forged. What is Bank A's position?
options: It must pay, as documents appear conforming
It must pay and then claim from the beneficiary
It must pay if the credit is irrevocable
It is under no obligation to execute the credit
explanation: Per 2/4/3 and 3/1/4, the bank must pay against conforming documents except upon proof of fraud or forgery, in which case it is under no obligation to execute.

title: Sale of Debt
q: Bank A sells a receivable to Company Y. When do the ownership and risk of the debt pass to Company Y?
options: Only once the debtor consents to the sale and acknowledges it
By any means that customarily lets it claim the debt
Only when the debtor pays the debt to Company Y in full
Only on registration of the sale before a court
explanation: Per 7/1, ownership of the debt and its risk transfer to the buyer by any means that customarily allows the buyer to claim the debt.

title: Trading in Currencies
q: Bank A has an account payable exposure in Currency Y and wants a permissible way to hedge against devaluation. Which method does the standard allow?
options: Buying Currency Y in the forward market at a fixed rate
Having a Mudarabah partner guarantee Currency Y losses
Selling goods on credit or by Murabahah in Currency Y
Giving a binding bilateral promise to buy Currency Y later
explanation: Per 2/4/2, where the exposure is an account payable, the Institution may hedge by selling goods on credit or by Murabahah in the currency of the exposure.

title: Ju’alah
q: Which of the following distinguishes Ju'alah from Ijarah under the standard?
options: Ju'alah requires the work to be clearly specified
Ju'alah requires acceptance by the worker
Ju'alah is binding from conclusion, Ijarah is not
Ju'alah is valid even if the other party is not known
explanation: Per clause 7, Ju'alah is valid despite uncertain work, needs no acceptance, pays on result, is valid with an unknown party, and as a rule is terminable.

title: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
q: Why, according to the Shari'ah basis, does Gharar not affect donation contracts as it does exchange-based contracts?
options: The donee incurs no loss, so no dispute arises
Donation contracts never involve uncertainty
Donation contracts are corollaries of exchange contracts
Donations are always made under a recognized need
explanation: Per the basis, Gharar in exchange contracts leads to unlawful acquisition of wealth; in donations no dispute arises since the recipient incurs no loss.

title: Insolvency
q: After being declared insolvent, Ahmad admits that he owes 50,000 to Mr. B in relation to his sequestered assets. What is the effect of this admission?
options: It is binding on all creditors, as an admission is the strongest evidence against oneself
No effect, unless creditors accept the debt predates the declaration
It is binding whenever the debt was in fact incurred earlier
It is binding provided Mr. B is not one of his relatives
explanation: Per 5/1, such an admission has no legal effect, whether the debt arose before or after the declaration, unless the creditors accept it was incurred before.

title: Combination of Contracts
q: Bank A offers a customer a sale of goods and, in the same contract, a loan to the same customer. What is the ruling?
options: Permissible, if the loan carries no interest
Permissible, since each contract is lawful alone
Permissible, if the sale is at market price
Not permissible: sale and lending is an explicit ban
explanation: Per 4/1, combining contracts must not include cases explicitly banned by Shari'ah, like combining sale and lending in one contract.

title: Waqf
q: A Waqf consultant is asked which topic the Waqf standard leaves out, despite its semblance to Waqf in certain aspects. Which one is it?
options: Detailed rulings of irṣād (state endowment)
Conditions of each constituting element of Waqf
Rulings on Waqf overseership and its management
Means by which the Institution invests Waqf sources
explanation: Per the Scope (1), the standard deals neither with detailed rulings of dynasty Waqf nor with irṣād (state endowment) or financial trust.

title: Islamic Reinsurance
q: Islamic Insurance Company X needs reinsurance cover and may use a traditional reinsurer under necessity. Where must it first seek cover?
options: With its own shareholders' funds only
With Islamic reinsurers, to the largest possible extent
With the cheapest reinsurer, whatever its type
With traditional reinsurers first, then with Islamic ones for the rest
explanation: Per 6/1, Islamic insurance companies should reinsure first with Islamic reinsurance companies to the largest possible extent.

title: Commercial Papers
q: Per the Shari'ah basis, why is endorsement of commercial paper permissible?
options: It is a gift from the endorser to the endorsee of the bill
It is a sale of debt at a discount to the endorsee
It does not go beyond Hawalah or Wakalah
It is a form of Mudarabah between endorser and endorsee
explanation: Per the basis, endorsement does not go beyond the meaning of either Hawalah (transfer) or Wakalah (agency), both of which are permissible.

title: Credit Agreement
q: A client's credit facility with Bank A is about to expire and both want to continue dealing. How should the renewal be done?
options: By entering into new contracts
By automatic rollover clauses in the original contracts
By adding a renewal commission to the existing debt
By extending the duration of the current contracts
explanation: Per 5/3/2/4/2, renewal and extension of facilities should be done by entering into new contracts rather than extending the duration of ongoing ones.

title: Settlement of Debt by Set-Off
q: Company X owes Company Y USD 10,000 and Y owes X USD 6,000, both due on 1 June and unencumbered. Neither party asks for anything. What happens?
options: Full set-off, with the 4,000 excess waived by operation of law
Compulsory set-off of 6,000; Y remains owed 4,000
Set-off only if Company Y requests it
No set-off without both parties' consent
explanation: Per 2/1/1-2/1/2, compulsory set-off occurs without request or consent; with unequal amounts, an equivalent amount is set off and the balance remains owed.

title: Islamic Reinsurance
q: Islamic insurance companies form a reinsurance fund. On whose behalf do the companies agree to form it?
options: On behalf of the regulator of the market
On behalf of their own shareholders, who contribute the capital of the fund
On behalf of the traditional reinsurers
On behalf of the insurance funds under their management
explanation: Per 2/1, Islamic reinsurance is an agreement among insurance companies, on behalf of the insurance funds under their management, to avoid part of the risks.

title: Payment Cards
q: Ahmad cancels a card the day after issuance and asks why the issuance fee is not refunded. What is the Shari'ah basis?
options: The fee is a deposit kept as security
The fee is a penalty for early cancellation of the card
The fee is for a specific job already completed
The fee is a gift (Hibah) to the issuer at issuance
explanation: Basis 5/2/1: issuance fees are against a specific job done by issuing the card, and the provider is entitled upon completion of the job.

title: Guarantees
q: Bank A undertakes to underwrite any shares left unsubscribed after an offer period. Which arrangement is permitted?
options: Taking them at a discount to the offer value
Taking them with a guaranteed resale price
Charging a commission for the underwriting undertaking itself
Taking them at offer value, with no fee for the underwriting
explanation: Per 6/7/1, the Institution may underwrite remaining shares at the offer value, without any consideration for the underwriting per se.

title: Competitions and Prizes
q: A company requires buying a coupon booklet to enter a draw, though it is reasonably known that customers buy it only to win the prize. What is the ruling?
options: Permissible, if the prize is announced publicly
Permissible, if all buyers have equal chances
Not permissible, since purchase is only for the prize
Permissible, since the booklet price is unchanged
explanation: Per 3/3/3/2, if customers would not buy except to win the prize, organizing the draw is not permissible.

title: Guarantees
q: Company Y guarantees a customer's debt to Bank A at the customer's own request. Which type of personal guarantee is this?
options: A guarantee with a right of recourse to the debtor
A non-recourse guarantee, since the debtor himself asked for it
A voluntary guarantee without recourse
A guarantee held on a trust basis
explanation: Per 3/1/2, a guarantee given at the debtor's request or with his consent carries recourse; a non-recourse guarantee is offered without his request or consent.

title: Stipulations and Ethics of Fatwa in the Institutional Framework
q: Bank A's board issues a Fatwa that a certain product is permissible. For practical reasons, Bank A decides not to offer it. What is required?
options: Seek another board's Fatwa that permits it
The rejection should be reported to the General Assembly
Follow it only if the General Assembly agrees
Offer it but report the rejection to the General Assembly
explanation: Per 6/1, when the Fatwa permits an act, the Institution may refrain for practical needs, but rejection of the Fatwa should be reported to the General Assembly.

title: Mortgage and its Contemporary Applications
q: Bank A, as mortgagee, pays for urgent repairs to a mortgaged building to prevent its decay. What right does it have?
options: Recourse on the mortgagor, or an equivalent period of use
No right, as it paid voluntarily without permission
Ownership of the building in proportion to the repair cost
Only a right to add a profit margin to the debt
explanation: Per 3/2/10, reparation and preservation costs fall on the mortgagor; if the mortgagee pays, with or without permission, he has recourse or an equivalent period of benefit.

title: Sale of Debt
q: Bank A sells a monetary receivable owed by Company X to Company Y in exchange for a car delivered on the spot. What is the ruling?
options: Not permitted without the debtor's consent
Permitted only if the car equals the debt
Permitted, as the commodity is delivered on spot
Not permitted; it can be sold only for cash
explanation: Per 5/2, a monetary debt may be sold for a commodity with spot delivery or for a usufruct or service whose delivery is ascertained.

title: Ijarah and Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek
q: Bank A insures a leased asset. After the contract is signed, the insurance cost rises above what the Bank anticipated when fixing the rent. May it charge the excess to the lessee?
options: Yes, but only half of the increase in cost
Yes, if the lessee is notified in advance in writing
Yes, as insurance costs always follow the leased asset
No, it may not charge cost beyond that anticipated
explanation: Per 5/1/8, the lessor bears insurance and may factor it into the rent, but after signing may not charge the lessee any cost exceeding that anticipated.

title: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
q: Bank A's Shari'ah board accepts an agency formed by any wording indicating delegation. On which fiqh principle does the standard base this?
options: Necessity makes the prohibited permissible, so delegation is allowed by any wording
In contracts, intentions and meanings count, not wording
Harm should be removed, and rigid wording causes harm to the parties
Gain accompanies liability for loss, so the agent's wording binds him
explanation: The basis grounds forming agency in any wording on the principle that what matters in contracts are intentions and meanings rather than wording and constructions.

title: Syndicated Financing
q: Participants agree at the outset that the syndicated financing is closed, so no Institution may exit before its end. What is the ruling?
options: Not permissible, as it contradicts the nature of Musharakah contracts
Permissible only for paid agency arrangements, not for Musharakah
Permissible; a closed syndication may bar premature exit
Not permissible, as partners may always exit whenever they wish to
explanation: Per 10/1, it is permissible to agree on a closed syndicated financing operation that does not allow premature exit.

title: Sharikah (Musharakah) and Modern Corporations
q: For final profit distribution, the partners use constructive valuation of Sharikah assets. How must outstanding receivables due in two years be valued?
options: At face value plus a time-value increment
At expected cash value after allowing for doubtful debts
At present value, discounted at a market interest rate
At the amount a buyer would pay for early settlement of the debt
explanation: Per 3/1/5/9, receivables are valued at expected cash value after allowance for doubtful debts; time value of money or discount for early payment is not allowed.

title: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
q: A co-owner with a right of Shuf'ah agrees to waive it in return for a payment from the buyer. What is the ruling?
options: Not permissible, as Shuf'ah is granted only to prevent harm
Permissible, if the waiver is documented in court
Permissible, as any financial right can be waived for a fee
Permissible, if the payment is below the property price
explanation: Per 10/2, it is not permissible to take consideration for transfer or waiver of rights granted only to prevent harm, such as the right of Shuf'ah.

title: Credit Agreement
q: Within the period of an approved facility, Bank A rejects a client's application to use it for a Murabahah. The client claims compensation. What is the ruling?
options: The Bank must pay a penalty agreed in the facility letter
The Bank must compensate the client for his actual harm
The Bank must refund any commitment fee the client paid
The Bank is not committed to pay any compensation
explanation: Per 5/2, the Institution is not committed to pay compensation on rejecting a request to utilize approved facilities, and the client is free to use them or not.

title: Financial Paper (Shares and Bonds)
q: Bank A pays Company X today for 10,000 shares of Corporation Y to be delivered in six months, on the basis of Salam. What is the ruling?
options: Permissible, if Corporation Y's activity is lawful
Not permissible, as Salam in shares is not allowed
Permissible, if the shares are described precisely
Permissible, if the price is paid in full now
explanation: Per 3/11, the contract of Salam is not permissible in shares.

title: Procrastinating Debtor
q: Bank A sets off a defaulter's overdue debt against his current account under a contract clause. Per the Shari'ah basis, what supports this right?
options: A court order, which is always required
The debtor's silence, deemed as his consent
The rule that deposits belong to the Bank once they are placed
The amicable right of recovery (Hadith to Abu Sufyan's wife)
explanation: Per the Basis, set-off rests on the amicable right of recovery (Hadith to Abu Sufyan's wife); it needs no consent but is best documented in the contract.

title: Islamic Reinsurance
q: Islamic Insurance Company X receives a surplus distribution from an Islamic reinsurance company. How is it treated?
options: As a reserve to be returned to the reinsurer at the end of the year
As income of X's shareholders
Lawful gain, credited to policyholders' account as revenue
As an unlawful gain to be given to charity
explanation: Per 9, all financial gains from Islamic reinsurers are lawful and credited to the account of policyholders (participant companies) as part of revenues.

title: Monetization (Tawarruq)
q: To speed up Monetization, Bank A arranges for Company T, a third party, to act as the agent of each client in selling the commodity the client bought from the Bank. What is the ruling?
options: The Bank should not arrange such a third-party proxy
Permitted, if Company T is paid a fee by the client
Permitted, provided the client has received the commodity
Permitted, since Company T is a party other than the Bank
explanation: Per 4/8, the Institution should not arrange proxy of a third party to sell, on behalf of the client, the commodity the client purchased from it.

title: Mortgage and its Contemporary Applications
q: A conventional lender asks Bank A to hold a mortgage as security for an interest-bearing loan it granted. Can a valid mortgage secure this debt?
options: Yes, if Bank A acts only as notary
Yes, if the interest is waived on default
Yes, since the mortgage is separate from the loan
No; the debt secured must be a permissible debt
explanation: Per 3/3/1, the secured debt must be permissible (e.g. sale price, Salam or Istisna'a commodity); it should not be an impermissible debt such as a usurious loan.

title: Istisna’a and Parallel Istisna’a
q: An Istisna'a stipulates that Bank A will produce the subject-matter using its own resources. The Bank later wants another company to build it. What is the position?
options: It may assign it via Parallel Istisna'a
It must abide by the condition and may not assign it
It may assign it if the quality is the same as promised
It may assign it with notice to the buyer
explanation: Per 3/1/4, if the contract stipulates production by the Institution's own resources, it must abide by this and has no right to assign production to another entity.

title: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
q: Bank B's existing shareholders convert it into an Islamic bank. From when must the bank dispose of interest and impermissible earnings?
options: From the bank's date of incorporation
From the date of the new licence
From the start of the financial period of conversion
From the first financial period after the conversion is complete
explanation: Per 8/1/2, for conversion by existing shareholders, disposal commences at the beginning of the financial period in which the conversion takes effect.

title: Istisna’a and Parallel Istisna’a
q: Bank A, as manufacturer in an Istisna'a, wants a penalty clause against the customer for late payment of the price. What is the ruling?
options: Not permitted against the purchaser for late payment
Permitted if paid to the Bank's charity fund
Permitted if the penalty is fair
Permitted, in the same way as for late delivery penalties
explanation: Per 6/6, a penalty clause may be stipulated for late delivery by the manufacturer, but not against the ultimate purchaser for default on payment.

title: Payment Cards
q: Why may a card issuer charge Ahmad the exchange rate difference when he returns goods bought by card, per the jurists' view cited?
options: The issuer is the seller of the goods bought by the card
The merchant is never liable for defects in goods sold by card
Return costs are a penalty imposed on the buyer by the issuer
The buyer bears the cost of returning the goods
explanation: Basis 5/7: jurists held the buyer bears the return burden, as his possession is liability-based and the right to return is his.

title: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
q: A paid agent has done part of the work when the subject matter is destroyed by a flood, with no fault of the agent. Must the principal pay?
options: Yes, the full fee for the whole agency term
No, damage of the subject matter cancels the fee
Yes, for the part of the work already performed
No, and the agent must indemnify the principal
explanation: Per 4/2/8, damage of the subject matter does not relieve the principal from paying for work performed; the agent indemnifies only for misconduct or negligence.

title: Financial Paper (Shares and Bonds)
q: A broker asks Bank A to lend it shares, to be repaid later with similar shares. Why does the Basis treat lending shares as impermissible?
options: At repayment the share does not represent the same assets
Shares are not truly owned by their holders
The broker would have to pay interest on the shares it borrows
Lending of any kind of asset is prohibited
explanation: Per the Basis, lending shares is impermissible because, due to the constant change in the corporation's assets, the share at repayment does not represent the same thing.

title: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
q: Shareholders of Bank D decide to convert it. Zakah was unpaid in past periods, partly on impermissible earnings. Must they pay it?
options: No, since those earnings will be given to charity in any case
Yes, for past periods, even on impermissible earnings
Only on permissible earnings of past periods
No, Zakah starts only from conversion
explanation: Per 11, converting shareholders must pay past Zakah even on impermissible revenues; Zakah is part of the obligation to dispose of such earnings.

title: Payment Cards
q: Bank A wants to join an international card network whose rules include interest on lending. What is the ruling?
options: Permitted only for debit cards with no fees
Not permitted under any circumstances, even if rules are avoided
Permitted, accepting all the network's terms as they stand
Permitted, provided Bank A avoids those violations
explanation: Per 5/3/1, Institutions may join card networks provided they avoid any Shari'ah violations stipulated, such as interest or penalty on lending.

title: Competitions and Prizes
q: Bank A launches a prize draw open exclusively to holders of its current accounts. What is the ruling?
options: Permissible if the prizes are in kind, not in cash, and of modest value
Impermissible to give prizes only to current accounts
Permissible if winners are chosen by draw
Permissible if paid from shareholders' funds and not from investment funds
explanation: Per 3/5/1, it is impermissible to assign prizes exclusively to holders of current accounts (see the standard on Qard).

title: Buyback
q: Bank A sells an asset with a unilateral promise from the buyer to resell it to the Bank. Where must this promise be documented?
options: In a deed separate from the first contract
Nowhere, to keep it non-binding
As a clause in the first sale contract
Only in the second contract, at performance
explanation: Per 5/1/2, the promise to purchase or sell must be documented in a separate deed from the first contract.

title: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
q: Partners agree profit ratios that differ from their capital ratios. Per the Hanbali view in the basis, why is this allowed?
options: Profit ratios must follow the scoring method
Loss may also be shared by agreed ratios
Profit is deserved for funds, work or guarantee
Profit is deserved only for contribution of funds
explanation: Per the basis, profit is deserved for contribution of funds, work or guarantee, so partners may set ratios not commensurate with their shares (Hanbali view).

title: Ijarah and Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek
q: Bank A has leased a building to Company X for two years. In the second year, it signs a lease of the same building with Company Y for the remaining period. What is the ruling?
options: Permitted if X is informed of the new lease in writing
Not permitted during the existing Ijarah period
Permitted as a successive lease for the rest of the period
Permitted if Y agrees to pay a higher rent than X pays
explanation: Per 4/2/2, once the lessor leases an asset for a period, it cannot sign another Ijarah with another lessee for the existing period or any remaining part of it.

title: Waqf
q: Under the standard, how is Waqf defined?
options: Appropriation of an asset and donating its benefit
Lending an asset for no consideration for a fixed period
Donating an asset's ownership while the donor keeps its benefit
Transfer of an asset's ownership to the poor for no price
explanation: Per 2/1, Waqf is the appropriation (allocation for a particular purpose) of an asset and donating its benefit.

title: Hawalah
q: Company X draws a bill of exchange on Bank A in favour of its creditor, but no debt exists between Company X and Bank A. How is this classified?
options: An agency for collection
A restricted Hawalah
An unrestricted Hawalah
An invalid transaction
explanation: Per 12/4/1-12/4/2, a bill to the drawer's creditor is Hawalah; with no debt between the drawer and the paying bank, it is an unrestricted Hawalah.

title: Waqf
q: Which analogy supports paying for the preservation of the Waqf asset before other avenues when revenue is short?
options: A partner's capital is repaid before any profit is shared
A guarantor pays before the debtor
A lessor's rent is paid before the maintenance of the property
An estate pays the deceased's debts before the heirs
explanation: Basis 9/10/1: by analogy, the estate gives preference to the rights of the deceased (debts, funeral costs) over the heirs' portions.

title: Stipulations and Ethics of Fatwa in the Institutional Framework
q: Bank A refuses to accept a Fatwa unless the board lists the detailed proofs for it. What is the ruling?
options: The Bank may refuse any Fatwa that comes without detailed proofs
The Bank may not impose this; the board refers to bases
The board must always list all detailed proofs
Proofs are needed only for prohibitions
explanation: Per 9/3, mentioning the proof is not a condition and the Institution may not impose it, but the board has to refer to the bases of its Fatwa.

title: Commercial Papers
q: A client with no balance draws a cheque on Bank A, which pays it (an overdraft). How is this treated and when is it permissible?
options: As a Hawalah, permissible with interest
As a guarantee, permissible for a fee
As a sale of debt, permissible at a discount
As a loan (Qard), permissible if void of Riba
explanation: Per 3/3(b), a cheque drawn without a balance (overdraft) is from the Shari'ah perspective a loan (Qard), permissible if void of Riba.

title: Loan (Qard)
q: Bank A charges current account holders a monthly fee for the services it renders to maintain their accounts. What is the ruling?
options: Permissible only for accounts that are overdrawn
Prohibited, as any charge on a Qard is Riba
Permissible to demand wages for services rendered
Prohibited, as the bank is the borrower
explanation: Per 10/1/2, it is permissible for the institution to demand wages for services rendered to the holders of current accounts.

title: Guarantees
q: A customer wants Bank A to issue a letter of guarantee that he will use to obtain an interest-based loan from another bank. May Bank A issue it?
options: No, it may not issue it for such a purpose
Yes, if the Bank charges no fee for it
Yes, if the customer provides full cover
Yes, as the guarantee itself bears no interest
explanation: Per 6/1/3, the Institution may not issue a letter of guarantee for an applicant who will use it to acquire an interest-based loan or a prohibited deal.

title: Murabahah
q: During the promise stage Bank A refers to a known benchmark index, then fixes its profit at signing as 6% of cost. What is the ruling?
options: Not permitted; the profit must be a lump sum
Permitted; the index was only a comfort indicator
Not permitted; benchmarks may never be mentioned
Permitted only if profit floats with the index
explanation: Per 4/6, a known indicator may be referred to in the promise stage as a comfort indicator, if profit at conclusion is a set percentage of cost.

title: Mudarabah
q: Company X owes Bank A 1 million. Bank A proposes to treat this debt as Mudarabah capital, with Company X as Mudarib. What is the ruling?
options: Not permissible to use a debt owed by the Mudarib as capital
Permissible if Company X has given adequate guarantees for the debt
Permissible if the profit ratio is agreed in advance
Permissible if the debt is already due and Company X is able to pay it
explanation: Per 7/3, it is not permissible to use a debt owed by the Mudarib or another party to the capital provider as capital in a Mudarabah contract.

title: Sale of Debt
q: Company X is owed a described transport service (mawsufa fi dhimma), not a specific one, and wants to sell this entitlement to Company Y for cash. What is the ruling?
options: Permitted, if the service is fully described
Permitted, with the provider's consent
Not permitted to sell such a service debt
Permitted, if sold for a commodity instead
explanation: Per 5/4, a usufruct or service debt that is mawsufa fi dhimma cannot be sold, whether for cash, commodity, usufruct or service.

title: Guarantees
q: Per the Shari'ah basis, how does the evidential value of attestation compare with written documentation?
options: Always weaker than writing, both traditionally and today
Rejected entirely as evidence by the traditional Fuqaha
Equal to writing in every era and every legal system
Traditionally stronger; modern laws favour writing
explanation: Per the Basis, traditional Fuqaha held attestation stronger than writing, but in modern times laws rely on witnesses rarely and favour documentary evidence.

title: Monetization (Tawarruq)
q: In Country Z, regulations allow a client to sell a commodity bought from Bank A only through Bank A itself. Under the Monetization standard, what is permitted?
options: The client may delegate Bank A to sell once he has received it
The client may delegate Bank A to sell at the time of the purchase
Bank A may appoint a third party to sell for the client
Monetization is not allowed at all in Country Z
explanation: Per 4/7, if regulations allow sale only through the same Institution, the client may delegate it after he actually or constructively receives the commodity.

title: Investment Sukuk
q: Istisna'a Sukuk funds have been converted, within the Istisna'a period, into assets owned by the holders. Why may these certificates be traded?
options: The ultimate purchaser has already paid in advance
The assets are properties that can be disposed of
The manufacturer guarantees the final sale price
Istisna'a debts may be traded at any price
explanation: Per the Basis, trading Istisna'a certificates after funds are converted into assets is permissible because such assets are properties that can be disposed of.

title: Settlement of Debt by Set-Off
q: Bank A's claim on Company X is secured by a mortgage; X's equal claim on Bank A is unsecured, same currency and maturity. When can set-off on demand occur?
options: Never, since the debts differ in quality
Only if the two parties sign a new agreement
If Bank A requests it and relinquishes the mortgage
If Company X requests it, even without Bank A's consent
explanation: Per 2/1/4(b), a mortgage makes a debt superior in quality; set-off on demand needs its creditor to request it and relinquish that privilege.

title: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
q: An investment agency contract stipulates that the agent guarantees the investors' capital. What is the ruling on this stipulation?
options: Permissible, as it protects the investors' capital against any loss
Permissible, if the guarantee is limited to a part of the capital
Permissible, if the agent is paid a separate fee for giving the guarantee
Not permissible: it turns the deal into an interest-based loan
explanation: Per 5/2 (citing SS 5, 2/2/2), combining agency and guarantee in one contract is not permissible; an agent's capital guarantee makes it an interest-based loan.

title: Zakah
q: A first-instance court orders Company X to pay indemnity, and Company X appeals. It books a provision. When can it be deducted from Zakatable assets?
options: Once a final verdict makes it due for payment
Immediately upon the initial verdict, since the court has already ordered payment
Never, as it is a provision
When the appeal is filed
explanation: Per 7/3/7, the indemnity provision is not deducted from Zakatable assets until it becomes due for payment by virtue of a final verdict.

title: Murabahah
q: Customer C signed a supply contract with Supplier S. C asks Bank A to take over that contract by assignment and then sell him the goods by Murabahah. What is the ruling?
options: Permissible as long as C has not paid Supplier S
Not permissible to assign C's contract to the Bank
Permissible if Supplier S consents to the assignment
Permissible if the Bank pays Supplier S directly
explanation: Per 2/2/2, any prior contractual relationship between customer and supplier must be genuinely excluded; assigning their contract to the Institution is not permissible.

title: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
q: Under a general agency over Ahmad's assets, the agent donates part of the assets to a charity without Ahmad's authorization. What is the ruling?
options: Allowed, if customary practice accepts such gifts from an agent
Allowed, if the donation serves Ahmad's reputation and is reasonable
Allowed, since general agency covers all disposals, including donations
Not allowed: general agency excludes donations unless authorized
explanation: Per 4/1/1, general agency covers all methods of disposing of assets but does not include making donations unless the principal authorizes it.

title: Mortgage and its Contemporary Applications
q: A mortgagor goes bankrupt. Bank A, his mortgagee, is owed 100, while the mortgaged asset sells for 60. How is Bank A treated?
options: Equal standing with other creditors for all 100
Priority over the 60; the remaining 40 is waived
Priority over the 60; equal standing with others for the 40
Priority over the whole 100, recoverable from all of his remaining assets
explanation: Per 3/5/3, on bankruptcy the mortgagee has priority from the sale value; for any excess debt he stands equal with other creditors.

title: Banking Services in Islamic Banks
q: Company X asks Bank A to act as its agent in concluding lease contracts with tenants. What may Bank A charge?
options: A fee for the contracting agency service
Nothing, as agency must be non-paid
A share of the rent as a partner
Interest on the rents it collects
explanation: Per 2/2, a customer may use the Institution as an agent for concluding contracts such as sale, purchase and lease, against a fee payable to it.

title: Zakah
q: Ahmad receives a monthly salary. At what point is Zakah due on his salary income?
options: On his annual gross salary at year end
On the portion that remains unexpended for a whole year
On each salary payment at the time of its receipt by Ahmad
Never, as salaries are exempt from Zakah
explanation: Per 3/1/3, Zakah is not due on wages and salaries upon receipt, but on that portion which remains unexpended for a whole year.

title: Waqf
q: Ahmad stipulated that his building is Waqf for ten years only. The ten years have now expired. What happens to the building?
options: It goes to general charitable causes
It remains Waqf, as Waqf is perpetual
It returns to Ahmad or, if he died, to his heirs
It is sold and the price is given to the poor
explanation: Per 2/4/1/5, Waqf may be limited to a period if stipulated; upon maturity of the term, the asset returns to the original owner or his heirs.

title: Ijarah and Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek
q: According to the Shari'ah basis, why is Ijarah also acceptable by reasoning?
options: It replaces the need for Murabahah
It is a way of lending money with a return
It lets the lessor avoid risks of ownership
It lets people use assets that they do not own
explanation: The basis: Ijarah is acceptable by reasoning as a convenient means for people to acquire the right to use assets they do not own.

title: Waqf
q: An overseer used cash Waqf to buy an apartment. A more beneficial investment now arises. What may he do?
options: Sell it only if its usufruct is totally lost or the apartment destroyed
Nothing; the apartment has become the Waqf asset and cannot be sold
Sell it; the cash amount remains the Waqf asset
Sell it, but only with the heirs' consent
explanation: Per 2/4/13/3, assets bought with cash Waqf are not the Waqf asset; they may be sold for a better investment, and the Waqf asset remains the cash.

title: Ijarah and Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek
q: Company X wants to use a building owned by a third party. It asks Bank A to acquire the usufruct of that building and lease it to X. Is this possible?
options: No, a usufruct cannot be the subject of an Ijarah
Yes, but only if X guarantees the owner's rentals
No, the Bank may lease only assets it owns outright
Yes, the Bank may acquire the usufruct and lease it on
explanation: Per 2/1, Ijarah is executed on an asset owned by the lessor or a usufruct owned by the sub-lessor; a customer may ask the Institution to acquire either.

title: Syndicated Financing
q: Which of the following is listed by the standard as a mode through which syndicated financing may be provided to customers?
options: Muzara'ah, Musaqat and Mugharasah
Discounting of commercial bills
Overdraft facilities with a fixed fee
Term loans at a fixed rate of interest
explanation: Per 4/6, Muzara'ah, Musaqat and Mugharasah are among the Shari'ah-compliant modes listed, with Murabahah, Ijarah, Salam, Istisna'a, Mudarabah and Sukuk.

title: Concession Contracts
q: In a construction concession, the licensee does the construction works and also provides the materials, and is paid by the right to use the project for a period. How is it adapted?
options: As Ju'alah, its Ju'l being a share of output
As Istisna'a, its value being the right to utilize the project
As Ijarah, its rent being the project itself handed to the State
As Mudarabah, with the project as capital
explanation: Per 6/2/1, if the licensee undertakes construction and materials (the predominant case), the contract is Istisna'a, its value being the right to utilize the project.

title: Istisna’a and Parallel Istisna’a
q: A contractor cannot continue an Istisna'a because the ultimate purchaser obstructed the work through misconduct. What is the contractor entitled to?
options: The value of the work done only, without compensation
The full contract price only, whatever work was done
The value of the work done plus compensation
Nothing, as the work is incomplete
explanation: Per 4/2/4, if failure is due to the purchaser's misconduct, the contractor is entitled to the value of the completed work and compensation for damage.

title: Ijarah and Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek
q: Bank A leases one holiday flat to several lessees for the same usufruct and duration, without fixing a period for each; each uses it in the time assigned to him by set rules. What is this?
options: A sale of the flat in undivided shares
A permissible form of Muhaya'ah (time-sharing)
Void, as each lessee's period is not fixed
Two contracts on the same asset and period
explanation: Per 4/2/3, a lease with several lessees entitled to the same usufruct without fixing a period per person is a form of Muhaya'ah (time-sharing).

title: Buyback
q: Company X sells goods for cash and later buys them back at a higher deferred price payable in other goods rather than cash. Is this among the permitted scenarios?
options: Yes, as the price in one contract is not cash
No, a price in kind makes it a deferred Sarf
No, any higher deferred price is 'Inah
Yes, but only if the goods changed in value
explanation: Per 3/5/2/4, buyback is permitted, even at a higher deferred price, if the price in one of the contracts is in a form other than cash.

title: Waqf
q: An overseer wants the Waqf to guarantee a supplier's debt. The Waqif did not stipulate it, it is not a Waqf purpose, and no authority permitted it. Is it allowed?
options: Yes, if the supplier is reliable
Yes, if the guarantee is for a short term
Yes, if the overseer bears the risk
No, the Waqf cannot guarantee it
explanation: Per 7, Waqf cannot guarantee third-party debts unless stipulated by the Waqif, among its purposes, or in its interest with authority permission.

title: Sale of Debt
q: Ahmad owes Bank A 100 grams of gold. They agree that he will settle it with 1,400 grams of silver instead. What is required?
options: Nothing, as a debt may be substituted freely
The silver must equal the gold in weight
The silver must be handed over in the session
The silver may be delivered within a month
explanation: Per 4/1/1/1(a), where the consideration is a Ribawi item of a different kind, it must be possessed in the session, even if quantities differ.

title: Documentary Credit
q: Bank B confirms Bank A's documentary credit. Per the Shari'ah basis, how is the confirming bank's undertaking characterised?
options: As an agency for the beneficiary seller
As a sale of the credit to Bank B
As a loan given to the issuing bank
As a back-up guarantee, which is permissible
explanation: Per the basis, the undertaking of the confirming bank and similar participating banks is an act of back-up guarantee, which is permissible in the Shari'ah.

title: Istisna’a and Parallel Istisna’a
q: Why does the Shari'ah basis allow the Istisna'a price to be deferred or paid in instalments without being a sale of debt for debt?
options: Because the price is not treated as a debt at all
Labour makes it like leasing, with deferred rents
Because Istisna'a is a form of Salam
Because the goods are delivered in full at signing
explanation: The basis: labour (transformation and added value) is a key part of the item, making Istisna'a similar to leasing where rentals may be deferred.

title: Hawalah
q: Ahmad and Zaid agree to transfer Ahmad's debt to Zaid without asking Bakr, the creditor. Is the Hawalah valid?
options: No, the transferee's consent is required
Yes, if Zaid is known to be solvent
Yes, the creditor's consent is not needed
Yes, if Bakr is notified afterwards
explanation: Per 6/1, the permissibility of Hawalah requires the consent of all parties: the transferor, the transferee and the payer.

title: Istisna’a and Parallel Istisna’a
q: A buyer refuses without good reason to take finished goods after being enabled to take possession. They stay with the manufacturer. Who bears safekeeping costs?
options: The manufacturer
The two parties equally
Nobody, until a court rules
The ultimate purchaser
explanation: Per 6/4, the goods remain with the manufacturer on trust, who is liable only for negligence or misconduct; the purchaser bears safekeeping expenses.

title: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
q: A converting bank offers a safe deposit box service that is naturally permissible. Does the conversion standard require it to change this activity or its profits?
options: No, naturally permissible activities are outside its scope
Yes, all pre-conversion activities must cease
Yes, it must be suspended until the conversion process ends
Yes, its past profits must be given to charity
explanation: Per the Scope (1), naturally permissible activities and profits made by permissible means are not the subject of conversion; the bank may continue them.

title: Hiring of Persons
q: Bank A rents a consultant's service and then sub-hires it to a client with the contract's permission. Per the Shari'ah basis, why is sub-hiring permissible?
options: The client becomes a partner of the Bank
Services are not owned by the hirer, so no transfer of them occurs
Owning the service enables the employer to transfer it
Sub-hiring is a form of agency without pay
explanation: The basis states sub-hiring is permissible because when the employer owns the service/work he becomes able to transfer it to someone else.

title: Zakah
q: Bank A agrees to act as agent for paying Zakah on behalf of some of its investment account holders. What is required?
options: The Bank may deduct Zakah from any client's account on its own
Funds must be available or submitted by the principals
The Bank must pay from its own funds first
The Bank must get a court order for each payment
explanation: Per 2/2/2, when the Institution accepts agency for payment of Zakah for equity or account holders, funds should be available or submitted by the principals.

title: Buyback
q: Bank A sells a commodity to Ahmad on deferred terms; by collusion, Bank A's 80%-owned subsidiary buys it back from him for less in cash. Is this a permitted scenario?
options: Yes, as the subsidiary is a separate entity
Yes, as the buyer differs from the first seller
No, the subsidiary is majority-owned by Bank A
Yes, if the second price is paid on spot
explanation: Per 3/5/2/3, a different buyer is permitted only if neither party is wholly or majority-owned by the other.

title: Sharikah (Musharakah) and Modern Corporations
q: Bank A (an Institution) plans a partnership with a conventional bank for a Shari'ah-acceptable project. Which arrangement is among the guarantees the standard calls for?
options: The conventional bank first converts to Islamic banking before signing
Operations managed or supervised by an entity observing Shari'ah rules
The conventional bank guarantees Bank A's capital against any loss
Profit is fixed in advance as a percentage of the capital invested
explanation: Per 3/1/1/2, assurances must be obtained that Shari'ah is observed, such as having the operations managed or supervised by an entity that observes Shari'ah rules.

title: Murabahah
q: Bank A authorises Agent B to buy an item in B's own name without disclosing the agency to the supplier. What is the ruling?
options: Permissible only if B is the purchase orderer
Not permissible; the agency must be disclosed
Permissible, and non-disclosure is preferable
Permissible, though disclosure is preferable
explanation: Per 3/1/7, the agent may act as principal without disclosing the agency, on behalf of the Institution; however, disclosure of the agent's role is preferable.

title: Islamic Insurance
q: Islamic Insurance Company T deducts part of the policyholders' funds as reserves for the insurance fund. Who owns these reserves?
options: The insurance fund; they never belong to the shareholders
The company, after three years
The shareholders, as managers of the fund who deducted them
The shareholders and policyholders jointly
explanation: Per 10/5, such deductions for policyholders' interest are permissible but should by no means belong to the shareholders; on liquidation they go to charity.

title: Possession (Qabd)
q: Bank A orders a vessel from a shipyard under Istisna'a. Absent any stipulation or custom, who bears the expenses of delivering the vessel?
options: The orderer (Bank A), who takes delivery of the vessel
The manufacturer (the shipyard)
Both parties equally, each bearing half of the expenses
The ultimate purchaser, who buys the vessel from Bank A
explanation: Per 4/1/4, in Istisna'a the manufacturer bears the expenses of delivering the subject matter, while the orderer bears those of delivering the price.

title: Insolvency
q: An insolvent debtor's admission that his property belongs to a friend is not enforced without the creditors' approval. What is the Shari'ah basis for this?
options: The principle that the deferred period has a share in the price
The Maliki view that admissions require a judge's approval
The rule that a debtor's admissions are never valid evidence
Preventing harm to creditors: "No harm and no reciprocal harm"
explanation: Per the basis, non-enforcement of the insolvent's admissions and ownership-transferring dispositions prevents harm to creditors, per the Hadith "No harm and no reciprocal harm".

title: Protection of Capital and Investments
q: Due to the Mudarib's negligence, a deal that would have produced profit was missed; the capital itself is intact. Can the Rabb al-Mal claim the expected profit?
options: No; the Mudarib is liable for loss of capital, not of profit
Yes, but only half of the expected profit, as a compromise
Yes, at the prevailing market rate of return for the period
Yes, the full amount of the profit that was expected from the deal
explanation: Per 3/7, in case of the Mudarib's misconduct, negligence or breach, the capital provider may hold him liable for loss of capital but not loss of profit.

title: Buyback
q: With prior collusion, Bank A sells a car to Ahmad for 120 payable in a year, then buys it back from him for 100 in cash. How is this classified?
options: A valid buyback, as the contracts are separate
A valid buyback, as the second price is lower
'Inah, which is prohibited
A valid Tawarruq, as Ahmad receives cash
explanation: Per 3/5/1/1, with collusion or custom, selling at a deferred price and buying back for less at spot constitutes 'Inah.

title: Payment Cards
q: Ahmad deposits an amount with Bank A specifically for a card he uses only up to that deposited balance. Which card type is this?
options: Credit Card
Prepaid Card
Charge Card
Debit Card
explanation: Per 3/2/1, in a Prepaid Card the cardholder deposits with the issuer a balance specifically for the card; it is a settlement, not credit, instrument.

title: Hiring of Persons
q: Per the Shari'ah basis, why does a private employee not guarantee what he works on, absent transgression or negligence?
options: He is not paid anything for his work until the contract is complete
The employer is presumed to be negligent instead
This is the general principle in trust-based contracts
He works for many employers at the same time
explanation: The basis: a private employee not guaranteeing absent transgression, negligence or breach is the general principle in trust-based contracts.

title: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
q: Company X, owner of assets, issues a binding promise to sell them to Bank A and asks Bank A for a fee in return for the promise. What is the ruling?
options: The fee is allowed if the promise is tradable
The fee is allowed, as a promise is a service
The promise is void as all promises are non-binding
The promise is allowed only without a counter-value
explanation: Per 5/2/3/3, a binding promise to sell or buy is a substitute for options only without specifying a counter-value for the promise, and it is not tradable.

title: Rules for Calculating Profit in Financial Transactions
q: A capital provider stipulates that the Mudarib must not invest in activities whose expected profit rate is below 6%. Is this stipulation permissible?
options: Yes, provided neither capital nor profit is guaranteed
No; the Mudarib must be left fully unrestricted
No; it amounts to guaranteeing the capital provider a 6% profit on his funds
Yes, and the Mudarib must make up any shortfall
explanation: Per 7/2, the capital provider may stipulate the Mudarib avoid activities below a specific expected profit rate, but capital and profit may not be guaranteed.

title: Hiring of Persons
q: A tailor serving many customers (a shared employee) accepts an order from Bank A's staff club while serving others. Is he restricted from working for others at the same time?
options: Yes, unless the first client permits it
No; a shared employee is not subject to that restriction
No, but only if he charges all clients equally
Yes; he must serve only one client at a time, in order of orders
explanation: Per 4/3, unlike a private employee, a shared employee working for more than one person is not restricted from working for others.

title: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
q: Company X agrees to sell described wheat for delivery in three months, with the price also payable in three months. The contract uses the word 'sale'. What is the ruling?
options: Not permitted: it is a Salam whose capital is not paid promptly
Permitted, if both parties are able to deliver
Permitted, as the word 'sale' rather than 'Salam' was used in it
Permitted, as a forward contract outside the exchange
explanation: Per 3/2/2/1, a described commodity with deferred price is not permitted, whether called sale or Salam, as it is Salam without prompt payment of capital.

title: Online Financial Dealings
q: A client accepts Bank A's online offer on Monday, but the Bank learns of the acceptance only on Wednesday. When did the contract become valid?
options: On Wednesday, when the Bank learned of the acceptance
When the Bank sends confirmation of receipt
On delivery of the subject matter to the client
On Monday, when the client accepted the offer
explanation: Per 6, an online contract is valid from the time the other party accepts the offer, whether or not the offering party has come to know of it.

title: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
q: Investors acquire a conventional bank in order to convert it. The bank earned interest before the acquisition. Must the new owners dispose of it?
options: Yes, for the last five financial periods
Yes, all past interest must go to charity
No, they are not obliged to dispose of it
Yes, if it remains in the bank's reserves
explanation: Per 8/1/1, new owners acquiring a conventional bank to convert it are not obliged to dispose of interest and impermissible earnings earned before acquisition.

title: Buyback
q: In a Tawarruq where Bank A's debt is secured by a pledge of the customer's shares, Bank A stipulates a right to sell the pledged shares at will. What is the ruling?
options: Permitted, since the shares are registered to it
Permitted, if Bank A bears any loss on them
Permitted, if the dividends are pledged too
Not permitted, though dividends may reduce the debt
explanation: Per 5/6/3/4(d), the pledgee may not stipulate selling the pledged securities; parties may agree that dividends pay off or reduce the debt.

title: Combination of Contracts
q: Bank A and a customer agree beforehand on a structure that violates no Shari'ah rule or objective and harms no one, as a Shari'ah exit. What is the ruling?
options: Permissible only if never disclosed to others
Prohibited, unless stated in the contract text
Permissible, as Muwata`ah for Shari'ah exits
Prohibited, as every prior agreement is a trick
explanation: Per 6/3/3, Muwata`ah for Shari'ah exits that do not violate Shari'ah rules or objectives or harm others is permissible.

title: Possession (Qabd)
q: Ahmad buys a laptop from a shop, and the shopkeeper physically hands it to him at the counter. What kind of possession has Ahmad taken?
options: Actual possession, through physical corporeal delivery
Constructive possession, through registration
Constructive possession, through relinquishment
Prior possession standing in place of a later one
explanation: Per 3/3, actual possession of movables takes place through physical corporeal delivery.

title: Insolvency
q: A lessee becomes insolvent in the middle of an Ijarah term. Regarding rent for the period in which the usufruct was already enjoyed, what is the lessor entitled to?
options: Full priority for the rent of the entire Ijarah term
That rent, on a pro-rata basis along with other creditors
Nothing, since the lessee is now insolvent
That rent only if he terminates the whole Ijarah
explanation: Per 5/5/2, the lessor is entitled, pro-rata with other creditors, to the rent for the period during which the usufruct was enjoyed.

title: Documentary Credit
q: An exporter holds an accepted bill of exchange due in six months under a credit and offers to sell it to Bank A today at less than its nominal value. What is the ruling?
options: Permissible if Bank A holds the bill to maturity
Permissible if the bill is accepted by a bank
Permissible if the discount equals actual expenses
Not permissible for Bank A to discount the bill
explanation: Per 3/7/2, the Institution may not discount accepted bills of exchange, i.e. purchase them before maturity at less than their nominal value.

title: Hiring of Persons
q: Company X owes its contractor three months of unpaid past wages. They agree to defer payment by six months in return for a 5% increase. What is the ruling?
options: Impermissible; unpaid past pay is a debt and cannot grow
Permissible, since both parties freely consented to it
Permissible as an ordinary amendment of the future pay
Permissible if the increase goes to the employee directly
explanation: Per 5/2/5, unpaid pay for past periods is a debt owed by the employer; stipulating an increase (rescheduling) is impermissible. Future pay may be amended by consent.

title: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
q: Company Y sells a heap of grain whose exact weight is unknown for a lump sum. The buyer views the heap at the time of sale. What is the ruling?
options: Void, since the quantity of the sold object is unknown
Void unless the price is stated per kilogram
Valid, as viewing makes the Gharar forgivable
Valid only if the heap is weighed before delivery
explanation: Per 5/2/1/5, Bay' al-Juzaf nullifies the contract except where Gharar is forgivable, such as viewing the commodity at the time of sale.

title: Waqf
q: A Waqf tenant fails to pay the rent. The superintendent wants to waive the debt as a favour. Per the Shari'ah basis, may he?
options: Yes, as manager he owns the Waqf's claims
No; the debt is owed to the Waqf, not to him
Yes, with the tenant's written request
Yes, if the amount is small
explanation: The basis: the Waqf has a legal personality separate from its superintendent; a party failing an obligation is indebted to the Waqf, so he cannot relieve the debtor.

title: Salam and Parallel Salam
q: Bank A and a seller disagree on how to describe the grade of cotton in a Salam. What is the reference for determining such descriptions?
options: Customary practice and the experience of experts
The buyer's own internal standards
Whatever the Shari'ah Supervisory Board decides
The seller's description alone
explanation: Per 3/2/6, the reference for descriptions used to specify al-Muslam Fihi is customary practice and the experience of experts.

title: Payment Cards
q: Bank B provides Shop X with POS devices, organizes its dealings with the card network and recovers the card payments for it. Which party to the card is Bank B?
options: The card network
The card issuer
The Acquirer
The card acceptor
explanation: Per 2/1/4 and 2/2/2, the Acquirer is the merchant's bank; it provides POS devices, organizes dealing with the network and acts as agent for recovery.

title: Online Financial Dealings
q: Bank A sends a sale offer to a client by e-mail. Which category of contract rulings applies to this deal?
options: Rulings on contracts signed in the presence of the two parties
Rulings on online bidding and auction contracts
Rulings on adhesion contracts subject to state control
Rulings on contracts signed in the absence of the two parties
explanation: Per 4/2, written communication, e-mail or site access is subject to the rulings on contracts in the absence of the two parties, as it resembles message contracting.

title: Islamic Insurance
q: It is proved that Ahmad deliberately gave false information when buying Islamic insurance cover. He now makes a claim. What may happen?
options: His indemnity is reduced only proportionately
He may be deprived of indemnity partially or fully
He receives full indemnity, as he donated
His contributions are returned with no indemnity
explanation: Per 8/1, a participant who committed fraud, deceit or gave false information is subject to partial or full deprivation from indemnity.

title: Buyback
q: By collusion, Ahmad sells an asset to Bank A for gold and later buys it back from the Bank on credit, paying in silver. What is the ruling?
options: Permitted, as an asset stands between the sales
Permitted, since gold and silver may be unequal
Permitted, if the silver amount is fixed today
Not permitted, as it results in deferred Sarf
explanation: Per 3/6, buyback must not result in deferred currency exchange, e.g., selling for gold or currency and buying back on credit in silver.

title: Options to Terminate Due to Breach of Trust (Trust-Based Options)
q: Ahmad discovers the seller added substances to make a product look better. After discovering this, he uses up the product entirely. What happens to his Khiyar al-Tadlis?
options: It lapses, as he consumed it after discovering the deception
It survives, since the deception was proven, and he may still revoke the sale after use
It converts into a right to compensation
It transfers to a right of exchange for a new item
explanation: Per 3/5, the option to revoke on grounds of deceptive conduct lapses if the item is consumed by the buyer after the deception is discovered.

title: Islamic Reinsurance
q: Under a reinsurance agreement, Reinsurer R must accept all risks within the scope agreed with Islamic Insurance Company X. A new risk in scope arises. May R refuse it?
options: No, unless the risk is above a loss limit
No; it is bound to accept all risks within the agreement's scope
Yes; it may study each risk individually and decline any it does not want
Yes, if the risk exceeds Company X's capacity
explanation: Per 4/2, in comprehensive reinsurance (reinsurance agreement) the reinsurer is committed to accept all the risks falling within the scope of the agreement.

title: Salam and Parallel Salam
q: Why does the Shari'ah basis treat granting the usufruct of an asset as immediate receipt of Salam capital?
options: Usufruct is received only when the term ends
Salam capital need not be received at all before delivery
Possessing part of a thing is like possessing the whole
Usufruct is a form of cash under commercial custom
explanation: The basis follows the Maliki view and the maxim 'Taking possession of part of a thing is like taking possession of the whole thing'; so it is not a sale of debt.

title: Waqf
q: Ahmad asks why he may make a Waqf on himself. Which basis does the standard give?
options: Analogy with charity given to oneself
The Waqif retains ownership of the asset
Analogy with a sale to oneself
Necessity of the Waqif's maintenance
explanation: Basis 2/4/4/2: self-Waqf rests on analogy with charity to self and hadiths such as "Start with yourself and spend it on yourself".

title: Buyback
q: Bank A manages a flexible investment deposit for another bank as Mudarib and undertakes to buy the underlying assets at their face value. What is the ruling?
options: Permitted, as a unilateral promise to buy the assets from the deposit
Not permitted; it may promise to buy at market value
Permitted, if it is a separate deed
Permitted, as the deposit is made for liquidity purposes only
explanation: Per 5/6/3/3(b), the manager may not undertake to buy the underlying assets at face value; a promise to buy at market value is permitted.

title: Waqf
q: An overseer leases a Waqf below fair rent with no preferred interest. Which maxim does the standard invoke against this?
options: Hardship begets facility, so rules are relaxed in difficulty
Custom is a decisive authority where no text exists
Certainty is not removed by doubt, so the first state remains
An overseer's act depends on the Waqf's interest
explanation: Basis 8/5: inna taṣarruf al-nāẓir alā al-waqf manuwṭ bi al-maṣlaḥa, the overseer's disposition of Waqf is contingent upon its interest.

title: Murabahah
q: A Murabahah contract says the car stays the Bank's property until full payment. Why is such a stipulation disallowed, per the Shari'ah basis?
options: It amounts to a sale of debt for debt between the parties
It makes the price unknown, as it varies with the payment period
It contradicts the immediate transfer of ownership in a sale
It is a form of commitment fee charged by the Bank
explanation: The basis: delaying transfer of ownership is against the effect of a sale, which is immediate transfer; delaying registration does not affect ownership.

title: Possession (Qabd)
q: Which of the following topics is excluded from the scope of the standard on Possession (Qabd)?
options: Constructive possession of ascertained movables
Possession in set-offs
Possession through bills of lading
Expenses of possession in a loan (Qard)
explanation: Per Scope (1), the standard does not cover possession in set-offs or the nature of possession regarding liability for compensation; these have their own standards.

title: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
q: A buyer stipulates a cooling-off option without any time limit. Per the Shari'ah basis, why must the option be timed?
options: Options are valid only for three days, as stated in the Hadith of Khalabah
Untimed options amount to Riba
The seller must know when to deliver, since delivery follows the option period
An untimed option causes Jahalah that may lead to dispute
explanation: Per the basis, an untimed option results in Jahalah (obscurity) which may lead to dispute; this is the majority view.

title: Zakah
q: Company X spends heavily on irrigation channels and on delivering the Zakah produce to recipients. Which cost may be deducted from Zakatable assets?
options: The cost of delivery to recipients
The irrigation channel expenses
Neither cost
Each of the two costs equally
explanation: Per 5/4/7 and 5/4/8, irrigation and land development expenses are not deducted, while the cost of delivery to recipients is deducted.

title: Salam and Parallel Salam
q: A trading company asks whether Salam may finance its working capital, given Salam is mostly used by farmers. What does the Shari'ah basis say?
options: Salam may be used only for exports
Salam is allowed only for small farmers
Salam is not limited to farming; traders may use it
Salam is limited to agricultural produce and farmers
explanation: The basis: though commonly used in agriculture, Salam's permissibility is not confined to it; it can be used in industry or trade.

title: Sale of Debt
q: Which narration does the standard cite for permitting the sale of an outstanding monetary debt to the debtor?
options: "Gold for gold, silver for silver... equal measure"
Ibn 'Umar selling camels in al-Baqi' for dinars
Imam Malik's report on Salam in the Muwatta
"Muslims act upon their conditions"
explanation: The Basis cites Ibn 'Umar: no harm if at the rate of that day, as long as you do not depart without concluding the transaction.

title: Concession Contracts
q: Bank A funds part of the capital for a concession project and undertakes to sell its share gradually to the State over the term. Which form is this?
options: Two-step Mudarabah
Parallel Ju'alah
Fixed Musharakah
Diminishing Musharakah
explanation: Per 7/4/2 and 8/3/2, in diminishing Musharakah the Institution contributes a share of capital and undertakes to sell its share gradually to the State.

title: Zakah
q: A government ministry holds large public funds and runs an insurance fund for public institutions. Is Zakah due on them?
options: No; Zakah is not obligatory on public wealth
Yes, at 2.5% of their year-end balance
Yes, but only on the insurance fund
Yes, if the funds are invested for profit
explanation: Per 3/1/5, Zakah is not obligatory on public wealth (public sector) or the insurance funds of public institutions.

title: Revocation of Contracts by Exercise of a Cooling-Off Option
q: A sale contract stipulates that the buyer will pay the seller a set amount if the seller waives his right to revoke. What is the ruling on this stipulation?
options: It is permissible if agreed at the time of waiver
It is permissible if the amount is fixed in advance
It is not permissible in a sale contract
It is permissible if the waiver is in writing
explanation: Per 10/1, it is not permissible to stipulate payment for waiver of revocation rights in a sale contract.

title: Buyback
q: Ahmad sells a machine for cash. Months later, with no prior collusion or custom, he buys it back from the buyer at a higher deferred price. What is the ruling?
options: Permitted only if the second price is spot
Prohibited, unless the machine's value changed
Prohibited, as a deferred price above spot is 'Inah
Permitted, as it is free of collusion and custom
explanation: Per 3/5/2/1, buyback is permitted, even if the deferred price is higher, when it is free of any collusion or customary practice.

title: Islamic Insurance
q: A licensed joint stock company is appointed to manage an Islamic insurance fund. On what contractual basis does it manage the insurance operations?
options: A remunerated Wakalah (agency) contract
A sale of cover in exchange for premiums
A Musharakah contract with the participants
A Mudarabah contract for underwriting
explanation: Per clause 3, where a joint stock company manages the fund, it assumes this job on the basis of a remunerated Wakalah (agency) contract.

title: Rules for Calculating Profit in Financial Transactions
q: Bank A calculates profit as an annualised percentage of the outstanding financing under an amortised payment schedule. When is this method permissible?
options: Only if the customer repays in equal monthly instalments
Always, even if the total sale price is left floating
When transparent, fully disclosed and the total price is fixed
Never; only flat-rate profit methods are permissible, as reducing balances are Riba-based
explanation: Per 10, annualised methods on total or outstanding amounts are permissible if transparent, fully disclosed and the total sale price is stated as a fixed amount.

title: Buyback
q: Company X sells shares to Bank A, but the contract leaves all dividends and the risk of price falls with Company X until it buys them back. Is this buyback permitted?
options: Yes, since legal title passed to Bank A at the time of sale
No, the first sale must be real, with its consequences
Yes, if the buyback is made in a separate contract signed later
Yes, if there is no collusion on a higher buyback price
explanation: Per 3/1, the sale must be real: the buyer is entitled to the yield, assumes price-change risk, and bears risk of loss on possession.

title: Protection of Capital and Investments
q: A Mudarib stores Mudarabah goods in an unlocked, unguarded warehouse, contrary to the usual means of protection, and they are stolen. Who bears the loss?
options: The Rabb al-Mal, since the Mudarib is a fiduciary and does not guarantee the capital
The two parties equally, as partners in the venture
The Mudarib, for failing to use usual means of protection
The Mudarib only if the contract expressly says so
explanation: Per 3/2, the investment manager must exercise due diligence to protect the funds; if he fails to do so using usual means of protection, he is liable.

title: Waqf
q: A candidate for a Waqf overseership board is highly competent and sane but lacks moral probity ('adālah). Is he eligible?
options: No, moral probity is one of the eligibility criteria
Yes, since competence is the only criterion for an overseer
Yes, as a board member rather than as a sole overseer
Yes, if the Waqif approves him
explanation: Per 3/5, the eligibility criteria of the overseer, as an individual or board member, are moral probity, sanity, discretion and competence.

title: Documentary Credit
q: Bank A structures a credit as a combination of contracts so it can take a higher fee that in effect prices its guarantee. What is the ruling?
options: Permissible as long as the fee is a lump sum, not a rate
Permissible, since each contract in the combination is valid on its own
Permissible if the client consents to it in writing and the fee is disclosed
Not permissible: combined contracts cannot mask a guarantee fee
explanation: Per 3/3/1(c), a combination of contracts may not be used as an excuse for prohibited transactions, such as a commission for a guarantee or a loan.

title: Waqf
q: An overseer insists he would charge his own son full market rent for a Waqf flat. Why does the standard still bar leasing it to his son?
options: A son can never be a lessee of any Waqf under any circumstance
Human nature raises fear of favouritism to self or child
Leases to relatives are void in all contracts under Shari'ah
The son would become a Waqf beneficiary
explanation: Basis 3/8/3: by human nature there is a fear of favouritism for himself or his child and of not choosing what is more favourable for the Waqf.

title: Documentary Credit
q: Company X has opened a valid credit in favour of its seller. Before the credit expires, the seller demands payment directly from Company X. Is he entitled?
options: Yes, at any time he chooses between the two
No, the buyer is fully discharged by opening it
No, not while the credit subsists and is valid
Yes, as opening the credit is not final payment
explanation: Per 2/4/2, opening the credit is not final payment, but the seller has no right to request payment from the buyer as long as the credit subsists and is valid.

title: Sharikah (Musharakah) and Modern Corporations
q: Why does the Shari'ah basis apply the general rules, especially of 'Inan, to diminishing Musharakah?
options: To keep it from becoming mere interest-based financing
Because the Institution manages it and bears the whole risk of loss
Because it has no juristic personality separate from that of the partners
Because it is a form of Mudarabah in which the customer is the Mudarib
explanation: Per the basis, applying 'Inan rules safeguards diminishing Musharakah from becoming a mere interest-based financing with payment beyond a share of income.

title: Loan (Qard)
q: Bank A agrees to grant a Qard to a customer on condition that the customer leases equipment from Bank A under Ijarah. What is the ruling?
options: Permissible, if the customer agrees in writing
Not permissible to stipulate an Ijarah within the Qard
Permissible, as the two contracts are separate
Permissible, if the Ijarah rental is at market rate
explanation: Per 7, it is not permissible to stipulate a contract of sale, Ijarah or other commutative contract within the contract of Qard.

title: Protection of Capital and Investments
q: Constructive liquidation of a Mudarabah shows profit of 100,000 added to the capital. Later the Mudarib's negligence wipes out that 100,000. Is he liable for it?
options: No, he is liable only for the original capital
No, since he is never liable for loss of profit
Yes, but only for half, as the Mudarib's share
Yes, since the profit had become part of the capital
explanation: Per 3/7, if liquidation shows profit added to capital and it is lost through the Mudarib's misconduct, negligence or breach, he must indemnify it as part of the capital.

title: Concession Contracts
q: Why may the State regulate mineral exploration by granting exclusive utilization rights, according to the Shari'ah basis?
options: Private persons may not hold mineral rights of any kind whatsoever
It realizes public interest and prevents disputes
Exploration is a form of Riba-free loan from the State to the licensee
The State owns all land absolutely, including privately held land
explanation: Per the Basis, State regulation realizes public interest and prevents disputes, as with fuqaha requiring State permission to develop wasteland.

title: Guarantees
q: Per the Shari'ah basis, which evidence supports guaranteeing a debt whose amount is not yet known?
options: The consensus that debts must be fixed first
The Hadith on the bankrupt's sold goods
The rule that Gharar is always tolerated
The general Hadith that the guarantor is liable
explanation: Per the Basis, the Hadith 'The guarantor is liable' makes no distinction between known and unknown, and the uncertainty causes no dispute; also the Yusuf verse.

title: Possession (Qabd)
q: Suppose the custom of treating bills of lading as possession of goods changed in a market. Per the Basis, what follows?
options: That mode would cease to be possession, as custom-based rules change
They become possession only with a court order
They remain possession only for perishable goods
They remain possession forever, as the rule is fixed by an explicit text
explanation: Per the Basis, where rules rest on custom they alter with a change in custom, except what the Shari'ah has specified; if custom changes, that mode ceases.

title: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
q: A seller holding an option to revoke for non-payment dies. Per the Shari'ah basis, why does the option not pass to his heirs?
options: Heirs must first obtain a court order
All options lapse on the death of either party, whoever holds them
It is a readiness and willingness to act, not transferable
The buyer's debt is cancelled upon the seller's death, ending the option
explanation: Per the basis, the option to revoke for non-payment abates on its owner's death because it constitutes a readiness and willingness to act, not transferable to heirs.

title: Islamic Insurance
q: Which Hadith does the basis cite as the ground for prohibiting commercial insurance?
