options: The Prophet prohibited sales which involve Gharar
The Prophet prohibited sale and lending together
The Prophet prohibited selling what one does not own
The Prophet prohibited two sales in one deal
explanation: The basis: commercial insurance is prohibited for Gharar, citing Abu Hurayrah: the Prophet prohibited sales which involve Gharar.

title: ’Arboun (Earnest Money)
q: Bank A proposes a currency exchange in which the customer pays 'Arboun and gets a period to confirm. On what basis does the standard reject 'Arboun in Sarf?
options: Sarf may be concluded only as a promise, not a contract
'Arboun may only be paid in kind, never in currency
It embeds a cooling-off option, while Sarf needs Qabd at the session
The exchange rate would remain unknown to the customer during the option period
explanation: Per the Basis, 'Arboun carries Khiyar al-Shart, impermissible in Sarf per the majority, as both countervalues must be possessed in Majlis al-'Aqd.

title: Mudarabah
q: A capital provider signs a Mudarabah but keeps the funds in his own locked account; the Mudarib has no access to them. What is the effect?
options: Valid, but the Mudarib then becomes a guarantor of the funds
Valid, as long as the capital is known in amount and currency
Valid, since the contract was signed by both of the parties and its terms are clear
Invalid: the capital must be available to the Mudarib
explanation: Per 7/4, for validity the capital must be wholly or partly put at the Mudarib's disposal, or he must have free access to it.

title: Trading in Currencies
q: Bank A expects a currency to decline and wants to protect its profit on a transaction by buying in the forward currency market. Is this allowed?
options: Yes, if the hedge does not exceed the exposure
No, forward dealing is prohibited even for hedging
Yes, if the forward rate equals the spot rate
Yes, because hedging is a legitimate purpose
explanation: Per 2/3, dealing in the forward currency market is prohibited even if the purpose is hedging against a loss of profit due to an expected decline.

title: Zakah
q: A non-profit educational institution with no specific owner, funded by allocated public property (Irsad), makes a surplus this year. Is Zakah due?
options: Yes, because it made a profit this year, as profit makes any institution Zakatable
Yes, on the market value of the allocated property
Yes, on its annual surplus at the rate of 2.5%, like a trading company
No; it is exempt like charitable Waqf, even with profits
explanation: Per 3/1/7, the exemption of charitable Waqf also applies to trust funds and Irsad for non-profit institutions with no specific owner, even if they make profits.

title: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
q: Company X holds a license to use a software product and wants to transfer this licence to Company Y. What is the ruling?
options: Not permitted; a license to use gives personal use only
Permitted, if Company Y pays a fair price
Permitted, as it is a usufruct owned by Company X, which may transfer it for a price
Permitted, if Company X stops using the software
explanation: Per 4/3, ownership of a license to use gives the licensee the right to personal use only, which cannot be transferred to a third party.

title: Investment Sukuk
q: A cultivator issues Muzara'ah Sukuk and uses the subscription amounts to buy farmland. What is the position of the subscribers?
options: They are the cultivators, entitled to a share of the produce
They are owners of the land, entitled to a share of the produce
They are lenders to the cultivator, entitled to repayment in full
They are lessees of the land, entitled to its usufruct
explanation: Per 5/1/5/9(b), where the cultivator issues the Sukuk, subscribers are owners of the land and holders take a share of the produce as agreed.

title: Arbitration
q: Bank A signs a financing agreement governed by a law that contradicts Shari'ah. What does the standard recommend to avoid being forced to apply that law in disputes?
options: Leaving disputes to the courts of the host country
Agreeing on arbitration only after a dispute arises
Stipulating Islamic arbitration in the agreement
Requiring the counterparty to waive all claims
explanation: Per 3/2, seeking Islamic arbitration should be stipulated in agreements so the parties cannot be forced to resort to laws that contradict Shari'ah.

title: Guarantees
q: Bank A prices a letter of guarantee at 1% per quarter of the guaranteed amount, as consideration for the guarantee itself. What is the ruling?
options: Not permissible, as it is a fee for the guarantee per se
Permissible if the guarantee is uncovered
Permissible if the letter of guarantee is fully covered in cash
Permissible as it reflects the risk taken
explanation: Per 6/1/1, no remuneration may be taken for a letter of guarantee per se (covered or not), as it is usually computed on amount and duration guaranteed.

title: ’Arboun (Earnest Money)
q: A buyer pays 'Arboun for a factory site and stipulates in the contract a refund if he fails to obtain licenses from the relevant authorities. Is this condition valid?
options: No, 'Arboun is non-refundable in all cases
No, it turns the 'Arboun into a refundable deposit
Yes, but only if the seller agrees after the contract
Yes, a refund may be stipulated for specific situations
explanation: Per item 10, the buyer may stipulate in the contract a refund of earnest money in specific situations, such as failure to obtain licenses.

title: Concession Contracts
q: Company X gets a utilization concession whose exploration effort is unknown, for a set percentage of the output. How does the Shari'ah classify it?
options: Mudarabah: the State is owner of capital
Ju'alah: the State is Ja'il, Company X is 'Amil
Salam: the State is buyer of the output
Ijarah: the State is lessor, Company X is lessee
explanation: Per 5/3, a utilization concession is a form of Ju'alah: the State is the Ja'il, the licensee the 'Amil and its amount the Ju'l.

title: Mudarabah
q: To what does the Shari'ah basis liken the Mudarib's preliminary entitlement to profit before final valuation?
options: The contract of Qard, in which the borrower returns the like
The contract of Ijarah, in which the usufruct is sold for rent
The contract of sharecropping
The contract of Salam, in which the price is paid in advance
explanation: Per the basis, the Mudarib's preliminary entitlement to realised profit, known absolutely only after actual or constructive valuation, is analogous to sharecropping.

title: Guarantees
q: In an Ijarah, Bank A as lessor requires the lessee to provide a guarantee covering damage to the leased asset from any cause. Is this allowed?
options: Yes, since the lessee holds and uses the asset throughout the lease
No, a lessor may never require any guarantee
Yes, if the lessee is given a lower rental
No, unless restricted to misconduct, negligence or breach
explanation: Per 2/3, the lessor bears the risk and the lessee holds the asset on trust; a guarantee may cover only misconduct, negligence or breach of contract.

title: Loan (Qard)
q: To avoid interest, Bank A and a correspondent bank agree on a ceiling for overdrafts each may draw on the other, with no claim for profit. What is the ruling?
options: Prohibited, as banks may not lend to each other
Permissible only if a profit rate is agreed
Permissible; there is no restriction on this
Prohibited as 'you lend me and I lend you'
explanation: Per 10/4, there is no restriction on agreeing with correspondents a ceiling on mutual overdrafts without any claim for profits (interest).

title: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
q: Bank A wants to charge a fee for opening investment accounts. How should this fee be set?
options: As a lump sum, charged once, preferably not above average actual cost
As a percentage of the deposit amount, charged annually for the account
As a share of the profit earned by the account
As a monthly charge based on the account balance
explanation: Per 2/2/4, the opening fee should be a lump sum, preferably not exceeding average actual cost, and charged once at the time of opening the account.

title: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
q: Bank A orders machinery to be manufactured under Istisna'a, with delivery and price both deferred to a later date. What is the ruling?
options: Invalid unless the machinery already exists
Valid, as Istisna'a is valid even when the price is delayed
Invalid, as the two counter-values are deferred
Valid only if the full price is paid to the maker at signing
explanation: Per 3/2/3, when the contract is Istisna'a, it is valid even when the price is delayed.

title: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
q: Per the Shari'ah basis, when does a suretyship (Kafalah) become affected by Gharar?
options: When it is made for an unknown period or an unknown amount
When it covers a future obligation not yet due at the time
When it is made subject to a condition
When it is paid for, as it becomes exchange-based
explanation: Per the basis, suretyship tolerates Gharar as a corollary contract; if paid for, it becomes an exchange-based contract and thus affected by Gharar.

title: Waqf
q: A Waqf deed over a warehouse says nothing about the duration of the Waqf. How long does the Waqf last?
options: It is perpetual, as that is the initial presumption
It lasts only for the beneficiaries' lifetime, then reverts to the Waqif
It lasts only for the Waqif's lifetime, then returns to his heirs
It is void for failing to specify a term
explanation: Per 2/4/1/5, the initial presumption is that Waqf is perpetual; it is limited to a period only if the Waqif stipulates so.

title: Salam and Parallel Salam
q: Bank A pays the capital of a Salam by granting the seller the use of a ship for one year, delivering the ship to him at once. What is the status of the capital?
options: Invalid; Salam capital must always be paid in cash
Valid; delivering the ship is immediate receipt
Valid only if the ship is later sold to him
Invalid; usufruct is received only over time
explanation: Per 3/1/1, the capital may be the usufruct of an asset such as a ship; granting access through delivery of the asset is regarded as immediate receipt.

title: Ijarah and Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek
q: Which precedent does the Shari'ah basis cite for the validity of a gift contingent on a condition, as used in Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek?
options: The case of Hibban Ibn Munqidh on options in sales
The practice of Umar Ibn Al-Khattab on 'Arboun in sales
The Prophet's gift to Negus, conditional on survival
The Prophet's purchase of a she-camel from Abu Bakr
explanation: The basis: a conditional gift is valid; the Prophet sent a gift to Negus on condition that he was alive when the messenger arrived.

title: Waqf
q: Company X wants to create a Waqf over its educational website and a set of digital applications. What is the ruling?
options: Not permitted; only real estate may be Waqf
Permitted only as a temporary Waqf
Permitted only if attached to real estate
Permitted, as Waqf of movable assets is valid
explanation: Per 2/4/7, it is permitted to create Waqf of movable assets such as vehicles, machinery, websites and digital applications.

title: Zakah
q: Bank A holds shares in Company Z for retention (Nama'), not trading. Company Z reports its Zakatable assets per share. How does Bank A pay Zakah?
options: On Company Z's Zakatable assets per share
On the market value of the shares at the end of the Zakah year
On the cost of the shares
On dividends received only
explanation: Per 4/2/4, for shares held for retention, Zakah is levied on the Zakatable assets per share if known; otherwise estimated; if none, on remaining net income.

title: Waqf
q: Ahmad makes Waqf of his 30% common share in a building that is leased to tenants. What is the Waqf entitled to?
options: Nothing, as the lease ends upon the Waqf
Its share of the rent from the building
The whole rent, as Waqf takes priority
Nothing until the building is divided
explanation: Per 2/4/11, Waqf over a common share is permitted; if the asset is leased, the Waqf is entitled to receive its share of the rent.

title: Liability of the Investment Manager
q: After a realized loss, a Mudarib voluntarily makes it good from his own funds. What basis does the standard give for allowing this?
options: It is a public interest (Maslahah Mursalah)
It is his waiver of a right with his consent
Benevolence: no blame lies on the doers of good
It is a third party's undertaking to donate
explanation: Per the Basis, he does so out of benevolence in this specific case, and there is no cause for blame upon the doers of good.

title: Mortgage and its Contemporary Applications
q: A client mortgages his current account to Bank A, where it is held. The Bank wants to use the balance in its operations. What is required?
options: Nothing; a current account is a loan that the Bank may freely use anyway
Agreement to convert it into a Mudarabah investment account
The client's verbal consent only, with no change
Payment of a fixed return to the client for the use
explanation: Per 5, the Institution should not use the mortgaged current account unless both agree to transfer it to an investment account under Mudarabah, avoiding free benefit.

title: Banking Services in Islamic Banks
q: Company X asks Bank A to collect its customers' cheques and debt notes and credit the proceeds to its account. What may the Bank do?
options: Collect them only free of charge
Collect them only after Shari'ah board approval
Collect them and receive a fee for the service
Buy them at a discount before maturity
explanation: Per 2/5/1, the Institution may collect cheques, debt notes and promissory notes, deposit the proceeds, and receive fees for such services.

title: Investment Sukuk
q: Sukuk holders demand a say in managing the assets their certificates represent. On what basis does the standard recognise their right to management?
options: Management rights arise only where the Sukuk are based on investment agency
They are creditors entitled to protect their loans to the issuer
The prospectus grants it to them as a contractual favour only
They own the property represented, and management is part of ownership
explanation: Per the Basis, holders have a right to management because they own the property their certificates represent, and management is part of ownership.

title: Monetization (Tawarruq)
q: Bank A's internal procedures execute the deferred purchase contract and the spot sale contract together in one step, so the customer never has a chance to receive the commodity. What is the ruling?
options: Prohibited, even if the link is only in the procedures
Permitted, if the customer voluntarily signed each contract
Permitted, since the link is not stipulated in the documents
Prohibited only if the link is written as a contract condition
explanation: Per 4/6, linking the two contracts so that the client loses his right to receive the commodity is prohibited, whether by stipulation, tradition or incorporation in procedures.

title: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
q: Company X pays gold as the capital of Salam to buy wheat for delivery in six months. Is this permissible?
options: No, the capital of Salam must be paid in currency, never in gold
Yes, if the wheat equals the gold in weight
Yes; the Salam subject is not gold, silver or currency
No, gold may not be used as payment in any deferred contract
explanation: Per 5/2/1, gold may be the capital of Salam provided the subject matter (al-Muslam Fehi) is not gold, silver or currencies.

title: Hawalah
q: Bakr finds that Zaid, the payer, has died bankrupt. Per the Shari'ah basis, what supports Bakr's recourse to the transferor?
options: The consensus that Hawalah never discharges the transferor at all
Uthman's report that a Muslim's right cannot go unfulfilled
The rule that death annuls all contracts
The Hadith that the guarantor is liable
explanation: Per the Basis, the Hanafi view rests on Uthman Ibn Affan's answer that the transferee returns to the transferor, as the right of a Muslim cannot go unfulfilled.

title: Al-Wakalah Bi Al-Istithmar (Investment Agency)
q: A client asks how an investment agency differs from Mudarabah, given both aim to grow wealth. What distinction does the Shari'ah basis draw?
options: Investment agency is a form of Ijarah; Mudarabah is a partnership
Investment agency is a gift; Mudarabah is a guarantee
Investment agency is a partnership in profit; Mudarabah is a contract of Ijarah for work
Investment agency is a loan; Mudarabah is a sale
explanation: Per the basis, investment agency, like Mudarabah and Musharakah, aims to increase wealth, but it is a form of Ijarah (hiring) while they are forms of partnership.

title: Islamic Reinsurance
q: Per the basis, why may the reinsurance company manage the reinsurance account either for a fee or free of charge?
options: Mudarabah allows the Mudarib to waive his share
The company owns the account and sets its own fee
Donation contracts permit any fee arrangement
Wakalah is permissible with or without remuneration
explanation: Per the basis, management rests on the agency (Wakalah) contract, which Fiqh scholars unanimously declare permissible with or without remuneration.

title: Ju’alah
q: Bank A undertakes a Ju'alah as worker for a client, then contracts out the work to Company Y under a parallel Ju'alah. When is this permissible?
options: Only if Company Y is paid the same Ju'l as Bank A receives from the client
Only if both Ju'alahs are linked in one contract with the same terms
If it was not stipulated that Bank A does the work itself
Never, an Institution must always do the work itself under Ju'alah
explanation: Per 9/1, an Institution may act as worker and contract out by parallel Ju'alah unless it is stipulated it will do the work itself; the two must not be linked.

title: Hawalah
q: The transferred debt is already due, but Zaid, the payer, requires that it be paid at an agreed future date. May Bakr, the transferee, demand earlier payment?
options: Yes, if Ahmad guarantees payment
Yes, since the debt was already due
Yes, after giving reasonable notice
No, not before the agreed date
explanation: Per 5/1/4, in a deferred Hawalah where the payer required future payment at an agreed date, the payer cannot be asked to pay before that date.

title: Buyback
q: Bank A buys a building for cash and renovates it extensively. Later, the original seller buys it back on deferred terms at a higher price. Is this permitted?
options: Yes, if the higher price reflects the asset's change
No, any deferred price above the original spot price is 'Inah
Yes, but only if the price is paid on spot
No, the original seller may never buy it back on deferred terms
explanation: Per 3/5/2/2, buyback is permitted where the price change is due to alterations in the asset's characteristics or value, not deferral.

title: Ijarah and Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek
q: After a lessee's default, Bank A forecloses on his security. What may the Bank deduct from the proceeds?
options: Future rentals for the full remaining term
Past rentals due plus legitimate compensation
All rentals, including those not yet due
Only past rentals, never compensation
explanation: Per 6/5, the lessor may deduct only rentals due for past periods, not future ones, plus legitimate compensation for the lessee's breach of contract.

title: Online Financial Dealings
q: A client finds that an online adhesion contract he joined carries an excessively unfair price. What remedy does the standard give him?
options: Resort to law to nullify the contract or amend its conditions
Unilateral withholding of payment until the price is reduced
Only a claim against the State for weak supervision
No remedy, since he accepted the terms by adhering
explanation: Per 8/3/4, for an unfair price or an unjust condition, the adhering party may resort to law for nullification of the contract or amendment of its conditions.

title: Hiring of Persons
q: A ship's crew hiring contract expires mid-voyage. Ending it now would cause harm. What does the standard provide?
options: The contract continues with no pay due
Hiring continues, at agreed pay or else normal pay
The contract continues at the old pay only
The contract ends and the crew is unpaid onward
explanation: Per 8/2/3, hiring ends at expiry but remains when needed for a reasonable excuse or to avoid harm, for pay agreed or else the normal pay for similar services.

title: Waqf
q: A cash Waqf of 1,000,000 is invested and grows to 1,080,000. How is the 80,000 treated?
options: As part of the Waqf asset itself, to be reinvested for growth
As the overseer's remuneration for managing the investment
As a return to the Waqif
As yield to be disbursed to the Waqf beneficiaries
explanation: Per 2/4/13/1, any excess cash over the Waqf amount is the yield, which shall be disbursed to the Waqf beneficiaries.

title: Financial Paper (Shares and Bonds)
q: Company X redeems Ahmad's shares during its life and gives him shares with lower profit rights and a claim at winding up only after capital shares are paid. What are these?
options: Preference shares, which are permissible
Bearer shares, which are permissible
Tamattu' shares, which are not permissible
Ordinary shares, which are permissible
explanation: Per 2/7, Tamattu' shares, given in place of redeemed shares with lesser profit and deferred liquidation rights, may not be issued.

title: Commercial Papers
q: Ahmad wants to transfer dollars he holds to pay a supplier in euros through a bank transfer. What does the standard require?
options: Convert at a rate fixed when the order is placed
Convert the currencies first, then make the transfer
Transfer the dollars without any conversion
Transfer the dollars, then convert at maturity
explanation: Per 7/3, where the currency differs, conversion must first be made (constructive possession sufficing), then the transfer: a combination of Sarf and Hawalah.

title: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
q: A client asks whether the standard on financial rights governs his Khiyar al-Shart (option to revoke within a set period) in a sale with Bank A. What is the answer?
options: Yes, as Khiyar al-Shart is a proprietary right
No; options are not recognised by the Shari'ah
No; Khiyarat are excluded, being covered elsewhere
Yes; it covers all rights that arise in sale contracts with Institutions
explanation: Per 1, the standard does not cover non-financial rights, Khiyarat (e.g. Khiyar al-Shart, Khiyar al-Naqd) or Waqf rights, as these are covered in separate standards.

title: Islamic Insurance
q: An Islamic insurance company manages and invests the policyholders' fund. What is the contractual relationship between the company and the fund?
options: Sale of cover for management; Qard for the investment
Musharakah for management; Ijarah for the investment of the fund
Mudarabah for both the management and the investment
Wakalah for management; Mudarabah or investment agency
explanation: Per 4/2, the company-fund relationship is Wakalah for management, and Mudarabah or investment agency for investment of the fund's assets.

title: Online Financial Dealings
q: Two years after learning that its website was trespassed, Bank A claims compensation. Under the standard, is the claim barred by time?
options: No; there is no specific time limit, subject to compatible rules
Yes; it must be claimed within one year of the incident
No; compensation is due even without any claim being made
Yes; compensation is due automatically and lapses if it is not paid on time
explanation: Per 8/1/6, compensation is due only when claimed, and claiming has no specific time limit after the trespass is known, observing compatible rules.

title: Procrastinating Debtor
q: Bank A's contract lets it recoup late amounts from the customer's accounts. The debt is in USD; his investment account is in EUR. How may the Bank proceed?
options: Recoup it at the rate on the contract date
It may not touch investment accounts
Recoup it at the then prevailing exchange rate
Recoup it only with his fresh consent
explanation: Per 2/5/3, a stipulated set-off from current or investment accounts needs no further consent; if currencies differ, the then prevailing rate is used.

title: Concession Contracts
q: A State agency charges Company X a fixed fee for the procedures of offering it a concession right, with no element of Riba or Gharar. What is the ruling?
options: Permissible, as a fee stipulated in the contract
Not permissible, as concessions must be granted free
Not permissible, as the State may not take fees
Permissible only if the fee is a share of output
explanation: Per 3/2, there is no Shari'ah objection to fees or compensation for procedures of offering concession rights, unless the deal involves Riba, Gharar or other banned practices.

title: Procrastinating Debtor
q: A contractor is late completing a building and owes an amount under the contract's penalty clause. Is his case within the procrastinating debtor standard?
options: No, penalty clauses on contractors fall outside the standard
Yes, he becomes a debtor by virtue of the penalty clause
No, only debtors under Murabahah are covered
Only if the contractor has become insolvent
explanation: Per the Scope (1), the standard covers a contractor or concessionaire who is late in completing work and becomes a debtor by virtue of a penalty clause.

title: Islamic Insurance
q: Per the basis, how does the company's role differ between Islamic and commercial insurance?
options: Mudarib in underwriting vs partner in the fund
Original party in its own name vs agent of the account
Guarantor of all claims vs agent of the policyholders' account
Agent of the account vs original party in its own name
explanation: The basis: in Islamic insurance the company is the agent of the insurance account; in commercial insurance it is an original party contracting in its own name.

title: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
q: Company X agrees to buy fuel from a supplier at the market price on the day of purchase, without stating a figure. What is the ruling on this price term?
options: Permitted; the Gharar in such a price is forgiven
Permitted only if a cap on the price is agreed
Void, as the price is left to an outside party
Void, because no amount is stated in the contract
explanation: Per 5/2/2, Gharar in the price is permitted when the sale is concluded at the market price on the day of purchase or the price people usually sell at.

title: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
q: A landowner holds a right of passage over his neighbour's land and agrees to waive it in return for a payment. What is the ruling?
options: Not permissible, as easements prevent harm like Shuf'ah
Permissible only if the waiver is without consideration
Permissible for an easement, unlike Shuf'ah
Not permissible, as easements have no monetary value
explanation: Per 10/3, it is permissible to take consideration for transfer or waiver of easement rights, by sale or otherwise.

title: Rules for Calculating Profit in Financial Transactions
q: A Murabahah customer cannot pay on time and asks for a longer term. Bank A proposes to extend the term and add further profit to the total amount. What is the ruling?
options: Permissible if the Shari'ah board approves the amount
Impermissible: rescheduling by raising profit for extension
Permissible, since the customer himself requested the extension and agreed to the profit
Permissible if the extension is shorter than one year
explanation: Per 9, where the profit rate is time-bound, re-scheduling debt by increasing the profit or total amount through extending the duration is impermissible.

title: Protection of Capital and Investments
q: In a capital protection structure, Partner A contributes 60% of a Musharakah's capital but stipulates that he will bear only 30% of any loss. Is this acceptable?
options: Yes, if both partners agree to it in writing, since Musharakah terms are set by agreement
Yes, if Partner A accepts a lower profit share
Yes, since it serves the aim of protecting capital
No; partners must bear losses per their shares in the capital
explanation: Per 4/1/1, a condition of capital protection instruments is that investment partners bear risks and losses according to their respective shares in the capital.

title: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
q: Ahmad, holding a cooling-off option, decides to revoke and records his decision in his own files, without informing the seller. Is the revocation valid?
options: Yes; his decision alone terminates the contract
No; the other party must know of the revocation
No, unless a court approves it
Yes, if made within the option period
explanation: Per 2/7/2, when the option owner revokes, the contract terminates, but it is required for the other party to know of the revocation for it to be valid.

title: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
q: A holder exits the Mudarabah with part of his funds before the period ends. Bank A sets the exit amount so that it earns less profit. How is this characterised?
options: Impermissible deprivation of the holder from the profit he is entitled to receive
Permissible only if the holder pays a fee
Permissible exit on the basis of supply and demand
Impermissible penalty imposed on the holder for withdrawing before the period ends
explanation: Per 4/9, the holder may exit, and the Institution may set the exit amount to earn no or less profit; this is exit on supply and demand, not deprivation from profit.

title: Debit Card, Charge Card and Credit Card
q: Bank A offers cardholders free conventional life insurance and discounts on airline reservations. Which of these privileges is permitted?
options: Only the discounts on airline reservations
Only the conventional life insurance
Each of them, since they are free gifts
Neither, as all card privileges are barred
explanation: Per 4/6, privileges prohibited by the Shari'ah, such as conventional life insurance, are barred; others, like airline or hotel discounts, are permitted.

title: Zakah
q: Company X has an interest-bearing loan with unpaid principal and unpaid interest outstanding. Can the unpaid interest be deducted from Zakatable assets?
options: Yes, but only half of the unpaid interest
Yes, as part of the company's current liabilities
Yes, if it is actually paid within the year
No; impermissible commitments are not recognized debts
explanation: Per 6/2/4, unpaid interest is not deducted from Zakatable assets, because impermissible commitments cannot lead to a Shari'ah-recognizable debt.

title: Mudarabah
q: Bank A restricts its Mudarabah to trading in a fruit that is out of season and very scarce, so the venture cannot make profit. What is the ruling on this restriction?
options: Acceptable if the Mudarib agreed to it in writing beforehand
Not acceptable: restricted commodities must be commonly available
Acceptable if the restriction is limited to a single year
Acceptable, since the capital provider may restrict freely
explanation: Per 9/2, restriction to certain commodities requires them to be commonly available; they must not be scarce, seasonal or in very limited supply.

title: Waqf
q: A Waqf holds Sukuk whose issuer is liquidated, and the Waqf receives the liquidation proceeds. Which rulings should then apply?
options: The rules on dissolving a family Waqf
The proceeds are distributed to beneficiaries as income
The proceeds return to the Waqif
The Shari'ah rulings on Istibdal (exchange of Waqf property)
explanation: Per 3/4/3/4, Waqf in Shari'ah-accepted shares and Sukuk is permissible; in case of liquidation, the rulings on Istibdal should be applied.

title: Mortgage and its Contemporary Applications
q: Investment accounts used as mortgage contain changing assets, involving some Gharar. Per the Maliki argument in the basis, why is this acceptable?
options: Who may lend undocumented may accept documentation with some Gharar
The Institution guarantees the account value
Gharar is never relevant to mortgage contracts, whatever the asset type
The account is converted into cash on mortgaging
explanation: Per the basis, the Malikis argue that since the mortgagee may lend without documentation, he can accept documentation with some Gharar: something is better than nothing.

title: Options to Revoke Contracts Due to Incomplete Performance
q: An Istisna'a contract for a building includes a clause excluding the manufacturer's liability for any defects (sale "as is where is"). Is this clause permissible?
options: Yes; Bay' al-Bara'ah is valid in every contract, including Istisna'a for a building
No, unless the buyer is a financial institution
No; excluding liability for defect is prohibited in Istisna'a
Yes, if the price is reduced in exchange
explanation: Per 2/2/4, a clause excluding the seller's liability for defect (Bay' al-Bara'ah) is prohibited in Ijarah and Istisna'a contracts.

title: Possession (Qabd)
q: Bank A leases equipment to a customer under Ijarah. Absent contrary stipulation or custom, who bears the expenses of delivering possession of the leased equipment?
options: The lessor, Bank A
The supplier of the equipment
The lessee, the customer
Both parties equally
explanation: Per 4/1/4, the expenses of possession of the leased property are borne by the lessor, while the lessee bears the expenses of delivering the rental.

title: Murabahah
q: Bank A and a customer want to exchange a bilateral promise before a Murabahah. When is such a bilateral promise permissible?
options: Only if the customer pays Hamish Jiddiyyah with it
Only if it is binding on both parties without option
Only if one or both parties have an option to cancel it
Only if it is signed after the Bank buys the item
explanation: Per 2/3/3, a bilateral promise is permissible only if there is an option to cancel exercisable by both promisors or by either one of them.

title: Sharikah (Musharakah) and Modern Corporations
q: Ali stipulated he would be a sleeping partner and provides 30% of the capital, yet asks for 50% of the profit. Is this permissible?
options: No, unless Ali brings additional capital to match his profit share
No, extra profit above capital share may not go to a sleeping partner
Yes, provided Ali also bears 50% of any loss of the Sharikah
Yes, the profit ratio may always be agreed freely among the partners
explanation: Per 3/1/5/3, profit may be disproportionate to capital provided the additional percentage over contribution is not in favour of a sleeping partner.

title: Waqf
q: A Waqf lacks funds to repair its leased building. The lessee offers to carry out the repairs. What may the overseer do?
options: Allow it only as a donation by the lessee
Allow it, and transfer part of the building's ownership to him
Refuse, as lessees may not repair Waqf assets
Allow it; the lessee has priority to remain as lessee until he recovers his debt
explanation: Per 4/3, if funds are insufficient, the overseer may allow the lessee to repair, and the lessee has priority to remain until he recovers his debt.

title: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
q: The lease of a shop ends, and the incumbent tenant agrees to hand over occupancy to a new tenant for a payment. What is the ruling?
options: Permitted, as goodwill belongs to the tenant who built up the customer base
Not permitted, as his right in the usufruct has expired
Permitted, if it does not exceed one month's rent
Permitted, if the owner receives a share of it
explanation: Per 8/3, after the end of the lease the incumbent tenant may not take any payment to hand over occupancy, because his right in the usufruct has expired.

title: Waqf
q: A Muslim donor wishes to make a Waqf for a hospital that serves a non-Muslim community, for a purpose involving no sin. What is the ruling?
options: Permissible only if Muslims share the income
Impermissible; beneficiaries must be Muslims
Permissible, since the cause involves no sin
Permissible only as a temporary Waqf
explanation: Per 3/3/2, it is permissible to make Waqf for the benefit of non-Muslims, provided the cause to be served does not involve a sin.

title: Waqf
q: After meeting the Waqf's needs and the avenues set by the Waqif, revenue remains. What may be done with it?
options: Keep it idle until the Waqf ends
Add it to the overseer's remuneration as a performance incentive
Return it to the Waqif or his heirs as the owner of the surplus
Invest it for the Waqf or give it to similar charities
explanation: Per 9/4, surplus revenue is invested for the Waqf, or disbursed in charitable causes similar to the Waqif's; otherwise to general charitable causes.

title: Loan (Qard)
q: Ahmad keeps funds in a current account with Bank A, which uses them in its business. What is the legal nature of the current account?
options: A loan: Bank A owns the funds and is liable to repay them
An investment account in which Ahmad shares in Bank A's profit
A Mudarabah with Ahmad as owner of capital
A deposit (Wadi'ah) held in trust by Bank A
explanation: Per 10/1/1, current accounts are loans and not deposits; the institution owns the amounts and a liability to repay them is established against it.

title: Competitions and Prizes
q: A store gives buyers of a product a ticket for a prize draw, and prices that product higher than the same product sold without a ticket. Is the draw permissible?
options: Yes, as the buyer still receives the product he paid for in full
Yes, if every buyer has an equal chance
No, the price must not be raised for the right to enter
Yes, if the prizes are Shari'ah compliant and the draw is fair
explanation: Per 3/3/3/1, the price of goods whose purchase qualifies for the draw must not be increased vis-a-vis the same goods without that right.

title: Payment Cards
q: Bank A issues a lending-based credit card and sets its issuance fee well above the actual direct cost. What is the ruling?
options: Not permitted; it may not exceed actual direct cost
Permitted, if the fee is disclosed to the customer in advance
Permitted, as fees follow the agreement signed with the cardholder
Permitted, if the card is not revolving
explanation: Per 5/1/1, fees charged by the issuer and linked to the loan in a credit card, such as issuance fees, may not exceed the actual direct cost.

title: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
q: A customer asks Bank A to apply the gold rulings to platinum that is marketed locally as 'white gold'. Under the standard, do the gold rulings apply?
options: Yes, since it is called white gold in that country
No, they do not apply to platinum even if so called
Only if the platinum is sold in ingot form
Yes, since all precious metals follow gold's rulings
explanation: Per 10/6, the gold rulings apply to white gold but not to metals such as platinum, palladium and nickel called white gold in some countries.

title: Waqf
q: A Waqf builds a maintenance reserve from its annual income. The beneficiaries demand a share of that reserve. What is their right?
options: Right to half of the reserve each year as part of their income
Full right, as all income of the Waqf belongs to the beneficiaries
Right to the whole reserve once the Waqf asset has been repaired
None, unless part of the reserve exceeds actual needs
explanation: Per 8/1/2, the beneficiaries have no right in the maintenance reserve unless part of it turns out to be in excess of actual needs; its returns join the principal.

title: Irrigation Partnership (Musaqat)
q: A Musaqat worker dies; the heirs decline to continue, and the owner completes the work. Once the crop materializes, what are the heirs entitled to?
options: A share proportionate to his work, uncapped
A market wage for the deceased's period, capped at his share
The deceased's full stipulated share, since the crop materialized during the contract
Nothing, as they declined to continue
explanation: Per 12/3, the successor gets a market wage for the period worked by the deceased, not exceeding his stipulated share of the crop.

title: Sale of Debt
q: Why may early discharge of a debt in another currency not be stipulated, anticipated or customary?
options: It would become a deferred currency exchange
It would involve excessive gharar
It would be extinction of debt in debt
It would be a sale of debt to a third party
explanation: Per the Basis for 4/1/1/2(b), such discharge would become a deferred currency exchange (sarf).

title: Trading in Currencies
q: A customer exchanges a one-pound note for coins of the same country worth 0.98 pound, both handed over on the spot. What is the ruling?
options: Permissible, since a note and a coin are different kinds
Permissible, as the difference is a minor handling cost
Permissible, because both were delivered hand to hand
Not permissible: equal amounts are required
explanation: Per 2/1/2, countervalues of the same currency must be equal even if one is paper money and the other coin, e.g. a one-pound note for a one-pound coin.

title: Financial Paper (Shares and Bonds)
q: A mixed company had prohibited income during the year but declared an overall loss and paid no dividends. Must its shareholders eliminate the prohibited income?
options: Yes, but only half of the prohibited income, the rest being offset
No; nothing is due if no dividend is paid to the shareholders
Yes, despite the loss and absence of distribution
No; the loss offsets the prohibited income earned during the year
explanation: Per 3/4/6/2, the prohibited income specific to the share must be eliminated whether or not profits are distributed and whether a profit or a loss is declared.

title: Payment Cards
q: Why does the Shari'ah basis make a seller who concealed a defect bear the return fees and exchange differences?
options: He holds the goods in trust for the buyer until return
He always bears all return costs
He is the card issuer's agent and acts on its behalf
He caused harm, and it is a discretionary sanction
explanation: Basis 5/7: a seller who caused harm should remove it; he is charged the return costs as a discretionary sanction for concealing the defect.

title: Concession Contracts
q: Company X pays the State a fee for an exploration license over an area for three years. What rights may this license give it?
options: The right to be sole explorer and to conduct exploration works
Only a non-exclusive right to survey the area for a limited period
Ownership of the land in the licensed area
The right to sell minerals without a concession
explanation: Per 5/2/2, an exploration license may entitle its holder to become the sole explorer in the area and to conduct the works required for exploration.

title: Islamic Insurance
q: Ahmad's car is covered by Islamic insurance for an insurance amount of 20,000. An accident causes an actual loss of 15,000. How much indemnity does he receive?
options: 15,000 plus his share of the surplus as of right
15,000, the lesser of the loss and the insured amount
20,000, the full insurance amount
17,500, the average of the two figures
explanation: Per 11/1, the participant receives either the loss he incurred or the insurance amount, whichever is less, as per regulations.

title: Sale of Debt
q: Ahmad simply repays part of his debt to Bank A, with no commutative arrangement involved. Is this governed by the standard on sale of debt?
options: Yes, as a sale of debt for cash at a discount
Yes, if repaid before the maturity date
No, such discharge of debt is outside its scope
Yes, as a sale of debt to the debtor himself
explanation: Per item 1, the standard does not deal with discharge of debt by the debtor, in whole or part, not done through a commutative arrangement.

title: Murabahah
q: Bank A plans to issue negotiable Sukuk whose underlying assets consist only of its Murabahah receivables. What is the ruling?
options: Permissible if the Murabahah sales were concluded validly
Impermissible, as the assets are receivables only
Permissible if the receivables are secured by mortgage
Permissible if the Sukuk holders consent to the risk
explanation: Per 2/2/7, it is impermissible to issue negotiable Sukuk where the underlying asset consists of Murabahah receivables or other receivables only.

title: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
q: Bank A buys goods from a supplier with a cooling-off option, planning to offer them to clients without any binding promise to purchase from them. Is this permissible?
options: No; Bank A may not hold an option as buyer
Yes, but it may not return the goods later
No; Bank A must first obtain a binding promise
Yes; it may return the goods if clients do not buy
explanation: Per 2/8/2, the institution may stipulate an option when buying from suppliers to offer items to clients without a binding promise, returning them if clients do not buy.

title: Debit Card, Charge Card and Credit Card
q: Ahmad's balance is 300. With Bank A's agreement, he uses his card to withdraw 500 in cash. When is this permissible?
options: If the excess carries a modest fixed return
Never, withdrawals may not exceed his balance
If no interest is charged on the excess
Only if the card is a revolving credit card
explanation: Per 4/5/1, a holder may withdraw within his available funds, or more with the issuer's agreement, provided no interest is charged.

title: Rules for Calculating Profit in Financial Transactions
q: A customer argues that a higher deferred price is just like interest. Per the Shari'ah basis, on what ground is the increase in a credit sale permitted?
options: "Allah has permitted sale", read as covering deferred sale
Custom, since all markets charge more for credit
The customer's consent, which validates any increase
Necessity, as Islamic banks cannot otherwise operate in a market based on credit
explanation: Per the basis, the increase is permitted by the Verse "Allah has permitted sale", referring to deferred sale, so the comparison between it and interest is addressed.

title: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
q: In a spot sale of an existing, ascertained commodity, delivery is delayed by a few days without any stipulation of delay. What is the effect on the contract?
options: The contract turns into a forward contract
The contract becomes a Salam contract
It does not affect the validity of the contract
The contract becomes void for lack of spot delivery
explanation: Per 3/1/4, delay without stipulation in delivery of an existing and ascertained commodity, or in accepting the spot price, does not affect validity.

title: Mudarabah
q: A Mudarib wishes to accept funds from another investor on a Mudarabah basis while managing Bank A's Mudarabah. Under what conditions may he?
options: With Bank A's permission, if his duties to Bank A are not affected
Freely, since an unrestricted Mudarib may do so at will, without telling Bank A
Never, since a Mudarib may manage only one Mudarabah at a time
Only if he guarantees Bank A's capital in return for its consent to this
explanation: Per 9/1/6(b), by permission of the capital provider, the Mudarib may accept funds from a third party if this does not affect his duties under the first Mudarabah.

title: Murabahah
q: After a Murabahah is executed, the customer refuses to take delivery at the prescribed time. The contract has a condition for this case. What may Bank A do?
options: Raise the price to cover storage costs
Revoke, or sell to a third party for his account
Keep the asset and also the price already paid by him
Charge him a daily fee for each day until delivery is taken
explanation: Per 4/11, the Institution may stipulate that on such refusal it may revoke the contract or sell the asset to a third party on the customer's behalf and account.

title: Sale of Debt
q: A Salam contract for wheat stipulates that at maturity the seller may deliver barley instead. What is the ruling on this term?
options: Permitted, if barley's value doesn't exceed wheat's
Permitted, as the substitution is after maturity
Permitted, since barley may be a Salam subject
Not permitted; substitution can't be stipulated
explanation: Per 4/1/1/3, substitution of the subject of Salam after maturity is permitted only without stipulating it in the contract.

title: Loan (Qard)
q: Bank A sets up exclusive booths for depositing and withdrawing, available only to its premium current account holders. What is the ruling?
options: Permissible only if the booths are offered for a fee
Prohibited, as all lenders must be treated equally
Permissible, as it relates to deposits and withdrawals
Prohibited, as it is a benefit in lieu of the Qard
explanation: Per 10/1/3, there is no restriction if the institution distinguishes between current account owners in what relates to deposits and withdrawals, like exclusive booths.

title: Obtaining and Deploying Liquidity
q: To raise liquidity, Bank A concludes an Istisna'a sale stipulating advance payment and a parallel Istisna'a purchase on instalments. Is advance payment obligatory in the Istisna'a sale?
options: No; advance payment is prohibited in Istisna'a
Yes, but only in the parallel Istisna'a purchase
Yes; the Istisna'a price must always be paid in advance
No; it may be stipulated, although it is not obligatory
explanation: Per 4/2/2, the institution may conclude an Istisna'a sale stipulating advance payment, although advance payment is not obligatory, with a parallel Istisna'a on deferred terms.

title: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
q: Why does the standard prohibit trading a promise (Wa'd) relating to gold through sale or purchase?
options: A promise cannot be the subject of a commutative contract
The promise lacks spot exchange of the countervalues at the session
The promise binds only one of the parties and so is unequal
Trading it would render the deposit a loan
explanation: Per the Basis, trading a promise in any form is impermissible because a promise cannot be used as the subject matter of a commutative contract.

title: Liability of the Investment Manager
q: A service agent collecting rentals for a Sukuk also commits to make up capital losses, and charges a fee well above the market rate for similar work. Is this acceptable?
options: Yes, if the fee is set in the service agency contract
No, its fee may not exceed the prevailing market rate
No, a service agent may never give such a commitment
Yes, the extra fee rewards its undertaking
explanation: Per 4/3/2/3, a paid service agent's fee must not exceed the market rate, to avoid a consideration for the undertaking, which must be voluntary.

title: Mudarabah
q: Ahmad gives Bilal funds under a contract titled 'Qirad', stating a profit ratio and Bilal's role as investor. Can this be a valid Mudarabah?
options: Yes, but only if a court registers the contract
No, only the word Mudarabah concludes the contract
Yes, Mudarabah may be concluded using the term Qirad
No, Qirad refers to an interest-free loan only
explanation: Per 4/1, the Mudarabah contract may be concluded using terms such as Mudarabah, Qirad or Mu'amalah.

title: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
q: Per the Shari'ah basis, why may a converting bank keep income it received under a qualified Ijtihad later seen as doubtful?
options: The income was earned before the conversion decision was taken
Shari'ah validates acts on a believed interpretation
The Shari'ah board may waive disposal of any such income
Doubtful income is always lawful to keep, whatever its source
explanation: Per the Basis, Shari'ah validates actions based on an interpretation believed valid until proved wrong, by analogy with insurgents who act on Ijtihad.

title: Hiring of Persons
q: A private employee hired from 1 May reports to work only on 15 May without excuse. What applies?
options: No pay for the gap; termination allowed unless a make-up is agreed
Full pay for the whole month, as the contract had already started
Pay for the gap is due, with a penalty deducted from his total pay
No pay for the gap, but the employer may not terminate the contract
explanation: Per 4/9, the employee gets no pay for the gap; the employer may terminate unless they agree on a compensatory period at the end of the contract.

title: Financial Paper (Shares and Bonds)
q: Ahmad bought shares; the sale formalities are complete and liability has passed to him, but final settlement is pending. May he sell them now?
options: Yes, but only back to the original seller
No, he must wait for final settlement first
No, he must wait for registration in his name
Yes, even though final settlement is not yet made
explanation: Per 3/7, the buyer may deal in the share after completion of the sale formalities and transfer of liability, even if final settlement has not been made.

title: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
q: On final liquidation of Bank A's investment base, some reserves for investment risk and rate of return remain. Per the Mubara'ah stipulation, where do they go?
options: They are returned to the last holders only
They are devoted to charitable purposes
They go to the Bank's shareholders
They are added to the Bank's general reserves
explanation: Per 5/4, the stipulation should indicate that on liquidation of the investment base the remaining reserves and allocations are devoted to charitable purposes.

title: Irrigation Partnership (Musaqat)
q: Two months into a binding Musaqat, before any crop materializes, the worker abandons the work and cannot be made to continue. What is he entitled to?
options: His full share once the crop materializes
A market wage for the two months worked
A share proportionate to the time worked
Nothing; he gets no share of the crop
explanation: Per 8/4, if the worker stops working before the crop materializes, he is not entitled to any share.

title: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
q: Ahmad asks his friend Karim to collect a debt for him without any fee. Karim hears the request, says nothing and does not object. What is the status of the agency?
options: Karim's silence counts as acceptance of the non-paid agency
Silence counts as acceptance only in paid agency, not in non-paid agency
The agency is void as no standard wording was used
No agency arises until Karim accepts it expressly, in writing or orally
explanation: Per 2/2/2, in accepting non-paid agency silence is sufficient acceptance, while a negative response indicates rejection.

title: Waqf
q: An overseer wishes to lease a Waqf shop to himself. How does the standard treat this?
options: It is allowed if he informs the Waqif
It is allowed at the fair rent if an expert confirms it
It is barred, as it raises doubt of favouritism
It is allowed if he pays the full year's rent in advance
explanation: Per 3/8/3, the overseer is barred from favouritism or any act raising doubt of it, such as leasing Waqf assets to himself or his son.

title: Commercial Papers
q: A holder sells a 100,000 bill not yet due for 105,000 in cash today. How does the standard classify this sale?
options: A permitted sale at a premium
Riba al-Fadl only
Riba al-Nasi'ah only
Riba al-Nasi'ah plus Riba al-Fadl
explanation: Per 6/2, selling commercial paper that has not become due for more than its value is Riba al-Nasi'ah plus Riba al-Fadl.

title: Hiring of Persons
q: Which practice does the Shari'ah basis cite to support hiring a person for a deferred service?
options: The Prophet's hiring of a scribe to record the Qur'an
The Prophet and Abu Bakr hiring a guide to serve after three days
Umar's taking of 'Arboun in the presence of the Sahabah
Umar's donation of his land in Khaybar as a Waqf for the poor and kin
explanation: The basis cites the Prophet and Abu Bakr hiring a man from Bani Al-Dail as a guide after three days; and hiring is a time-based contract.

title: Procrastinating Debtor
q: Bank A still holds a Murabahah asset when the buyer becomes bankrupt. Per the Shari'ah basis, why may it take the asset ahead of other creditors?
options: The sale is void due to the buyer's non-payment of the price
The asset is deemed mortgaged to the Bank
A Hadith gives the seller priority over other creditors
The Bank's claim ranks first as a loan
explanation: Per the Basis, Abu Hurayrah reported that a seller who retains the asset when the buyer becomes bankrupt is more qualified to take it than other creditors.

title: Impact of Contingent Incidents on Commitments
q: Before actual or legal delivery to Bank A, part of the goods owed to it is damaged by a heavenly factor (Sabab Samawi) the supplier could not avoid. What right does Bank A have?
options: The right of option regarding the commitment
A right to demand a penalty for late delivery of the goods
No right; it must accept the remaining goods as they are
Only a claim for the full price of the damaged part
explanation: Per 5/2, in partial damage before actual or legal delivery caused by an unavoidable heavenly factor (Sabab Samawi), the committing party has the right of option.

title: Hiring of Persons
q: Per the Shari'ah basis, on what ground may the Institution take a seriousness margin from a party pledging to hire its services?
options: The general rule of Kafalah
The rules of Rahn on existing debts
Need and interest
The analogy with 'Arboun in sale
explanation: The basis states that permissibility of receiving a seriousness margin from the party pledging to hire is based on need and interest.

title: Competitions and Prizes
q: Bank A offers a draw-based prize to customers who use its fund transfer service. Under what condition is this permissible?
options: Only current account holders may enter the draw
No additional amount is charged on the service fees
The prize is paid out of investment account funds
The customer pays a small fee to enter the draw
explanation: Per 3/5/3, a draw-based prize on financing, currency exchange or fund transfers is permissible if no extra amount is charged on fees for it.

title: Irrigation Partnership (Musaqat)
q: Which of the following does the Shari'ah basis cite as Sunnah evidence for the permissibility of Musaqat?
options: The Hadith on the wealth of orphans and Zakah
The Prophet's interdiction of Mu'adh's property and sale of it to pay his creditors
The Hadith on overcharging a trusting buyer
The Prophet gave Khaybar to its people for half of its yield
explanation: Per the basis, the Prophet gave the land of Khaybar to its inhabitants to work and cultivate for half its yield; Ijma', common sense and analogy with Mudarabah also apply.

title: Credit Agreement
q: Bank A wants to charge a fee on the unused part of a client's approved facility, as traditional banks do for loans and overdrafts. What is the ruling?
options: Not permitted; it is the fee of interest-bearing facilities
Permitted if called a financing fee and not a loan fee
Permitted, as the Bank reserved and kept funds available for the client
Permitted if the client uses less than half of the limit
explanation: Per 5/3/2/1, the Institution should not charge the commitment fee (loan fee, overdraft facility fee, financing fee) of traditional interest-bearing facilities.

title: Loan (Qard)
q: Bank A lent Company X funds for a fixed period of one year. After four months, Bank A demands repayment. Must Company X repay now?
options: Yes, if Bank A gives Company X one month's notice before demanding it
No, unless Company X's business is profitable
Yes; a Qard is always repayable on demand
No; the lender may not demand it before the period ends
explanation: Per 6, a period may be stipulated in Qard; the borrower need not repay before it ends, nor can the lender demand repayment before the end of the period.

title: Sharikah (Musharakah) and Modern Corporations
q: Company X offers, as its whole contribution to a new Sharikah, the receivables its customers owe it. What is the ruling?
options: Permitted if valued at a discount for early payment by debtors
Permitted if valued at their face amount in currency
Not permitted: debts alone cannot be a capital contribution
Permitted if the debtors are partners themselves
explanation: Per 3/1/2/4, it is not permitted that debts (receivables) alone be used as a contribution to the Sharikah capital.

title: Waqf
q: A donor gives cash to a Waqf as a gift, without intending it to be a Waqf. How is the cash treated?
options: Owned by the Waqf, but not recognized as a Waqf asset
Returned to the donor if not used within the financial year
Treated as the overseer's property
Treated as a Waqf asset in all cases, whatever the donor intended
explanation: Per 9/5/3, if the donor intended other than Waqf (e.g., gift), the asset is owned by the Waqf but is not recognized as a Waqf asset.

title: Istisna’a and Parallel Istisna’a
q: Bank A buys turbines by Istisna'a for June delivery, paying cash to give the maker liquidity. It then sells similar turbines by Parallel Istisna'a. Which delivery date is acceptable for that sale?
options: Any date the buyer prefers
July, after the original June delivery
May, before the original delivery
Exactly the signing date of the sale
explanation: Per 7/1, in this Parallel Istisna'a the delivery date in the parallel sale must not precede that in the original purchase, and the contracts stay separate.

title: Commercial Papers
q: The holder of a promissory note requires the issuer to provide a piece of land as tangible security for payment. How is this security treated?
options: As a mortgage (Rahn), governed by the rules of Rahn
As a sale of the land to the holder of the note
As a guarantee for which a fee may be charged
As a Hawalah of the debt onto the land's value
explanation: Per 8/3, tangible security stipulated by the holder of commercial paper to secure his right is deemed a mortgage (Rahn) and governed by its rules.

title: Al-Wakalah Bi Al-Istithmar (Investment Agency)
q: Bank A's agency contract gives it a fixed fee plus all profit above an expected 8%. The investment earns 10%. Is Bank A's claim to the extra 2% valid?
options: Yes, but only if the fixed fee is waived
Yes; the excess may be given as a performance incentive
Yes, but only for half of the excess profit
No; an agent is entitled to its fixed fee only, and any excess profit belongs to the principal
explanation: Per 5/4 and 6/5, the agent may be entitled, in addition to its fee, to all or part of any amount above the expected profit as a performance incentive.

title: Possession (Qabd)
q: Bank A buys 100 tons of steel in the seller's warehouse. The seller weighs and sets them aside and releases them so Bank A can take them without obstacle; nothing is moved. Has Bank A taken possession?
options: Yes, but only once Bank A resells the steel to one of its customers
No, possession requires transporting the steel to Bank A
No, possession of steel requires physical delivery by hand
Yes, constructive possession after ascertainment and relinquishment
explanation: Per 3/3, constructive possession of movables occurs, after ascertainment, by relinquishing them to the entitled person without obstacle, even with no transportation.

title: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
q: Before converting, Bank B committed to provide a non-permissible service to a client. What must it do after converting?
options: Assign the obligation to a conventional bank in return for a fee
Perform it and donate the fee received
Terminate it, refunding the price even with compensation
Perform it, as the contract is binding
explanation: Per 9/1/2, the bank must strive to terminate obligations to provide non-permissible services by refunding the consideration, even if it must pay compensation.

title: Salam and Parallel Salam
q: Bank A sold 1,000 tons of rice by Salam to Company X. To meet this, it buys similar rice by a separate Salam from a farmer. What is the Bank's role in the second contract?
options: Buyer in an independent Parallel Salam
Agent of Company X in a single deal
Seller, as in the first contract
Guarantor of the farmer's delivery
explanation: Per 6/1, the seller may make a separate, independent Salam with a third party to acquire similar goods; the seller in the first becomes buyer in the second.

title: Guarantees
q: A trainee says failing to put a deferred deal in writing is a sin. Per the Shari'ah basis, whose view is this?
options: The consensus of all the Fuqaha
The majority's view; Ibn Hazm saw writing as merely recommended
Ibn Hazm's; the majority regard writing as recommended
The view of the Hanafis alone
explanation: Per the Basis, the majority hold written documentation is recommended; Ibn Hazm held it obligatory, relying on the literal meaning of the verse of debt.

title: Zakah
q: Company X is building a hotel to operate (not to sell). During construction, part of it generates rental income. How is Zakah treated?
options: No Zakah of any kind until construction ends
Zakah on the full construction cost to date, as the hotel is still an asset under development
Zakah on the market value of the whole project
Zakah on the unexpended income, added to Zakatable assets
explanation: Per 4/2/3, for capital projects not for trading, Zakah is due on the unexpended part of income they generate, added to Zakatable assets at year end.

title: Murabahah
q: Bank A stipulates in a Murabahah that it is free from responsibility for defects (Bay' al-Bara'ah). Which risk can it NOT exclude by this condition?
options: Defects the supplier also knew about
Destruction before the customer's possession
All hidden defects of the asset unknown to the Bank
Some specified defects of the asset named in the contract
explanation: Per 4/9, the Institution may disclaim all or some defects, but not destruction before the customer's possession or diminution of the quantity sold.

title: Buyback
q: Company X sells Sukuk to Bank A with a unilateral promise from Company X to buy them back. Which pricing complies with the standard?
options: Both the sale and the buyback at a spot price
Both sales at deferred prices fixed today
Sale at spot, buyback at a higher deferred price
Sale on deferred terms, buyback at lower spot
explanation: Per 5/1/1, with a promise to buy back or resell, both contracts (the first sale and the subsequent one) must be for a spot price.

title: Salam and Parallel Salam
q: Bank A signs a Salam for a fruit that is normally not available at the delivery place on the agreed delivery date. Which condition is missing?
options: Immediate payment of the capital in the same session
Common availability at the delivery place and date
A known place of delivery stated in the contract
A known quantity of the fruit, stated by weight or measure
explanation: Per 3/2/8, al-Muslam Fihi must be commonly available under normal circumstances where it should be on the delivery date, so the seller can deliver.

title: Buyback
q: An asset is resold, without collusion, to a party other than its original seller in a tripartite setting. What basis does the standard give for permitting this?
options: A public interest in liquidity
The buyer's retention of the legal deed
The absence of any 'Inah implication
An analogy to Suftajah
explanation: Per the Basis, collusion-free, value-changed or tripartite repurchase is permitted due to the absence of Einah implication.

title: Arbitration
q: Two months after issuing his verdict, an arbitrator wishes to change it simply because he has reconsidered. When may he retreat from his verdict?
options: At any time before the verdict is executed
Whenever he changes his opinion
Whenever either party asks him to, before the decision is executed
Only when he declares he committed a mistake in it
explanation: Per 13/3, the arbitrator has no right to retreat from his verdict unless he declares a mistake; then he can cancel or amend it per Shari'ah.

title: Payment Cards
q: Ahmad's debit card account has a zero balance. He asks Bank A to let the card finance his purchases until salary day. What is the nature of a debit card?
options: A revolving financing instrument for the cardholder's purchases
A settlement instrument linked to the available balance
A credit instrument within a fixed limit set by the issuer
A credit instrument with a grace period
explanation: Per 3/1/1, the debit card is a settlement instrument, not a credit (lending or financing) instrument, so it is linked to the available balance.

title: Salam and Parallel Salam
q: Why does the Shari'ah basis reject a Salam for the produce of one specific farm?
options: Farm produce cannot be measured or weighed accurately
Salam is limited to manufactured goods
The farm may yield nothing by delivery (Gharar)
The seller cannot own his farm's produce
explanation: The basis: per the Hadith ('but not for the products of the kin of so and so'), produce from a specific farm may not exist at delivery, leading to Gharar.

title: Mortgage and its Contemporary Applications
q: One building is mortgaged to Bank A and Bank B with the same rank. A third mortgagee wants the same rank. How is the right shared and whose consent is needed?
options: Consent of all; right shared in proportion to their debts
Consent of the mortgagor only; shared equally
No consent needed; first come, first served
Consent of the first mortgagee only; the right is shared equally
explanation: Per 3/2/3, where mortgages are of the same rank, all parties must consent and the mortgage right is shared in proportion to their respective debts.

title: ’Arboun (Earnest Money)
q: Under an 'Arboun sale, Company X takes delivery of a machine during the option period and simply stores it in its warehouse. Has Company X confirmed the contract?
options: No, because delivery is not allowed during the option period
Yes, any delivery during the option period confirms the sale
Yes, since liability moves to it, the option ends
No, taking delivery on its own does not indicate confirmation
explanation: Per item 7, the buyer may take delivery during the option period; this alone does not indicate confirmation unless his conduct shows acceptance.

title: Sharikah (Musharakah) and Modern Corporations
q: Bank A requires its partner to provide a mortgage over his house, to be used only if he commits misconduct, negligence or breach of contract. What is the ruling?
options: Not permissible, as it amounts to guaranteeing capital
Not permissible, as partners act on a trust basis
Permissible, as it secures misconduct, negligence or breach
Permissible only if it also covers ordinary business losses
explanation: Per 3/1/4/2, a partner may stipulate that another partner provides a personal guarantee or mortgage to cover misconduct, negligence or breach of contract.

title: Possession (Qabd)
q: Bank A grants a Qard and requires promissory notes and documents to record the loan. Who bears the cost of preparing these documents?
options: Both parties equally
The borrower
Whoever drafts the documents
The lender, Bank A
explanation: Per 4/2/2, the expenses of drawing up documents and promissory notes needed for a loan contract, its implementation or documentation, are borne by the borrower.

title: Documentary Credit
q: Under a documentary credit, the beneficiary presents documents that do not conform to the credit instructions. What may the bank do?
options: It must pay, since the documents were presented in time
It must inspect the goods before deciding anything
It must reject them and cancel the credit at once
Accept, reject or seek amendment of the documents
explanation: Per 2/2/4, if the documents do not conform to instructions, the bank reserves the right to accept, reject or seek amendment of the documents.

title: Al-Wakalah Bi Al-Istithmar (Investment Agency)
q: Midway through an investment agency, the principal unilaterally notifies Bank A that it may now invest only in real estate. What is the status of this new restriction?
options: Invalid; neither party may unilaterally amend the restrictions
Valid provided the agent's agreed fee remains unchanged
Valid, since the principal is the owner of the invested funds
Valid if notice is given to the agent thirty days in advance
explanation: Per 3/4, it is not permissible for any one of the parties to unilaterally amend the restrictions in the agency contract.

title: Options to Terminate Due to Breach of Trust (Trust-Based Options)
q: At an auction, the seller's associate keeps raising the bid with no intention to buy, and Ahmad wins at an inflated price. How does the standard treat this?
options: It is normal auction practice, so the sale is final and Ahmad has no option to revoke
It is Najsh, giving Ahmad an option to revoke for verbal deception
It entitles Ahmad only to a reduction of the price
It gives no option, as no statement was made to Ahmad
explanation: Per 2/2(b) and 2/3/1, raising bids by phantom bidding (Munajashah or Najsh) is verbal deception giving the buyer the option to revoke.

title: Concession Contracts
q: Company X holds a concession license and wants to securitize it to raise funds. What is the ruling?
options: Permissible per Shari'ah rulings and the licensor's conditions
Not permissible without the State as co-issuer
Not permissible, as a license is not property
Permissible only by selling the whole license outright to an investor
explanation: Per 9, a concession license is a financial right; its owner may sell, lease, mortgage, share or securitize it per Shari'ah rulings and the licensor's conditions.

title: Zakah
q: Bank A calculates its Zakah base by the net assets method. Which of the following is deducted from its Zakatable assets?
options: The provision for slow-moving and perishable goods
The statutory and voluntary reserves of the Bank
Rights of holders of non-restricted investment accounts
The paid-up capital and share premium of the Bank
explanation: Per 2/1/1, the Zakah base equals Zakatable assets minus current liabilities, rights of non-restricted investment account holders, minority, Waqf and charitable rights, etc.

title: Trading in Currencies
q: Ahmad buys USD from a money changer against local currency. He pays now, and the changer will deliver the USD tomorrow. What is the status of the deal?
options: Valid, if the exchange rate is fixed at the time of contracting
Valid, since Ahmad's payment is actual possession
Valid, because the two currencies differ in kind
Invalid: both sides must be possessed before parting
explanation: Per 2/1/1 and 2/6/2, both parties must take possession (actual or constructive) of both countervalues before dispersing; one-sided possession is not enough.

title: Protection of Capital and Investments
q: A fund manager obtains Takaful cover, on behalf of the investors, against the risks of the manager's own negligence, death or bankruptcy. Is this permissible?
options: Yes, but only against the risk of the manager's death
Yes; the manager may obtain Takaful cover on the investors' behalf
No; only the investors themselves may obtain such cover
No, since it covers the manager's own negligence, which no cover may insure against
explanation: Per 4/2/1, Takaful may cover misconduct, negligence, breach, procrastination, death or bankruptcy, obtained by investors or by the manager on their behalf.

title: Murabahah
q: Bank A asks the purchase orderer to bear the transport risk of goods it is buying. Why is this disallowed, per the Shari'ah basis?
options: Transport risk is always borne by the supplier alone
It would be a commitment fee in disguise
The owner bears the risk, as profit goes with risk
The customer is the agent of the supplier in all cases
explanation: The basis: the goods' safety is the owner's responsibility; the customer is not the owner, and the right to profit is associated with bearing risk.

title: Loan (Qard)
q: Two brothers have exchanged gifts every year for a long time. One borrows from the other and continues the usual gift during the loan period. What is the ruling?
options: Prohibited unless the gift is deducted from the debt
Permissible only after the loan has been repaid
Prohibited, as any gift during the Qard is Riba
Permissible, as the practice existed before the Qard
explanation: Per 5/1, benefits during the Qard are not permissible when given for its sake, unless the practice continued between the parties from before the Qard.

title: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
q: Ahmad instructs his agent to sell a car for 10,000. The agent sells it for 11,000. Has the agent breached the agency contract?
options: No, acts that serve the principal's interest are not a breach
Yes, any departure from the set price is a breach of the agency contract
No, but Ahmad may declare the sale invalid and recover the car
Yes, and the extra 1,000 belongs to the agent as his reward for the sale
explanation: Per 5/2, breach does not include acts that serve the principal's interest, such as selling at a higher or buying at a lower price.

title: Documentary Credit
q: Bank A partners with a client in goods the client already bought, then plans to sell its share back to him on deferred payment. Per the Shari'ah basis, why is this barred?
options: It is a guarantee given for a fee, which is not permitted
It amounts to a sale-buy back (Bay' al-'Inah)
It is a sale of a debt for a debt, as the price is deferred
It is a sale before taking possession of the goods by the Bank
explanation: Per the basis, selling the Institution's share in goods purchased by the client back to him for deferred payment amounts to Bay' al-'Inah, prohibited by Shari'ah.

title: Sharikah (Musharakah) and Modern Corporations
q: In a diminishing Musharakah, the customer promises to set aside part of his profit share to buy Bank A's units at intervals. What is the ruling?
options: Permissible as a way to acquire the Institution's equity
Not permissible, as profit must be distributed
Not permissible, as it is a lump sum from profit
Permissible only if the units are bought at face value
explanation: Per 5/8, acquisition may include the client's promise to set aside a portion of his profit or return to acquire a percentage of the Institution's equity.

title: Hiring of Persons
q: An employee's pay was due in advance, but he agreed to wait two months. Later the employer claims a right to always pay two months late. What is the position?
options: The employer has now acquired a right to pay two months late
The contract becomes void because its terms were changed
The delay was a respite he granted, not a right of the employer
The pay is converted into deferred pay for the rest of the term
explanation: Per 6/2, when the employee accepts a delay of pay due in advance, this is a respite he willingly granted and can by no means be considered a right of the employer.

title: Combination of Contracts
q: Two parties agree beforehand to a Bay' al-Wafa` structure to obtain a return on money. What is the ruling on this Muwata`ah and the contract?
options: The Muwata`ah is valid if the price is fair and the buyer takes possession
The contract is valid but the Muwata`ah is void
The contract and Muwata`ah are valid if the Shari'ah board approves them
The Muwata`ah is prohibited and the contract is invalid
explanation: Per 6/3/1, Muwata`ah to form up Riba tricks, such as Bay' al-'Inah, Bay' al-Wafa` or Riba al-Fadl, is prohibited and the contract so designed is invalid.

title: Waqf
q: Ahmad made Waqf of shares in a permissible company. The company later turned into a prohibited one. What must be done?
options: The shares must be substituted
Substitution is allowed but optional
Shares are kept and income purified
The Waqf ends and shares go to Ahmad
