explanation: Per 10/1/3, substituting Waqf assets is required if the subject turned prohibited, e.g., permissible shares that later turned prohibited.

title: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
q: Shop X sells items where a programmed machine picks, at random, which of several goods the buyer receives for the fixed price. What is the ruling?
options: Valid, as the Gharar is only medium
Valid, as the price is fixed and known
Valid if the buyer has an option to return the item
Void: the sold item is randomly selected
explanation: Per 5/1/2, sales become void when the sold item is randomly selected, like Bay' al-Hasah, including via a programmed machine.

title: Arbitration
q: While deciding a dispute over delayed delivery, an arbitrator also rules on a separate lease issue that the parties never referred to him. What is the position?
options: It is valid, since the parties are the same as in the referred dispute
It is binding if issued in the same decision
It is outside his mandate unless the parties agree
It is valid if it serves justice between them
explanation: Per 11/3, arbitration should not go beyond the subject matter of dispute, as further issues fall outside the arbitrator's mandate unless the parties agree.

title: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
q: Company X leases gold jewelry to a customer for an event, with the rent payable in arrears. Is this lease permissible?
options: No, gold is a Ribawi item that cannot be leased
Yes, as its corpus is not consumed in the lease
Yes, but only if the leased gold is ingots
No, rent for gold must be paid in advance
explanation: Per 5/3/1, gold may be leased, as jewelry or ingots, if its corpus is not consumed; rent may be in advance or in arrears.

title: Salam and Parallel Salam
q: Bank A and a seller part without the Salam capital being paid, leaving it for a month. Per the Shari'ah basis, what does this turn the transaction into?
options: A valid deferred Salam
A permitted Parallel Salam
A Murabahah to the purchase orderer
A prohibited sale of debt for debt
explanation: The basis: delay in paying capital with dispersal of the parties renders the transaction a sale of debt for debt, prohibited by scholarly consensus.

title: Mortgage and its Contemporary Applications
q: A rented asset, mortgaged with the owner's permission, perishes in the mortgagor's hands without his transgression or negligence. Must he compensate the owner?
options: Yes, at half its value on the date of perish
Yes, as with a borrowed asset in all cases
No; for a rented asset, only transgression or negligence
No, but the mortgagee must compensate the owner for its full value
explanation: Per 3/2/6, a borrowed mortgage perishing requires compensation to the owner, but for a rented asset only if due to transgression or negligence of the mortgagor.

title: Procrastinating Debtor
q: Bank A wants to put a defaulting debtor on a black list and warn other companies that enquire about him. Is this allowed?
options: Only after a court declares him bankrupt
Yes, as a non-material punishment for default
No, it is prohibited slander of the debtor
Only with the debtor's prior written consent
explanation: Per 2/4, the Institution may list a defaulting debtor as undesirable and warn other companies on enquiry or when black lists are exchanged.

title: Documentary Credit
q: A correspondent bank requires that a credit be subject to the uniform practices for documentary credit, which include interest clauses. What should Bank A do?
options: Qualify it as not violating Shari'ah, stating interest will not apply
Accept them in full and give any interest it receives to charity afterwards
Accept the practices in full as an accepted international industry standard
Refuse any reference at all to the uniform credit practices
explanation: Per 3/7/1, such a reference must be qualified so it does not violate Shari'ah, and it must be explicitly stated that any interest provision will not be acted upon.

title: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
q: Why is a lump sum or percentage of capital as a party's return prohibited in Mudarabah, per the basis?
options: It makes the expenses too high for the Mudarib, who must pay them from his own pocket
It conflicts with the scoring method of distribution
It eliminates profit sharing, the essence of the partnership
It requires constructive liquidation every month
explanation: Per the basis, it eliminates profit sharing, a fundamental aspect of Mudarabah; e.g. if profit only equals the lump sum, the partnership's essence is lost.

title: Options to Terminate Due to Breach of Trust (Trust-Based Options)
q: Which Hadith does the Shari'ah basis cite for revoking a contract due to price gouging of a trusting buyer?
options: "Overcharging a trusting buyer (Mustarsil) is forbidden"
"Muslims are bound by their conditions", cited for binding contractual stipulations
"No harm and no reciprocal harm"
"Allah has permitted sale and prohibited Riba"
explanation: Per the basis, the Hadith states "Overcharging a trusting buyer (Mustarsil) is forbidden"; a variant narration says it is Riba.

title: Ijarah and Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek
q: Why does the Shari'ah basis say that things that perish by use cannot be leased?
options: Their rentals cannot be specified in advance
They cannot be delivered on time
Such things cannot be insured by the lessor against loss
The subject of a lease is usufruct, not the asset
explanation: The basis: the leased asset must be usable while preserved, because the subject of a lease is usufruct, not the asset; things that perish by use cannot be leased.

title: Waqf
q: In his charitable Waqf, Ahmad stipulates that revenue goes first to the poor among his progeny, and the remainder to charitable causes. What is the ruling?
options: Valid only if no other poor persons exist
Valid, and the condition must be complied with
Void, as charitable Waqf excludes relatives
Void, as it turns the Waqf into a Private Waqf
explanation: Per 2/6/3, the Waqif may stipulate that charitable Waqf revenue be disbursed first to the poor from his progeny, then to charitable causes.

title: Al-Wakalah Bi Al-Istithmar (Investment Agency)
q: Bank A's investment agency fee is linked to a benchmark known to both parties, referred to before each period after the first period's fee is fixed. No limits are set. What is missing?
options: A cap and a floor setting maximum and minimum limits
Conversion of the fee into a share of the profit
Nothing; a known benchmark is sufficient by itself
The principal's right to cancel before each period
explanation: Per 5/1, a fee linked to a known benchmark referred to before each period is permissible but should be capped and floored with maximum and minimum limits.

title: Documentary Credit
q: Per the Shari'ah basis, why can a revocable documentary credit not be classified as a guarantee contract?
options: A guarantee cannot secure the price of a sale
Guarantees cannot be given by a bank to a seller
An option is not permissible in guarantee contracts
Guarantees must always be paid in cash at once
explanation: Per the basis, a revocable credit is a form of agency; it is not a guarantee because it conflicts with guarantee requirements and an option is not permitted in guarantee.

title: Al-Wakalah Bi Al-Istithmar (Investment Agency)
q: With the principal's consent, Bank A set aside part of the profit as a profit equalisation reserve. At liquidation, a balance remains. What happens to it?
options: It goes to Bank A as an additional incentive for its management of the investment
It is returned to the principal, with Bank A's fee unaffected
It reduces Bank A's incentive for those periods
It is shared equally by Bank A and the principal
explanation: Per 6/7, upon liquidation the reserve balance is returned to the principal without affecting the agent's fixed fee or incentive for the periods concerned.

title: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
q: A discriminating minor appoints an agent to sell his bicycle. The agent sells it at a fair price. What is the status of the sale?
options: It is void from the outset and cannot be approved
It is valid because the price equals the market price
It is valid and binding on the minor immediately
It remains pending the approval of the minor's guardian
explanation: Per 3/1/2, in acts that may be harmful or useful like buying and selling, a partially capable person's agent's acts remain pending the guardian's approval.

title: Stipulations and Ethics of Fatwa in the Institutional Framework
q: Bank A's management prefers to ask a well-known outside scholar rather than its own Shari'ah board for a Fatwa on a new product. What does the standard say?
options: It must ask its central bank's Fatwa body first
It may ask an outside scholar if the board is busy
Under the rules, it has to seek Fatwa from its own board
It may ask any scholar it trusts, without restriction
explanation: Per 3/5, though a seeker may choose the best source, under the rules and regulations Institutions have to seek Fatwa from their own boards.

title: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
q: Company X, as agent, buys a commodity for Bank A and then wants to buy it from Bank A for itself. What is required?
options: No step, as the agent already holds the commodity
Only a single advice from Bank A confirming the sale
Only the agent's notice to Bank A that it has bought the commodity
Two independent offers and acceptances between the two parties
explanation: Per 4/1/3, the agent may buy for himself only by distinguishing the two liabilities through two independent offers and acceptances, e.g. by exchanging two advices.

title: Buyback
q: Bank A buys a commodity spot from Company X and sells it on credit to Ahmad; all parties collude that Ahmad resells it spot to Company X for less. What is the ruling?
options: Not permitted, due to collusion among all parties
Permitted, if each sale is a separate contract
Permitted, as Bank A is not the final buyer
Permitted, since three parties are involved
explanation: Per 4/4, buying spot to sell on credit to a third party is not permitted if all parties collude to resell to the first seller spot for less.

title: Waqf
q: A government proposes to pool all Waqf revenues into the public treasury and manage them with state funds. What does the standard say?
options: It is permitted for Charitable Waqfs only
Waqfs must stay independent of public treasury funds
It is required, as Waqfs are public property
It is permitted if the state protects the Waqfs
explanation: Per 3/4/1, Waqfs must be independent of public treasury funds in administration, finance and accounting, while the state's protective role is regarded.

title: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
q: Bank A's Shari'ah board rejects a broker acting for both buyer and seller in one deal. Per the basis, what is the main reason?
options: Because the broker would earn two separate fees
Because agency cannot cover sale contracts
To avoid giving both offer and acceptance to one party
Because the broker would have to guarantee the price
explanation: The basis, following the Hanafi and predominant Shafi'i view, bars it to avoid assigning offer and acceptance to one party and prevent self bias.

title: Options to Revoke Contracts Due to Incomplete Performance
q: Bank A sells Company X 100 cartons in one deal. Before delivery, 20 cartons are destroyed. Company X did not foresee this. What are its options?
options: Revoke only if more than half are destroyed
Revoke, or accept 80 cartons at their portion of the price
Accept 80 cartons and pay the full price, as the destruction was not caused by the seller
Accept 80 cartons and claim extra compensation
explanation: Per 3/3/3 and 3/4, if part of the sold items is destroyed before delivery, the buyer may revoke or accept the remainder for the corresponding portion of the price.

title: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
q: Ahmad carried out Tahjir on a plot but left it unutilised for three years, with no different regulatory period. What is the status of his right?
options: It expires
It passes automatically to the state treasury as ownership
It remains valid indefinitely
It becomes full ownership
explanation: Per 9/4, the right of Tahjir expires if the land is not utilised for three years, or as provided by applicable regulations.

title: Payment Cards
q: An acquirer agrees with the card network to settle the amounts owed to it in a currency other than that of the goods' price. When is this permitted?
options: Only if the card network bears the exchange rate risk alone
Never, as it is a sale of debt for debt between the parties
Always, without any condition, as it is a settlement of dues
When the exchange rate is known, with SS 59 conditions
explanation: Per 5/5/3, the acquirer may agree on settlement in another currency provided the exchange rate is known and 4/1/1/2 of SS 59 is observed.

title: Istisna’a and Parallel Istisna’a
q: Bank A buys equipment from a contractor for cash and sells it back to the same contractor on deferred terms at a higher price, labelled Istisna'a. What is the ruling?
options: Not permissible, as it is an interest-based device
Permissible, as the price is agreed by both parties
Permissible if the equipment is new
Permissible if the contractor won it by competitive bidding
explanation: Per 2/2/4, buying from the contractor for cash and selling back to him deferred at a higher price is a device for interest-based financing ('Inah).

title: Online Financial Dealings
q: Bank A and a client conclude a Murabahah over an online video call, each in a different city. Which rulings apply to the contract signing session?
options: The rulings on contracts signed in the absence of the two parties
The rulings on contracts signed in the presence of the two parties
The rulings on message contracting through a messenger
No session rulings, as the parties are in different places
explanation: Per 4/1, audio or audiovisual contracting is subject to the rulings for contracts in the presence of both parties, e.g. Itihad al-Majlis and succession of offer and acceptance.

title: Combination of Contracts
q: On the same day, Ahmad buys a car from Bank A and rents a warehouse from it. Neither contract is a condition of the other, and there was no prior agreement. How is this classified?
options: Combining contracts by Muwata`ah without any condition
Combining contracts with one as a condition in the other
Combining contracts without condition and without Muwata`ah
Agreeing to choose the contractual form in the future
explanation: Per 2/1/1, one form is combining more than one contract without imposing any as a condition in the other and without prior agreement (Muwata`ah).

title: Payment Cards
q: Ahmad wants to buy gold jewellery and pay with his credit card. What is the ruling?
options: Not permitted, as gold requires cash at hand
Permitted only if paid within the grace period
Permitted only with a debit card
Permitted to pay the price of gold by credit card
explanation: Per 5/4, it is permitted to carry out currency exchange and pay the price of gold and silver using debit, prepaid or credit cards.

title: Irrigation Partnership (Musaqat)
q: The trees under a Musaqat become unable to bear fruit. Per the Shari'ah basis, why does the contract terminate?
options: "Neither harm nor malice": he would otherwise work gratis
The owner may then take the land back for free, as the worker's right ends with the trees
The worker's share automatically becomes a wage
Musaqat must always yield a minimum profit
explanation: Per the basis, termination rests on the Hadith "There should be neither harm nor malice", as the worker would be excessively harmed by working without compensation.

title: Concession Contracts
q: The State inspects a licensee's management of an airport and finds a breach of contract conditions. What may it do under the standard?
options: Impose any penalty it deems fit
Only warn the licensee, without penalties
Take the airport's revenue as compensation
Impose the penalties stipulated in the contract
explanation: Per 10/5, the licensor may monitor and inspect the contract's conditions and impose the penalties stipulated in the contract for breach.

title: Sale of Debt
q: Why does the standard permit a creditor to sell a debt to the debtor himself without first taking possession of it?
options: Debts owed by the debtor are not Ribawi
The debtor is deemed to possess what he owes
The debt's risk is already with the creditor
Such a sale is an assignment (Hawala)
explanation: Per the Basis, the debtor is deemed the possessor of what he owes, like selling usurped property to the usurper already holding it.

title: Sharikah (Musharakah) and Modern Corporations
q: Which evidence does the Shari'ah basis cite for distributing profit on constructive valuation?
options: The saying of Ali Ibn Abu Talib that loss is by the ratio of capital
Ibn Umar's sale of camels at Al-Baqi' for dinars, taking dirhams
The hadith on valuing a slave partly freed by a co-owner
The hadith of Al-Sa'ib, the Prophet's partner
explanation: The basis cites its use in Zakah and theft and the hadith: if a co-owner frees his part of a slave, the slave is valued by fair value and freed.

title: Hawalah
q: Per the Shari'ah basis, which Hadith shows that transfer of debt is legal?
options: Allah curses the one who gives Riba and the one who takes it
The guarantor is liable for what he guarantees
Muslims are bound by the conditions they made
If one of you is transferred to a solvent person, he must accept
explanation: Per the Basis, the Prophet ordered that one transferred to a solvent person must accept the transfer, which shows Hawalah is legal; Ijma' also supports it.

title: Documentary Credit
q: In a Musharakah to import goods, Bank A wants to sell its share to its partner by deferred Murabahah after receipt of the goods. What condition applies?
options: The sale must not rest on prior binding promises or the Musharakah
The partner must first buy the goods directly from the supplier
The sale must be at the original face value of Bank A's share
The sale must be made on a spot basis only, never deferred
explanation: Per 3/6/1, after receipt of goods the Institution may sell its share by spot or deferred Murabahah if not based on prior binding promises or stipulated in the Musharakah.

title: Protection of Capital and Investments
q: A Musharakah contract stipulates that the managing partner guarantees the capital absolutely. Per the Shari'ah basis, why is this condition void?
options: It is valid in Shari'ah but cannot be enforced before a court
It strips the contract of its essence, turning it into a guaranteed loan
It gives the managing partner an excessive share of the profit
It is void only if it was not disclosed to the other partners before the contract was signed
explanation: Per the basis, such a condition strips partnership and agency contracts of their essential content, turning them into a guaranteed loan, and violates their trust-based nature.

title: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
q: Bank A cannot terminate a long-term interest-based loan it granted before its decision to convert. What must it do with the interest?
options: Keep it, as it was earned on a loan predating the conversion
Add it to the bank's capital reserves
Dispose of it to charity as the standard sets out
Write off the principal amount instead
explanation: Per 7/2, the bank must try to terminate pre-conversion interest loans; if unable, it must dispose of the interest earned as explained in 10/2.

title: Ijarah and Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek
q: Bank A takes 'Arboun at the execution of a lease, and the lessee may terminate within a set period. If the lease proceeds, how is the 'Arboun treated?
options: As an advance payment of the rental
As a security held for misuse
As a fee earned by the Bank
As a deposit refunded at lease end
explanation: Per 4/1/4, 'Arboun may be taken at execution of the lease with the lessee's right to terminate within a period, and it is treated as an advance payment of rental.

title: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
q: Bank A appoints Ahmad as agent to buy and take possession of gold. Afterwards, Ahmad buys that gold from Bank A by offer and acceptance. Who then bears liability for it?
options: The supplier, until the gold is delivered again
Bank A, since Ahmad remains its agent
Bank A, until Ahmad pays the full price
Ahmad, as purchaser in the latter contract
explanation: Per 5/1/3, after purchase and possession the agent may buy from the principal by Ijab and Qabul, and liability transfers to him as purchaser.

title: Commercial Papers
q: A trainee asks why a promissory note is permissible. Which evidence does the Shari'ah basis cite?
options: The hadith 'Muslims abide by their conditions'
The command to fulfil obligations
The command to write down debts for a fixed period
The hadith on Banu Al-Nadir's debts
explanation: Per the basis, a promissory note is a document acknowledging a debt, and Allah commanded securing debts: 'When you contract a debt for a fixed period, write it down.'

title: Sharikah (Musharakah) and Modern Corporations
q: A partnership in commendum fails with debts exceeding its assets. What is the liability of a sleeping partner?
options: Nil, since sleeping partners bear no losses
Limited to the lots he owns, not his personal assets
Joint with the managing partners from personal wealth
Unlimited, but only after the managing partners pay
explanation: Per 4/3/1/2, managing partners are jointly liable from personal wealth, while each sleeping partner's liability is limited to the number of lots he owns.

title: Istisna’a and Parallel Istisna’a
q: An Istisna'a makes the manufacturer the buyer's agent to sell the goods if the buyer delays taking delivery. The sale brings less than the contract price. What follows?
options: The maker has recourse to the buyer for the balance
The buyer may cancel the contract and take his money back
The maker bears the shortfall itself as the buyer's agent
The shortfall is written off
explanation: Per 6/5, the manufacturer sells on the buyer's behalf, keeps the price and returns any surplus; if short, it has recourse to the buyer, who bears sale expenses.

title: Sale of Debt
q: Bank A owes Company Y and directs it to collect the amount from Company X, which owes Bank A. How does the standard treat this?
options: As a sale of monetary debt for cash
As an assignment of debt, not a sale of debt
As a prohibited sale of debt for debt between the three parties
As a division of debt among claimants
explanation: Per 5/1, an assignment of debt (Hawala) is not considered a sale of debt; see the standard on Hawala.

title: Waqf
q: Per the Shari'ah basis, why is Waqf regarded as the ongoing charity (Sadaqah Jariyah) mentioned in the Hadith?
options: The asset must be a mosque, a well or a school
The Waqif keeps ownership of the asset for all time
The beneficiary neither owns the asset nor disposes of it
The income is paid only after the death of the Waqif himself
explanation: The basis states Waqf is the ongoing charity in the Hadith because the beneficiary does not own the Waqf asset and accordingly cannot dispose of it.

title: Financial Paper (Shares and Bonds)
q: Company X's memorandum of association lists dealing in interest among its objectives, though actual interest income is small. May Bank A invest in its shares?
options: Yes, as its interest income is below 5% of income
Yes, if its interest-based debt is under the 30% limit of capitalization
Yes, if Bank A eliminates the interest income later
No; such an objective in the memorandum bars investment
explanation: Per 3/4/1, the exemption requires that the corporation not state in its memorandum that one of its objectives is dealing in interest or prohibited goods.

title: Buyback
q: In a sale of land to Bank A, the sale contract stipulates that the seller will buy the land back from the Bank on a set date. What is the ruling on this term?
options: Not permitted, as the buyback is stipulated in the sale
Permitted, if the buyback is at a spot price at the later date
Permitted, if a separate deed records it later
Permitted, as both prices are disclosed to the parties up front
explanation: Per 3/3, the second contract should not be stipulated within the first contract.

title: Sharikah (Musharakah) and Modern Corporations
q: A stock company restricts its liability to its paid-up capital. What condition does the standard attach to this?
options: A court approves the limitation upon incorporation
Shareholders guarantee any shortfall from their personal assets on a pro rata basis
The company holds no debt above its paid-up capital at any time during its life
The limitation is made public to inform the company's customers
explanation: Per 4/1/2/9, restricting the company's liability to paid-up capital is permissible if made public, so customers know its financial position without uncertainty.

title: Credit Agreement
q: Bank A wants to charge a client a fee for allocating and specifying a facility limit for him, payable whether or not any deal is concluded. Is this allowed?
options: Yes, but only if the client actually uses the facility
No; mere willingness to deal does not justify remuneration
Yes, if it equals the actual cost of allocating the limit
Yes, if the fee is disclosed in the facility letter in advance
explanation: Per 5/3/1/2, commission for offering credit facilities is impermissible, as mere willingness to enter a lending and borrowing transaction does not justify remuneration.

title: Sharikah (Musharakah) and Modern Corporations
q: Why does the Shari'ah basis allow current account balances to be used as Sharikah capital although they are loans?
options: They become the bank's own capital once they are deposited
They are deposits held on trust by the bank, not loans
They are presumed possessed as available to holders on demand
Banks guarantee a fixed return on current account balances
explanation: Per the basis, current accounts are presumed possessed by the holders because the Institutions must pay on demand irrespective of their financial situation.

title: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
q: An agent gets a fixed fee plus a pledged share of profit. Per the Shari'ah basis, how may that extra share be characterized?
options: As a Mudarabah profit share
As a guarantee of minimum return
As a deferred part of the price
As a conditional gift or as Ju'alah
explanation: The basis: the pledge to give the agent a share of profit is a pledge to donate, so it can be a conditional gift or Ju'alah (or a subsidiary addition).

title: Istisna’a and Parallel Istisna’a
q: A customer gives Bank A price quotations he obtained from several builders before an Istisna'a. How may the Bank use them?
options: Only to fix the Istisna'a price at cost plus
To help assess costs and its prospective profit
It may not use them; that would be Murabahah
Only by assigning those builders' contracts to itself
explanation: Per 2/1/2, the Institution may benefit from price offers obtained by the customer to evaluate expenses and compute prospective profit.

title: Arbitration
q: Two traders ask an arbitrator to rule on whether one of them should receive a Hudud penalty for an offence. May this be arbitrated?
options: No; Hudud are a right of Allah and not subject to arbitration
Yes, provided the verdict is later registered in court
Yes, if the arbitrator is a qualified Muslim scholar
Yes, if both parties consent to the arbitrator's verdict
explanation: Per 7/2/1, arbitration is impermissible in what constitutes a right of Allah, such as Hudud.

title: Commercial Papers
q: Under the law, a fixed amount is mandatorily held in a drawer's account for a cheque drawn between banks, so it is legally deemed certified. May it be used to buy silver?
options: No, only physical cash is possession for silver
Yes, but only once the cheque has been cleared
Yes, its receipt is constructive possession of its amount
No, only a banker's cheque is constructive possession
explanation: Per 7/1, a banker's cheque, certified cheque or one legally deemed certified (an amount mandatorily maintained) is constructive possession, usable to buy gold or silver.

title: Trading in Currencies
q: Company X, not a party to a Musharakah, volunteers to guarantee one partner against currency losses. When is this permissible?
options: When the guarantee is stated in the Musharakah contract
When the guarantee is not stated in the Musharakah contract
When the other partner requests it as a condition
Never, as all guarantees of currency risk are void
explanation: Per 2/9/3, a third party may volunteer to guarantee against currency risks, provided the guarantee is not stated in the contract.

title: Islamic Insurance
q: A government runs a compulsory social insurance scheme for workers. Does the Islamic Insurance standard cover this scheme?
options: Yes, if the scheme invests through Mudarabah
Yes, it covers every form of cooperative cover
No, unless non-Muslims also participate
No, state-arranged social insurance is excluded
explanation: Per clause 1, the standard does not cover social insurance schemes arranged by the state.

title: Sale of Debt
q: In a Salam for gas, after maturity the buyer agrees to take oil instead, without this having been stipulated in the contract. What limit applies to the oil?
options: No limit, as substitution is after maturity
Its value must equal the original Salam capital
Its market value can't exceed the gas's at delivery
Its quantity must equal the quantity of gas
explanation: Per 4/1/1/3, the substitute's market value must not exceed that of the subject of Salam at delivery time, and it must be fit as subject of Salam.

title: Competitions and Prizes
q: Company X sells its own discount card for an annual fee. The fee covers only discounts on Company X's goods, with no other services. What is the ruling?
options: Not permissible, as it involves Gharar and Jahalah
Permissible, as the discount is a Tabarru'
Permissible, as the issuer is deemed a broker
Permissible if the fee is below expected discounts
explanation: Per 3/6/2/2/2 Scenario (2), a card whose fee is exclusively for discounts from the same issuer is not permissible, as it involves Gharar and Jahalah.

title: Mudarabah
q: A capital provider tells the Mudarib: 'Do business according to your expertise.' What limits still apply to the Mudarib's actions?
options: He must obtain the capital provider's approval before each single transaction
None, he may act in any way he deems fit since the mandate is absolute
He must act in the parties' interest and per business custom
He may only trade in the capital provider's own city
explanation: Per 5/1, in an unrestricted Mudarabah the Mudarib's freedom must be exercised in the parties' interests and the profit objective, per business customs.

title: Waqf
q: Ahmad's Waqf deed does not reserve a right to dismiss the overseer. The overseer has been negligent. May Ahmad dismiss him?
options: Yes, negligence is a ground for the Waqif to dismiss
No, as the deed did not reserve that right to the Waqif
No, an overseer once appointed is permanent
No, only a judge may dismiss him, whatever the deed provides
explanation: Per 3/10/2, the Waqif may dismiss the overseer if so stipulated, if dismissal serves the Waqf, or if the overseer committed misconduct or negligence.

title: Stipulations and Ethics of Fatwa in the Institutional Framework
q: Which matter falls within the scope of Fatwa in an Institution, according to the standard?
options: Personal family disputes of the Bank's staff and shareholders
Operational financial rulings and related issues e.g. Zakah
Political questions in the host country
Rulings on all acts of worship of the public
explanation: Per clause 4, Fatwa in Institutions is confined to operational financial rulings and related issues, such as some rulings on worship and Zakah.

title: Hawalah
q: In an unrestricted Hawalah, Zaid objects that he never agreed to pay Ahmad's creditor. Per the Shari'ah basis, why is Zaid's consent needed?
options: His consent replaces the consent of the transferee
He must agree to waive any recourse against Ahmad
He must agree to the exchange rate used for the debt
There is no liability without first accepting it
explanation: Per the Basis, the payer must consent in unrestricted Hawalah because it makes him liable, and in principle there is no liability without prior acceptance of it.

title: Syndicated Financing
q: A board member objects that Bank A cannot be a partner with a non-Muslim conventional bank. Per the Shari'ah basis, what really matters?
options: That the deal is only with banks of the same country
The deal's conformity to Shari'ah, not the faith of the dealer
That the non-Muslim partner pays a higher fee than Muslim partners
That the non-Muslim partner holds only a minority share in the syndicate
explanation: The basis: partnership with a non-Muslim is not prohibited except for banned dealings; what matters is the deal's conformity to Shari'ah, not who made it.

title: Sharikah (Musharakah) and Modern Corporations
q: Partners agree that any profit above 1 million belongs to the managing partner, and profit up to that ceiling is shared 50:50. Is this allowed?
options: No, profit must always follow capital shares
No, this is a lump sum that violates profit sharing
Yes, but only if the managing partner is a sleeping partner
Yes, profit above a ceiling may be given to a particular partner
explanation: Per 3/1/5/8 (subject to 3/1/5/3), it is permissible to agree that profit above a certain ceiling belongs to a particular partner.

title: Unilateral and Bilateral Promise
q: Two institutions exchange back-to-back bilateral promises designed to replicate a derivative that Shari'ah prohibits. What is the ruling?
options: Impermissible, as a circumvention of a Shari'ah prohibition
Permissible if each promise is non-binding
Permissible if the subject matters differ
Permissible, since promises are not contracts and create no binding obligation
explanation: Per 6, back-to-back bilateral promises entered to circumvent Shari'ah prohibitions, such as back-to-back derivatives, are impermissible.

title: Mortgage and its Contemporary Applications
q: Bank A's mortgage contract states that on default the Bank automatically becomes owner of the mortgaged land. What is the ruling?
options: Permitted, as both parties agreed to it
Permitted, if the default lasts over 90 days
This condition is not permitted
Permitted, if the land's value equals the debt
explanation: Per 3/4/2, the mortgagee may not stipulate that he owns the asset on default, but he may purchase it from the mortgagor at market value.

title: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
q: How does the standard characterize gold in principle?
options: An ordinary commodity unless minted as currency
A Ribawi item exempt from al-Sarf when made into jewelry
A non-fungible item that may be sold on deferred terms
A fungible Ribawi item subject to the rulings of al-Sarf
explanation: Per item 2, gold is in principle a fungible item (measured by weight), a Ribawi commodity, and subject to the rulings of currency exchange (al-Sarf).

title: Islamic Reinsurance
q: Islamic Insurance Company X can obtain full cover from Islamic reinsurers but prefers a traditional reinsurer for lower cost. May it reinsure with the traditional reinsurer?
options: Yes, if the Shari'ah Board approves the arrangement after signing it
Yes, if the cost saving is passed to participants
No; only a transitional need amounting to necessity permits it
Yes, if the traditional reinsurer is highly rated
explanation: Per 3/1/1 and 3/2, reinsuring with Islamic reinsurers is permissible; with traditional ones it is impermissible except as a transitional arrangement from public need amounting to necessity.

title: Financial Paper (Shares and Bonds)
q: Which of the following is outside the scope of the standard on Financial Paper (Shares and Bonds)?
options: Pledging and lending of shares
Investment Sukuk
Options and swaps based on shares
Issuance of interest-bearing bonds
explanation: Per Scope (1), the standard covers shares and interest-bearing bonds, but not investment Sukuk, which have a separate specific standard.

title: Insolvency
q: Bank A, owed a deferred price not yet due, joins a demand for Ahmad's insolvency. Per the Shari'ah basis, why is a demand on undue debt not warranted?
options: No demand lies for undue debt, as the deferred period has a share in the price
Debts arising from Murabahah are never subject to insolvency
Deferred debts are extinguished upon any insolvency, so Bank A would lose its claim
Bank A must first prove that it is the sole creditor
explanation: The basis states insolvency must be demanded by owners of due debts: there is no demand for undue debt, as the deferred period has a share in the price.

title: Guarantees
q: Bank A discharges Ahmad from a debt that Bakr had guaranteed. What happens to Bakr's liability?
options: He remains liable for the full debt
He becomes the principal debtor
He remains liable for half the debt
He is automatically discharged
explanation: Per 3/3/2, if the creditor discharges the debtor, the guarantor is automatically discharged; discharging the guarantor does not discharge the debtor.

title: Waqf
q: Per the Shari'ah basis, on which schools' views does the permissibility of temporary Waqf rest?
options: The Maliki and Imami Schools, and a view of Abu Yusuf
The Hanafi and Shafi'i Schools, by consensus
The Hanbali School alone, as an exception
The Shafi'i and Hanbali Schools, against the Maliki
explanation: The basis states permissibility of temporary Waqf rests on the Maliki and Imami Schools, and what is reported of Abu Yusuf of the Hanafi School.

title: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
q: Bank A's account terms promise holders 5% of their capital annually as their share of profit. What is the ruling?
options: Permissible, if it is called an expected return
Impermissible; profit must be shared in ratios
Permissible, if the Bank has enough reserves
Permissible, as the percentage is fixed and known
explanation: Per 4/1, profit must be distributed in ratios, never as a lump sum, a percentage of capital, or any method that could avoid sharing of profit.

title: Mortgage and its Contemporary Applications
q: A client who mortgaged his house to Bank A dies before repaying the debt. What happens to the mortgage contract?
options: It terminates and the Bank becomes owner of the house
It terminates and the debt becomes unsecured
It remains valid and his inheritors substitute him
It remains valid only if the heirs renew it
explanation: Per 3/1/5, the death of the mortgagor or mortgagee has no effect on the validity of the mortgage; the respective inheritors substitute the dead party.

title: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
q: Which Hadith does the basis cite for the rule that no profit is sought before preservation of capital?
options: Profit is distributed as agreed, while loss follows capital contribution
When someone liberates a co-owned slave he should pay partners
The one who mortgages should get benefits and bear expenses
A prayer performer is like a merchant: profit only after capital
explanation: Per the basis, the Hadith likens a prayer performer to a merchant who obtains profit only after preserving his capital; profit is an increment on the principal.

title: Monetization (Tawarruq)
q: Bank A sells a commodity to Ahmad for 110 payable in one year and, at the same session, buys it back from him for 100 paid in cash. How is this arrangement classified?
options: It is 'Inah, which is strictly prohibited
It is Monetization, permitted because a real commodity exists
It is a valid Murabahah followed by a valid spot sale
It is Monetization, permitted if the commodity was received
explanation: Per 2 and 4/5, selling back for a lower spot price to the same party from whom the commodity was bought is 'Inah, strictly prohibited; Monetization requires sale to a third party.

title: Sharikah (Musharakah) and Modern Corporations
q: After a loss occurs, and without any prior condition in the contract, one partner volunteers to bear the entire loss. What is the ruling?
options: Void unless approved by a court
Valid only if he is the managing partner
Valid, as it was not a prior condition
Void, since losses must follow capital shares
explanation: Per 3/1/5/4, it is valid that one partner takes, without any prior condition, the responsibility of bearing the loss at the time of the loss.

title: Payment Cards
q: Bank A issues Ahmad a card that deducts every purchase directly from the available balance of his current account with the Bank. Which card type is this?
options: Prepaid Card
Debit Card
Credit Card
Charge Card
explanation: Per 1/1 and 3/1/1, a Debit Card is a settlement instrument linked to the available balance in the cardholder's account with the card issuer.

title: Sharikah (Musharakah) and Modern Corporations
q: Partners agree profit is shared 60:40 in year one and 50:50 in year two, depending on the profit level. Under what condition is this variable method allowed?
options: It must not likely preclude any partner from sharing in profit
It must match the partners' capital ratios in both periods
It is allowed only if the loss ratios vary in the same way
It must be approved again by all partners at each period's end
explanation: Per 3/1/5/5, any permanent or variable profit allocation method is allowed if it does not lead to the likelihood of a partner being precluded from profit.

title: Waqf
q: Company X is a juridical person and wishes to create a Waqf over one of its buildings. What does the standard require for the creation?
options: The written consent of all of the company's creditors and lenders
A resolution of the owners or whoever has that authority
The acceptance of the intended Waqf beneficiaries and the overseer
A court order authorizing the Waqf
explanation: Per 2/4/3/2, a juridical person's Waqf is created by a resolution from the owners or those with authority, provided it does not contravene laws.

title: Sale of Debt
q: Three partners split a single debt among themselves according to their shares. Why is this not treated as a sale of debt?
options: It is appurtenant to other assets
It is a form of sulh among the partners
Such division is a separation, not a sale
It is a Hawala to each of the partners
explanation: Per the Basis for 6/1-6/2, dividing single or multiple debts among partners is a separation, not a sale (6/3 is treated as sulh).

title: Combination of Contracts
q: Citing Al-Qarafi, why does the basis bar combining contracts that contradict each other?
options: Such contracts always involve excessive Gharar
They cannot be concluded by offer and acceptance
Contradictory contracts always involve Riba, whatever their objectives
Contracts are means to objectives and cannot serve opposite ones
explanation: The basis cites Al-Qarafi: contracts are devices to achieve specific objectives; one requirement cannot fit two contradicting positions at once.

title: Mortgage and its Contemporary Applications
q: In a deferred-price Murabahah, Bank A stipulates that the customer, after possessing the car, mortgage it to the Bank against the deferred price. What is the ruling?
options: Permissible only before the customer possesses the car
Permissible for the seller to stipulate
Impermissible unless a third-party guarantor is added
Impermissible, as the Bank cannot take the sold good as mortgage
explanation: Per 3/2/7, the seller may stipulate that the buyer, after actual or constructive possession, mortgage the good to him against the deferred price.

title: Murabahah
q: Bank A wants to refinance a Murabahah by renewing it on the same commodity with the same customer. Under which prohibited heading does this fall, per the Shari'ah basis?
options: Gharar in the subject matter
Sale before acquisition
Sale of debt
Bay' al-Bara'ah
explanation: The basis: tradable Murabahah securities and refinancing a Murabahah fall under the sale of debt, which Shari'ah prohibits.

title: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
q: Converting Bank A used to charge interest on uncovered documentary credits. What alternative does the standard require?
options: Charging interest on the credit and donating it all to charity
Charging a commission for the facility itself
Charging a percentage of the credit amount
Treating them through Murabahah, Musharakah or Mudarabah
explanation: Per 5, the bank may not receive interest for services; an Islamic alternative is needed, e.g. uncovered credits via Murabahah, Musharakah or Mudarabah.

title: Hiring of Persons
q: Bank A agrees to provide a client with a fully specified training programme to be delivered next year. The Bank does not yet own it. Must the client pay in advance?
options: No, unless the contract is a Salam or Salaf contract
Yes, at least half must be paid at signing
No, and the Bank must own the service first
Yes, as future services require advance pay under every contract
explanation: Per 5/1/6, future well-described services need not be owned at signing, and the pay need not be in advance unless the contract is Salam or Salaf.

title: Obtaining and Deploying Liquidity
q: Bank A may need to liquidate assets before distributing profits to investors. What is the Shari'ah basis for linking profit distribution to liquidity?
options: Investors are entitled only to cash, never to assets
Profits may only be paid from central bank support funds, never from the investors' assets
No profit exists until capital is protected, which liquidation achieves
Distribution before liquidation would amount to Riba
explanation: Per the basis, profit distribution depends on liquidity because there is no profit except after protection of capital, realised by liquidating the assets.

title: Murabahah
q: Bank A approves a Murabahah credit facility limit for Company X and charges a fee for providing the facility. What is the ruling?
options: Not permissible to charge a fee for the facility
Permissible if it is a fixed lump sum amount
Permissible if added to the Murabahah cost
Permissible if Company X uses the facility
explanation: Per 2/4/2, it is not permissible for the Institution to receive a fee for providing a credit facility.

title: Documentary Credit
q: Bank A is asked to act as intermediary, by payment or notification, so a beneficiary can sell deferred payment documents to the confirming bank below nominal value. What is the ruling?
options: Permissible for export credits but not for import credits
Not permissible for Bank A to act as intermediary in this
Permissible if Bank A charges only a fixed fee for its role
Permissible, as Bank A itself is not the buyer of documents
explanation: Per 3/7/3, the Institution may not trade in deferred payment documents below nominal value, nor act as intermediary between beneficiary and bank to facilitate it.

title: Debit Card, Charge Card and Credit Card
q: Bank A's card gives credit up to a ceiling; the holder must pay all purchases by the end of a set period after receiving a statement. How is it classified?
options: A debit card, as payment is made in full
A credit card, as it carries a credit ceiling
A credit card, as it is also a means of payment
A charge card, as it gives no revolving credit
explanation: Per 2/2/1-2/2/3, a charge card gives credit up to a ceiling for a set period, without revolving credit: the holder pays by the end of the credit period.

title: Buyback
q: Bank A buys a factory from Company X and then leases it back to Company X under Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek. What is the ruling?
options: Permitted only if the rent is paid in advance for the full term
Permitted, subject to the Ijarah standard's provisions
Prohibited, as it is 'Inah in all cases where the seller leases back
Prohibited, as a seller cannot become lessee
explanation: Per 5/2, buying a tangible asset and leasing it to its seller under Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek is permitted, subject to the Ijarah standard.

title: Ijarah and Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek
q: A lessee pays a monthly rental late. Bank A's contract adds 2% to the rental due for each month of delay, for the Bank's own account. What is the ruling?
options: Permissible up to the Bank's actual cost of funds
Permissible if the lessee is solvent and delays without excuse
Not permissible; no increase for delay is allowed
Permissible if stated clearly in the written contract
explanation: Per 6/3, no increase in the rental due may be stipulated by the lessor in case of delay in payment by the lessee.

title: Waqf
q: Ahmad declares his farm a Waqf to take effect upon his death. The farm equals half of his estate. How is this treated?
options: As a binding Waqf from the date of the declaration
As a valid Waqf over the whole farm upon his death
As a void Waqf, since it depends on death
As a bequest that cannot exceed one-third of his estate
explanation: Per 2/4/1/4, a Waqf contingent upon the Waqif's death is a bequest; it takes effect upon death and shall not exceed one-third of his estate.

title: Hiring of Persons
q: Bank A signs a hiring contract on 1 March with an IT expert, agreeing that his work will start on 1 June. What is this arrangement called and is it valid?
options: Deferred hiring, and it is valid
Forward hiring, and it is void
Conditional hiring, valid only with a guarantor
Deferred hiring, valid only if paid in advance
explanation: Per 4/8, the hiring period starts at signing unless the parties agree on a specific start date; this is known as deferred hiring (to be executed in the future).

title: Islamic Insurance
q: A group of traders agree to pay contributions into a fund to cover injuries from fire risks they all face. In Islamic Insurance, how are these contributions paid?
options: As Mudarabah capital owned by the company
As loans repayable to each trader at year end
As donations to a fund with its own legal entity
As premiums owned by the managing company
explanation: Per clause 2, contributions are paid as donations, establishing a fund with the status of a legal entity and independent financial liability.

title: Financial Paper (Shares and Bonds)
q: Company X records shareholders' names in an electronic register only, not on certificates. Why is this valid, per the Basis?
options: The Lawgiver set no particular form for recording rights
Only bearer shares need to be recorded in a register
Shares do not represent any ownership right at all
Written records of rights are never required in Shari'ah
explanation: Per the Basis, the Lawgiver wishes rights to be established through writing and other forms but has not determined a particular form.

title: Hawalah
q: Ahmad, who owes Bakr nothing, directs Bakr to collect 1,000 from Zaid, who owes Ahmad that amount. How is this transaction characterised?
options: A restricted Hawalah, since Zaid owes Ahmad that amount
An unrestricted Hawalah, since Bakr collects from Zaid
A transfer of right by sale of the debt to Bakr
An agency for collection, not a Hawalah
explanation: Per 6/2, Hawalah requires the transferor to be a debtor to the transferee; if a non-debtor transfers another, it is an agency contract for collection.

title: Sharikah (Musharakah) and Modern Corporations
q: A partner is appointed manager by a separate independent contract with a wage. Per the Shari'ah basis, why is the wage allowed?
options: Wages are part of his profit share, paid in advance of the final distribution
He acts as an employee of the company, not as a partner
The wage is a gift from the other partners and not a binding obligation
He bears more risk than the other partners, so he is compensated with a wage
explanation: Per the basis, under a separate independent contract the partner becomes an employee of the company and is not acting in the capacity of a partner.

title: Mortgage and its Contemporary Applications
q: A client offers shares of a company with permissible original activities, but where Riba-based dealings form a predominant part of its activities. May Bank A accept them as mortgage?
options: No; such shares are among papers that cannot be mortgaged
Yes, if the Bank purifies the dividends
Yes, if the company is listed on an exchange
Yes, since its original activities are permissible, whatever the share of Riba dealings
explanation: Per 4/3, impermissible mortgages include shares of companies with permissible original activities but where Riba-based dealings are a predominant part.

title: Murabahah
q: The supplier's owner is the customer's wife. Why does the Shari'ah basis allow Murabahah in such a case, absent 'Inah?
options: The Bank bears no risk in such deals
Both parties have independent legal liability
Family sales are exempt from 'Inah rules
The wife's consent cures any defect
explanation: The basis: a relative or spouse may be the supplier because both have independent legal liability, unless they are involved in an 'Inah transaction.

title: Unilateral and Bilateral Promise
q: Bank A promises to sell a specific commodity to Company X in three months, and Company X promises to buy that same commodity from Bank A. What does the standard call this?
options: A master agreement for future transactions
Two unrelated unilateral promises
A concluded sale with a deferred delivery
A bilateral promise
explanation: Per 2/2, a bilateral promise is the exchange of two back-to-back promises between two parties, each promising a future act relating to the same subject matter.

title: Financial Paper (Shares and Bonds)
q: Ahmad resells shares before final registration formalities are completed. What justifies this, per the Basis?
options: The broker guarantees delivery of the shares to him
Shares are debts that may be traded without limits
Daman has passed to him via constructive possession
Registration of shares has no legal effect at all
explanation: Per the Basis, transactions are allowed before final registration because liability for loss (Daman) passes to the buyer through constructive possession.

title: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
q: Why are options impermissible, according to the Shari'ah basis of the standard?
options: They always involve deferring the two counter-values of the contract
They are concluded outside organized markets
They give rights to only one of the parties
Their subject-matter is not wealth that can be deemed compensation
explanation: Per the Basis, options are impermissible because the subject-matter of the contract is not wealth that can be deemed compensation under the Shari'ah.

title: Combination of Contracts
q: Bank A and a customer stipulate their Muwata`ah as part of the contract. What is its effect?
options: It becomes binding on Bank A only, not the customer
It becomes a condition precedent subject to Shari'ah rulings
It has no effect on the contract, being only a moral promise between the parties
It replaces the contract and needs no further rulings
explanation: Per 6/2/2, Muwata`ah stipulated in the contract becomes a condition precedent, and the contract becomes subject to rulings on permissibility, enforceability and validity.

title: Guarantees
q: Company Z, not a party to a Mudarabah, voluntarily undertakes to compensate the investors for any investment loss. When is this permissible?
options: If it is not linked in any way to the Mudarabah contract
If it is stated as one of the terms of the Mudarabah contract
If the Mudarib co-signs the undertaking
If Company Z receives a fee for it
explanation: Per 6/6, a third party (not the Mudarib, agent or partner) may volunteer to compensate investment loss, if not linked in any way to the financing contract.

title: Investment Sukuk
q: Certificates are issued to provide educational benefits from a university meeting stated specifications, without naming the university. How are these certificates classified?
options: Certificates of ownership of services of a specified party
Certificates of ownership of usufructs of existing assets
Certificates of ownership of described future services
Investment agency certificates managed by the university
explanation: Per 3/2/4, services from a described provider (a university not named) are described future services; a nominated university falls under 3/2/3.

title: Trading in Currencies
q: Bank A e-mails a customer an offer to sell USD at a set rate, open for two days. After one day, before any reply, Bank A wants to withdraw it. Is this allowed?
options: Yes, offers sent electronically are never binding
Yes, at any time before acceptance is received
Yes, if it compensates the customer for the change
No, the offer binds the offeror for its stated period
explanation: Per 2/8/2, an offer made for a stated period and sent by a prescribed means of communication remains binding on the offeror during that period.

title: Financial Paper (Shares and Bonds)
q: At subscription, Company X adds a fixed and reasonable percentage to the share value to cover the expenses of issuance. What is the ruling?
options: Permissible at any rate the board decides
Permissible, as long as the percentage is fixed and reasonable
Permissible only if paid from the company's profits
Not permissible, as it is an excess over the nominal value of the share
explanation: Per 2/2, a determined percentage may be added to the share value at subscription to cover issuance expenses if it is fixed and reasonable.

title: Syndicated Financing
q: A Mudarib in a syndicate offers to safeguard the capital providers against exchange rate fluctuations. Per the basis, why is this prohibited?
options: It amounts to the Mudarib guaranteeing the capital
It is a form of commitment commission
It turns the Mudarabah into an agency with an unspecified fee
Exchange rates cannot be known on the contract date
explanation: The basis: such a commitment leads to the impermissible case of a partner or Mudarib guaranteeing the other party against loss of capital.

title: Istisna’a and Parallel Istisna’a
q: An Istisna'a customer pays early and Bank A grants an unstipulated rebate. Which precedent does the Shari'ah basis cite?
options: The case of Hibban Ibn Munqidh on the option in a sale
The Prophet's request that a carpenter make a pulpit for him
The Prophet asking Ubay Ibn Ka'b to write off part of a debt
The Prophet's gift to Negus, conditional on survival
explanation: The basis: discount for unconditional early payment rests on the Prophet's saying in the case of Ubay Ibn Ka'b and his debtor: 'Write off a portion of your debt'.

title: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
q: After liquidation, Bank A's shareholders, as Mudarib, decide to give up part of their profit share to the account holders. What must the Bank do?
options: Nothing, as it is a purely internal matter
Treat it as a binding term for future periods
Obtain approval of each account holder
Disclose that relinquishment
explanation: Per 5/6, when the shareholders as Mudarib relinquish part of their profit share to accountholders after liquidation, the Institution should disclose that.

title: Mudarabah
q: In a three-year Mudarabah with a 50:50 ratio, year 1 loses 100,000 and year 2 earns 150,000. Nothing has been distributed. What profit is shareable at the end of year 2?
options: 150,000 less the Mudarib's share of the year 1 loss
Nothing at all until the Mudarib repays the loss
50,000, after the loss is set off against later profits
150,000, as each year's result stands on its own
explanation: Per 8/7, no profit is recognised unless capital is intact; losses are compensated by profits of future operations and brought forward against them.

title: Murabahah
q: Bank A concludes a Murabahah where the profit will be set by the LIBOR rate prevailing on each future instalment date. What is the ruling?
options: Permitted, if a ceiling rate is stated in the contract
Not permitted, as profit is left to future variation
Permitted, if the customer agrees to it in writing
Permitted, as LIBOR is a known and published public rate
explanation: Per 4/6, price and profit must be fixed and known at signing; they may not depend on future variations such as a future LIBOR rate.

title: Combination of Contracts
q: Per the basis, why is a Muwata`ah preceding a contemporary set like Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek treated as binding?
options: It is part of a whole system that collapses if one part fails
Because a court must enforce every promise made before a contract
Because it is always written into each contract by the Bank's practice
Because it turns the set into a single sale
explanation: The basis: current banking tradition treats such Muwata`ah as binding; it is part of a system that collapses when any component loses balance.

title: Sale of Debt
q: The debtor gives Bank A a unilateral binding promise to buy his debt, and the promised sale meets the rules for selling debt to the debtor. Is this permitted?
options: No, only a bilateral promise is valid
No, any promise to sell a debt is barred
Yes, but only if the promise is non-binding
Yes, a unilaterally binding promise is permitted
explanation: Per 4/2, if the rules of 4/1 are met in the promised sale, a unilaterally binding promise is permitted.

title: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
q: Bank A appoints Company X to buy a commodity at a spot price and sell it on Bank A's behalf to a third party at a deferred price. How may Company X's compensation be set?
options: As interest on the deferred amount
As an amount or a percentage of the purchase price
Only as an undivided share of the profit
As a share of the deferred price owed by the buyer
explanation: Per 4/1/1, in investment agency the agent's compensation may be set as an amount or a percentage of the commodity's purchase price.

title: Istisna’a and Parallel Istisna’a
q: Bank A completes a building under an Istisna'a. Must the Bank and the customer exchange a new offer and acceptance to sell the completed building?
options: Yes, unless the price was paid in advance
Yes, as in a Murabahah, after the Bank takes possession
No, the binding Istisna'a already governs the sale
Yes, a sale needs a separate final contract
explanation: Per 2/2/2, Istisna'a is binding, so no new offer and acceptance is needed after completion, unlike the promise in Murabahah.

title: Settlement of Debt by Set-Off
q: X owes Y 5,000 due now; Y owes X 5,000 of the same currency due in six months. Neither has asked for set-off. Does a compulsory set-off occur?
options: No, compulsory set-off requires equal maturity
Yes, with a discount for the earlier maturity
Yes, as each party is creditor and debtor
Yes, as the amounts and currency are equal
explanation: Per 2/1/2(b), compulsory set-off requires the debts to be equal in kind, type, description and maturity.

title: Sharikah (Musharakah) and Modern Corporations
q: In a partnership in commendum, the contract gives a sleeping partner a profit equal to 10% of his capital. What is the ruling?
options: Permissible if the managing partners agree
Permissible if profit exceeds 10% of capital
Permissible, as he cannot manage the company
Not permissible
explanation: Per 4/3/2/2, it is not permissible to stipulate that a sleeping partner has a right to profit as a percentage of the capital or a lump sum.

title: Sale of Debt
q: Two partners hold three separate debts owed by different debtors. They agree that each will keep particular debts according to his share. Is this permitted?
options: Yes, multiple debts may be divided by shares
Only if each partner takes part of every single debt
No, it is a prohibited sale of debt for debt among the partners
Only if the debtors consent to it
explanation: Per 6/2, claimants in multiple debts may divide them so that each reserves one debt or more based on his share.

title: Murabahah
q: A jeweller asks Bank A to sell him 1 kg of gold by Murabahah with the price payable in 6 months. What is the ruling?
options: Permitted for gold but not for currencies
Not permitted for gold, silver or currencies
Permitted if the profit is a lump sum amount
Permitted if the gold is in the Bank's possession
explanation: Per 2/2/6, Murabahah on deferred payment terms is not permitted where the asset is gold, silver or currencies.

title: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
q: In the basis, the right of Shirb is distinguished from the right of Shafah. What is the right of Shirb specifically?
options: The right of humans and animals to drink
The right of passage to a water source
The right to water crops and trees
The right to use water for ablution
explanation: Per the basis, Shirb is specifically for watering crops and trees, while Shafah is the right of humans and animals to drink and use water for ablution, bathing, etc.

title: Islamic Insurance
q: Islamic Insurance Company T pays a claim for a car hit by a negligent driver. It then sues the driver and recovers money. Where must the proceeds go?
options: Into the insurance account
To the company as its own revenue
To the participant on top of his indemnity
To the shareholders as a special dividend
explanation: Per 10/6, the company claims indemnity from the injuring party, representing the participants, and deposits the proceeds in the insurance account.

title: Guarantees
q: A leased machine needs major maintenance to keep providing the benefits agreed under the lease. Who bears the expense?
options: The lessee, as user of the asset
The two parties equally
The lessor
The lessee, through the guarantee
explanation: Per 2/3, the lessor bears the expense of major maintenance needed to keep the leased property providing the contractual benefits, and related insurance.

title: Zakah
q: Ahmad paid a cash security for an electricity connection. He could not invest it, and it is refunded years later. When and how is Zakah paid?
options: Never, as it is a security
On refund, for one year
Every year while it is held
On refund, for all past years
explanation: Per 5/1/5/3, Zakah on cash security for services such as electricity is paid by its owner on refund for one year, unless he was enabled to invest it.

title: Ijarah and Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek
q: A customer breaks his promise to take an asset on Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek. Bank A then leases it to a third party on the same basis. What may the customer be charged?
options: All rentals the customer would have paid over the lease
The Bank's expected profit on the lease over its full term
Cost of the asset minus its market value at the date of breach
Cost of the asset minus total rentals from the third party
explanation: Per 2/3, for a promise of Ijarah with transfer of ownership, the breaching promisor is charged the difference between the asset's cost and total rentals from the third-party lease.

title: Loan (Qard)
q: Why does the borrower own the loaned wealth only upon possession, according to the Shari'ah basis?
options: Possession is needed to fix the price of the loan
Qard is purely commutative, so ownership passes like a sale on credit
Qard is mainly donation, so like Hibah it is owned on possession
The lender keeps ownership until repayment
explanation: Per the Basis, Qard combines commutative and donation aspects with donation predominant, so its rule is like Hibah, in which ownership passes with possession.

title: Indices
q: Bank A uses LIBOR to set the profit in a Murabahah promise. The contract is concluded on a fixed profit that will not change with later index moves. What is the ruling?
options: Permissible, since the profit is fixed at the contract
Not permissible for Murabahah to the purchase orderer
Permissible only if profit floats with LIBOR
Not permissible, as LIBOR is an interest rate
explanation: Per 5/3, an index like LIBOR may be a basis for Murabahah profit, provided the contract is concluded on a specific profit not varying with later index changes.

title: Waqf
q: A Waqf building is destroyed by an earthquake. The overseer had managed it properly with no negligence or breach. Is he liable?
options: Yes, as a guarantor of the Waqf assets even without any breach
Yes, for half of the loss caused by the earthquake
Yes, unless the building was insured against earthquakes
No, as he holds the Waqf in a fiduciary capacity
explanation: Per 3/7/5, the overseer has a fiduciary capacity and is not liable except for misconduct, negligence or breach of the Waqif's conditions.

title: Payment Cards
q: Bank A cancels Ahmad's card because he kept using it for Shari'ah-prohibited purchases. How is the treatment of the fees determined?
options: As a cancellation not caused by Ahmad, so fees are returned pro rata
As if Ahmad himself requested the cancellation
All fees are refunded in full, since Bank A cancelled
All fees are doubled as a penalty for the prohibited usage
explanation: Per 5/2/5, cancellation by the issuer for a valid Shari'ah reason attributed to the holder follows the ruling of cancellation at his request.

title: Combination of Contracts
q: On what does the basis rely for allowing the sale of a debt for a debt within a subsidiary contract?
options: Imam Malik's view in Al-Muwatta` on a slave owed a debt
Ibn Al-Qayyim's view on two separate sales combined in one contract
Al-Sayuti's view on implicit sales and the forgiveness of Gharar in them
Al-Qarafi's view on contradictory contracts
explanation: The basis relies on the slave Hadith and Imam Malik's view in Al-Muwatta` allowing sale of a slave whose money is a debt, even if sold on deferred payment.

title: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
q: Bank A wants a 30-day cooling-off option when buying a building. A colleague says such options can never exceed three days. What does the standard say?
options: The minimum is three days for any option
No fixed minimum or maximum, unless contrary to custom
The maximum is one month for real estate and three days for movables
The maximum is three days, following the Hadith of the 3-day option
explanation: Per 2/2/2, there is no minimum or maximum time limit except where it is contrary to what is customarily acceptable for the subject matter.

title: Financial Paper (Shares and Bonds)
q: Ahmad sells shares he does not own, relying on his broker's promise to lend him the shares at the time of delivery. What is the ruling?
options: Permissible, if the shares are bought back on the same trading day
Permissible, as the broker's promise secures delivery
Not permissible; the broker's promise is of no consequence
Permissible, if the company's activity is lawful
explanation: Per 3/6, selling shares the seller does not own (short sale) is not permissible, and the broker's promise to lend them at delivery is of no consequence.

title: Debit Card, Charge Card and Credit Card
q: Bank A wants to charge cardholders for cash withdrawals made with its card. Which fee structure does the standard permit?
options: A fee set as a percentage of the amount withdrawn
A percentage fee only on amounts above the balance
A fee that rises with the time until repayment
A flat fee proportionate to the service offered
explanation: Per 4/5/2, the issuer may charge a flat service fee for cash withdrawal, proportionate to the service, but not a fee that varies with the amount withdrawn.

title: Financial Paper (Shares and Bonds)
q: Company X wants to give founders' shares extra voting rights, with no priority in profits or liquidation. What is the ruling?
options: Permissible only if they also get priority in the distribution of profit
Not permissible, as all shares must be identical
Permissible, as the feature is procedural or administrative
Not permissible, as it treats shareholders unjustly
explanation: Per 2/6, certain shares may be granted procedural or administrative features, like voting rights, in addition to ordinary share rights.

title: Debit Card, Charge Card and Credit Card
q: Bank A charges its cardholders a membership fee, a renewal fee, and a fee for replacing a lost card. Is this allowed?
options: No, card fees may be charged to merchants only
Yes, the standard permits these fees
Only the replacement fee is permissible
Only if each fee varies with the amount spent
explanation: Per 4/3, the issuing Institution may charge the cardholder membership fees, renewal fees and replacement fees.

title: Arbitration
q: An arbitration decision does not state its Shari'ah basis or reasoning, and no law requires reasoning. What is the effect on its validity?
options: It is valid only if the parties consent
It is void for lack of reasoning, whatever the applicable law says
It must be reissued with reasoning
It remains valid; reasoning is preferable, not a condition
explanation: Per 11/6, mentioning the basis of the decision (reasoning) is preferable but not a condition for valid arbitration, unless the law so requires.

title: Sale of Debt
q: Bank A groups debts and tangible assets in an internal portfolio not registered with the authorities and sells it in one leg. Which rules apply?
options: The rules for sale of debt to a third party
The commingled-entity rules, if assets exceed 50%
No debt rules, since the assets are combined
The rules for ongoing operating entities
explanation: Per 8/3, debts combined with assets without a registered entity (e.g., accounting separation, unregistered portfolio) follow item 5's rules.

title: Syndicated Financing
q: Per the Shari'ah basis, why is receiving a commitment commission prohibited?
options: It is paid before any work has been done by the lead bank on the deal
It is paid for the right of contracting, a matter of will
It is paid by the customer, not by the partners in the syndicate
It always exceeds the actual cost incurred in arranging the financing
explanation: The basis: commitment commission is paid for exercising the right of contracting, a matter of will and desire, not a subject matter of compensatory deals.

title: Guarantees
q: Bank A wants to secure its debt obligations against doubtful or bad debts through insurance. Which cover is permitted?
options: Conventional credit insurance
Either Islamic or conventional insurance
Islamic insurance coverage only
Conventional insurance, if Islamic is unavailable
explanation: Per 6/4, subscribing to Islamic insurance as security for debt obligations is permissible; insuring debts on a conventional insurance basis is not.

title: Investment Sukuk
q: Sukuk represent the usufruct of a described future building that has not yet been ascertained. An investor wants to buy them on the market. What is the ruling?
options: Permissible if the price does not exceed the nominal value
Permissible only after the building has been fully leased out
Freely permissible, as the usufruct is already owned by the certificate holders
Not permissible except by observing the rules for disposal of receivables
explanation: Per 5/2/8, usufruct Sukuk of a described asset may not be traded before the asset is ascertained, except by observing the rules for disposal of receivables.

title: Guarantees
q: A Murabahah contract requires Ahmad to provide a guarantor, but he fails to do so. What may Bank A do?
options: Sue to force him to provide one, or terminate the contract
Nothing, as a condition to provide a guarantor is unenforceable
Raise the agreed Murabahah profit
Charge him a monthly late penalty
explanation: Per 3/3/5, if a debtor fails to provide a stipulated guarantor, the Institution may initiate legal action to force him to provide one or terminate the contract.

title: Concession Contracts
q: A management concession is treated as Mudarabah though its capital is a facility, not cash. What view does the Basis rely on?
options: Mudarabah capital may be any debt owed by the State to the licensee
Facilities count as cash by custom
The Hanbalis permit Mudarabah on income-generating assets
The State is exempt from Mudarabah rules
explanation: Per the Basis, the Hanbalis permit Mudarabah on income-generating assets like animals; net profit is shared after allocations to preserve the project's capital.

title: Hiring of Persons
q: Which Qur'anic verse does the Shari'ah basis cite as evidence for the permissibility of hiring of persons?
options: "Then if they give suck to the children for you, give them their payment"
"When you contract a debt for a fixed period, write it down"
"Help you one another in Al-Birr and Al-Taqwa"
"O you who believe! Fulfill (your) obligations. Lawful to you are the beasts of cattle"
explanation: The basis cites the verse: "Then if they give suck to the children for you, give them their due payment" (Al-Talaq: 6) for permissibility of hiring.

title: Waqf
q: A Waqf building in a deserted area yields no income and no funds exist to develop it. The superintendent agrees a sale at fair value. What else is required?
options: Approval of the tenant in occupation
Permission of the judiciary
Consent of the Waqif's heirs
A vote of the beneficiaries
explanation: Per 9/3, Istibdal conditions include no income and no development funds, no excessive injustice in price, Waqf interest, and permission of the judiciary.

title: Guarantees
q: Without any stipulation in the agency contract, Bakr, an investment agent, voluntarily gives his clients an independent guarantee. He is later removed as agent. Status?
options: His guarantee ends with the agency
He is liable only for his negligence
The guarantee was void from the start
He remains liable as guarantor
explanation: Per 2/2/2, a voluntary guarantee given independently of the agency contract makes the agent a guarantor in another capacity; he stays liable after discharge.

title: Obtaining and Deploying Liquidity
q: In a Sukuk issuance, Bank A is only the lessee of the Sukuk assets and is not their manager. What purchase undertaking may it give?
options: A promise at a price fixed by the subscribers later
No promise to purchase of any kind
A promise to purchase the assets at face value
A promise to purchase only at the market price
explanation: Per 4/2/5, if the institution is only the lessee and not the manager of the Sukuk assets, it may promise to purchase them at face value.

title: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
q: Bank A holds a mortgage over a client's land as security for his Murabahah debt. How is the Bank's right in the land classified?
options: A secondary proprietary right protecting a personal right
A personal right against the client, with no link to specific property
A right to an intangible asset
A primary proprietary right of full ownership
explanation: Per 3/2/2, secondary proprietary rights only protect fulfilment of personal rights, e.g. the creditor's rights in security provided by an obligor.

title: Payment Cards
q: At a shop, Ahmad has 1,000 entered on the POS terminal for his card, but receives only 950 in cash in the card's currency. What is the ruling?
options: Permitted, if the card is a debit card
Permitted, as the 50 is a service fee
Permitted, if Ahmad agrees beforehand
Not permitted
explanation: Per 5/8/2, using the card at an acceptor to get cash in the card currency less than the amount entered on the POS is not permitted.

title: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
q: A paid agent completes useful partial work, then stops without any reasonable excuse, causing the principal an actual loss. What is the agent's position?
options: Entitled to nothing, and liable for the principal's loss and the lost profit
Paid for the part done; liable for the principal's actual loss
