Allowed with the beneficiaries' approval
Allowed, since the rent is above market
Not allowed except through the judiciary
explanation: Per 5/3/2, the superintendent shall not lease the Waqf to himself or his dependant son, even at more than the normal rent, except through the judiciary.

title: Stipulations and Ethics of Fatwa in the Institutional Framework
q: Which precedent does the basis cite for rectifying a wrong Fatwa?
options: Umar's revised Fatwa on brothers' inheritance
Ali's ruling on a gift before receipt
Uthman's compilation of the Qur'an
Abu Bakr's ruling on those who refused to pay Zakah
explanation: The basis cites Umar, who denied some brothers inheritance and later granted it, saying the former case followed his old Fatwa and the new the new one.

title: Online Financial Dealings
q: Money is stolen from Bank A's site, which had taken all possible protective measures and gave no pledge of liability. The thief cannot be charged. Who is responsible?
options: Bank A, as owner of the website through which the theft took place
Bank A and the client, equally
The client whose money was stolen
The one who facilitated the act of theft
explanation: Per 8/1/7, liability rests on the direct thief, otherwise on the facilitator; the site owner is not chargeable if it took all measures and gave no pledge.

title: Mudarabah
q: Parties agree that profit up to 15% of capital is shared 70:30, and any profit above that ceiling goes to the Mudarib. What is the ruling?
options: Permissible only if the excess goes to the capital provider
Permissible; this ceiling arrangement is an exception
Void, as profit is linked to capital
Void, as it is a lump-sum stipulation
explanation: Per 8/5, the lump-sum rule does not apply where parties agree profit over a ceiling goes to one party, and profit up to it is shared as agreed.

title: Investment Sukuk
q: Bank A plans to issue tradable Sukuk representing its portfolio of deferred Murabahah receivables owed by customers. Is this permissible?
options: Yes, since any asset may be divided into equal shares
Yes, if the Shari'ah Supervisory Board approves the prospectus beforehand
No; debts owed as a liability may not be securitized for trading
Yes, if the receivables are sold at their face value
explanation: Per 5/1/2, tangible assets, usufructs and services may be securitized, but debts owed as a liability may not be securitized for trading.

title: Istisna’a and Parallel Istisna’a
q: After production, the manufacturer enables the buyer to take control of the goods. Later the goods are damaged with no negligence by the manufacturer. Who bears the loss?
options: The manufacturer, until the goods are physically delivered
The Institution that financed the Istisna'a
Both parties equally, as neither was negligent
The ultimate purchaser
explanation: Per 6/3, delivery may be constructive by enabling the buyer to take control; the manufacturer's liability then ends and the purchaser's liability begins.

title: Waqf
q: A perpetual Waqf building is totally destroyed and nothing of the Waqf asset remains. What happens to the Waqf?
options: It continues, as perpetual Waqf never ends
It ends with the total loss of the Waqf asset
It passes to the overseer's liability
The Waqif must rebuild it
explanation: Per 11, Waqf ends with the total loss of the Waqf asset, whether the Waqf is temporary, restricted, or perpetual.

title: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
q: Bank A pays a premium to acquire a right, but not an obligation, to buy shares at a set price within three months. What is the ruling?
options: Permitted, if the premium is small relative to the share price
Permitted, if Bank A genuinely intends to exercise it within the period
Not permitted, either in its formation or in its trading
Permitted, if traded only on a regulated exchange with a clearing house
explanation: Per 5/2/1-5/2/2, options grant a right without obligation to buy or sell at a set price and period; they are not permitted in formation or trading.

title: Sharikah (Musharakah) and Modern Corporations
q: Mid-year, the partners want to allocate revenues as profit before deducting operating costs and taxes. What does the standard require before allocation of profit?
options: Costs, expenses and taxes deducted, capital kept intact
Only the managing partner's fee must be deducted first
Only taxes need be deducted before profit is allocated to partners
Nothing; revenue may be allocated as received
explanation: Per 3/1/5/6, profit may not be allocated unless operating costs, expenses and taxes are deducted and the capital of the Sharikah is maintained intact.

title: Options to Terminate Due to Breach of Trust (Trust-Based Options)
q: After buying a property, Ahmad pledged it to Bank B as security. He then discovered he had been grossly overcharged. What is the status of his Khiyar al-Ghabn?
options: It remains, subject to Bank B's consent
It converts into a right to a price reduction
It remains, as the pledge was made before he discovered the gouging
It lapses, as a third-party right attached to the item
explanation: Per 4/5(a), Khiyar al-Ghabn lapses on consumption of the item, and the attachment of a third-party right over it has the same legal effect.

title: Ijarah and Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek
q: A farmer leases a tractor from a cooperative and agrees that the rental will be ploughing the cooperative's land for a season. Is this a valid rental?
options: No, rental must be paid in cash
Yes, but only if it is valued in cash
Yes, rental may be a benefit (service)
No, rental may be cash or goods only
explanation: Per 5/2/1, the lease rental may be in cash, in kind (goods) or a benefit (service), and must be specified.

title: Combination of Contracts
q: An Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek set provides for Muwata`ah in the contract. The customer later wants to ignore it. What is the ruling?
options: It binds only Bank A, not the customer
It stays binding, subject to permissible banking practice
It is binding only after the last rental
It is not binding, as it preceded the contract and was never written into it
explanation: Per 7/2, Muwata`ah provided for in the contract and used to combine contracts should be observed and remains binding, subject to permissible conventions.

title: Islamic Insurance
q: Ahmad fails to notify Islamic Insurance Company T of an insured accident within the period in the policy, causing an actual loss to the fund. What may the company do?
options: Claim the actual loss caused to the insurance account
Charge him a fixed penalty set in the policy
Cancel his policy and keep all his contributions
Nothing, as notice is only a recommendation
explanation: Per 8/3, if the participant fails to notify, the company may claim indemnity from him for the actual loss incurred by the insurance account.

title: Concession Contracts
q: Why is a mining licensee entitled to build refineries and acquire transport facilities, per the Basis?
options: They are part of the Ju'l paid by the State for the exploration
The State must provide them free of charge to every licensee
The licensee owns the land of the concession and everything on it
They are complementary requirements of utilization
explanation: Per the Basis, rights to production and transport devices are complementary requirements of utilization; the same applies to related easement rights.

title: Unilateral and Bilateral Promise
q: Ahmad lends 100,000 to Company X. In a separate letter, X promises to let Ahmad use its warehouse free of charge during the loan. What is the ruling on this promise?
options: Prohibited, even though it is in a separate document
Permissible, as it is outside the loan contract
Permissible if the warehouse use is of small value
Permissible, as a promise is not legally binding
explanation: Per 3/2, any promise in a loan that procures benefit for the lender beyond repayment is prohibited even if given in a document separate from the loan contract.

title: Murabahah
q: Bank A takes a mortgage from a Murabahah customer. May it stipulate that it can sell the mortgaged asset to recover its debt without going to court?
options: Yes, but it may keep the full proceeds of the sale
Yes, via the customer's assignment to the Bank
No, unless the customer is declared insolvent by a court
No, only a court may order the sale of a mortgaged asset
explanation: Per 5/5, the Institution may stipulate an assignment from the customer enabling it to sell the mortgaged asset without recourse to the judiciary.

title: Buyback
q: Bank A sells bonds to Bank B for cash and buys them back in a month at a higher price, while Bank A keeps their yield and risk. How does the standard characterize this?
options: A Tawarruq with a pledge of securities
A valid sale with a unilateral promise
A riba-based loan secured by financial assets
A valid buyback, as both prices are cash
explanation: Per 5/6/2, a conventional repo is a riba-based loan secured by financial assets; the price difference (repo rate) is interest.

title: Istisna’a and Parallel Istisna’a
q: Why does the Shari'ah basis bar selling Istisna'a items before taking actual or constructive possession of them?
options: It doubles the profit made by the Institution on the deal
It is selling a non-existent item one does not own
It breaches the defect liability rule
It makes the price unknown to the final buyer
explanation: The basis: selling items before possession is selling a non-existent item and what one does not own, as it is not available to the seller at contracting.

title: Payment Cards
q: Bank A argues that a credit card issuance fee above actual cost is just a service fee. Why does the Shari'ah basis reject this?
options: The fee is unknown to the holder and so it is gharar
The fee is a form of gambling on the cardholder's usage
It is an artifice for a loan that carries benefit
Service fees are always prohibited when charged by a lender
explanation: Basis 5/1/1: an increase over actual direct cost is an artifice to charge an increase over the loan, i.e., a loan carrying benefit for the lender.

title: Zakah
q: A Zakah fund wants to invest Zakah money in a project. Which condition applies under the standard?
options: Only after the urgent needs of recipients are met
Only in projects run by the payer itself
Only if the return is guaranteed by the Bank
The project must remain owned by the Institution
explanation: Per 10/4, Zakah may be invested if need arises, after meeting recipients' urgent needs, with safeguards, and owned by recipients or supervised by the Shari'ah body.

title: Procrastinating Debtor
q: Ahmad cannot pay a due debt to Bank A because he is genuinely insolvent. Per the Shari'ah basis, how should he be treated?
options: All his instalments fall due immediately
He must compensate the Bank for the delay
He may be publicly dishonoured and punished
He should be granted a grace period
explanation: Per the Basis, punishment applies to a solvent defaulter, whereas an insolvent debtor should be granted a grace period.

title: Waqf
q: Bank A's board resolves to create a Waqf over some of its assets, subject to the approval of the supervisory authority. What is the status of this Waqf?
options: Valid only as a bequest within one-third
Void, since the contingency creates excessive gharar
Valid, as Waqf may be contingent upon a condition
Void, as Waqf must always take effect immediately
explanation: Per 2/4/1/3, the presumption is immediate effect, but Waqf may be contingent upon a condition, e.g., the supervisory authority's approval.

title: Buyback
q: Company X and Bank A use a third party so that a commodity returns to Company X at a cash price lower than its deferred price. How does the standard view this?
options: Permitted, as a tripartite setting excludes 'Inah
Permitted, if the third party is independent
Void only as a contingent sale
A stratagem for 'Inah; the third party changes nothing
explanation: Per the Basis for 4/4, it is a stratagem for Einah; engaging the third party does not change the essence of the transaction.

title: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
q: Co-owners divide their land and demarcate boundaries and paths; then one sells his part. Per the Hadith in the basis, is there a right of Shuf'ah?
options: Yes; co-owners always keep Shuf'ah, even after boundaries and paths are set
No; once boundaries and paths are set there is no Shuf'ah
Yes, if the sale is to an outsider
Yes, if claimed within one year
explanation: Per the basis, Abu Salamah narrated the Prophet ruled for Shuf'ah in undivided property; if boundaries are assigned and paths demarcated, there is no Shuf'ah.

title: Financial Paper (Shares and Bonds)
q: A corporation's objective and usual activity is dealing in gold, silver and currencies (Sirafah). How must its shares be traded?
options: In the light of the rules of Sarf
Only under the rules of Salam
Freely, like any trading company
Only under the rules of Istisna'a
explanation: Per 3/19, if the corporation's objective and usual activity is dealing in gold, silver or currencies (Sirafah), trading in its shares must follow the rules of Sarf.

title: Zakah
q: Bank A covers a documentary credit for importing trade goods: it paid opening expenses and amounts retained by intermediary banks. What is Zakatable before the goods are owned?
options: The expenses and the retained amounts, as both are paid by the Bank for the goods
Neither, until the goods arrive
The amounts retained for the credit, not the expenses
Only the expenses of opening the credit
explanation: Per 5/2/6/7, Zakah is paid on the amounts retained for the credit, not the expenses; once the goods are owned, Zakah is on their market value.

title: Waqf
q: A Waqf has no income this year, and the superintendent wants to borrow so as to pay the beneficiaries their usual shares. What is the ruling?
options: Allowed, as beneficiaries' rights come before all else
Allowed if repayable from next year's expected income
Allowed with the judiciary's permission in such a case
Not allowed; borrowing may not be to spend on beneficiaries
explanation: Per 5/3/6/3, borrowing for the Waqf should not be for the sake of spending on the beneficiaries of the Waqf.

title: Mudarabah
q: Bank A and Company X sign a memorandum of understanding for Mudarabah financing of up to 10 million over two years, to be implemented through successive transactions. Is this permissible?
options: Yes, and the memorandum itself transfers the 10 million at once
Yes, if later implemented through specific or successive Mudarabahs
No, a Mudarabah cannot be tied to a defined sum and duration
No, each Mudarabah must be negotiated without any framework
explanation: Per 3/1, Mudarabah financing may be concluded under a general framework or MoU for a sum and duration, later implemented in specific or successive transactions.

title: Concession Contracts
q: A licensee's pay for building a bridge is set as a sum of money, recovered through bridge tolls. The period ends before the full sum is received. What is its position?
options: It keeps utilizing the project until the full sum is received
It may raise tolls without the licensor's consent
It may sell the bridge to a third party
It must hand over the bridge at the end and lose the unpaid balance
explanation: Per 6/3/2, where pay is a sum of money, the licensee keeps the project and utilizes it until receipt of the full amount, unless a clearance deal is made.

title: Investment Sukuk
q: Which of the following falls outside the scope of the standard on Investment Sukuk?
options: Certificates of ownership of usufructs of existing or future assets
Muzara'ah (sharecropping) certificates for agricultural land
Certificates of investment funds and portfolios
Investment agency (Wakalah) certificates issued for a specific project
explanation: Per Scope (1), the standard does not cover shares of joint stock companies, certificates of funds and investment portfolios.

title: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
q: How does the basis reconcile the Hadith 'The neighbour of the house has a greater right to the house' with the Hadiths limiting Shuf'ah?
options: By limiting it to movable property only
By applying it to a neighbour who is co-owner or shares easements
By treating the neighbour Hadith as abrogated by the later Hadiths
By applying it to all adjacent neighbours
explanation: Per the basis, the Hadiths are reconciled by ascribing the neighbour Hadith to a neighbour who is also a co-owner or shares easement rights.

title: Obtaining and Deploying Liquidity
q: Under the standard on obtaining and deploying liquidity, what does the term "liquidity" refer to?
options: Cash or that which can be easily converted to cash
Funds obtained through central bank support facilities
Cash balances held in current accounts only
Any asset recorded on the institution's balance sheet
explanation: Per 2/1, liquidity refers to cash or that which can be easily converted to cash.

title: Guarantees
q: Per the Shari'ah basis, why is Islamic insurance an acceptable security for bad debts while conventional insurance is not?
options: It is provided in return for a set consideration
It is free of any element of guarantee
It guarantees full recovery of every debt
It rests on donation, where Gharar is tolerable
explanation: Per the Basis, Islamic insurance is based on donation for mutual benefit, so Gharar is tolerable and the guarantee is not given for conditional consideration.

title: Mudarabah
q: A capital provider contributes trucks instead of cash as Mudarabah capital. How is the capital determined?
options: By the trucks' value, per experts or as the parties agree
By the trucks' original purchase price, with no new valuation needed at contract
By the total rent the trucks will earn over the term
It cannot be done, as capital must always be paid in cash at the contract date
explanation: Per 7/1, capital may be tangible assets; their value is the contribution, determined by experts or as agreed by the parties.

title: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
q: Per the Shari'ah basis, why is a cooling-off option invalid in Sarf and Salam contracts?
options: They involve deferred delivery on both sides
It contravenes the Qabd stipulated in those contracts
Their prices fluctuate too quickly for any option period to be workable
Those contracts are non-binding by nature, so an option adds nothing to them
explanation: Per the basis, stipulating such an option in contracts that entail taking possession (Qabd) is invalid as it contravenes the Qabd stipulated in Sarf and Salam.

title: Insolvency
q: Shortly before his declaration of insolvency, during a period the competent authority assesses as a period of uncertainty, Ahmad endowed a building as Waqf. What is the effect?
options: It is valid, but the building's rent goes to the creditors
It is valid, since endowment is an act of charity
It has no legal effect, as the rule extends to that period
It is valid, since it preceded the declaration
explanation: Per 5/3, the lack of legal effect of sale, gift or endowment also applies during the period of uncertainty preceding the declaration, as assessed by the authority.

title: Ijarah and Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek
q: Bank A buys a machine from Company X and will lease it back to X. The purchase contract says the sale is conditional on X taking the lease. What is the ruling?
options: Leasing back to the seller is never allowed
Valid, as the lease is the purpose of the deal
Valid, if the rent is fixed in the purchase
The lease must not be a condition of the purchase
explanation: Per 3/2, an asset may be acquired from a party and leased to it, but the Ijarah should not be stipulated as a condition of the purchase contract.

title: Mortgage and its Contemporary Applications
q: Why must a mortgaged asset be Shari'ah-permissible property, per the basis?
options: Impermissible assets cannot be insured by the mortgagor under Islamic insurance
Impermissible assets have no market value at all
It must be sold to settle the debt, and banned objects cannot be
Only permissible assets may be held in trust by banks
explanation: Per the basis, the objective is to sell the asset to settle the debt; a Muslim cannot repay debts with Shari'ah-banned objects such as alcohol and swine.

title: Financial Paper (Shares and Bonds)
q: A company holding mostly receivables adds a small amount of tangible assets solely so that its shares can be traded freely. How does the standard view this?
options: Acceptable, if a Shari'ah board approves it
Acceptable, as any amount of tangible assets makes the shares tradable
Acceptable, if the tangible assets are owned
Not acceptable, as a legal device for trading in debts
explanation: Per 3/20, the rule must not be used as a means for trading in debts by merging parts of tangible assets and benefits with debts as a legal device.

title: Islamic Insurance
q: Islamic Insurance Company T manages a fund and invests its assets as Mudarib. Which of the following is Islamic Insurance Company T entitled to?
options: The insurance surplus at the end of the year
The agency fee and its share of the investment profits
The reserves and provisions of the fund
The contributions and the returns on them, as manager of the fund
explanation: Per 3/1, the company gets its capital and returns, the agency fee, and its share of profits from investing insurance assets via Mudarabah or investment agency.

title: Ijarah and Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek
q: Bank A leases a hall to Company X for January to June, and the same hall to Company Y for July to December. What is the ruling?
options: Permissible as successive leases
Permissible only with Company X's consent
Permissible only if both pay the same rent
Not permissible; one asset, one lessee
explanation: Per 4/2/1, one asset may be leased to several lessees for different periods, provided two contracts are not made for the same period (successive leases).

title: Waqf
q: Ahmad's debts exceed the value of his assets, though no bankruptcy or interdiction ruling was issued. He creates a Waqf over his house. What is the ruling?
options: It is valid, since no interdiction ruling was ever issued against him
It is not concluded at all, like a prodigal's Waqf
It is contingent upon the authorization of his creditors
It is valid but treated as a bequest limited to one third
explanation: Per 2/4/3/3, Waqf by one interdicted for debt depends on creditors' authorization; the same applies if debts exceed assets without a ruling.

title: Sharikah (Musharakah) and Modern Corporations
q: In a partnership in creditworthiness (Sharikat al-Wujuh), goods bought on credit are sold at a loss. How is the loss borne?
options: By the liability ratio each partner undertook for purchases on credit
By the agreed profit-sharing ratio between the partners, whatever liability each undertook
Equally among the partners per head, whatever was agreed
By the partner who negotiated the purchases on credit
explanation: Per 3/2/3, profit follows the agreement, but loss is borne by each partner according to the ratio he undertook in the assets purchased on credit.

title: Ijarah and Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek
q: Bank A's lease contract states that the Bank bears no liability for any defect impairing the intended use of the leased equipment. Is this clause valid?
options: Yes, if the lessee accepts it in writing
No, the lessor may not exclude such liability
Yes, if the rental is reduced in return
Yes, for defects caused by events outside its control
explanation: Per 5/1/5, the lessor must accept responsibility for defects impairing intended use and may not exclude liability, even for events outside its control.

title: Liability of the Investment Manager
q: A Mudarib's misconduct causes a loss. Before it, the fund had realized a profit of 100; experts estimate a further 50 would have been earned. What does his liability cover?
options: The capital plus the 100 and the expected 50
The capital plus the 50 opportunity cost only
Only the capital, excluding any profit
The capital plus the 100 realized profit only
explanation: Per 7/1, liability covers capital and profit realized before the loss, but not lost profit (opportunity cost) or unrealized expected profits.

title: Payment Cards
q: Why does the standard prohibit a card that rolls over the cardholder's loan through Tawarruq with the issuer?
options: It is an artifice to delay the loan with an increase
The card issuer cannot be a seller of commodities to its holder
Tawarruq is prohibited in all cases, even when properly structured
The commodity is never possessed by the cardholder or issuer
explanation: Basis 6/3/2: revolving the debt via Tawarruq from the lender to settle the loan is an artifice to delay settlement with an increase.

title: Impact of Contingent Incidents on Commitments
q: In an Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek, ownership cannot be transferred for a reason the lessee cannot stop. The rent was set above the normal rent of similar property. What applies?
options: All rent paid is refunded and the lessee pays nothing for use
The lessor must transfer ownership despite the obstacle
The rent above the normal rent of similar property is dropped
The lessee loses all rent paid, as he had full use of the property during the lease
explanation: Per 5/5, in Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek the rent exceeding normal rent of similar property is dropped when ownership cannot be transferred for a reason the lessee cannot stop.

title: Waqf
q: Ahmad bought a shop with an option to rescind held by a third party, then made the shop Waqf. The option holder later refused to authorize it. What is the result?
options: The Waqf turns into a bequest of one-third
The Waqf is null and void from the start
The Waqf is void only from the date of refusal
The Waqf continues over the price Ahmad paid
explanation: Per 2/4/5/2, such a Waqf depends on the option holder's authorization; if it is not granted, the Waqf is deemed null and void from the start.

title: Ju’alah
q: Company X wants someone to find water on its land, but no one can say how much drilling will be needed. Why does Ju'alah suit this better than Ijarah?
options: Ju'alah requires the work to be precisely specified, which suits drilling better
Ijarah cannot be used by companies for drilling or other exploration work
Ju'alah fixes the time the work will take in advance
Ju'alah needs only a determined result, not specified work
explanation: Per clause 3, Ju'alah is valid with uncertainty in the work if the end result is determined, so it suits activities for which Ijarah, needing specified work, does not.

title: Guarantees
q: Bakr guaranteed Ahmad's debt with no condition on the order of claims. Ahmad is solvent and the debt is due. May Bank A claim directly from Bakr?
options: Yes, it may claim from either of them
Only after a judgment against Ahmad
No, it must claim from Ahmad first
No, unless Ahmad becomes insolvent
explanation: Per 3/3/1, the creditor may claim from either debtor or guarantor, unless the guarantor stipulated at contracting that the debtor be claimed first.

title: Combination of Contracts
q: A party grants an asset to Ahmad as a gift and, at the same time, sells the same asset to him. What is the ruling on this combination?
options: Permissible, as both gift and sale are lawful when concluded separately
Permissible, if the gift precedes the sale
Permissible, if the price is only nominal
Not permissible: the two contracts contradict each other
explanation: Per 4/4, combined contracts must not contradict each other, e.g. granting an asset as a gift while selling or leasing it simultaneously.

title: Murabahah
q: Under the customer's authority, Bank A sells a Murabahah asset after the customer fails to pay on the due date. The sale yields more than the debt. What must the Bank do?
options: Keep the surplus as a late payment fee
Recover its due and return the balance
Keep all proceeds as compensation
Give the surplus to charitable causes
explanation: Per 5/4, if the Institution sells the asset on default, it must confine itself to the amount due to it and return the balance to the customer.

title: Loan (Qard)
q: Company X uses its credit standing to raise a loan for Ahmad from a lender and stipulates a reward for this service. What is the ruling?
options: Prohibited, as any reward linked to a loan is Riba, even for a service
Permissible only if the reward is paid by the lender and not the borrower
Permissible, as long as it is not a device (Hilah) for Riba
Prohibited unless Company X guarantees the loan
explanation: Per 8, it is permissible to stipulate a reward for raising loans for another as long as it is not a fictional device (Hilah) for dealing in Riba.

title: Sharikah (Musharakah) and Modern Corporations
q: Subscribers to a new stock company pay the first instalment of their shares and the rest is deferred. Under what condition is this permissible?
options: Instalments cover all shares; liability is confined to subscribed shares
Only the paid instalment counts and the rest is waived
The deferred instalments carry a fixed markup to compensate the company for the delay
The subscribers pledge their shares to an interest-based lender to fund the rest
explanation: Per 4/1/2/5, instalment subscription is allowed provided the instalments cover all the shares and the company's liability is confined to the value of subscribed shares.

title: Waqf
q: Ahmad makes Waqf of specific Sukuk for a period equal to their term. At cancellation, the issuer repays the principal amount (not a return). Who gets it?
options: The Waqif and beneficiaries equally
The Waqf, to be reinvested in new Sukuk
Ahmad, the Waqif
The Waqf beneficiaries as revenue
explanation: Per 2/4/15/1(b)(3), if the Waqf period equals the Sukuk term, the amount paid at cancellation is for the Waqif, unless paid as a return (then revenue).

title: Possession (Qabd)
q: Company X receives a bank draft drawn on Bank B, though the actual cash is paid only some days later. How is Company X's receipt of the draft treated?
options: As no possession until the cash is received
As a mere promise of payment by Bank B
As actual possession of the cash itself
As constructive possession of the amount payable
explanation: Per 5/1, possession of a bank draft or cheque is constructive possession of the amount payable by the drawee bank, even if actual payment is delayed.

title: Istisna’a and Parallel Istisna’a
q: A customer insists that Bank A itself manufacture his order. Why does the Shari'ah basis accept such a condition?
options: It lets the Bank charge a higher profit
He may want a maker known for competence and quality
It makes Parallel Istisna'a unnecessary
It removes the Bank's liability for defects in the goods
explanation: The basis: the buyer may be interested in a particular supplier's distinguished competence and the quality of its manufacturing or construction.

title: Mortgage and its Contemporary Applications
q: Those who validate a mortgage signed before the debt contract compare it, per the basis, to which arrangement?
options: An 'Arboun paid in advance in a sale
A Hamish Jiddiyyah paid with a promise to purchase, which the buyer forfeits if he withdraws
A Wadi'ah deposit kept on trust basis
A darak guarantee against a third party claim on the asset
explanation: Per the basis, a mortgage before the debt documents a valid right and is for something in the future, similar to a guarantee and a darak guarantee.

title: Istisna’a and Parallel Istisna’a
q: After an Istisna'a is concluded, the customer and the contractor agree to add an extra floor to the building. On what condition is this permissible?
options: Adjust the deadline but not the price
Adjust the price and allow a reasonable period
Keep the original price and deadline
Only if a new Istisna'a contract replaces the old one
explanation: Per 4/1/1, amending or adding specifications is permissible if the price is adjusted and a reasonable period is granted for the new requirements.

title: Stipulations and Ethics of Fatwa in the Institutional Framework
q: A Shari'ah board member of Bank A owns a stake in a company that wants to sell assets to the Bank. The Bank seeks Fatwa on this deal. What does the standard require?
options: The member may vote if he discloses his stake to the other members
The member may issue the Fatwa alone
The member must have no personal interest in the matter
The interest matters only if it exceeds 5%
explanation: Per 5/3, the board member shall have no personal interest in the matter for which the Institution seeks Fatwa.

title: Waqf
q: A Waqf shop is leased below the normal rent. A new tenant offers the normal rent of similar property. What may the superintendent do?
options: End the old lease unless the old tenant accepts the increase
Nothing at all until the old lease term expires
Lease to both tenants and split the shop between them
Raise the rent without needing the old tenant's acceptance
explanation: Per 6/2, if a new tenant can pay the normal rent, the superintendent may terminate the previous contract unless the old tenant accepts the rent increment.

title: Banking Services in Islamic Banks
q: A customer objects that a fee set as a percentage of the service value is unknown. Per the basis, why is it permissible?
options: Unknown fees are allowed in banking services, as customary practice
Once calculated, it becomes like a lump sum amount
Percentage fees are a form of Mudarabah
The customer may refuse to pay it later
explanation: The basis: the fee may be a lump sum or a percentage of the service value, because when the percentage is calculated it becomes like a lump sum.

title: Protection of Capital and Investments
q: Company Z offers to guarantee a fund's capital for a fee. Besides being akin to conventional insurance, what Shari'ah basis does the standard give for prohibiting it?
options: The extent of loss is unknown at inception, causing excessive ambiguity
A guarantee is valid only for debts, never for any capital
Guarantees may be given only by the investment manager
The fee would be too small to cover the potential loss, so the guarantor would be harmed
explanation: Per the basis, a fee-based guarantee entails excessive ambiguity since the extent of loss is unknown at inception, and giving a guarantee for a fee is prohibited.

title: Obtaining and Deploying Liquidity
q: Bank A's treasury committee is drafting its liquidity management objective. Which formulation matches the standard's definition of liquidity management?
options: Investing all available cash in long-term assets for return
Holding maximum cash in reserve to cover any withdrawal at all times, whatever the cost to returns
Balancing swift, cheap obtaining of liquidity with its effective deployment
Drawing on central bank facilities whenever cash is short
explanation: Per 2/2, liquidity management means achieving a balance between obtaining liquidity as swiftly and cheaply as possible and investing and deploying it effectively.

title: Mortgage and its Contemporary Applications
q: Ahmad's zakatable assets are mortgaged to Bank A and he cannot dispose of them. Who must pay the Zakah on them?
options: Ahmad and Bank A in proportion to the debt
No one, since disposal is restricted
Bank A, as the possessor of the asset
Ahmad, as the owner of the mortgaged asset
explanation: Per 9/1, the owner of the mortgaged asset pays Zakah if due; his inability to dispose of the mortgaged asset does not relieve him from Zakah.

title: Combination of Contracts
q: A combined set contains a subsidiary contract with an element of Gharar that would invalidate it if concluded alone. What is the ruling?
options: The Gharar is overlooked only if minor in amount
The Gharar may be overlooked in the subsidiary contract
The subsidiary contract must be removed
The whole set is void due to the Gharar in one of its contracts
explanation: Per 5/2/1, Gharar, which affects financial contracts, may be overlooked in implicit and subsidiary contracts.

title: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
q: A seller releases a commodity to Bank A and facilitates its taking, but the Bank has not physically taken it. What kind of holding has occurred?
options: Actual holding
No holding until the goods are moved
Holding only for goods sold by Juzaf
Constructive holding
explanation: Per 5/6, constructive holding indicates the act of releasing the commodity and facilitating the process of its holding.

title: Sale of Debt
q: Ahmad borrowed USD 1,000 under a loan contract and now repays it in local currency. Which exchange rate applies?
options: The rate on the loan's maturity date
Any rate the two parties agree upon
The rate prevailing on the day of settlement
The rate on the day the loan was granted
explanation: Per 4/1/1/2(c), discharge in another currency is at the rate on the settlement day if the debt resulted from a loan contract.

title: Settlement of Debt by Set-Off
q: Per the Shari'ah basis, why is settling debts by set-off in line with the objectives of the Shari'ah?
options: It discharges liability without futile recovery processes
It lets creditors earn a return on their debts
It is expressly ordered for all debts in the text of the Quran
It removes the need for any consent of parties
explanation: Per the Basis, set-off has been practised without disapproval and serves Shari'ah objectives by discharging debts without futile recovery processes.

title: Murabahah
q: Bank A asks the purchase orderer to guarantee the goods against damage and destruction while they are shipped and stored for the Bank. What is the ruling?
options: Permitted if he suggested the supplier
Permitted, since he will buy the goods anyway
Permitted if it is offset by a lower mark-up
Not permitted to impose this guarantee on him
explanation: Per 2/5/2, it is not permitted to impose on the purchase orderer a guarantee for hazards such as damage and destruction during shipment or storage.

title: ’Arboun (Earnest Money)
q: Which maxim underlies the seller's liability for the sale item before delivery and the buyer's liability after delivery in an 'Arboun sale?
options: Al-Kharaj Bi al-Daman: revenue follows liability
He who voluntarily binds himself must honor the condition
Ownership passes at contract; liability follows Qabd
Contracts are interpreted by their intent and meaning, not by their words
explanation: The Basis cites the maxim: ownership is established upon conclusion of the contract, while liability is contingent upon delivery (Qabd).

title: Procrastinating Debtor
q: A customer challenges Bank A's clause obliging him to donate to charity if he defaults. Per the Shari'ah basis, what is this clause based on?
options: A commitment to donate, established in the Maliki school
A penalty clause, as accepted in the Hanbali school of law
A right of set-off against his accounts
Compensation for the creditor's actual loss
explanation: Per the Basis, this is a commitment to make a donation, well established in the Maliki school (Ibn Nafi' and Ibn Dinar).

title: Concession Contracts
q: Minerals are found under Ahmad's private land. One view puts them at the State's (Bayt al-Mal's) disposal. What reason does the Basis give for this view?
options: Ahmad did not pay the Kharaj on his land
No one, the landlord included, brought the minerals into being
The State always owns private land
Private land ownership never extends to resources under the ground
explanation: Per the Basis, this view holds that no one, including the landlord, can claim to have brought the minerals into being, which removes disputes with the discoverer.

title: Waqf
q: Ahmad argues he may take back his Waqf since Waqf is a voluntary act. Which evidence does the standard cite for its binding nature?
options: The maxim that harm is to be removed, so owners may retract
Consensus that gifts are revocable before Qabd, as with any donation
Analogy with a bequest, which the testator may revoke at any time
Umar's Khaybar land: not to be sold, gifted or inherited
explanation: Basis 2/3: Umar (RA) gave the land in charity on condition it not be sold, gifted or inherited, showing the Waqf's binding nature.

title: Payment Cards
q: Bank A plans to offer cardholders free conventional life insurance as a card benefit. What is the ruling?
options: Permitted if cardholders consent
Permitted, as it is offered for free by the insurer to holders
Not permitted, as it is a prohibited benefit
Permitted for premium cards only, with a separate premium
explanation: Per 5/6/1, the issuer may not provide benefits prohibited by Shari'ah, such as conventional life insurance or free access to prohibited places.

title: Waqf
q: Per the Shari'ah basis, which school's view is followed in allowing a Waqf for a non-charitable but permissible purpose?
options: The Hanafi School; the Maliki School requires charity
The Maliki School; the Hanafi School requires charity
The Shafi'i School; the Hanbali School requires charity
The Hanbali School; all others require charity
explanation: The basis: since Waqf is a donation, the only condition is a permissible purpose (Maliki view), whereas the Hanafi School holds the purpose should be charitable.

title: Hawalah
q: A client endorses a bill of exchange to Bank A, asking it to collect the amount and credit his account. How is this classified, and may the Bank charge?
options: Agency, permissible with or without a fee
Hawalah, with no fee permitted
Hawalah, with a fee based on the amount
Agency, which must always be free of fee
explanation: Per 12/5/2, endorsing a bill so the Institution collects and credits the client is not Hawalah but agency, permissible with or without consideration.

title: Mortgage and its Contemporary Applications
q: Bank A's mortgage over a client's land is possessed legally through registration in the land registry, not by physically holding the land. How is it treated?
options: As invalid, since actual possession by hand is required
As a mere promise to mortgage until physical delivery
As a formal mortgage, with the same rulings as seizure mortgage
As valid, but with weaker rulings than a seizure mortgage held by hand
explanation: Per 3/1/2, possession may be actual (seizure mortgage) or legal via registration (security or formal mortgage); both types are subject to the same rulings.

title: Obtaining and Deploying Liquidity
q: Bank A deploys surplus cash by buying wheat on Salam and, in a separate contract, appoints the Salam seller to sell the wheat to his customers. When may the wheat be sold?
options: After Bank A takes physical or constructive delivery
Only after the seller returns the Salam price
Never; the Salam seller cannot sell on the bank's behalf
At any time, even before the delivery date
explanation: Per 5/3, commodities bought on Salam may be sold after taking physical or constructive delivery, personally or by appointing the seller, in a separate contract, as agent.

title: Protection of Capital and Investments
q: A fund manager wants to protect a fund against exchange-rate fluctuation and inflation using Shari'ah-compliant instruments. What is the ruling?
options: Not permissible; only loss of the capital itself may be protected, not currency or inflation
Permissible; such risks may be covered by compliant instruments
Permissible only through conventional swaps and options
Permissible only if the manager guarantees the outcome
explanation: Per 3/3, Shari'ah-compliant instruments and processes may protect investment from risks such as loss of capital, depreciation, inflation or exchange-rate fluctuation.

title: Waqf
q: Ahmad states: "I made this house a Waqf for myself and then for charitable causes." What is the status of this Waqf?
options: Valid only for the charitable part, the self-benefit being void
Void, as a Waqif cannot benefit from a Waqf he has created himself
Valid only if Ahmad is poor
Valid; the Waqif may stipulate himself as beneficiary
explanation: Per 2/4/4/2, it is valid to stipulate that the Waqf beneficiary is the Waqif, e.g., a Waqf for himself and then for charitable causes.

title: Payment Cards
q: Bank A lets its debit cardholders overdraw their balance against a monthly charge. What is the ruling?
options: Permitted, for customers with good history
Permitted, as the monthly charge is a service fee for the overdraft
Not permitted, as it is lending against interest
Permitted, if the charge is a fixed lump sum, not a percentage
explanation: Per 4/1/1, a debit card must not result in lending against interest, like overdrawing the card against a consideration.

title: Procrastinating Debtor
q: Bank A stipulates that late payers must deliver goods worth 1% of the debt for each month of delay. Is this stipulation valid?
options: Yes, as it is not cash compensation
Yes, if the debtor agreed at contracting
Yes, since the amount is pre-determined
No, compensation in any form is not permitted
explanation: Per 2/1/2, financial compensation for delay may not be stipulated, whether in cash or in other consideration, and whether pre-determined or not.

title: Payment Cards
q: Bank A designs a card: it lends Ahmad interest-free, then at due date has him settle the loan via Tawarruq from Bank A, leaving a larger debt. What is the ruling?
options: Permitted if the profit is modest
Not permitted, as a rollover of the debt
Permitted, as Tawarruq is via Murabahah
Permitted if Bank A acts as agent
explanation: Per 6/3/2, a card based on lending then rollover (qalb al-dayn) via Tawarruq, resulting in a debt more than the loan, is not permitted.

title: Murabahah
q: Bank A wants to take 'Arboun from Customer C at the time C signs his promise to purchase. What is the ruling?
options: Not permitted; 'Arboun is taken on concluding the sale
Permitted only for a binding promise
Permitted, as it shows how serious C is about his promise
Permitted if refunded in full when the sale is done
explanation: Per 2/5/6, 'Arboun may be taken upon conclusion of the Murabahah sale, but not during the stage at which the customer has given his promise to purchase.

title: Sharikah (Musharakah) and Modern Corporations
q: In a diminishing Musharakah, Bank A's contract states that the customer shall buy Bank A's units every quarter as part of the partnership contract itself. What is the ruling?
options: Permitted if the price is the market value
Permitted if the customer signs each sale separately
Permitted, as it is the essence of diminishing Musharakah
Not permitted; only an independent promise to buy is allowed
explanation: Per 5/1, the buying and selling must not be stipulated in the partnership contract; the buyer may give only a promise to buy, independent of that contract.

title: Options to Terminate Due to Breach of Trust (Trust-Based Options)
q: An elderly customer trusts a shopkeeper not to overcharge him, so he does not negotiate, and is charged far above the fair price. How does the standard classify him?
options: A party who consented, with no option
A party to Najsh, entitled to Khiyar al-Taghrir for the inflated price he was charged
A Mustarsil, a victim of price gouging with Khiyar al-Ghabn
A victim of Tadlis, with Khiyar al-Tadlis
explanation: Per 4/3/1, sale to a Mustarsil, a purchaser who does not negotiate because he trusts the seller, is an example of price gouging.

title: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
q: A farmer sells unripe fruits on his trees to Company X, apart from the trees and without any stipulation to await harvesting. What is the ruling?
options: Void: the Gharar relates to the primary subject matter
Valid if the buyer pays the full price in advance
Valid: unripe fruits involve only medium Gharar
Valid: the Gharar is in a corollary of the trees
explanation: Per 4/3, Gharar in the primary subject matter, as when unripe fruits are sold apart from the trees without stipulating awaiting harvest, nullifies the contract.

title: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
q: Bank A offers units in an exchange-traded fund (ETF) whose entire assets are gold. Which rulings govern trading in these units?
options: The rulings for currencies
The rulings for gold
The rulings for gold only above 50% purity
The rulings for shares of ordinary companies
explanation: Per 10/3, Sukuk, investment fund units and ETF units whose entire assets are gold are subject to the rulings for gold.

title: Sharikah (Musharakah) and Modern Corporations
q: Bank A enters a Sharikah with a customer and asks that the contract stipulate that the customer guarantees Bank A's capital. What is the ruling?
options: Permitted if the customer is the managing partner
Permitted if the customer receives a higher profit ratio in return
Not permitted: a partner may not guarantee another's capital
Permitted if the guarantee is limited to half of the capital
explanation: Per 3/1/4/1, partners hold Sharikah assets on trust; it is not permitted to stipulate that a partner guarantees the capital of another partner.

title: Irrigation Partnership (Musaqat)
q: An owner offers his Musaqat worker a lump sum of 5,000 instead of a share of the crop. Per the Shari'ah basis, why is a share required?
options: The worker must bear the risk of the land
A lump sum diverts the contract from Musaqat's features
A lump sum is always Riba in any contract, because it fixes the return in advance
Cash payments are not allowed in farming
explanation: Per the basis, specifying lump-sum compensation diverts the contract from the features of Musaqat, based on the Khaybar Hadith; a known share averts Jahalah.

title: Documentary Credit
q: A seller stipulates in the sale contract that the buyer must pay through a documentary credit. What is the status of this condition?
options: Void, as it adds a condition to the sale
Valid, but only a recommendation to the buyer
Valid only if the buyer's bank is an Institution
Valid, and its performance is binding on the buyer
explanation: Per 3/2/1, the seller may stipulate payment through documentary credit; such a condition is valid and its performance is binding upon the buyer.

title: Sale of Debt
q: Bank A sells a special purpose company holding debts and tangible assets, but undertakes to bear the risks of those assets after the sale. Is this permitted?
options: No, the buyer must bear the risks of the assets
Yes, if tangible assets exceed 50% of the company's asset value
Yes, if the company is registered
Yes, but only for the first year after the sale
explanation: Per 8/2/1, the sale must transfer ownership and risk to the buyer; it is not permitted to stipulate that the seller bears the risks at any stage.

title: Islamic Insurance
q: An Islamic insurance car policy states that the participant bears the first 500 of every claim. What is the ruling on this condition?
options: Void, as it turns the donation into a sale
Void, as indemnity must cover the whole of the loss suffered
Binding only on participants who never claim
Binding, as long as it does not contradict Shari'ah
explanation: Per 9/1, special conditions such as charging the participant with a portion of the indemnity are binding if they do not contradict Shari'ah or the contract.

title: Zakah
q: Company X failed to pay Zakah for several past years. Does that past Zakah lapse due to the passage of time?
options: Yes, if the company was unaware
Yes, after three years, as the right of the recipients lapses by prescription
No; Zakah does not cease by prescription
Yes, after one year, as the Zakah year has passed
explanation: Per 10/5, Zakah does not cease to be valid by prescription.

title: Sale of Debt
q: Why does the standard prohibit a bilaterally binding promise to sell a debt to the debtor?
options: It contains excessive gharar as to the price and the debt
It is a means to achieve riba artificially
It turns the debt into Salam capital, which is not allowed
It requires the debtor's consent
explanation: Per the Basis for 4/2, a bilaterally binding promise in this form is a means to achieve riba artificially.

title: Loan (Qard)
q: Bank A wants its Qard service charge to include a share of staff salaries and office rent. Is this allowed?
options: No; indirect expenses are not part of actual expenses
Yes, if the Shari'ah Supervisory Board is informed
Yes, if they are allocated on a reasonable basis
Yes, as all costs of running loans may be recovered
explanation: Per 9/2, indirect expenses such as employee salaries, rentals of space, assets and transport, and general management expenses are not included in actual expenses.

title: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
q: Ahmad and Omar co-own a fleet of trucks not attached to any real estate. Omar sells his share. Does Ahmad have a right of Shuf'ah?
options: Yes; Shuf'ah applies to any co-owned property
No, unless the trucks are all used together in a single joint business
Yes, if he claims it immediately
No; Shuf'ah covers only immovables and movables attached to them
explanation: Per 7/1/1, the right of Shuf'ah exists only in relation to immovable property or movable property attached to it.

title: Zakah
q: Company X owns a building leased to tenants (Mustaghallat), not held for trade. How is Zakah applied?
options: No Zakah at all, either on the building or on its rent
Zakah on the building's market value at each year end, as it is an asset of the company
No Zakah on the building; Zakah on unexpended rent at year end
Zakah on the full gross rent at the time it is received
explanation: Per 3/1/4 and 4/2/1, leased assets not for trade are not Zakatable; the unexpended rental is added to other Zakatable assets at year end.

title: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
q: Converting Bank B owns premises that were designated for non-permissible activities. What should it do with them?
options: Sell them and donate the full sale price to charity at once
Change them to locations for permissible operations
Demolish them, as prohibited assets cannot be reused
Leave them unused permanently, to avoid any doubt
explanation: Per 8/1/6, property assets designated for non-permissible activities should be changed to locations designated for permissible operations and services.

title: Settlement of Debt by Set-Off
q: Bank A accepts a cheque and set-off with the drawer then takes place through the clearing-house. How is this set-off classified?
options: Either type, depending on which conditions are met
Always a contractual set-off, as the drawer agreed to it
Always a compulsory set-off, as the clearing-house imposes it
Not a set-off at all, but a transfer of debt (Hawalah)
explanation: Per 4/2, set-off between an Institution accepting a cheque and the drawer through the clearing-house may be compulsory or contractual, per the conditions met.

title: Sale of Debt
q: Bank A securitizes its monetary receivables into tradable certificates. Against what may these certificates be traded?
options: Other debt-based certificates
Cash at a discount to face value
Only a commodity, usufruct or service
Cash, but only at face value
explanation: Per 9/5/2, securities based on monetary debts may trade only against a commodity, usufruct or service with ascertained delivery, per 5/2.

title: Guarantees
q: Company Z guarantees to refund the price to a buyer if the sold commodity proves to belong to someone other than the seller. What is this guarantee called?
options: A subscription guarantee
Hamish Jiddiyyah
'Arboun
Daman al-Dark
explanation: Per 3/2, a guarantee to refund the price if the sold item belongs to another is Daman al-Dark, a market (business) guarantee of contractual obligation.

title: Concession Contracts
q: A ministry plans to award a mining concession to a favoured company without giving other qualified bidders any chance. What does the standard require when offering concessions?
options: Justice, equality of chances and realization of public interest
Awarding the concession to the highest financial bidder in all cases
Awarding it to whoever first applies for it
Awarding it only to companies owned by the State
explanation: Per 4, when offering concession rights, due consideration should be given to justice, equality of chances and realization of public interest.

title: Waqf
q: Ahmad makes a temporary Waqf of units in an investment fund. The deed does not say whether the Waqf is of the units or of their value. What is the Waqf asset?
options: The periodic distributions only
Those particular fund units
The value of the units at creation
The fund's underlying assets
explanation: Per 2/4/15/1(b), the presumption is that the Waqf asset is those particular Sukuk or units, unless the Waqif stipulated that it is for the value.

title: Ijarah and Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek
q: An identified leased vehicle is totally destroyed without the lessee's fault. The lease says the remaining instalments are still payable. What is the position?
options: The lease continues with a substitute vehicle
The lease ends, but the instalments stay due
The lease ends; that stipulation is not allowed
The lessee must pay half the remaining rent
explanation: Per 7/1/3, Ijarah on an identified asset terminates on its total destruction, and it may not be stipulated that the remaining instalments be paid.

title: Credit Agreement
q: What is the Shari'ah status of a credit facility agreement signed between Bank A and a client before any utilization?
options: It is a binding loan contract for the full approved limit
Mutual understanding and exchange of non-binding promises
It is a bilateral binding promise enforceable by the courts
It is a binding sale contract from the date of signing
explanation: Per 4, the decision and the facility agreement are means of mutual understanding and exchange of non-binding promises; utilization depends on the contract used.

title: Waqf
q: Ahmad's Waqf deed reserves his right to amend the Waqf's terms and conditions. What is the ruling?
options: Valid only for appointing the overseer
Void, since a Waqf is binding on creation and cannot be amended
Valid, including the right to revoke the Waqf altogether
Valid, if it does not prejudice the essence of the Waqf
explanation: Per 2/6/6, the Waqif may stipulate the right to amend the Waqf's terms and conditions provided it does not prejudice the essence of Waqf.

title: Istisna’a and Parallel Istisna’a
q: A contractor stops building on the purchaser's land due to his own misconduct. What is the purchaser's position regarding the partly built structure?
options: He pays its value and claims his actual damage
He pays the full contract price
He takes it without paying anything for the work done
He pays its value with no damage claim
explanation: Per 4/2/4, where failure is due to the contractor's misconduct, the purchaser is liable only for the structure's value and the builder compensates actual damage.

title: Ju’alah
q: Company X engages Ahmad under Ju'alah to obtain financing for it from banks. Which outcome may validly be the subject of this Ju'alah?
options: Securing a loan with interest set by custom
Securing a deferred-payment Murabahah facility
Securing an interest-bearing loan from a bank
Securing an interbank loan with interest
explanation: Per 8/3/2, Ju'alah for facilities requires a valid subject, such as Murabahah on deferred payment, and not raising interest-bearing loans.

title: Mudarabah
q: A Mudarabah contract is later concluded on the basis of a memorandum of understanding that is silent in the contract itself. What is the status of the memorandum's contents?
options: They apply only if repeated word for word in the new contract
They bind only the Mudarib and never bind the capital provider who signed the contract
They lapse once the actual Mudarabah contract has been signed
They are part of the contract unless originally exempted from it
explanation: Per 3/3, the MoU contents become an integral part of any future contract unless the parties had originally agreed to exempt themselves from some obligations.

title: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
q: Bank A's treasury proposes to buy futures contracts on crude oil and trade them before maturity. What is the ruling?
options: Not permitted, either in their formation or in trading them
Permitted, for hedging purposes only and not for speculation
Permitted to trade them, but not to form them at the outset
Permitted, if the contracts are ended by actual delivery of the oil
explanation: Per 3/3 and 5/1/2, futures transactions are not permitted according to the Shari'ah, either through their formation or through trading in them.

title: Mudarabah
q: A Mudarib hires a specialist for work that is not, by custom, the Mudarib's responsibility. May the specialist be paid from the Mudarabah funds?
options: No, only from the Mudarib's own funds
No, such work may not be hired out
Yes, at the prevailing rate
Yes, at any rate the Mudarib agrees
explanation: Per 9/4, the Mudarib may hire, against the Mudarabah funds and at the prevailing rate, another party for work not customarily the Mudarib's responsibility.

title: Revocation of Contracts by Exercise of a Cooling-Off Option
q: A credit facility lets Bank A revoke upon breach of a restrictive covenant. The customer breached it but fully cured the breach before Bank A sought to revoke. Is revocation valid?
options: Yes, provided the bank notifies the customer first
Yes, a breach at any time gives a permanent right
No, covenant breaches cannot trigger revocation
No, the cause must exist at the time of revocation
explanation: Per 6/1, a valid revocation requires the cause triggering the option to exist at the time of the revocation.

title: Mudarabah
q: A Mudarabah contract omits the profit ratio. Local custom is to share Mudarabah profit equally. How is profit distributed?
options: Equally, following the customary practice
By the ratio of capital to labour value
Entirely to the capital provider
The contract is void and the Mudarib gets a wage
explanation: Per 8/4, if no ratio is stipulated, customary practice applies; if custom is equal distribution, profit is distributed equally.

title: Salam and Parallel Salam
q: According to the Shari'ah basis, how does the buyer in a Salam contract usually benefit?
options: By charging the seller a fee for financing
By acquiring the commodity below market price
By selling the commodity before delivery
By receiving interest on the capital paid
explanation: The basis: Salam finances those needing working capital, and the buyer benefits by acquiring the commodity at a price below the market price.

title: Obtaining and Deploying Liquidity
q: Islamic Bank A faces a one-week cash gap and considers an interest-bearing overdraft from a conventional bank. What is the ruling?
options: Permitted for one week as a matter of necessity, since the gap is short and temporary
Permitted if the facility is arranged through a subsidiary
Prohibited, whether direct, by overdraft or by a commission-based facility
Permitted if the interest paid is small and fixed in advance
explanation: Per 4/1, obtaining liquidity through interest-bearing loans is prohibited, whether directly or through overdrafts or interest-bearing or commission-based facilities.

title: Stipulations and Ethics of Fatwa in the Institutional Framework
q: Two years after a Fatwa approved a product, the underlying reasons of that Fatwa no longer exist. What should Bank A do?
options: Continue relying on the original Fatwa
Discontinue the product at once without asking the board
Ask another board to confirm the old Fatwa
Seek the Fatwa again by presenting the new developments
explanation: Per 6/2, Fatwa should be sought again on new developments, such as changed conception, new circumstances or non-existence of underlying reasons.

title: Mortgage and its Contemporary Applications
q: On default, a mortgaged asset is sold for 120 against a debt of 100 owed to Bank A. What happens to the remaining 20?
options: Bank A keeps it as compensation for delay
It is held as security for future debts
It is given to the mortgagor
It is donated to charity on the mortgagor's behalf
explanation: Per 3/4/1, after repaying the mortgagee's debt, the remaining value of the sold mortgaged asset is given to the mortgagor.

title: Possession (Qabd)
q: How does the standard define possession (Qabd)?
options: The gathering of a thing or what takes its rule, per customary practice
The physical transfer of a thing from hand to hand in every case
The payment of the full price of a thing to its seller
The registration of ownership of the thing in an official government register
explanation: Per 2, possession is the gathering of a thing or what takes its rule, according to the requirements of customary practice.

title: Sharikah (Musharakah) and Modern Corporations
q: Two years into a Sharikah with equal capital, the partners want to change the profit ratio from 50:50 to 60:40. What is the ruling?
options: Not permitted once the contract has been concluded by offer and acceptance
Permissible at any time, while losses remain shared by capital shares
Permissible only at liquidation of the partnership, not during its term
Permissible only if the loss-sharing ratio is also changed to 60:40
explanation: Per 3/1/1/4, partners may amend the terms and profit ratio at any time, taking into account that losses are shared according to each partner's share in capital.

title: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
q: Bank A and Bank B conclude a currency exchange with a 3-day cooling-off option for Bank A. Is the option valid?
options: No; currency exchange requires spot payment of both sides
No, since only the seller may hold the option
Yes, provided the period does not exceed 3 days and is fixed in the contract
Yes, as the cooling-off option applies to any financial contract between banks
explanation: Per 2/3, cooling-off options do not apply to contracts requiring spot payment of both countervalues such as currency exchange, nor to Salam or non-binding contracts.

title: Procrastinating Debtor
q: Bank A incurs legal and other expenses to recover a debt from a procrastinating debtor. Who bears these expenses?
options: The court, as a public cost
The two parties equally
Bank A, as the creditor
The procrastinating debtor
explanation: Per 2/1/4, the procrastinating debtor is liable for legal and other expenses incurred by the creditor to recover his debt.

title: Obtaining and Deploying Liquidity
q: Bank A needs cash. It sells its office building for immediate cash and then leases it back on rent payable in arrears. How does the standard treat this?
options: As prohibited, being a disguised interest-bearing loan
As permissible only for assets the bank does not use
As a permissible mode of obtaining liquidity
As permissible only if the rent is paid in advance
explanation: Per 4/2/3, the institution may sell some of its assets for immediate cash and then, if required, lease them back on rent payable in arrears.

title: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
q: Bank A takes a customer's gold as a pledge and stipulates a right to lease it out, undertaking to return it at maturity. Is this stipulation valid?
options: Yes, since the pledgor agreed to it in the contract
No, even with an undertaking to return it
Yes, if the rent is credited to the debt
Yes, since Bank A will return the same gold
explanation: Per 7/1/4, the pledgee may not stipulate a right to sell, re-pledge or lease the pledged gold, even if it undertakes to return it.

title: Murabahah
q: Why does the Shari'ah basis disallow a promise that is binding on both the Institution and the customer?
options: It turns the Murabahah into 'Inah between the parties
It is a form of commitment fee charged by the Bank
It leaves the mark-up unknown to both the Bank and customer
It amounts to a contract before the item is acquired
explanation: The basis: a bilateral binding promise amounts to a contract prior to acquisition of the item to be sold.

title: Investment Sukuk
q: Ahmad holds 10% of the Sukuk of a project that suffers a loss. How is the loss allocated to him?
options: He bears 10% of the loss, in proportion to his holding
It is shared equally among all holders regardless of holding
The issuer bears it up to the nominal value of his Sukuk
He bears none, as Sukuk holders are creditors of the issuer
explanation: Per 4/5, holders share the return as stated in the prospectus and bear losses in proportion to the certificates they hold.

title: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
q: Ahmad opens a savings account at Bank A that carries no authorization to invest the funds for his benefit. Which rulings apply to it?
options: The rulings on unrestricted investment accounts
The rulings on investment agency accounts
The rulings on current accounts
The rulings on restricted investment accounts
explanation: Per 2/2/3, savings accounts without authorization to invest for the holder are subject to the rulings on current accounts; with such authorization, investment account rulings.

title: Murabahah
q: A customer breaches his binding promise. Bank A's cost was 100,000; it resells the item to a third party for 92,000. Its expected mark-up was 10,000. How much may it deduct from Hamish Jiddiyyah?
options: The entire Hamish Jiddiyyah
explanation: Per 2/5/4, the Institution may deduct only actual damage: cost minus the third-party price (100,000 - 92,000). Lost mark-up is not included.

title: Ijarah and Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek
q: In an Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek, title cannot pass because the asset is destroyed without the lessee's fault, so rentals are adjusted to market rate. To what does the basis liken this?
options: Refunding 'Arboun after deducting the actual damage incurred
Rebating part of a debt paid before its due date
Reducing the price of a crop hit by natural calamities
Returning goods within a three-day option period
explanation: The basis: retrospective adjustment to market rental protects the lessee and is analogous to discounting the price of a sold crop damaged by natural calamities.

title: Concession Contracts
q: A licensee is paid for building a project only by the right to use it for a period before handing it over. Why is this a valid price, per the Basis?
options: The State owes the licensee nothing
Usufruct counts as a gift from the State
Istisna'a needs no price at all when the orderer is the State itself
In Istisna'a, usufruct of the product may serve as its price
explanation: Per the Basis, in Istisna'a temporary benefit from the product may be its price; the price may be money or usufruct, including of the product itself.

title: Salam and Parallel Salam
q: A Salam contract is concluded on the basis of an earlier memorandum of understanding, and the parties say nothing about it at signing. What is the status of the memorandum's terms?
options: They become part and parcel of the contract
They bind only the seller, not the buyer
They are merely moral, not contractual
They lapse once the contract is signed
explanation: Per 2/1/2, the memorandum's contents become part of the contract, unless the parties agreed at conclusion to exempt themselves from some obligations.

title: Debit Card, Charge Card and Credit Card
q: Ahmad buys gold from a jeweller using his charge card issued by Bank A. When is this purchase permissible?
options: Only if he repays the issuer within the free credit period
When the issuer can settle the jeweller without delay
Never, as gold must be bought only with cash in hand
Only with a debit card, never a charge card
explanation: Per 4/4, gold, silver or currency may be bought with a debit or charge card where the issuer can settle the amount due to the merchant without delay.

title: Guarantees
q: A customer pays a Hamish Jiddiyyah of 5,000 and breaks his binding promise. Bank A bought the asset for 100,000 and resells it for 97,000. What may it keep?
options: Nothing, as no contract was concluded
The full 5,000 as forfeited 'Arboun
5,000 plus a claim for lost profit
3,000 for actual damage, refunding 2,000
explanation: Per 6/8/2, Hamish Jiddiyyah is held on trust; on breach the Institution may deduct only actual damage: cost minus the sale price to a third party.

title: Zakah
q: Company X harvests 500 kg of dates and 400 kg of wheat from its farms. What is the Zakah position, given the 653 kg Nisab?
options: Zakah on 900 kg, since crops of different kinds are added together to reach the Nisab
Zakah on the dates only
No Zakah; different kinds cannot be added together
Zakah on both, as the total exceeds Nisab
explanation: Per 5/4/1 and 5/4/2, the Nisab is 653 kg; types of the same kind may be added, but different kinds of produce cannot; each kind has its own Nisab.

title: Waqf
q: A Waqif stipulated that his Waqf house be benefited from by residence for poor students. The superintendent finds leasing it would serve better. What applies?
options: Leasing makes the Waqf void
It may be used by residence or by leasing
It may only be used by residence
It may be leased only with court permission
explanation: Per 4/1/4, when the Waqif stipulates benefit through residence, the Waqf can be benefited from in that manner or through leasing, and vice versa.

title: Loan (Qard)
q: Ahmad offers to lend Company X a unique antique painting by way of Qard, to be returned later in kind. Is this a valid subject-matter of Qard?
options: No; the subject-matter must be known fungible (Mithli) wealth
Yes; any valuable property may be lent as Qard if returned in kind
No; only cash may be the subject-matter of Qard
Yes, if its market value is agreed in advance
explanation: Per 3/4, the subject-matter of Qard must be known fungible (Mithli) marketable wealth.

title: Irrigation Partnership (Musaqat)
q: An owner argues his Musaqat worker should guarantee the crop. Per the Shari'ah basis, why does the worker act in a fiduciary capacity?
options: He is a lessee of the land under the contract
He has no share in the crop until division, so he cannot be a partner
He is a guarantor appointed by the owner
He is the owner's agent in preserving the trees and fruits
explanation: Per the basis, the worker acts in a fiduciary capacity rather than a position of liability because he is an agent on behalf of the owner in caring for trees and fruits.

title: Hiring of Persons
q: Bank A receives a seriousness guarantee from a client who pledged to hire its services. Which of the following is a permitted way to hold this amount?
options: Use it freely as the Bank's own funds without any return to the client
Lend it to other clients at a fixed return
Invest it for the client by Mudarabah or investment agency
Treat it as the Bank's income on receipt
explanation: Per 3/2, the guarantee amount may be kept as a deposit not disposed of, invested for the client via Mudarabah or investment agency, or frozen in his current account.

title: Commercial Papers
q: Bank A asks whether the Commercial Papers standard governs a new instrument that has some attributes of commercial paper but is not a bill, note or cheque. What is the answer?
options: No, the standard covers only cheques among bank instruments
No, the standard covers only bills, promissory notes and cheques
Yes, it covers any instrument with commercial paper attributes
Yes, if the instrument is issued under the Geneva Convention
explanation: Per clause 1, the standard covers bills of exchange, promissory notes and cheques, and not anything else possessing the attributes of commercial paper.

title: Investment Sukuk
q: The manufactured asset under Istisna'a Sukuk has been delivered to the ultimate purchaser on deferred payment. Why is trading in the certificates now subject to debt-trading rules?
options: It represents the price owed by the purchaser, a monetary debt
The Istisna'a contract is rescinded upon delivery
The manufactured asset has been consumed and so no longer exists
Ownership of the asset reverts to the manufacturer
explanation: Per the Basis, after delivery to the ultimate purchaser the certificate represents the price in the purchaser's liability, a monetary debt, so debt-trading rules apply.

title: Financial Paper (Shares and Bonds)
q: Bank A did not subscribe to a bond issue but wants to buy the bonds in the secondary market and pledge them. What is the ruling?
options: Only pledging is prohibited, not buying
Permitted, if bought below face value
Prohibited, as trading and pledging bonds are barred
Permitted, since Bank A was not the original lender to the issuer
explanation: Per 5, trading in bonds, sale and purchase, is prohibited, and so is their pledging and endorsement.

title: Procrastinating Debtor
q: A supply contractor owes Bank A 20,000 under a penalty clause but refuses to pay. The Bank still owes him 50,000 under the contract. What may the Bank do?
options: Charge him an extra penalty on top for his refusal to pay
Deduct the 20,000 from the amount it owes him
Cancel the contract and keep the 50,000 it still owes him
Waive the penalty as unenforceable
explanation: Per 2/3, if the contractor refuses to pay a penalty, default rulings apply, and the amount may be deducted from amounts outstanding to the contractor.

title: Mortgage and its Contemporary Applications
q: Bank A and a client agree to place a mortgaged machine with a notary. Later the Bank wants to move it to its own warehouse. May it?
options: Yes, after notifying the notary and the client in writing in advance
Yes, since the Bank is the mortgagee
No, unless the client is in default
No; neither party may transfer it to another location
explanation: Per 3/1/3, the mortgage can be kept by a notary agreed by both parties; when kept by a notary, neither party has the right to transfer it elsewhere.

title: Monetization (Tawarruq)
q: A customer with prior interest-based debts asks Bank A to use Monetization to help him settle them. According to the Shari'ah basis, what is the position?
options: Permitted after ensuring his genuine intent to stop usurious dealings
Never permitted, since it would help him benefit from a Riba transaction
Permitted without conditions, as any Monetization is lawful
Permitted only if the debts are owed to an Islamic bank
explanation: Per the Shari'ah basis, Monetization may help clients dispose of previous interest-based debts after ensuring they genuinely intend not to deal in usurious transactions again.

title: Sharikah (Musharakah) and Modern Corporations
q: A manufacturing firm contributes its net assets, which include some receivables, as its share in a Sharikah. Is the inclusion of receivables acceptable?
options: No, any debt in a contribution invalidates the capital
Yes, since the debts are inseparable from the other assets
No, the receivables must first be removed from the net assets
Yes, but only if the receivables exceed the tangible assets
explanation: Per 3/1/2/4, debts may form part of the capital contribution where inseparable from other assets, e.g. a manufacturing firm contributing its net assets.

title: Investment Sukuk
q: Sukuk proceeds are used, under a Mugharasah contract, to plant trees and cover the work and expenses of the plantation. What do the certificate holders become entitled to?
options: A share in both the land and the plantation
A fixed rental paid by the owner of the land
A share in the crop only, without any share in land
Return of their capital plus an agreed fixed profit
explanation: Per 3/9, Mugharasah Sukuk holders become entitled to a share in the land and the plantation.

title: Sale of Debt
q: A debtor repays a currency loan at the rate of the loan date rather than the settlement day. Why does the standard reject this?
options: It turns the loan into a Salam contract
