explanation: The basis: the employee is entitled since he fulfilled the condition of being at the employer's disposal, while the employer has no excuse for not benefiting.

title: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
q: Bank A sells land to Company X, with a cooling-off option held by Bank A alone. During the option period, who owns the land?
options: Company X, from the moment of contract, subject to Bank A's right to revoke
Company X, once it pays the price
Bank A; ownership does not transfer to Company X
Both jointly, in proportion to the price paid, until the option expires
explanation: Per 2/5/1, if the option is held by both parties or only the seller, ownership of neither countervalue transfers and rights remain solely with the seller.

title: Arbitration
q: Bank A and Company X had no arbitration clause. A dispute arises and the law of their country imposes arbitration on them. Is this a recognized form of resorting to arbitration?
options: No; arbitration is valid only if agreed in the original contract
No; arbitration must be agreed at the time of dispute
Yes, but only if both parties later sign a new contract
Yes; arbitration can also be legally imposed on the parties
explanation: Per 3/1, arbitration can be sought by agreement at the time of dispute, by a previous agreement, or it can be legally imposed on the two parties.

title: Mudarabah
q: Bank A holds a guarantee from its Mudarib. The Mudarabah loses money due to a general recession, with no fault by the Mudarib. May Bank A enforce the guarantee?
options: No, guarantees are never permitted in a Mudarabah
No, only for misconduct, negligence or breach of terms
Yes, but only up to the amount of the profit expected from the Mudarabah
Yes, guarantees in Mudarabah cover every capital loss, whatever its cause
explanation: Per clause 6, the capital provider may obtain adequate guarantees but may not enforce them except in cases of misconduct, negligence or breach of contract.

title: Sale of Debt
q: Under a permitted new Murabaha, the sale proceeds are credited to the customer's account at Bank A. When may he choose to settle his first debt with them?
options: After one working day following receipt
Immediately, by automatic debit on receipt
Only after the new Murabaha matures
Never, as proceeds can't settle the old debt
explanation: Per 4/1/3/4(c), the customer may freely dispose of the proceeds, including settling the first debt after one working day following receipt.

title: Credit Agreement
q: Under the Fatwa cited in the basis, how must the contract for preparing a client's credit study relate to the financing contracts?
options: It must be part of the facility letter for the limit
It must be merged into the Mudarabah or Musharakah deal
It must be a special contract fully separate from them
It must be a clause inside the Murabahah contract
explanation: The cited Fatwa (Aayan: 189) requires special contracts for the study, completely separate from the financing and legal contracts of the deals.

title: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
q: After deciding to convert, Bank A wants to keep its non-permissible transactions running for two more years for convenience. Is this allowed?
options: Yes, until the existing contracts mature
Yes, if done within the announced period
Yes, if the resulting profits are given to charity meanwhile
No, delay is allowed only for necessity or pressing need
explanation: Per 2/1, pre-decision transactions must in principle cease or be disposed of immediately; delay is not permissible unless it is a necessity or pressing need.

title: Commercial Papers
q: Bank A issues travellers' cheques and wants to charge a commission on issue and on payment. What is the ruling?
options: Permissible for intermediation, provided it includes no Riba
Permissible only as a percentage for each day held
Permissible only on issue, never at the time of payment
Not permissible, as travellers' cheques are loans
explanation: Per 3/3(e), the institution issuing travellers' cheques may take commission for intermediation on issue or at payment, provided this does not include Riba.

title: Financial Paper (Shares and Bonds)
q: Company X holds interest-taking deposits equal to 25% of its market capitalization. Its other ratios are within limits. May Bank A invest in its shares?
options: Yes, as such deposits are not counted at all in the permitted ratios
Yes; interest-taking deposits are within the 30% limit
No; the limit for such deposits is 10% of the market capitalization
No; any interest-taking deposits bar investment in the company's shares
explanation: Per 3/4/3, total interest-taking deposits must not exceed 30% of market capitalization; such deposits remain prohibited whatever their amount.

title: Investment Sukuk
q: Company X issues Mudarabah Sukuk to manage a trading activity with the subscription funds. What are the roles of Company X and the subscribers?
options: Company X is the owner of capital; subscribers are the Mudarib
Company X is an investment agent; subscribers are principals
Company X is a borrower; subscribers are its creditors
Company X is the Mudarib; subscribers are the owners of capital
explanation: Per 5/1/5/7, in Mudarabah Sukuk the issuer is the Mudarib, the subscribers are the owners of capital and the funds are the Mudarabah capital.

title: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
q: Which evidence does the standard cite for classifying gold as a Ribawi item?
options: The consensus of jurists on the permissibility of Salam with gold
The maxim that the majority is tantamount to the whole in ruling
'Ubaidah bin al-Samit's Hadith: gold for gold, like for like
The precedent of early jurists on endowing money
explanation: The Basis cites the Hadith narrated by 'Ubaidah bin al-Samit: "Gold for gold... like for like... hand in hand."

title: Documentary Credit
q: A client wants to buy imported goods from Bank A through Murabahah financing of a documentary credit. Who should buy the goods from the supplier?
options: The client, with Bank A paying the price to the supplier as a loan
Bank A, which then sells them to the client by Murabahah
The supplier's bank, acting as agent of the client for the purchase
The client, who then sells them to Bank A before it resells them to him
explanation: Per 3/5/2, the Institution should be the party that purchases from the supplier and then sells to the client through Murabahah.

title: Al-Wakalah Bi Al-Istithmar (Investment Agency)
q: A fixed-term investment agency gives the principal a right to terminate unilaterally if the agent's Shari'ah supervision licence is withdrawn. Is this clause permissible?
options: Yes; a unilateral right may be stipulated for specific circumstances
Yes, but such a right may be given only to the agent
Yes, but only in an unremunerated investment agency
No; a binding contract of fixed term can contain no right of unilateral termination
explanation: Per 4/2, where the parties agreed not to terminate for a specified period, the contract may stipulate one party's right to terminate unilaterally in specific circumstances.

title: Mortgage and its Contemporary Applications
q: A client offers Bank A preference shares and interest-based bonds as mortgage for a Murabahah debt. What is the ruling?
options: Permissible, as the Bank only holds them as security
Permissible if the bonds are government-issued
Permissible, if the Bank donates the interest earned
Impermissible, as Shari'ah bars their issue and trading
explanation: Per 4/3, papers that may not be issued or transacted under Shari'ah, e.g. interest-based bonds, preference shares and enjoyment shares, cannot be mortgaged.

title: Loan (Qard)
q: Company X lends Ahmad 5,000 on condition that Ahmad lets Company X use his delivery van free of charge during the loan period. What is the ruling?
options: Permitted, as the benefit is a use of property, not tangible property
Permitted, provided the loan has a fixed period
Prohibited: a stipulated benefit for the lender is Riba
Permitted, as no extra money is repaid
explanation: Per 4/1, a stipulated excess for the lender amounts to Riba whether it is a tangible thing or a benefit.

title: Waqf
q: A Waqf's annual income is ready for distribution, but its building needs scheduled maintenance. The Waqif set no condition on maintenance. What should the superintendent do?
options: Maintain only if the Waqif had stipulated it
Distribute first, then maintain from next year's income
Seek the beneficiaries' consent before maintaining
Spend on maintenance before distributing to beneficiaries
explanation: Per 8/1/1, spending on maintenance and renovation precedes distribution of income, and does not require a prior condition stipulated by the Waqif.

title: Sharikah (Musharakah) and Modern Corporations
q: Per the Shari'ah basis, why is a joint-liability partner barred from bringing in a substitute without the other partners' consent?
options: The partner's personality and personal assets matter to them
Shares in such companies cannot be sold at all, even with the other partners' consent
The substitute would be a sleeping partner without any liability for the company's debts
It would change the company's juristic personality and so dissolve it by law
explanation: Per the basis, the partner's personality is significant because the company's liability includes his personal assets, and a substitute may be in a weaker position.

title: Zakah
q: Company X has trade goods in its Zakah base at market value and has booked a provision for decline in their value. Is the provision deducted?
options: Yes, but only up to 50% of the provision
No, since the goods are already at market value
Yes, if the provision is approved by auditors
Yes, in full as a liability of the company
explanation: Per 7/2/2, as Zakah uses market value, provisions on current assets are not deducted, unless assets are valued at book value above exchange value.

title: Insolvency
q: Company X is declared insolvent. Customer Y owes X a deferred amount due in one year. How is this receivable treated?
options: It is excluded from the insolvency assets
It is written off to protect Customer Y
It stays deferred, joins the insolvency assets and is paid out when collected
It becomes due immediately upon X's insolvency, so Customer Y must pay it at once to the creditors
explanation: Per 5/7, undue debts owed to the insolvent do not become due; they are included in the insolvency assets and distributed to creditors as and when paid.

title: Documentary Credit
q: A seller requires the buyer to open a credit as a condition of the sale. Per the Shari'ah basis, what is this condition likened to?
options: A stipulation to pay part of the price in advance, as in Salam
A stipulation that the seller may revoke the sale if payment is late
A stipulation for a penalty on late payment of the price by the buyer
A stipulation to provide a specific guarantor for payment
explanation: Per the basis, making a credit a condition in the sale is similar to a stipulation to provide a specific guarantor for payment, a valid condition in the contract's interest.

title: Irrigation Partnership (Musaqat)
q: The parties to a Musaqat obtain Takaful cover for the orchard's crop. Nothing is agreed on who pays. How is the Takaful cost borne?
options: By the owner alone, as owner of the trees
Equally, regardless of their shares
By both parties, in proportion to their shares
By the worker alone, as manager of the work
explanation: Per 8/2, the worker and owner bear the partnership's expenses, including Takaful insurance, in proportion to their shares unless agreed otherwise.

title: Liability of the Investment Manager
q: Why does the standard exclude opportunity cost from the investment manager's liability, even where misconduct is established?
options: It is covered by the presumption of non-liability
It is non-existing and unrealized Mal
Rab Al Maal has waived it by consent
His possession of the funds is fiduciary
explanation: Per the Basis, opportunity cost is non-existing, unrealized money (Mal) and cannot lead to liability; realized profit is treated as capital.

title: Mortgage and its Contemporary Applications
q: A mortgaged current account is converted by agreement into an investment account at Bank A. What are the parties' roles?
options: The holder is Rab al-Mal and the Bank is Mudarib
The holder and the Bank are Musharakah partners
The Bank is Rab al-Mal and the holder is Mudarib
The holder is lender and the Bank is borrower
explanation: Per 5, on transfer to an investment account the holder gets his profit share as owner of capital (Rab al-Mal) and the Institution as worker (Mudarib).

title: Islamic Reinsurance
q: A reinsurance company acting as agent claims it must guarantee the reinsurance account's losses. Per the basis, what is the rule?
options: An agent guarantees half of any loss
An agent guarantees only for transgression, negligence or breach
An agent guarantees if it charges a fee
An agent always guarantees the principal's funds whether at fault or not
explanation: Per the basis, by unanimous agreement of Fiqh scholars an agent should not guarantee except in case of transgression, negligence or breach of the contract.

title: Buyback
q: Why may a partner in a joint enterprise promise to buy his partner's share at market value but not at a predetermined price?
options: Market value reflects the partnership's profit or loss
Market value avoids a deferred Sarf between the partners' shares
The partner is an outsider to the other's share
A set price makes the promise a contingent sale of the share
explanation: Per the Basis, a predetermined price contradicts profit and loss sharing; market value reflects the partnership's profit or loss at execution.

title: Waqf
q: Ahmad creates a Waqf whose revenue will go to poor persons and a university research centre. Based on the Waqf beneficiary, what type of Waqf is this?
options: Joint Waqf
Private or Dynasty Waqf
Self Waqf
Charitable Waqf
explanation: Per 2/2/1/1, a Charitable Waqf is one whose revenue and benefit go to general charitable causes such as poor persons, research centres and universities.

title: Mudarabah
q: Per the Shari'ah basis, why is a Mudarabah initially a non-binding contract?
options: The capital is a loan payable on demand
The profit ratio is not yet known at signing
The Mudarib is an agent, and agency is not binding
The capital provider is a guarantor of the Mudarib
explanation: Per the basis, the Mudarib uses the provider's funds with consent as an agent, and an agency contract is not binding.

title: Istisna’a and Parallel Istisna’a
q: Bank A acts as the builder (contractor) for a customer's office tower under an Istisna'a. Does the Istisna'a standard cover the Bank in this role?
options: Yes, it covers the Institution as purchaser or maker
No, it covers the Institution only as the ultimate purchaser
No, construction contracts fall outside Istisna'a
Only if the Bank builds with its own staff
explanation: Per clause 1, the standard covers Istisna'a and Parallel Istisna'a whether the Institution is the ultimate purchaser or the manufacturer or builder.

title: Murabahah
q: After a customer has given his promise, but before the Murabahah is executed, Bank A wants to increase the mark-up. Can it do so?
options: No, the terms of a promise can never be revised
Only with the customer's consent
Yes, unilaterally, as only the customer is bound
Yes, by giving the customer written notice
explanation: Per 2/3/4, the terms of the promise (deferment, mark-up, etc.) may be revised before execution, but only by mutual consent of both parties.

title: Loan (Qard)
q: A trainee asks why the subject-matter of Qard must be fungible. What reason does the Shari'ah basis give?
options: Non-fungible items cannot be possessed by the borrower under a loan
Fungible items cannot be the subject of Riba, so they suit a loan
Only fungible items have a market price, which the borrower must repay
Only a fungible item can be returned by a similar substitute
explanation: Per the Basis, only a fungible item can be returned by the borrower; fungible items are also compensated by similar substitutes in usurpation and destruction.

title: Liability of the Investment Manager
q: Bank A, as investment agent, is instructed not to invest in real estate but does so anyway, and the property falls in value. Is Bank A liable for the loss?
options: No, unless the loss exceeds half of the capital
Yes, but only up to the agency fee it received
Yes, because it breached the conditions
No, its possession is fiduciary in all cases
explanation: Per 3/1, the investment manager is not liable unless there is misconduct, negligence, or breach of conditions; here conditions were breached.

title: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
q: Bank A's unrestricted investment accounts incur a loss with no transgression, negligence or breach by the Bank. Who bears the loss?
options: The Bank as Mudarib, from its own funds
The Bank and the holders in the profit-sharing ratio
The shareholders, as the Bank guarantees the investment accounts' capital
The account holders, in proportion to their shares in the capital
explanation: Per 2/1/1, holders of unrestricted accounts bear all losses in proportion to their capital shares, except losses from transgression, negligence or breach, borne by the Institution.

title: Concession Contracts
q: The State grants Company X the right to manage a port for an annual fee of 5% of the port's total income. How is the contract adapted?
options: As Mudarabah
As Ijarah
As Ju'alah
As Istisna'a
explanation: Per 10/2/1, where the management concession price is a lump sum or percentage of total income, the contract between the State and licensee is Ijarah.

title: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
q: Per the basis, why is selling abstract rights such as Shuf'ah or options impermissible?
options: They are rights in rem attached to property and so are inseparable from the owner
They are protected as intangible assets
No Shari'ah monetary value, plus Gharar and Jahalah
They can be inherited by the heirs
explanation: Per the basis, the impermissibility of selling the abstract rights in item 10 rests on their lack of monetary value in Shari'ah and the presence of Gharar and Jahalah.

title: Sharikah (Musharakah) and Modern Corporations
q: In a Sharikat al-'Inan with no restriction on management, partner Ahmad sells partnership goods on deferred payment and rents out a partnership asset without consulting others. Was he entitled?
options: Yes, each partner may in principle do such acts in the partnership's interest
Yes, but only for spot sales; renting out partnership assets needs consent
No, deferred sales require the prior consent of all the other partners
No, only the partner with the largest capital share may act for the partnership
explanation: Per 3/1/3/1, each partner may in principle act for the partnership in spot or deferred sales, renting its assets and what is customary in trading.

title: Sale of Debt
q: Bank A sells a receivable to Company Y in a permitted form without asking the debtor; their original contract is silent on this. Is the sale valid?
options: No, the debtor must consent to any sale
Yes, the debtor's consent is not required
Yes, but only if the debt is secured
No, unless the debtor is notified first
explanation: Per 5/6, the debtor's consent is not required for sale of the debt to a third party unless the debtor and creditor agreed otherwise.

title: Impact of Contingent Incidents on Commitments
q: Bank A and a client mutually agree to end a Murabahah facility early. A trainee calls this a contingent incident. Is he right?
options: No; termination by mutual consent is not a contingent incident
No; it is a contingent incident only if a court approves the ending
Yes, provided the termination causes harm to one of the parties
Yes; any early ending of a commitment, however it arises, is a contingent incident
explanation: Per 1 and 2, contingent incidents are sudden events with significant influence on commitments; termination on mutual consent or by a party's contractual right is distinct.

title: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
q: A trader sells a quantity of buried root crops (underground commodities) still in the ground to Company Y. How does the standard classify and treat this Gharar?
options: Excessive Gharar, which nullifies the contract
Medium Gharar, which makes the contract voidable
Minor Gharar, which nullifies only the price clause
Medium Gharar, which does not affect the contract
explanation: Per 4/2/3, sale of underground commodities is an example of medium Gharar, which does not affect the contract.

title: Guarantees
q: A depositor demands that Bank A, holding his goods on trust, be liable for their loss in all cases. Per the Shari'ah basis, why is the Bank not liable?
options: The depositor waived his rights by depositing
Deposits are owned by the trustee once received
A trustee is liable only for misconduct, negligence or breach
Loss of trust assets is borne by the trustee as a matter of principle
explanation: Per the Basis, a trustee is not liable for loss except for misconduct, negligence or violation of conditions; otherwise liability conflicts with the nature of trusts.

title: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
q: Bank A leases a warehouse to Company X at a fixed monthly rent, but the lease contract specifies no period at all. What is the status of the lease?
options: Valid, but either party may end it on notice
Void, as this is excessive Gharar
Valid, as the Gharar is only medium
Valid, as the monthly rent is known
explanation: Per 4/2/1, signing a lease contract for an unspecified period is an example of excessive Gharar, which sets the contract null and void.

title: Zakah
q: Company X has an end-of-service benefits provision; part is due for payment this year but unpaid. What may be deducted from Zakatable assets?
options: Nothing in any case
The entire provision balance, as it is a liability of the company towards its employees
Only the part that is paid or due this year
Half of the provision
explanation: Per 7/3/6, end-of-service provisions are not deducted as merely allocated; they are deducted only when actually paid or when due in the current year.

title: Ju’alah
q: A worker starts a Ju'alah task, then walks away from it on his own. The parties had made no special agreement. What can he claim?
options: Nothing from the offeror
A pro rata share of the reward
The full reward if the offeror benefited
Reasonable wages for work done
explanation: Per 6/3-6/4, if the worker terminates after commencing work, he is not entitled to a reward and has no claim against the offeror unless otherwise agreed.

title: Debit Card, Charge Card and Credit Card
q: Bank A charges merchants that accept its card a commission of 2% of the purchase price of goods bought with the card. What is the ruling?
options: Permissible only if borne by the cardholder
Not permissible, as it is interest on the credit
Permissible only as a flat fee per transaction
Permissible as a percentage of the purchase price
explanation: Per 4/2, the issuer may charge the party accepting the card a commission at a percentage of the purchase price of items and services bought with it.

title: Insolvency
q: Ahmad, facing an insolvency claim, plans a long trip abroad that would harm his creditors. What may the creditors seek?
options: An absolute travel ban for the whole period of the claim, even if guarantors are provided
Nothing, as travel can be restricted only after a declaration
Prevention of the travel unless he appoints a surety for his attendance
An order that he pay all debts in full before departing
explanation: Per 4/2/7, creditors may seek to prevent travel that harms them where the debtor does not appoint a surety to ensure his attendance, providing guarantors.

title: Al-Wakalah Bi Al-Istithmar (Investment Agency)
q: With the principal's consent, Bank A appointed Company Y as sub-agent. Bank A now wishes to dismiss Company Y. Can it?
options: No; only the principal can dismiss Company Y
Yes, as the agent who appointed it
No; nobody may dismiss it before term ends
Yes, with notice to the principal
explanation: Per 9/2, a sub-agent appointed with the principal's consent can be dismissed only by the principal, unless the agent was authorised to appoint any sub-agent at will.

title: Banking Services in Islamic Banks
q: Bank A arranges for a third party to underwrite a company's share subscription. May Bank A charge a fee for this arrangement?
options: No, any fee linked to underwriting is barred, even for arrangement
Yes, it may receive fees for arranging the third party
No, unless Bank A also underwrites itself
Yes, but only its actual expenses
explanation: Per 2/3/2, the Institution may arrange, and receive fees for, engaging a third party to underwrite the subscription.

title: Liability of the Investment Manager
q: The Mudarib in Mudaraba Sukuk undertakes to purchase the underlying assets from the certificateholders at maturity. At which price is this undertaking permitted?
options: At the face value of the Sukuk at issuance
At a price specified when making the contract
At the original capital plus expected profit
At the net asset value at the time of purchase
explanation: Per 3/5/1, an undertaking at a price specified at contract is prohibited; it is permitted at NAV, market value, fair value or a price agreed at purchase.

title: Indices
q: A buyer's binding pledge to buy a commodity states that any rise in a set index since a given date, compared with the commodity price, will be added to the price. Ruling?
options: Not permissible, as pledges cannot be indexed
Permissible only if the index is a falling one
Permissible
Not permissible, as the price becomes unknown
explanation: Per 5/7, fulfillment of a binding pledge of a buyer or seller may be linked to the rate of change of an index versus the commodity price at a set date.

title: Concession Contracts
q: Before production starts, the State sets how a licensee must dispose of its share of the extracted minerals and the value to be paid to it. Is this within the State's rights?
options: No; only market forces may set the value
Yes, but only after production has begun
No; the licensee freely owns its share
Yes, taking into account public interest
explanation: Per 5/7/1, the State may determine in advance how the licensee disposes of its share of the products and the value paid, taking public interest into account.

title: Ijarah and Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek
q: In January, Bank A signs an Ijarah contract under which the lease period starts in March. What is this arrangement?
options: A valid future Ijarah
Valid only if rent is paid from January
A promise to lease, not a contract
Void, as Ijarah must start on signing
explanation: Per 4/1/2, the period starts on execution unless the parties agree on a future commencement date, resulting in a future Ijarah.

title: Impact of Contingent Incidents on Commitments
q: On which evidence are the rulings on Jawa'ih (calamities) based?
options: The view of Al-Shatibi that Shari'ah has no room for futility
The Hadith forbidding Bay' al-Sinin and permitting discounts on calamities
The consensus that a lessor may cancel a lease for any excuse
The Hadith that an extorter is indebted with what he takes until he returns it
explanation: Per the basis, Jawa'ih rulings rest on the Hadith in which the Prophet forbade Bay' al-Sinin and permitted value discounts on calamities.

title: Murabahah
q: Goods insured by Bank A are destroyed before their sale to the customer. The insurance payout exceeds their purchase price. Who is entitled to the payout?
options: Bank A exclusively
Bank A up to cost; the rest to the customer
Bank A and the customer equally
The customer, as the intended buyer
explanation: Per 3/2/6, insurance before sale lies with the Institution as owner; any recovery belongs to it exclusively, even if it exceeds the purchase price.

title: Hiring of Persons
q: A hiring contract for a private employee is silent on when pay is made. When is the pay due, and what may the employee do if it is delayed despite notice?
options: At signing; he may then sue for damages only, but not stop work
At signing; he may then demand a late fee
Monthly by default; he must keep working
At expiry of the hiring period; he may then stop work
explanation: Per 7/2/1(a), absent agreement, pay is due after complete service or at expiry of the period for private employment; if delayed despite notice he may stop work.

title: Istisna’a and Parallel Istisna’a
q: An Istisna'a includes a fair penalty clause for late delivery by the manufacturer. The delay is due to force majeure. Is the penalty due?
options: Yes, but reduced by half for force majeure
Yes, a penalty clause applies regardless of the cause
No, it applies only if delay is not force majeure
No, penalty clauses are never allowed
explanation: Per 6/6, a fair penalty for late delivery may be stipulated, but compensation is permissible only if the delay is not due to force majeure.

title: Financial Paper (Shares and Bonds)
q: During subscription, before business starts, a new corporation's assets are exclusively cash. Ahmad wants to sell his shares. On what terms is this permissible?
options: At nominal value, with deferred payment allowed
Only at nominal value, with delivery of possession
Only under the rules of dealing in debts
At any market price agreed by the parties
explanation: Per 3/17, when the assets are exclusively cash, shares may be traded only at nominal value and with delivery of possession.

title: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
q: Why is a contract involving Gharar in its form (offer and acceptance) null and void, according to the Shari'ah basis?
options: Its price becomes unknown to the parties until delivery
Its subject matter cannot be delivered
It turns the contract into a donation
It stays unconcluded, as finalization is only probable
explanation: Per the basis, a contract with Gharar in its form remains unconcluded; such Gharar makes finalization of the contract probable rather than definite.

title: Arbitration
q: Per the Shari'ah basis, what conditions should, in principle, govern the selection of arbitrators?
options: Only the conditions agreed by the parties
Shari'ah conditions for selecting judges, incl. non-partiality
Only the licensing rules of the host country
Only the experience requirements of the Institution and the parties
explanation: The basis states that selection of arbitrators should in principle follow the same Shari'ah conditions for selection of judges, including non-partiality.

title: Salam and Parallel Salam
q: Bank A wants a Salam for branded products made in approximate units with standardised specifications, regularly available at any time. May they be al-Muslam Fihi?
options: Yes, they are goods without significant variation
No, Salam is limited to agricultural crops and livestock
No, manufactured goods can be sold by Istisna'a only
Yes, but only if one specific unit is named in the contract
explanation: Per 3/2/2, products identified by trademarks and standard specifications and commonly available are items where variations make no difference (read with 3/2/8).

title: Guarantees
q: Per the Shari'ah basis, why may a creditor demand all instalments on default instead of waiting for each due date?
options: The creditor is owed compensation for delay
The guarantor's liability ends on default
The debtor might hide his assets and claim insolvency
Deferred instalments are unlawful in principle under Shari'ah
explanation: Per the Basis, the creditor may accelerate because during the delay the debtor may conceal assets and claim insolvency; deferral is the debtor's right he may forgo.

title: Mortgage and its Contemporary Applications
q: A farmer offers Bank A a stock of fresh vegetables as mortgage for a debt. May perishable objects be mortgaged?
options: Yes, but only if the debt matures within a week
Yes, as they can be sold and replaced by their value
No; only tangible durable assets may be mortgaged
No; perishable objects cannot be possessed
explanation: Per 3/2/2, perishable objects can be mortgaged as they can be sold and replaced by their value.

title: Sharikah (Musharakah) and Modern Corporations
q: In a three-partner Sharikah with no agreed term, one partner gives due notice and withdraws. What is the effect?
options: He takes his share; the other partners' partnership continues
He may not withdraw until the venture is complete
The whole partnership terminates automatically, as it lacks an agreed term
He forfeits his share as a penalty for leaving
explanation: Per 3/1/6/1, each partner may withdraw after due notice and take his share; this does not necessitate termination of the remaining partners' partnership.

title: Commercial Papers
q: Which practice of the Companions does the Shari'ah basis cite to support dealing in bills of exchange?
options: Al-'Abbas set conditions on the travel of his Mudarib with his capital
Umar gave an orphan's funds to a trader for trade in Iraq
Ibn Abbas took silver at Mecca and wrote notes payable at Kufa
Abu Qatadah took on the two dinars of debt of a deceased man
explanation: The basis cites Ibn Abbas taking silver from traders at Mecca and writing a demand note payable at Kufa, and Ibn Al-Zubayr's similar notes on his brother in Iraq.

title: Financial Paper (Shares and Bonds)
q: A retail company with permissible primary activity earns 7% of its total income from prohibited sources. May Bank A invest in its shares?
options: Yes, as its primary activity is permissible
Yes, as prohibited income is below 10%
Yes, if Bank A eliminates the 7% portion
No; prohibited income exceeds 5% of total income
explanation: Per 3/4/4, income from a prohibited component must not exceed 5% of the corporation's total income, whatever its source.

title: Waqf
q: Ahmad declares a Waqf effective from next year. By analogy to which contract does the Shari'ah basis justify such a future-dated Waqf?
options: Ijarah (lease)
'Ariyah (lending)
Wasiyyah (will)
Hibah (gift) with possession
explanation: The basis states that permissibility of declaring Waqf effective from a future date is viewed by analogy between Waqf and Wasiyyah (will).

title: Zakah
q: Company X keeps a current account with Bank B and (against Shari'ah) receives interest on it. How should it treat this for Zakah?
options: Pay no Zakah at all on a current account balance
Pay Zakah on the principal plus all the interest
Pay Zakah on the interest only and keep the principal
Pay Zakah on the principal and donate all the interest
explanation: Per 5/1/3/1, Zakah is paid from current accounts with other Institutions; any interest (prohibited) is donated entirely to charitable purposes.

title: Indices
q: Two parties agree that one will pay the other if a share index closes above 5,000 next month, with no assets bought or sold. They call it a hedge. What is the ruling?
options: Prohibited, even if practiced for hedging
Permissible, if the amounts are small
Permissible, if the index is an Islamic one
Permissible, since its purpose is hedging
explanation: Per 6/1, paying or receiving money on mere index readings without buying or selling real assets is prohibited even if practiced for hedging.

title: Debit Card, Charge Card and Credit Card
q: Bank A issues a card only to customers with available funds; purchases and withdrawals are debited to the account at once. Which feature marks it as a debit card?
options: It gives revolving credit within a set ceiling
It gives no credit and is limited to the credit balance
It must be settled in full at the end of a credit period
It gives free credit until the monthly statement is issued
explanation: Per 2/1/1-2/1/2, a debit card is issued against available funds, debits the account immediately up to the credit balance, and provides no credit.

title: Islamic Reinsurance
q: Per the basis, what supports Islamic insurers reinsuring with traditional reinsurers in some cases?
options: The view that Gharar does not affect exchange-based reinsurance contracts
The lower cost of traditional reinsurance cover
The agency nature of traditional reinsurers
Practical necessity and dire public need ranking as necessity
explanation: Per the basis, permissibility rests on practical necessity from lack of Islamic cover and dire public need ranking as necessity, recognised by Qur'an and Sunnah.

title: Possession (Qabd)
q: Two traders exchange gold for gold. Which evidence does the standard cite as the basis for actual physical possession in gold, silver and currencies?
options: The verse: 'No ground can there be against those who do good'
The hadith of Ubadah Ibn Al-Samit: 'like for like... from hand to hand'
The hadith: 'He who buys food is not to sell it until he has measured it'
The maxim: 'Gains are based on the bearing of costs'
explanation: Per the Basis, actual possession in gold, silver and currencies rests on the hadith of Ubadah Ibn Al-Samit: 'Gold for gold... like for like... from hand to hand.'

title: Guarantees
q: Bank A charges an applicant administrative expenses for issuing a final letter of guarantee. What limit applies to these charges?
options: They may not exceed 1% of the guaranteed amount
They must reflect the amount and the duration of the guarantee
They may not exceed what others charge for such services
No limit applies, as expenses are freely agreed
explanation: Per 6/1/2, administrative expenses may be charged for preliminary or final letters of guarantee, provided they do not exceed the commission others charge.

title: Islamic Reinsurance
q: Per the basis, why does Gharar not invalidate cooperative (solidarity) reinsurance?
options: Gharar does not affect donation-based contracts
Gharar is permitted in all insurance contracts
The reinsurer guarantees all claims in advance
Cooperative reinsurance involves no uncertainty at all
explanation: Per the basis, cooperative insurance rests on cooperation and donation, and it is a well-known Fiqh axiom that Gharar does not affect donation-based contracts.

title: Possession (Qabd)
q: A trainee asks whether the standard on Possession (Qabd) governs possession of a car taken by usurpation (Ghasb). What is the answer?
options: Yes; it covers every form of possession, whether by contract or not
No; it covers only possession of immovable property
No; acts other than contracts, like Ghasb, fall outside its scope
Yes, but only as regards the usurper's liability for compensation
explanation: Per Scope (1), the standard covers possession in contracts and does not cover acts other than contracts, like possession in usurpation (Ghasb).

title: Waqf
q: Bank A offers a Waqf superintendent financing secured by a mortgage over the Waqf building. May the superintendent mortgage the Waqf asset?
options: Yes, if the debt is for the Waqf's benefit
No; mortgaging Waqf assets is not allowed
Yes, for a short-term debt only
Yes, if the beneficiaries agree
explanation: Per 5/3/4, the superintendent shall not mortgage the Waqf assets for a debt to be obtained for the Waqf or the beneficiaries.

title: Mudarabah
q: In an unrestricted Mudarabah, the Mudarib appoints another person to buy a commodity and sells goods on deferred payment. Were these actions within his powers?
options: Yes, each is within an unrestricted Mudarib's powers
No, deferred sales need the capital provider's consent
No, he must personally do all the work himself
Only the appointment is allowed, not deferred sales
explanation: Per 9/1/2 and 9/1/5, an unrestricted Mudarib may appoint another to carry out work, such as buying a commodity, and may buy and sell on deferred payment.

title: Islamic Insurance
q: A student asks why Gharar does not invalidate cooperative insurance. Per the basis, what is the answer?
options: Necessity removes the effect of Gharar
The company guarantees all the claims, so no uncertainty remains
The amounts involved are always small, so the Gharar is minor
It rests on donation, where Gharar has no impact
explanation: The basis: cooperative insurance rests on cooperation and donation, not Mu'awadah, and per the Maliki School Gharar has no impact on donation contracts.

title: Zakah
q: Company X received rent in advance for services not yet provided, and separately received earnest money on a sale whose goods are undelivered. Which is deducted?
options: Each of the two amounts in full
Neither of the two amounts
The prepaid income for undelivered services
The earnest money received on the sale
explanation: Per 6/3/9, prepaid income for undelivered services is deducted since not finally owned; earnest money on exchange contracts is owned and not deducted.

title: Murabahah
q: Bank A argues it may charge a commitment fee because it reserved funds for the customer. Why is such a fee impermissible, per the Shari'ah basis?
options: It is paid for a right to contract, which is not exchangeable
It is not proportional to the work and effort done by the Bank
It is paid to a third party rather than to the Bank itself
It is part of the cost of the item sold to the customer
explanation: The basis: a commitment fee is in exchange for the right to contract, a mere intention and wish that is not a subject of exchange.

title: Waqf
q: A financier and a Waqf develop Waqf land via Diminishing Musharaka ending in transfer of the buildings to the Waqf. What is the status of the land?
options: It is pledged to secure the financier's share
It is sold to the financier and leased back to the Waqf for the term
It becomes jointly owned with the financier in proportion to the funds
It is not part of the Musharaka; building rents are shared
explanation: Per 8/6/2, the Waqf land is not the subject of Musharaka; building rental revenues are shared until the Waqf owns all the buildings.

title: Mortgage and its Contemporary Applications
q: A client offers Bank A a stock of wine as mortgage for a Murabahah debt. What is the ruling?
options: Acceptable, if the client is not a Muslim
Not acceptable; it must be Shari'ah-permissible property
Acceptable, if its value exceeds the debt amount
Acceptable, if the Bank never takes physical possession
explanation: Per 3/2/1, the mortgaged asset must be Shari'ah-permissible property, well specified, and deliverable.

title: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
q: Bank A buys shares of a non-gold company holding some gold, without spot exchange. Which maxim does the standard cite for exempting this from al-Sarf?
options: What is barred in itself may be allowed as an accessory
A promise cannot be the subject of a sale
A certificate is as good as physical possession
In ruling, the majority is tantamount to the whole in a mixed item
explanation: Per the Basis for 3/1/2, the maxim: a thing not permissible in itself may be permissible as an accessory (and implicitly).

title: Istisna’a and Parallel Istisna’a
q: As manufacturer in an Istisna'a, Bank A has a Parallel Istisna'a with a builder. Before delivery to the customer, who bears ownership risk and insurance costs?
options: The customer, as the ultimate purchaser
The builder, under the terms of the Parallel Istisna'a
Bank A, which cannot shift that risk to the builder
The builder and the customer equally
explanation: Per 7/3, the Institution as producer bears ownership risk, maintenance and insurance before delivery and may not transfer its risk towards the customer to the maker.

title: Unilateral and Bilateral Promise
q: An importer and Bank A use a binding bilateral promise when opening a letter of credit, as the seller does not yet own the goods. What does the Shari'ah basis rely on?
options: The consensus that a promise always creates a contract
An IIFA resolution permitting it where law, public interest or custom requires
The Hadith "Muslims are bound by their conditions"
The rule that all bilateral promises bind both parties, as they are equal to contracts
explanation: The basis cites an IIFA resolution: where a sale cannot be concluded as the seller does not own the goods, and public interest, law or custom requires (e.g. LCs), it may bind.

title: Financial Paper (Shares and Bonds)
q: What is the Shari'ah basis for permitting the issuance of shares of a corporation with permissible objectives?
options: The custom of stock markets, without other evidence
The rule that necessity permits what is prohibited
The rule that a Qard may yield a benefit to the lender if agreed
Evidences on contracts, partnership, 'Inan and Mudarabah
explanation: Per the Basis, it rests on the generality of evidences on abiding by contracts and conditions, partnership, 'Inan, Mudarabah, Musaqat and Muzara'ah.

title: Trading in Currencies
q: To hedge devaluation, Bank A lends Bank B USD interest-free, and Bank B lends Bank A the equivalent in EUR. When is this permissible?
options: If no extra benefit is given and they are not linked
If each loan carries the same modest rate of return
If both loans are repaid at a pre-agreed forward exchange rate
If the two loans are made conditional on each other
explanation: Per 2/4/1, back to back interest-free loans in different currencies are allowed without extra benefit, provided the two loans are not contractually connected.

title: Istisna’a and Parallel Istisna’a
q: A manufacturer offers to deliver conforming items two months early. The buyer refuses but has no good reason. What is the position?
options: Early delivery cancels the contract
The buyer may refuse until the due date
The buyer may accept at a discount
The buyer is obliged to accept them
explanation: Per 6/2, early delivery of conforming items is allowed; the buyer must accept unless he has a good reason for refusing.

title: Zakah
q: Company X has slow-moving trade goods and has made a provision for them. How are they treated for Zakah?
options: Valued at cost, since they are slow-moving; the provision is deducted from their value
Valued at market price as they are; the provision is not deducted
Excluded entirely from Zakatable assets
Valued at market price; the provision is also deducted
explanation: Per 5/2/6/1 and 7/3/3, slow-moving goods may be valued at market price in their current form; an allocation for them is not deducted from Zakatable assets.

title: Waqf
q: Ahmad signs a letter to a charity: "I undertake to create a Waqf over my land for you." Has a Waqf been concluded?
options: Yes, once the charity accepts the undertaking and takes possession
Yes, but it is treated as a bequest limited to one third
No, an undertaking to create a Waqf does not conclude it
Yes, since Waqf may be deferred to a future date
explanation: Per 2/4/1/2, the form of Waqf creation must be conclusive (jāzima); Waqf cannot be concluded with an undertaking to create Waqf.

title: Loan (Qard)
q: Bank A's current account funds are lost through no negligence of the bank. Why must Bank A still repay the holders, per the Basis?
options: Regulators require banks to insure all deposits against loss of any kind
Current accounts are Qard, so the bank guarantees repayment
Current accounts are Wadi'ah, so the bank is a trustee liable only for negligence
The bank promised a return on current accounts and must honour its promise
explanation: Per the Basis, the bank must return a similar amount even on loss without negligence; this is the purpose of Qard, unlike Wadi'ah, a trust not guaranteed absent negligence.

title: Sharikah (Musharakah) and Modern Corporations
q: Which of the following is listed by the standard among the traditional Fiqh-nominate partnerships rather than the modern corporations?
options: Allotment (Muhassah) partnership, a private form of company
Partnership in commendum, with managing and sleeping partners
Sharikat al-Wujuh (partnership of creditworthiness or reputation)
Company limited by shares, with managing and sleeping partners
explanation: Per 2/2/1, the traditional Fiqh-nominate partnerships are Sharikat al-'Inan, Sharikat al-Wujuh (or Al-Dhimam) and Sharikat al-A'mal; the others are modern corporations.

title: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
q: Under an either-or option, Ahmad takes delivery of three items priced 300, 600 and 900, to buy one. All three are destroyed in his possession. What must he pay?
options: 1,800: the price of all three items
900: the price of the dearest item
300: the price of the cheapest item
600: one third of each item's price
explanation: Per 4/2/1, if all items are destroyed and prices differ, the buyer pays the average price for the number purchased, e.g. one third of each item's price for one of three.

title: Mudarabah
q: Midway through a Mudarabah, accounts show a profit. When does the Mudarib's entitlement to his share become absolute?
options: Only after distribution on actual or constructive valuation
On the date when the Mudarabah contract was concluded
Only when the capital provider pays him a separate fee
As soon as any profit appears in the interim accounts
explanation: Per 8/8, the Mudarib is entitled once profit is realised, but this is subject to retention to protect capital and becomes absolute only after distribution.

title: Waqf
q: An overseer plans a 30-year Ijarah of Waqf land. What does the standard prefer for such a long-term lease?
options: Full rent for 30 years paid in advance
A fixed rent set once for all 30 years, to give the tenant certainty
A rent below the fair rate, to secure a long-term tenant
Variable rent linked to a benchmark, at least fair
explanation: Per 8/4, long Ijarah needs evident interest; in long-term Ijarah, a variable rent linked to a known benchmark is preferable, at least the fair rate.

title: Buyback
q: Bank A sells a commodity on deferred terms. The buyer later offers it in a public auction for cash, and Bank A wins the bid at a lower cash price. What is the ruling?
options: Permitted, even at a lower cash price
Permitted only above the deferred price
Prohibited unless a third party outbids it
Prohibited, as it is 'Inah through an auction
explanation: Per 4/3, it is permitted to sell on deferred terms and buy back from the auction, even at a lower cash price.

title: Payment Cards
q: Abroad, a shop lets Ahmad pay in his card's currency, with conversion done by an independent entity at a rate above actual cost. May Ahmad choose this?
options: Yes, only if his card is not lending-based
Yes, and that exchange need not abide by actual cost
No, he must pay in the local currency of the country he is in
No, the rate must equal the actual cost incurred by the issuer
explanation: Per 5/5/2, the holder may choose to pay in the card currency; the exchange is by an independent entity and need not abide by actual cost.

title: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
q: A non-paid agent has started a construction task that cannot be halted without harming the principal. The agent now wants to withdraw. What is the ruling?
options: He may withdraw only if he pays the principal compensation
He may withdraw at once, as non-paid agency is not binding on the agent
The agency is binding until work can be suspended without injury
The agency is binding until the whole project is completed
explanation: Per 4/3/3, agency remains binding when the agent commences tasks that cannot be discontinued without injury, until they can be suspended without injury.

title: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
q: A commodity contract defers both the delivery and the price. Which reason does the Basis give for prohibiting it?
options: The commodity may perish before delivery
The price cannot be known in advance
It is not organized on an exchange under financial supervision
It creates two liabilities, like delaying the capital of Salam
explanation: Per the Basis, delaying both counter-values creates two liabilities, and the jurists prohibit delaying the capital of Salam; it also opposes the contract's requirements.

title: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
q: Converting Bank B plans to use its interest earnings to fund training for its own staff. Is this allowed?
options: No, though training people other than its staff is allowed
Yes, since training is one of the charitable channels listed
Yes, if management approves the budget
Yes, if the staff are newly recruited
explanation: Per 10/2, the bank may not use such money directly or indirectly for its own benefit; listed channels include training people other than the bank's staff.

title: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
q: The principal under an ordinary agency to buy goods dies before the agent completes the purchase. What is the status of the agency?
options: It continues if the agency was a paid one
It passes automatically to the principal's heirs
It expires with the death of the principal
It continues until the purchase is completed
explanation: Per 7/1/1, the agency contract expires when the principal or the agent dies or loses legal capacity, or the Institution is bankrupt or liquidated.

title: Possession (Qabd)
q: Ahmad deposits gold bars with Company X as Wadi'ah and later withdraws them; both steps involve handling costs. Who bears these costs?
options: Both parties equally
The depositor, Ahmad
The depositary, Company X
Company X on deposit; Ahmad on withdrawal
explanation: Per 4/3, the expenses of deposit and withdrawal in a contract of deposit (Wadi'ah) are borne by the depositor (the owner of the deposit).

title: Stipulations and Ethics of Fatwa in the Institutional Framework
q: Bank A's board issues a Fatwa prohibiting a product that management strongly favors. What must Bank A do?
options: Seek another board's Fatwa that permits it
Refrain from it but report to the General Assembly
Follow it only if the General Assembly and management agree
Follow the Fatwa, whether management is satisfied or not
explanation: Per 6/1, the Institution is obliged to follow a Fatwa entailing enforcement or prohibition, regardless of management's satisfaction.

title: Procrastinating Debtor
q: Bank A wants to enforce an agreed acceleration clause against a procrastinating debtor who missed an instalment. What does the standard consider preferable?
options: Applying it at once on the missed due date without any notice
Notifying him and allowing a reasonable period first
Adding a late charge on the debtor before accelerating it
Obtaining a court order first before applying the clause
explanation: Per 2/1/6, it is preferable to implement the acceleration clause only after notifying the debtor and after a reasonable period of time has lapsed.

title: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
q: Bank A manages some investment accounts on the basis of investment agency rather than Mudarabah. Does the standard on profit distribution in investment accounts cover them?
options: Yes, but only restricted accounts under agency
No; such accounts are treated as current accounts
No; agency-based accounts need a separate standard
Yes; it covers all investment accounts of the Institution
explanation: Per 1, the standard covers Mudarabah-based investment accounts and does not cover accounts managed on the basis of investment agency, which require a separate standard.

title: Documentary Credit
q: A client has already bought goods and Bank A then joins him in a partnership over them. May Bank A sell its share to the client on deferred payment?
options: No, it may not sell its share to the client on a deferred basis
No, unless the client gave Bank A a binding promise beforehand
Yes, by deferred Murabahah once the goods have been received
Yes, provided the price is the market value of Bank A's share
explanation: Per 3/6/2, the Institution may partner with the client in goods the client purchased, on condition that it does not sell its share to the client on a deferred basis.

title: Hawalah
q: In a restricted Hawalah, Zaid's debt to Ahmad was secured by a mortgage. After the Hawalah, who holds the rights and legal protections against Zaid?
options: The mortgage lapses on the Hawalah
Ahmad and Bakr share them equally
Bakr, the transferee, in Ahmad's place
Ahmad keeps the mortgage rights
explanation: Per 9/2, in restricted Hawalah the transferee takes the place of the transferor in respect of all rights, legal protections and obligations against the payer.

title: Sharikah (Musharakah) and Modern Corporations
q: Bank A and a customer are partners. The customer is appointed manager under a separate contract, independent of the Sharikah, and may be dismissed at any time. May he earn a specific remuneration?
options: Yes, but only if the remuneration is a percentage of capital
Yes, as the appointment is independent of the Sharikah contract
No, unless the Sharikah contract is amended to include the fee
No, a partner may never receive remuneration for management work
explanation: Per 3/1/3/5, a partner may be appointed by an independent contract, dismissable without amending the Sharikah, and may then earn a specific remuneration.

title: Waqf
q: Why is a Waqf valid even if the Waqif names no avenue of disposal?
options: Because the overseer is the true beneficiary of the unnamed Waqf
Because Waqf requires no Waqif intention
Because the court becomes the owner of the unallocated asset
By analogy with absolute charity, vows and sacrifices
explanation: Basis 2/4/1/6: Waqf is alienation to seek Allah's pleasure; by analogy with absolute charity, vows, sacrifices and bequest, it is valid.

title: Insolvency
q: Bank A's Murabahah receivable from Ahmad falls due in two years, while his other creditors' debts are already due. Can Bank A, on its own, demand a declaration of insolvency now?
options: No; creditors of undue debts have no present right to demand it
Yes; any creditor may demand it regardless of maturity, since the debtor is already in default
No, unless Ahmad has first refused a request to travel
Yes, provided Bank A's receivable is the largest debt
explanation: Per 4/3/1 and 5/5/1, the application is by creditors of due debts; creditors of undue debts have no present right to demand a declaration of insolvency.

title: Ijarah and Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek
q: A lessee owes two unpaid past rentals. Bank A and the lessee agree to restructure rentals. Which rentals may they increase?
options: All rentals, if the term is extended
Past rentals, if the lessee consents
Only future rentals for unused periods
The unpaid past rentals as well
explanation: Per 5/2/5, future rentals may be amended by agreement; unpaid rentals of past periods become a debt owed by the lessee and cannot be increased.

title: Payment Cards
q: Bank A charged Ahmad one aggregate card fee without splitting it between issuance and other services. Ahmad cancels mid-year. What may Bank A retain?
options: A pro rata amount for the period since issuance
Only the issuance part, as it estimates it
The entire aggregate fee
Nothing, since the fee was not itemized
explanation: Per 5/2/3, for an undifferentiated aggregate fee, the issuer may retain a proportionate amount for the period from issuance to cancellation.

title: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
q: Bank A is an unsecured creditor of Company X, while Bank B holds a proprietary right over Company X's building. What can Bank A do that differs from Bank B?
options: It has priority over Bank B on the building
It cannot enforce its right by claiming any specific property
It can seize Company X's building directly using permissible means
It can enforce its right against any asset it chooses
explanation: Per 3/2/3, the owner of a proprietary right can directly enforce it over specific property; the owner of a personal right cannot claim any specific property.

title: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
q: Bank A distributed profit to investment account holders mid-year, but at year-end the capital was not fully protected. How is the earlier distribution treated?
options: As a gift from the Bank to the holders
As a loan from the holders to the Bank
As realized profit that cannot be adjusted
As an advance payment, not realized profit
explanation: Per 3/1/1, profit is not realized before protecting the capital; any amount distributed before that is an advance payment rather than realized profit.

title: Islamic Insurance
q: Ahmad wants cover against losses arising from his own decision to stop operating his shop. Can this risk be insured?
options: Yes, any risk can be covered by Islamic insurance
Yes, if the Shari'ah board is notified
No, it must not depend on his absolute will
Yes, if the contribution reflects the risk
explanation: Per 7/3, the insured risk should be one that could probably occur, not related to the absolute will of the participant, and not prohibited.

title: Options to Terminate Due to Breach of Trust (Trust-Based Options)
q: A seller hid a machine's defect by adding a substance. Before the buyer revokes, the machine's condition improves to no less than its original specification. Can he still revoke?
options: No; the deception must be continuing at revocation
Yes; the seller's deceptive conduct suffices
Yes, but only with compensation to the seller
No, unless the seller admits the deception
explanation: Per 3/2/3, the deception must be continuing; if the item's condition improves to not less than the original specification before revocation, no right to revoke remains.

title: Ijarah and Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek
q: In an Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek, the lessee paid rentals above market rate. The asset is destroyed with no fault of the lessee, so the lease cannot continue. What follows?
options: The lessee loses the excess he paid above the market rental
The lessee must pay the Bank the full value of the asset
The lessee receives back the full cost of the asset
Rental is adjusted and the excess over market refunded
explanation: Per 8/8, the rental is adjusted to prevailing market value and the excess over the market rate is refunded to the lessee.

title: Murabahah
q: Per the Shari'ah basis of the standard, what is a Murabahah concluded with a prior promise to buy from a person seeking goods through the Institution called?
options: Bay' al-Bara'ah, a sale free from liability for defects
Banking Murabahah, or Murabahah to the purchase orderer
Tawliyyah, a sale at cost price without any profit
Ordinary Murabahah, a sale at cost plus a disclosed profit
explanation: The basis defines Murabahah without a prior promise as ordinary Murabahah, and with a prior promise as banking Murabahah (to the purchase orderer).

title: Unilateral and Bilateral Promise
q: In a diminishing Musharakah, the client promised to buy units of Bank A's share at stipulated intervals. The client now wants to stop buying. Is his promise binding?
options: No; it is only a religious obligation
Yes, but only for the first purchase of units
Yes; the client's promise is legally binding
No; only Bank A's promises are binding
explanation: Per 5/2 with 3/5, the client's promise in diminishing Musharakah to buy units of the institution's share at stipulated intervals is legally binding.

title: Protection of Capital and Investments
q: An investor asks Bank A whether its commitment to "protect" his capital means the Bank guarantees it. How does the standard distinguish protection from guarantee?
options: They are synonyms; both mean that the manager undertakes to bear any loss of the capital
Protection is narrower, covering only destruction of capital
A guarantee is wider, covering inflation and exchange rates
Protection is safeguarding; a guarantee is an undertaking to bear any loss
explanation: Per 2, protection is wider than a guarantee: a guarantee is a party's undertaking to bear any loss, while protection refers to safeguarding capital.

title: Ijarah and Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek
q: Bank A sells a leased building to Investor Z, who knows of the lease and accepts it. The lessee was not asked. What is the outcome?
options: Valid, but the remaining rentals stay with the Bank
Valid; Z replaces the Bank for the remaining rentals
Valid, but the lease ends once the sale is concluded
Void, as the sale needed the lessee's prior consent
explanation: Per 7/1/2, the lessor may sell to a third party without the lessee's consent; a buyer who knows of and accepts the lease takes the place of the lessor.

title: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
q: An investment account holder demands that Bank A guarantee repayment of his deposit after an investment loss with no fault of the Bank. What is the ruling?
options: No; investment accounts are held on trust
The Bank guarantees it if it was held for over a year
The Bank must guarantee it, as all deposits are guaranteed
The Bank guarantees half of it as Mudarib
explanation: Per 2/2/1-2/2/2, investment accounts are held on trust and not guaranteed except for transgression, negligence or breach; profit or loss is distributed as agreed.

title: Waqf
q: Shares held as Waqf turn prohibited. Which hadith does the standard cite for requiring their substitution?
options: "Muslims are held to their conditions, except those that make lawful unlawful"
"If you wish, hold the property as a Waqf and give its fruit as charity"
"Start with yourself and spend on yourself, then on your family"
"Allah is Good, and He accepts only that which is good"
explanation: Basis 10/1/3: a Waqf asset must be permissible, and the Prophet said Allah is Good and accepts only what is good; also by analogy with one repenting.

title: Protection of Capital and Investments
q: In a Mudarabah fund, the Mudarib undertakes to buy the fund's assets at maturity at their nominal price, to reassure investors. What is the ruling?
options: Permissible if investors pay a fee for the promise
Not permissible, as it makes the manager bear the loss
Permissible, as it is only a unilateral promise
Permissible if the price is agreed at the outset
explanation: Per 5/3, a commitment by or obligating the manager to purchase the investment assets at nominal price or at an initially agreed price is not permissible.

title: Investment Sukuk
q: Certificates of ownership of an existing leased building have just been issued and ownership of the building has passed to the holders. When may they be traded?
options: Only after the first rental instalment is received
Never, since they represent rental receivables
Immediately upon issue and up to the date of maturity
Only on the maturity date of the Sukuk
explanation: Per 5/2/4, Sukuk of ownership of existing leased assets may be traded immediately upon issue until maturity, after ownership passes to the holders.

title: Al-Wakalah Bi Al-Istithmar (Investment Agency)
q: Company X signs an investment agency contract with Bank A in March, stating that the appointment takes effect from 1 July. Is this permissible?
options: Yes; it may take effect on a specified future date
Yes, but only if the whole fee is paid in advance
No; an agency must take effect upon signing
Yes, but only for an unrestricted investment agency
explanation: Per 3/2, the appointment of an agent may be contingent on conditions or made to take effect on a specified future date.

title: Investment Sukuk
q: Istisna'a Sukuk proceeds were immediately paid as the price in a parallel Istisna'a contract. How is trading in these certificates treated?
options: It is freely permissible like trading in assets
It is permissible at market price without restriction
It is subject only to the rules of Salam
It is subject to the rules of disposal of debts
explanation: Per 5/2/13, if funds are immediately paid as price in a parallel Istisna'a or the item is delivered to the ultimate purchaser, trading follows debt rules.

title: Stipulations and Ethics of Fatwa in the Institutional Framework
q: Per the Shari'ah basis, why is the board bound to issue Fatwa to its Institution?
options: The relationship set by the General Assembly's decision
The board is paid per Fatwa issued
Fatwa is a personal duty of every scholar towards every Institution
The regulator requires each Fatwa to be filed
explanation: The basis: the board's duty to issue Fatwa to the Institution arises from the relationship binding them by decision of the General Assembly (equity owners).

title: Zakah
q: Company X bought fertilizers on deferred payment for its farm. How are they treated in calculating Zakah on the produce?
options: Not Zakatable, and never deductible in any case
Not Zakatable, and deductible since obtained through debt
Zakatable as part of the farm's current assets, whether bought on credit or in cash
Deductible from the Zakah base even if paid in cash
explanation: Per 5/4/5, fertilizers and insecticides are not Zakatable assets and are not deducted from the Zakah base unless they were obtained through debt.

title: Buyback
q: Two banks agree a bilateral loans points system, with extra points to one bank as a penalty if the other repays its counter-loan late. Is this permitted?
options: Yes, if points are never converted to cash
Yes, if the penalty is agreed at borrowing
No, no party may receive extra or penalty points
Yes, since penalties ensure timely repayment
explanation: Per 5/6/3/2(a), the points system must be fair; preferential terms or extra points, including as a penalty for late repayment, are not permitted.

title: Unilateral and Bilateral Promise
q: Under a legally binding promise, the agreed date arrives. Bank A, the promisee, offers to sell the asset to the customer, the promisor. What is the status?
options: The sale was already concluded on the date automatically
The customer may freely accept or reject the offer
The sale needs no acceptance once the offer is made
The customer is bound religiously and legally to accept
explanation: Per 3/8, the promised contract is not automatic; offer and acceptance must be exchanged; if the promisee makes the offer under a binding promise, the promisor must accept.

title: Zakah
q: Company X made an advance payment to a contractor on signing a construction contract. Is this advance part of Company X's Zakatable assets?
options: Yes, as a receivable from the contractor, repayable if the contract is not performed
Yes, until the work is delivered
No, since it is no longer owned by Company X
Yes, at half its value
explanation: Per 5/3/4/5, no Zakah is paid on advance payments on signing contracts, since they are no longer owned by the Institution.

title: Financial Paper (Shares and Bonds)
q: Ahmad wants to sell shares he does not yet own. What reason does the Basis give for prohibiting this short sale?
options: He sells what he neither owns nor is liable for
Short sales always involve paying interest to the broker
The price of shares is always unknown at sale
Shares cannot be sold before dividends are paid
explanation: Per the Basis, a short sale leads to the sale of something not within the liability of the seller nor in his ownership, which is prohibited.

title: Impact of Contingent Incidents on Commitments
q: A buyer finds that the sold asset was seized unlawfully and belongs to another person, so the commitment is ineffective. What is the Shari'ah basis for this?
options: The seller's good faith validates the sale of the asset
Unlawful seizure is not recognised as a basis of ownership
The buyer's Qabd cures any defect in the seller's title
Possession for a long period always confers ownership
explanation: Per the basis, unlawful seizure is unrecognizable as a basis of ownership: 'An extorter is indebted with what he takes until he returns it back'.

title: Waqf
q: Ahmad declares his apartment building a Waqf. A year later he wants to sell it to settle a personal expense. What is the ruling?
options: He cannot; the Waqf is binding and ended his ownership
He can, since a Waqf is a revocable gift to the beneficiaries
He can, if he donates the sale price to charity
He can, with the beneficiaries' consent
explanation: Per 2/2, Waqf is a binding commitment; declaring a property as Waqf spontaneously deprives its donating owner of the right of ownership.

title: Ijarah and Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek
q: A lease runs from 1 March, but Bank A delivers the asset on 1 April. Nothing else was agreed. What happens to March's rental?
options: Full rent is due as the contract is signed
Half the March rent is due as compensation
No rental is due for March; rent is reduced
March's rent is due once delivery takes place
explanation: Per 4/1/3, no rental is due between the agreed and actual delivery dates, unless it is agreed to extend the lease by an equivalent period after expiry.

title: Waqf
q: Critics say cash cannot be Waqf because the same coins cannot be retained. What is the standard's answer?
options: Cash Waqf is merely a loan to beneficiaries
Cash Waqf is valid only if the same coins are kept in a vault
Cash must first be turned into real estate before it can be Waqf
Coins are not specific; their substitutes take their place
explanation: Basis 2/4/13/1: Waqf's objective is achieved in cash Waqf; money cannot be specific by identification, and its substitute will be in its place.

title: Ijarah and Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek
q: Bank A appoints a customer as its agent to buy equipment that the customer will later lease from the Bank. What does the standard say about this agency?
options: Permissible only if the customer pays the price
Permissible, but another agent is preferred if possible
Permissible, and the customer is the preferred agent for it
Not permissible; the Bank must buy the equipment directly
explanation: Per 3/7, the Institution may appoint the customer as agent to acquire the asset, but it is always preferred that the agent be someone other than the customer.

title: Sharikah (Musharakah) and Modern Corporations
q: In a diminishing Musharakah, the customer leases Bank A's share of the jointly owned property. Who is responsible for periodical maintenance?
options: Each partner, for his own share
The customer, as lessee of the whole property
The customer, once he owns over half
Bank A, as the majority owner
explanation: Per 5/9, either partner may lease the other's share for a specified amount and duration; each partner remains responsible for the periodical maintenance of his share.

title: Protection of Capital and Investments
q: Company Z offers to guarantee a fund's capital against any loss in exchange for an annual fee. How does the standard classify this?
options: Permissible, as it is a form of Takaful
Impermissible; it is a form of conventional insurance
Permissible if Company Z is independent of the manager
Permissible if the fee is reasonable and disclosed
explanation: Per 5/4, a third party's undertaking to guarantee the capital for a fee is not permissible; it is a form of conventional insurance.

title: Waqf
q: Which reasoning supports the standard's acceptance of a Waqf limited by time?
options: Perpetual Waqf is disliked in Shari'ah, so only temporary is valid
Ownership cannot be relinquished forever
General Waqf texts cover perpetual and temporary Waqf
A temporary Waqf is in fact a lease of the asset to the beneficiaries
explanation: Basis 2/4/1/5: some Waqf texts are general, applying to perpetual and temporary Waqf; Waqf is a donation whose scope is broadened.

title: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
q: Ahmad buys a car with a 7-day cooling-off option and test-drives it once to check its performance. Does this test drive cancel his option?
options: Yes; any use of the item confirms the contract and ends the option
Yes, unless the seller was present and agreed to the test drive
No, but he must pay a fee for using the car
No; testing cancels it only if repeated without need
explanation: Per 2/4/2, the option owner may test the item without losing the right to revoke, unless he does so repetitively without need or acts as owner contrary to terms or custom.

title: Buyback
q: Ahmad repudiates his promise to buy an asset for 110 from Bank A, which cost the Bank 100. On the performance date Bank A sells it to a third party for 95. What may it claim?
options: 5: the cost minus the third-party price
10: the profit lost on the promised price
15: the promised price minus the sale price
110: the full promised price
explanation: Per 5/1/7, actual damage for a promise to purchase is cost minus the third-party sale price on the performance date; lost profit is excluded.

title: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
q: Bank A holds the ownership certificates of a customer's warehoused gold pledged to it. When does this amount to possession of the pledged gold?
options: Never, as a pledge needs physical possession
When the owner can't dispose of it without them
Only once the gold is moved to Bank A's vault
Only if the gold is jewelry rather than ingots
explanation: Per 7/1/5, holding ownership certificates is constructive possession as long as the pledgor cannot dispose of the gold without presenting them.

title: Ijarah and Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek
q: Bank A wants floating rentals for a 10-year Ijarah tied to a benchmark. What must it do for the first rental period?
options: Set it as an average of past benchmarks
Link it to the benchmark like later periods
Specify its rental as a lump sum
Leave it open until the period ends
explanation: Per 5/2/3, with a floating rental, the first period's rental must be specified as a lump sum; later periods may follow a benchmark.

title: Sharikah (Musharakah) and Modern Corporations
q: Why does the Shari'ah basis reject a partner contributing receivables alone as Sharikah capital?
options: Receivables have no monetary value until they are collected in cash
Only the Institution may contribute debts, and individuals may not
Debts can never be owned or transferred between persons under Shari'ah rules
They are not assets in possession and may lead to Riba
explanation: Per the basis, debts cannot actually be used in operations as they are not assets in possession, and this may lead to Riba when the partner is the debtor.

title: Ijarah and Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek
q: Bank A is asked to lease a vehicle to carry prohibited merchandise. Which principle does the Shari'ah basis apply in barring this?
options: The rental would be uncertain until the goods arrive
The lessor would be an accomplice in doing evil
The lessee would not own the usufruct of the vehicle
The vehicle would perish by its use in transport
explanation: The basis: leasing for impermissible use makes the lessor an accomplice in evil, contrary to 'Help you one another in Al-Birr and At-Taqwa'.

title: Mudarabah
q: A Mudarib takes customary personal expenses from the funds though the contract is silent. Which principle in the Shari'ah basis supports him?
options: Harm must be removed at any cost
Necessity makes the prohibited permissible
What is known by custom applies as a condition
Certainty is not removed by doubt
explanation: Per the basis, what is known by custom is deemed to apply as a condition even if not clearly stipulated, so custom permits common personal expenses.

title: Sale of Debt
q: Partners jointly own cash, tangible assets and debts. They agree that one takes the debts, another the cash and the third the assets. What is the ruling?
options: Not permitted unless the debtors consent
Not permitted: debts can't be swapped for cash
Permitted only if each gets part of each asset
Permitted by agreement among the partners
explanation: Per 6/3, partners owning debts, tangible assets and cash may agree that some take debts, some cash and others tangible assets.
