explanation: Per 3/2/2, the agent must be aware of his status; an act done before he knows he is an agent does not fall under the agency (it may fall under Fodooli rules).

title: Istisna’a and Parallel Istisna’a
q: Bank A offers a customer: 1,000,000 if the plant is delivered in 12 months, or 950,000 if delivered in 18 months; one offer is chosen at conclusion. Is this allowed?
options: No, it is a sale of debt for debt
Yes, price may vary with the delivery date
No, the price must be one single fixed amount
Yes, but the choice may be left open
explanation: Per 3/2/4, the Istisna'a price may vary with delivery date, and several offers may be negotiated provided only one is finally chosen to conclude the contract.

title: Zakah
q: Company X, a textile trader, faces a severe trade recession and has little cash. May it pay its Zakah on trade goods in kind?
options: Yes, if the interest of Zakah recipients is achieved
No; Zakah on trade goods may be paid only in cash, as it is assessed at market value
Yes, at any time and with no condition
Only with the regulator's approval
explanation: Per 5/2/4, Zakah on articles of trade is in principle paid in cash, but in a trade recession it can be paid in kind if recipients' interest is achieved.

title: Hiring of Persons
q: Company X pledged to hire Bank A's services and paid a seriousness guarantee of 50,000. It then withdraws, causing the Bank actual harm of 20,000. How much may the Bank deduct?
options: Nothing, since a pledge is not binding
Only 20,000, the actual harm caused
20,000 plus the Bank's expected lost profit
The full 50,000 as a penalty for withdrawal
explanation: Per 3/2, upon the client's withdrawal, the deduction from the guarantee amount should not exceed the actual harm caused to the Institution.

title: Sharikah (Musharakah) and Modern Corporations
q: A company proposes Tamattu' (enjoyment) shares: they share in net profit without voting and are gradually redeemed through profit distributions before termination. What is the ruling?
options: Permitted for bearer shareholders only
Permitted if holders agree in advance
Not permitted to issue them
Permitted if they carry voting rights
explanation: Per 4/1/2/15, it is not permitted to issue Tamattu' (enjoyment) shares, which share in net profit without voting and are gradually redeemed from profits.

title: Hawalah
q: Bakr claims the transferred debt from Zaid, who refuses, saying he only ever owed money to Ahmad. What is Zaid's position?
options: He is obliged to pay Bakr
He may refuse and pay Ahmad instead
He may pay only if Ahmad confirms
He may refuse until the original due date
explanation: Per 9/1, the transferee may claim the debt from the payer per the Hawalah terms; the payer is obliged to pay and has no right to refuse.

title: Financial Paper (Shares and Bonds)
q: Bank A manages an equity fund that invests in shares of mixed companies. Who is responsible for eliminating the prohibited income?
options: The companies whose shares are held
Each fund investor individually
The custodian bank of the fund
Bank A, as it is managing the operations
explanation: Per 3/4/6/6, the responsibility for elimination falls on the institution when it trades for itself or manages the operations.

title: Payment Cards
q: Bank A cancels Ahmad's card mid-term due to a restructuring of its card products, with no fault from Ahmad. What applies to the fees?
options: Bank A keeps all the fees already paid, as the card was issued
Bank A returns issuance and service fees pro rata
Bank A keeps the fees for a year
Bank A returns only the issuance fee and keeps the service fees
explanation: Per 5/2/5, if cancellation is for a reason not attributed to the cardholder, the issuer returns issuance and service fees pro rata for the remaining period.

title: Investment Sukuk
q: Bank A undertakes to buy any unsubscribed portion of a Sukuk issue and asks the issuer for an underwriting commission. What is the ruling?
options: Underwriting is not allowed as it is a mere promise to buy
Both the underwriting and the commission are permissible
Allowed by binding promise, but no commission may be taken
The commission is allowed if it is a fixed lump sum
explanation: Per 5/1/9, an institution may underwrite the unsubscribed issue on a binding promise, but should not receive any commission for the underwriting.

title: Hiring of Persons
q: An employee hired to deliver a well-defined future service dies before delivery. Per the Shari'ah basis, why does the contract not become void?
options: The service, as a debt, is considered existent
The employee's heirs become the new employer
The employer has waived the service
The pay has already been earned in full
explanation: The basis: a contract for a future service does not become void on the employee's death because the service, as a debt, is considered existent.

title: Monetization (Tawarruq)
q: A customer buys a commodity from Bank A on deferred payment and sells it for cash to Broker X. By prior understanding, Broker X then sells it back to Bank A. What is the ruling?
options: Permitted, since the customer sold to a third party, not the Bank
Permitted, provided the Bank's repurchase price is the market price
Permitted, if Broker X pays the customer on spot
Prohibited: the commodity may not return to the seller by collusion
explanation: Per 4/5, the commodity shall not return to the seller by prior agreement or collusion between the parties, or according to tradition, to avoid 'Inah.

title: Sale of Debt
q: Ahmad owes Bank A USD 1,000 and agrees to settle it in euros. He pays half of the euro amount now and the rest next week. Is this permitted?
options: No, the converted amount must be paid in the session
Yes, if the rate of the day is used for the whole amount
Yes, since the debt itself was already due before the conversion
Yes, if the remainder is secured by a pledge
explanation: Per 4/1/1/2(a), the substitute must be possessed in the session so that no part of the converted debt remains outstanding.

title: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
q: In an external conversion, the assets of the bank being acquired carry impermissible mortgages. What must the buyer stipulate?
options: That the mortgages stay until they lapse
That the seller replace them with permissible mortgages
That depositors guarantee the mortgages
That the buyer will pay the interest secured by the mortgages
explanation: Per 9/3, shareholders must accelerate redemption of impermissible mortgages; in external conversion, the buyer must stipulate that the seller replaces them.

title: Mudarabah
q: A Mudarib travels abroad for the Mudarabah. No amount for living expenses was agreed with the capital provider. What may he take from the Mudarabah funds?
options: A fixed daily amount set by the Mudarib himself
Nothing, unless an amount was agreed in advance
Living and travel expenses as per custom and reason
Only travel costs, never living expenses
explanation: Per 9/7, absent agreement the Mudarib takes living expenses by custom and reason, and is also entitled to travelling expenses by custom and reason.

title: Insolvency
q: Creditors Ali and Omar obtained a declaration of Ahmad's insolvency. Before the distribution, creditor Karim appears with a proven claim. What is Karim entitled to?
options: Nothing, since he did not join the application
Only what remains after Ali and Omar are paid in full
Payment only after the declaration is revoked
A pro-rata share of the distribution
explanation: Per 4/4, creditors need not prove they are the sole creditors; another creditor appearing before distribution is entitled to a pro-rata share.

title: Loan (Qard)
q: Ahmad borrowed 1,000 with no stipulation or custom of any excess. At repayment, out of goodwill, he voluntarily returns 1,050. What is the ruling?
options: Prohibited, as any excess over a Qard is Riba
Permissible only if the lender requests it
Permissible, as an unstipulated excess at repayment
Permissible only if the Qard was in kind, not cash
explanation: Per 5/2, an excess in quantity or quality at repayment is permissible when not stipulated or customary, whether the Qard is cash or kind.

title: Protection of Capital and Investments
q: A fund protects capital with Murabahah and uses the rest to buy assets under 'Arboun contracts. The assets' value then falls sharply. What happens?
options: The Murabahah buyers must bear the decline in value
The sellers must refund the 'Arboun to the fund
The fund must complete the purchases and sell at a loss, as the 'Arboun binds it
The purchases are not completed; loss is limited to the 'Arboun
explanation: Per 4/2/7(d), if asset values decline, the purchase contracts are not completed and the loss is limited to the 'Arboun amount, with capital protected by Murabahah.

title: Zakah
q: Bank A sold a car in Murabahah for 120 (cost 100) on deferred payment; the full 120 is outstanding. On what amount does the Bank pay Zakah?
options: 100, the cost of the car, with profit added on collection
120, the total price including profit
20, the profit only, as the cost is not Zakatable until paid
Nothing until collection
explanation: Per 5/3/4/9, Zakah on Murabahah debtors is payable on the total price including profits, as with cash debts under 5/3/1.

title: Stipulations and Ethics of Fatwa in the Institutional Framework
q: Which Qur'anic verse does the basis cite for choosing the easier of two permissible rulings?
options: Allah intends for you ease, not difficulty
Do not consume one another's wealth unjustly
Fulfill (all) obligations
Allah has permitted trade and forbidden Riba
explanation: The basis cites Al-Baqarah 185: "Allah intends for you ease..." and the Hadith "Make things easier not harder", after reviewing the specific proofs.

title: Sharikah (Musharakah) and Modern Corporations
q: An investor buys shares with an interest-based loan from his broker, mortgaging the shares as security. What is the ruling?
options: Permitted if the broker is licensed
Permitted if the shares are Shari'ah-compliant
Permitted, as the shares secure the loan
Not permitted
explanation: Per 4/1/2/6, it is not permitted to purchase shares using interest-based loans from a broker or other person against mortgaging the shares.

title: Obtaining and Deploying Liquidity
q: Bank A does not sell its commodities but evaluates them to arrive at the expected monetary value they could realise. In the traditional terminology cited by the standard, this is:
options: Tandid by estimation
Liquidity management
Securitisation of assets
Actual Tandid
explanation: Per the basis, liquidity is traditionally Tandid: actual Tandid is selling commodities for cash; Tandid by estimation is evaluating them to arrive at expected monetary value.

title: Sharikah (Musharakah) and Modern Corporations
q: A partner asks why contributions in a different currency must be converted at the current exchange rate. Which evidence does the Shari'ah basis cite?
options: The hadith of the co-owner who frees a slave
Ibn Umar's camel sales at Al-Baqi' at the day's rate
The partnership of Al-Sa'ib with the Prophet
The saying of Ali Ibn Abu Talib on loss sharing
explanation: Per the basis, conversion is a currency exchange allowed at the current rate, as the Prophet endorsed Ibn Umar's sales at Al-Baqi' at the current rate.

title: Ijarah and Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek
q: Bank A leases a delivery van to Ahmad, who overloads it far beyond common practice and damages it. Which duty did Ahmad breach?
options: Paying all rentals in advance
Carrying out major maintenance of the van
Using the asset suitably and avoiding misuse
Insuring the asset at his own expense
explanation: Per 5/1/4, the lessee must use the asset in a suitable manner per common practice and avoid causing damage by misuse through misconduct or negligence.

title: Online Financial Dealings
q: After an online auction ends, the highest bidder wants to retreat. When is he barred from doing so?
options: Only if the auction was run by an Institution
If the seller made the offer binding for a period or practice requires it
Never; once the auction is over he is free to retreat from his highest bid
Only if he had paid a deposit when placing his bid
explanation: Per 4/3, after bidding ends he may not retreat if the seller conditioned the offer to remain binding for a period, or if normal practice necessitates it.

title: Zakah
q: A client withholds 5% of contract payments as retention from Bank A until the project is complete; the Bank cannot invest it. How is Zakah treated?
options: No Zakah while held; one year's Zakah on receipt
Zakah every year while it is held, as it remains owned by the Bank
No Zakah at any time
Zakah for all years on receipt
explanation: Per 5/3/4/4, if the Institution cannot invest retention amounts it pays no Zakah on them; on receipt it pays Zakah for only one year.

title: Hawalah
q: Ahmad issues a cheque on his current account at Bank A to Bakr, to whom he owes that amount. How is this characterised?
options: Hawalah: Bank A transferor, Ahmad payer, Bakr transferee
Sale: Bakr buys Ahmad's balance at Bank A
Agency: Bakr collects on behalf of Ahmad
Hawalah: Ahmad transferor, Bank A payer, Bakr transferee
explanation: Per 12/1, a cheque on a current account to the issuer's creditor is Hawalah, with issuer, bank and beneficiary as transferor, payer and transferee.

title: Mortgage and its Contemporary Applications
q: Bank A issues a back-to-back documentary credit for a client against another credit. Per the basis, why is this permissible?
options: Documentary credits are Mudarabah investments that may be pledged freely
Documentary credits involve no debt at all
A credit creates a bank debt to the client, which may be mortgaged
The second credit is a gift from the bank
explanation: Per the basis, a documentary credit results in a debt owed by the bank to the client, and such debt can be mortgaged to obtain a new debt.

title: Ijarah and Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek
q: In an Ijarah Mawsufah fi al-Dhimmah, the vehicle delivered to the lessee is destroyed. Nothing else was agreed. What must the lessor do?
options: Provide a substitute of similar specification
Nothing, as the lease automatically ends
Refund all rentals paid so far
Repair it at the lessee's cost
explanation: Per 7/1/6, in a lease of a described asset the owner must offer a substitute of similar specification and the Ijarah continues; if impossible, it terminates.

title: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
q: A guarantor gives Kafalah for any future debts Company X may incur toward Bank A, for an unspecified period. What is the effect of this Gharar?
options: Valid only for debts existing on the date of signing
Void, as the period of Kafalah must be known
The Kafalah is permissible despite this Gharar
Void, as Kafalah cannot cover future obligations
explanation: Per 6/2, Kafalah can involve Gharar not permitted in sale: it can be conditional, for an unknown period, or relate to a future obligation.

title: Mortgage and its Contemporary Applications
q: On a client's default, Bank A wants to buy the mortgaged land from him and take from the price what it is owed. Is this allowed?
options: No; the mortgagee may never acquire the asset
Yes, if it purchases at market value
Yes, at the value fixed in the mortgage contract
Yes, at a discount reflecting the client's default
explanation: Per 3/4/2, though ownership on default may not be stipulated, the mortgagee may purchase the asset from the mortgagor at market value and take its due portion.

title: Waqf
q: Ahmad declares a shop as Waqf, keeping its rental income for himself while alive and naming a hospital to receive it after his death. Which type of Waqf is this?
options: Joint Waqf (al-Waqf al-Mushtarak) for charity and kin
Temporary Waqf for the period of his own lifetime
Family Waqf (al-Waqf al-Ahli) for his relatives
Self-dedicated Waqf (al-Waqf 'Ala al-Nafs)
explanation: Per 2/3/4, in a self-dedicated Waqf the donor retains the income for himself while alive and indicates the charitable purpose entitled after his death.

title: Waqf
q: Why does the standard make the Waqf of a person interdicted for debt depend on his creditors' permission?
options: Because Waqf of debtors is a bequest
Because the creditors own his assets
To repel harm from the creditors
Because debt removes legal capacity
explanation: The basis for suspending Waqf by one interdicted for debt until creditors permit it is to repel harm from the creditors.

title: Waqf
q: An upper floor is declared Waqf, but the owner of the lower floor cannot construct his floor. Under the right of Ta'alli, what may be done?
options: The Waqf lapses until the lower floor is built
Build the lower floor at Waqf cost, repaid from its rent
The Waqf may build only if the owner pays in advance
The lower-floor owner must sell his land to the Waqf
explanation: Per 3/4/5, the lower floor can be built at the Waqf's cost (with authorities' permission) and the cost reimbursed to the Waqf from its leasing income.

title: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
q: Why does the standard prohibit a conditional sale and Khiyar al-Shart in gold trading?
options: They conflict with the option for defect
They turn the sale into a loan with benefits
They make the promise tradable, which is barred
They contravene the requirement of spot exchange
explanation: Per the Basis, conditional sales and Khiyar al-Shart in gold trading contravene the Shari'ah requirement for spot exchange of countervalues.

title: Sale of Debt
q: Bank A's financing contract stipulates that the customer will discharge his USD debt in local currency before its maturity. What is the ruling on this term?
options: Not permitted; such early discharge can't be stipulated
Permitted, if the customer is solvent and agrees in writing
Permitted, as early discharge favors the debtor
Permitted, if the settlement-day rate is used for the conversion
explanation: Per 4/1/1/2(b), discharge in another currency before the due time must not be stipulated, anticipated, or a customary practice.

title: Possession (Qabd)
q: Ahmad sells a locked shop. Following the Hanafi view cited in the Basis, what suffices for delivery of possession?
options: Moving all goods out of the shop first
Handing over the key along with relinquishment
Registering the sale before any handover
Ahmad remaining present while the buyer enters
explanation: Per the Basis, Hanafi jurists hold that for locked immovable property, delivering the key along with relinquishment suffices, enabling the possessor to open it easily.

title: Banking Services in Islamic Banks
q: Jewels kept by a customer in Bank A's safe deposit vault are lost, with no misconduct or negligence by the Bank in keeping the vault. Is the Bank liable?
options: No, only for misconduct or negligence in keeping it
Yes, if the customer declared the jewels
Yes, it guarantees all items in the vault as their keeper for a fee
Yes, up to the amount of the vault fee
explanation: Per 2/7/2, the Institution ensures the vault's safety but does not guarantee items kept in it except for misconduct or negligence in keeping the vault.

title: Payment Cards
q: Bank A waives the card fee only for current account debit cards, while still charging the fee on cards for saving and investment accounts. What is the ruling?
options: Permitted, if the waiver is temporary
Permitted, as a marketing incentive
Permitted, as current accounts carry no profit
Not permitted
explanation: Per 4/1/2, the current account card fee should not be exclusively exempted or lowered if saving/investment account cards carry a fee.

title: Concession Contracts
q: A management concession price is set as a percentage of the project's net profit after expenses and allocations. How is it adapted?
options: As Ju'alah, with the profit share as Ju'l for managing the facility
As Musharakah, with cash contributed by the State as capital
As Mudarabah, with the facility itself as capital
As Ijarah, with the profit share as rent for the facility
explanation: Per 10/2/1, if the price is a percentage of net profit, the contract is Mudarabah, in which the capital is the original facility or the project itself.

title: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
q: Per the Shari'ah basis, why may impermissible earnings be donated to charity, becoming lawful for the beneficiaries?
options: Transfer of ownership changes their prohibited character
Charity purifies the whole capital of the bank that gives it
Beneficiaries are not bound by Shari'ah
The earnings were lawful from the outset
explanation: Per the Basis, transferring ownership changes the prohibited characterisation; what is prohibited for one may be permissible for another (the usurped goat Hadith).

title: Hiring of Persons
q: A contractor and Company X agree: if the work is done in 30 days the pay is 10,000; if done in 20 days it is 12,000. What is the ruling?
options: Impermissible, as two sales in one sale
Permissible only if the lower rate is paid first
Permissible; more than one rate of pay may be agreed
Impermissible, as the pay is uncertain
explanation: Per 5/2/9, the parties may agree upon more than one rate of pay, e.g. one rate if done within a certain period and a higher rate for a shorter period.

title: Murabahah
q: Customer C accepted a supplier's offer but argues no sale exists because he has not paid yet, so Bank A can still do Murabahah. Why is he wrong, per the Shari'ah basis?
options: The supplier's offer had no addressee, so acceptance failed
Payment results from the contract; it is not a condition
Payment is always made before acceptance can take place
Acceptance is binding only after delivery of the goods
explanation: The basis: the sale is concluded once C accepts; payment of the price is a consequence of a contract, not a condition of its validity.

title: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
q: Bank A sells equipment to Company X and the contract states that the price will be determined later by an outside expert. What is the ruling?
options: Valid if the expert is named in the contract
Valid with a right of objection for the buyer
Valid, since a neutral third party fixes the price
Void, due to Gharar in the price
explanation: Per 5/2/2, Gharar arises when the price is left to be determined by one of the parties or a third party, and it nullifies the sale contract.

title: Waqf
q: Ahmad, suffering a fatal illness, declares his land a Waqf. According to the Shari'ah basis, which rulings govern this Waqf?
options: The rules for Waqf of an irrational person
The ordinary rules of Waqf by a healthy person
The rulings applicable to the will of such a person
The rules of gifts with immediate possession
explanation: The basis states that Waqf by a person suffering a fatal illness should be subject to the rulings applicable to the will of such person.

title: Waqf
q: An overseer wants to substitute a tangible Waqf building. Which approval is required?
options: Only the beneficiaries' approval, given by a majority vote
Only the overseer's own assessment
The approval of the Waqif's heirs and the overseer together
The authority's approval or a valid Shari'ah pronouncement
explanation: Per 10/1/5/5, substitution of tangible Waqf assets should be per the relevant authority's approval, if any, or a valid Shari'ah pronouncement.

title: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
q: Why does the Shari'ah basis consider Gharar from failure in delivery as nullifying a sale?
options: The seller gets the price while the buyer may not get the item
Such sales are donation contracts by nature
The price in such sales is always unknown to one of the parties
The seller loses the option of viewing the item
explanation: Per the basis, a sale safeguards both parties' rights; if the seller gets the price while the buyer cannot get the sold object, the contract's objective is violated.

title: Online Financial Dealings
q: Bank A e-mails an offer to sell a property and states that it remains valid for 10 days. On day 4, before the client replies, the Bank wants to withdraw. Can it?
options: Yes, if it notifies the client by e-mail
No; it may not withdraw during the specified period
No, unless the client has not opened the e-mail
Yes, any time before the client's acceptance
explanation: Per 4/2/2, where the offering party specifies a validity period, acceptance time covers the whole period and the offeror has no right to withdraw during it.

title: Murabahah
q: Ahmad tells Bank A informally that he would like to acquire a car through the Bank. Nothing is signed. What is the status of this expressed wish?
options: It is not a promise unless expressed in due form
It is a binding promise to purchase the car
It is a concluded Murabahah awaiting delivery
It becomes a binding promise once the Bank buys the car
explanation: Per 2/1/3, the customer's wish to acquire the item does not constitute a promise or commitment except when it has been expressed in due form.

title: Documentary Credit
q: A credit secures a currency exchange contract. What must hold for the credit's subject to be permissible?
options: Only the amount of the currencies must be fixed in advance
The exchange must be valid in its elements, conditions and type
Only the credit's own terms need be valid in Shari'ah
The bank need not consider the underlying contract at all
explanation: Per 3/1/3, the contract relied upon (currency exchange, ordinary sale or another) must be valid in Shari'ah in its elements, conditions and type of transaction.

title: Waqf
q: Per the Shari'ah basis, why may the superintendent borrow to protect the Waqf but not to pay beneficiaries when there is no income?
options: Beneficiaries are never entitled to any income at all
Any debt taken for the beneficiaries' shares necessarily involves Riba
Borrowing prevents the Waqf's ruin; unpaid shares do not
The Waqif's heirs must pay the beneficiaries instead
explanation: The basis: borrowing safeguards the Waqf against being useless, whereas refraining from paying beneficiaries when there is no income involves no such harm.

title: Mudarabah
q: Bank A, as capital provider, stipulates that its own staff will work alongside the Mudarib in buying and selling for the Mudarabah. What is the ruling?
options: Permitted if the Mudarib's profit share is raised to compensate for the interference
Permitted if Bank A's staff bear part of any loss that results
Permitted in a restricted Mudarabah, where the provider may set such terms
Not permitted for the capital provider to stipulate this
explanation: Per 9/3, the capital provider may not stipulate a right to work with the Mudarib and be involved in selling and buying, or supplying and ordering.

title: Guarantees
q: A buyer pays 'Arboun when concluding a sale and does not terminate within the agreed option period. What becomes of the 'Arboun?
options: It becomes part of the price
It remains held on trust
It is kept by the seller as a fee
It is refunded to the buyer
explanation: Per 6/8/3, if the contract is not terminated within the option period, the 'Arboun is considered part of the consideration for the contract.

title: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
q: Bank A opens an account in which customers deposit gold of a specific weight and karatage, as a current account. Which rulings govern this account?
options: The rulings for joint ownership of gold
The rulings for investment accounts
The rulings for Hamish Jiddiyyah
The rulings for current accounts
explanation: Per 10/8, a gold-denominated current account is permissible and subject to the rulings for current accounts (see the standard on Qard).

title: Waqf
q: A non-Muslim businessman creates a Waqf over a building for a public hospital. What is the ruling?
options: Invalid, as Waqf is purely an act of worship
Valid, subject to observing the rulings and conditions of Waqf
Valid only where its beneficiaries are non-Muslims as well
Valid only after a Shari'ah board ratifies it
explanation: Per 2/4/3/5, Waqf by a non-Muslim is valid subject to observing the rulings and conditions of Waqf.

title: Documentary Credit
q: Bank A proposes to charge 0.5% of the credit amount for each month the credit remains open. What is the ruling on this commission?
options: Permissible, as a percentage of the amount is allowed and duration does not matter
Permissible for import credits only, not for export credits
Not permissible: the duration must not affect the commission
Permissible if the actual costs of the credit are also covered by it
explanation: Per 3/3/1, a fee may be a lump sum or a percentage of the credit amount, provided the duration of the credit is not considered in determining it.

title: Murabahah
q: Bank A's purchase contract with the supplier of an item later turns out to be void. What is the effect on its Murabahah with the customer?
options: It remains valid, but the mark-up must be reduced
It is also void, as the Bank lacked complete title
It remains valid, as the customer acted in good faith
It is voidable only at the customer's option
explanation: Per 3/1/1, the Murabahah is void if the contract with the supplier is void, because the Institution would fail to acquire complete title to the item.

title: Sale of Debt
q: Company X bought 500 tons of wheat by Salam and, before taking possession, sells that wheat debt to a third party for cash. What is the ruling?
options: Not permitted before taking possession
Permitted, as the wheat is precisely described
Permitted, if sold at its Salam price
Permitted, if sold for a commodity, not cash
explanation: Per 5/3, a commodity debt may not be sold before taking possession, whether for cash, commodity, usufruct or service.

title: Payment Cards
q: Bank A charges a replacement fee on its prepaid card that exceeds the actual cost of replacement. The card involves no lending. What is the ruling?
options: Not permitted on any prepaid card
Permitted only if half is refunded
Permitted, as such fees follow the agreement
Not permitted above the actual direct cost
explanation: Per 5/1/2/3, fees in cards that involve no lending (issuance, renewal, replacement, etc.) are not restricted to actual cost.

title: Mortgage and its Contemporary Applications
q: A client mortgages to Bank A a debt owed to him by Company X; other creditors of the client also claim that debt. Who has the stronger claim?
options: Company X decides whom to pay first
The earliest creditor of the client, whoever it is
All creditors share it in proportion to their claims
Bank A, as mortgagee, is more entitled to it
explanation: Per 3/2/12, when a debt is mortgaged, the mortgagee becomes more entitled to it than anyone else.

title: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
q: A sale contract signed today gives the buyer a 15-day cooling-off option starting six months from now. Is this valid?
options: Yes, since its duration is clearly specified at the time of contracting
Yes, if the buyer pays part of the price in advance
No; the option period must begin with the contract
No, because options may never exceed three days from the contract date
explanation: Per 2/2/3, the stipulated cooling-off period must coincide with the beginning of the contract period.

title: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
q: A seller tells Ahmad: "This machine is yours for 1,000 cash or 2,000 deferred," and they part without settling on either price. What is the ruling?
options: Valid at the higher deferred price by default
Void, as combining two sales in one sale
Valid, and the buyer later chooses the price
Valid at the lower cash price by default
explanation: Per 5/1/1, selling for 1,000 cash or 2,000 deferred without concluding either deal is Bay'atayn Fi Bay'ah, which nullifies the contract.

title: Waqf
q: A Waqif stipulates that his Waqf may never be exchanged (Istibdal) under any circumstances. What is the effect of this condition?
options: The condition binds only during his lifetime
The condition is binding as a Waqif condition
The whole Waqf becomes void
The condition is rejected; the Waqf remains valid
explanation: Per 4/1/3, absolute forbiddance of Istibdal is an invalid condition; such a condition is rejected while the Waqf remains valid.

title: Loan (Qard)
q: Bank A charges credit card holders a fee of 3% of every cash amount withdrawn from an ATM. What is the ruling?
options: Not permissible: the charge may not be linked to the amount
Permissible, if it is capped at a maximum amount
Permissible, as it is a charge for services
Permissible, if the percentage rate is disclosed to the cardholder in advance
explanation: Per 10/3/2, ATM cash withdrawal charges on credit cards must be a certain amount within reasonable limits; linking the charge to the amount withdrawn is not permissible.

title: Procrastinating Debtor
q: Bank A's Murabahah contract obliges the customer, if he procrastinates, to donate a percentage of the debt to charitable causes through the Bank. Ruling?
options: Not permissible, as it is a penalty on a debt
Permissible only if a court orders each individual donation
Permissible if the Bank keeps it as income
Permissible, as an undertaking by the debtor to donate
explanation: Per 2/1/8, a debtor's undertaking to donate an amount or percentage of the debt to charity through the Institution if he procrastinates is permissible.

title: Sharikah (Musharakah) and Modern Corporations
q: Before signing, Bank A learns that the funds a conventional bank will contribute to a proposed Sharikah clearly come from non-permissible sources. May Bank A proceed?
options: No, partnership is not permissible when this has become evident
Yes, since the funds are mixed once contributed to capital
Yes, provided the conventional bank manages the operations
Yes, if Bank A takes a higher profit share as purification
explanation: Per 3/1/1/2, partnership with non-Muslims or conventional banks is permissible unless it has become evident that their funds are from non-permissible sources.

title: Islamic Reinsurance
q: Allocations deducted from a solidarity reinsurance fund remain unpaid on liquidation. Per the basis, how are they treated?
options: Returned to participants in proportion to contributions
Spent on charitable purposes, not given to participants
Transferred to the shareholders' equity
Paid to the company as Mudarib
explanation: Per the basis (j), such unpaid allocations at liquidation are spent on charitable purposes and not given to participants, unlike in commercial reinsurance.

title: ’Arboun (Earnest Money)
q: A buyer pays 'Arboun for a cow. During the option period, before delivery, the cow gives birth to a calf. Absent any stipulation, how is the calf treated?
options: It is sold separately and its price divided equally
It belongs to the seller since delivery has not occurred
It is considered part of the sale item
It belongs to the buyer only if he later revokes
explanation: Per 8/2, separate growth during the option period, before or after delivery, is in principle part of the sale item, unless the liable party stipulates otherwise.

title: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
q: A restricted investment account suffers a loss because Bank A invested in a project outside the one specified by the account holder. Who bears the loss?
options: The holder, as restricted accounts bear all losses
The Bank, as it arises from breach of the contract
The holder and the Bank equally
The account holder, in proportion to his capital
explanation: Per 2/1/2, the holder bears losses in proportion to his capital share, except losses from transgression, negligence or breach of contract, borne by the Institution.

title: Waqf
q: A scholar objects that a Waqf deferred to a future date involves gharar. How does the standard's Shari'ah basis answer this?
options: Deferral to a known date removes all gharar from the contract
Gharar is accepted when the Waqif is wealthy
Gharar has no effect in donation contracts like Waqf
Gharar is lifted by registering the deed with the authorities
explanation: Basis 2/4/1/3: the cause for barring suspension or deferral is gharar, which is non-effective in donation contracts such as Waqf.

title: Online Financial Dealings
q: Bank A's website is trespassed, causing it direct financial loss and actual loss of earnings. What does the compensation comprise?
options: Both the direct financial loss and the actual loss of earnings
Only a fixed penalty set in advance by the Bank
Only the direct financial loss, excluding loss of earnings
Only the expected profit the Bank had planned to earn
explanation: Per 8/1/5, compensation for trespassing comprises direct financial loss as well as actual loss of earnings; expert advice may be sought.

title: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
q: A Mudarabah investment account contract sets no profit ratios at signing, and there is no normal practice to refer to. What is the result?
options: Ratios are set later by the Bank at distribution
The Mudarib takes the whole profit as reward for the work he performed
Profit is shared equally between the two parties
Void; the Mudarib gets a normal wage and Rab al-Mal all profit
explanation: Per 4/2, if ratios are unspecified and no normal practice exists, the Mudarabah is void; the Mudarib gets the wage for similar work and all profit goes to Rab al-Mal.

title: Combination of Contracts
q: A finance house offers hire-purchase in its traditional form, where one contract is at once a lease and a sale of the asset. What is the ruling?
options: Permissible, if the rentals equal the asset price
Permissible, as it is like Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek
Not permissible, as leasing and selling contradict here
Permissible, if ownership passes at the end
explanation: Per 4/4, leasing with selling (hire-purchase in its traditional form) is listed among contradictory contracts that may not be combined.

title: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
q: Without any need or urgency and with no authority, Karim sells Ahmad's goods to a buyer. Ahmad later approves the sale. From when is the sale effective?
options: From the date the buyer takes delivery of the goods from Karim
From the date of Karim's act, as approval is retroactive
It is not effective; a new contract is needed between Ahmad and the buyer
From the date of Ahmad's approval only, as approval is not retroactive
explanation: Per 8/4, when the owner approves the act of the uncommissioned agent, the contract becomes effective under agency rules, retroactively from the date of the act.

title: Sale of Debt
q: Sukuk proceeds are used partly for Murabaha transactions and partly for tangible assets such as Ijarah assets. How is trading in these Sukuk governed?
options: They may never be traded, as they hold debts
They trade freely, as an ongoing business
They may trade only at their face value
As a commingled entity, incl. the tangible ratio
explanation: Per 8/4, trading such Sukuk is subject to 8/2 (incl. the tangible asset ratio), provided the issuance guarantees nothing impermissible.

title: Online Financial Dealings
q: Bank A wants to use electronic signatures to verify the identities of dealers on its website. When is this acceptable?
options: When it is adoptable under the prevailing rules and regulations
Never; identity may be proved only by the dealer's personal presence
Only when the dealer also signs a paper copy later
Only for contracts below a certain monetary limit
explanation: Per 8/2/2, the electronic signature is acceptable for verifying dealers' identities if it is adoptable by virtue of the prevailing rules and regulations.

title: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
q: Company X's bylaws give existing shareholders priority to subscribe in a capital increase. How is each shareholder's priority right determined?
options: Equally among all shareholders, whatever their holdings before the issuance
In proportion to his respective share before the issuance
Only for shareholders with a majority stake
According to the order of applications
explanation: Per 13/1, bylaws may give existing shareholders priority to subscribe; each may subscribe in proportion to his respective share prior to the issuance.

title: Al-Wakalah Bi Al-Istithmar (Investment Agency)
q: Under an unrestricted investment agency, Bank A puts the principal's funds into a type of venture that customary practice would never accept for such funds. Was Bank A free to do so?
options: No; it remains bound by custom and the principal's best interests
Yes, as long as the agreed agency fee was not exceeded
No; an unrestricted agent may invest only in Murabahah deals
Yes; an unrestricted agent may invest in anything at all
explanation: Per 3/3, an unrestricted agency is still restricted by customary practice and requires the agent to act in the principal's best interests.

title: Payment Cards
q: Bank A requires charge cardholders to deposit a cash guarantee and insists it be placed in a current account. What does the standard require?
options: The deposit must be placed in a current account, as it is a guarantee
No cash guarantee may ever be requested from a charge cardholder
Giving the option of a current or an investment account
The deposit must be in an investment account
explanation: Per 4/3/2, the issuer should not stipulate depositing the guarantee in the current account; the holder chooses a current or investment account.

title: Mudarabah
q: Midway through a Mudarabah, the parties agree to change the profit ratio from 60:40 to 50:50 for the next year only. What is the ruling?
options: Not permitted once the contract has been concluded
Permitted only if approved by an independent third party
Permitted only at the final liquidation of the Mudarabah
Permissible to change it at any time and set its duration
explanation: Per 8/3, the parties may change the profit distribution ratio at any time and define the duration for which the agreement remains valid.

title: Waqf
q: Ahmad declares his house a Waqf for his nephew Bilal. Bilal has not yet expressed acceptance. Is the Waqf created?
options: No, a specific beneficiary must accept it first, as with a gift
Yes, Waqf does not require the beneficiary's acceptance
No, not until Bilal takes possession of the house itself
Yes, but it remains revocable by Ahmad until Bilal accepts it
explanation: Per 2/4/1/1, an offer from the Waqif creates Waqf; it does not require acceptance of the Waqf beneficiary, whether specific or not.

title: Murabahah
q: Bank A paid insurance on goods during its ownership, before selling them by Murabahah. How may it treat this expense?
options: Include it in the Murabahah cost price
Bear it only, with no addition to cost
Deduct it from the Hamish Jiddiyyah
Charge it to the customer as a separate fee
explanation: Per 3/2/6, the Institution may include insurance expenses in the Murabahah cost price; insurance must be on a Takaful basis whenever possible.

title: Competitions and Prizes
q: Two competitors in a race each put up SR 1,000, and the winner takes the whole amount. Is this reward-based competition permissible?
options: Yes, if the race is in a permissible activity
Yes, since the two competitors contribute equally
No, a reward from more than one competitor is barred
Yes, provided a third party holds the money
explanation: Per 2/3/2/2, the reward must come from a third party or one competitor; if offered by more than one competitor, it is not permissible.

title: Mudarabah
q: A Mudarib invested prudently within the contract terms, but a market fall caused a 20% loss of the capital. Who bears the loss?
options: Both parties equally, as partners in the Mudarabah who share profit and loss
The Mudarib, up to the amount of his expected profit
The Mudarib, who must restore the capital in full from his own assets
The capital provider; the Mudarib is a trustee, not liable
explanation: Per 4/4, the Mudarib invests on a trust basis and is not liable for losses except in case of misconduct, negligence or breach of the contract terms.

title: Murabahah
q: Which precedent does the Shari'ah basis cite for allowing a rebate when a Murabahah debtor pays early?
options: The practice of Umar Ibn Al-Khattab on 'Arboun in sale contracts
The Prophet asking Ubay Ibn Ka'b to write off part of a debt
The Prophet's purchase of a she-camel from Abu Bakr
The Hadith of Hibban Ibn Munqidh on options
explanation: The basis: early payment discount is a settlement; in Ubay Ibn Ka'b's case the Prophet suggested: 'write off a portion of your debt.'

title: Guarantees
q: Bank A requires both a personal guarantee and a mortgage of security in one Murabahah contract. What is the ruling?
options: Permissible only if the guarantor owns the mortgaged asset
Permissible only if each is in a separate document
Only one form of security may be taken per contract
Permissible to include several guarantees in one contract
explanation: Per 2/1/2, there is no Shari'ah objection to including a number of guarantees in one contract, such as a personal guarantee together with a mortgage.

title: Waqf
q: A Waqf's revenue cannot cover all of: preserving the Waqf asset, employees' dues and beneficiaries' shares. Which is paid first?
options: Preservation of the Waqf asset
The administrative employees' dues
The relevant parties dealing with the Waqf
The beneficiaries' shares
explanation: Per 9/10/1, in competition of avenues, preservation of the Waqf asset comes first, then obligations to employees and parties, then per the Waqif.

title: Possession (Qabd)
q: A heap of grain is sold by estimate without being weighed or measured. The seller relinquishes it to the buyer, enabling him to take it without obstacle. What is the status of possession?
options: Possession occurs only if the sale is registered officially
No possession until the grain is physically transported
Constructive possession is realised by the relinquishment
No possession, as grain must always be weighed first
explanation: Per 3/3, relinquishment is constructive possession even where measures are applicable but not applied, as in sale by estimate.

title: Rules for Calculating Profit in Financial Transactions
q: Bank A sells a car for 100,000 cash or 120,000 payable over two years. Is the higher credit price permissible?
options: Yes, but only if the increase equals the prevailing interest rate
Yes, if built into the price and the debt never rises for late payment
Yes, and more may be added to the debt if payment is late
No; any extra price charged for deferment of payment is Riba
explanation: Per 5, profit in credit sales may exceed cash sales if incorporated into the price and the debt is not increased due to late payment.

title: Ijarah and Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek
q: A customer breaks his promise to take an asset on operating Ijarah. Bank A keeps the asset and does not sell it. What compensation may the Bank claim?
options: None, since the asset was not sold
A fixed amount stated in the promise
The difference between cost and market value
The first year's expected rentals
explanation: Per 2/3, in operating Ijarah the charge is cost minus the third-party selling price; if the asset is not sold, the promisee is not entitled to any compensation.

title: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
q: An item that is 70% gold mixed with copper is sold by Bank A for pure gold on spot. What condition applies to the weight of the pure gold?
options: It must equal the gold contained in the item
It must equal the item's total weight
No weight condition applies to such alloys
It must outweigh the gold contained in the item
explanation: Per 3/3/1/1 (second form, first type), the pure gold must weigh more than the gold in the alloy, the excess being for the non-gold substance.

title: Zakah
q: Company X chose to postpone Zakah on a sound outstanding debt until it is collected. When it collects the debt after three years, what must it pay?
options: No Zakah, as it chose to postpone
Zakah only on the profit component
Zakah for the whole past period
Zakah for one year only
explanation: Per 5/3/2, the Institution can postpone Zakah on outstanding debts until collection, but on collection it has to pay Zakah for the whole past period.

title: Documentary Credit
q: Bank A is asked to confirm (endorse) a credit issued by Bank B, with no services required of Bank A. What may Bank A charge?
options: Only the actual expenses it incurs
A percentage fee for the confirmation risk
Actual expenses plus a fee for the guarantee
A lump-sum fee for guaranteeing payment
explanation: Per 3/3/1(a), guarantee per se is not priced; confirming another bank's credit is an addition over guarantee, so only actual expenses may be charged.

title: Syndicated Financing
q: Four Institutions arrange a syndicated financing. Who should supervise its arrangement, implementation and follow-up?
options: The Shari'ah supervisory board of the borrower only, as the beneficiary
The central bank of the lead manager's country only, as the regulator
The participating Institutions' Shari'ah supervisory boards
The lead manager's internal audit department only, with no board role
explanation: Per 5/4, it takes place under the participants' Shari'ah supervisory boards; preferably a joint committee of them makes decisions binding on all parties.

title: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
q: Converting Bank A asks which Shari'ah governance bodies it must set up as part of the necessary measures for conversion. What does the standard require?
options: A Zakah committee in place of a Shari'ah board
Only a Shari'ah adviser for new products
Only an external Shari'ah auditor appointed on a yearly contract basis
A Shari'ah supervisory board and internal compliance department
explanation: Per 3/4, the bank must form a Shari'ah supervisory board and an internal Shari'ah compliance department per AAOIFI Governance Standards.

title: Monetization (Tawarruq)
q: Why does the Shari'ah basis allow a client to appoint the Institution as his selling agent where the law bars him from selling directly?
options: Because constructive receipt is not required in such cases
To safeguard the deal from being nullified by the law
Because agency of the Institution is permitted in all cases
Because the Institution bears the risk of the commodity
explanation: The Shari'ah basis states that permitting the Institution's agency where the client by law cannot sell directly is meant to safeguard the deal from nullification by law.

title: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
q: Bank B buys in Salam a commodity that is not usually available in the market on the agreed delivery date. What is the ruling on this contract?
options: Valid if the seller provides a guarantor
Valid, since the Gharar is only minor
Void, due to excessive Gharar
Valid, as Salam is an exception for non-owned goods
explanation: Per 4/2/1, sale of a Salam commodity that is not usually available on the date of delivery is an example of excessive Gharar that nullifies the contract.

title: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
q: Bank A wants to buy gold through a Salam contract, paying the capital of Salam in currency at the session. What is the ruling?
options: Permissible, as the capital is paid at the session
Not permissible, as the capital may not be currency
Permissible, as Salam always defers the subject
Permissible, if the gold is precisely described
explanation: Per 5/2/2, gold may be bought through Salam provided the capital of Salam is not gold, silver or currencies.

title: Waqf
q: Ahmad makes Waqf of his current account balance held at Bank A. What is the ruling?
options: Valid, even though the balance is a debt owed by the bank
Invalid, as a debt cannot be a Waqf asset
Valid only if converted into real estate
Valid only after he withdraws the balance in physical cash
explanation: Per 2/4/13/1, Waqf over cash is permitted even if it is an outstanding debt, e.g., current account balances.

title: Competitions and Prizes
q: Bank A's marketing team designs a competition, with a modest reward from shareholders' funds and due regard to public interest. What else is required before launch?
options: A promise that every participant wins a prize
Approval of the investment account holders
A fee from each participant to cover costs
Approval of the Bank's Shari'ah Supervisory Board
explanation: Per 2/3/3/3, a competition organized or sponsored by the Institution must be approved by its Shari'ah Supervisory Board.

title: Islamic Insurance
q: Ahmad's insured warehouse is completely destroyed by fire, a covered risk. What happens to his policy and his claim?
options: The policy continues for the remaining period
The policy expires, but his right to indemnity remains
The claim is paid only if he renews the policy
The policy expires and his claim lapses with it, as nothing remains insured
explanation: Per 13/3, complete damage of the insured property ends the policy, without nullifying the participant's entitlement to indemnity, subject to conditions.

title: Guarantees
q: Bank A sells goods on deferred payment and stipulates a guarantee in the body of the same sale contract. Does this affect the permissibility of the sale?
options: No, but only if the guarantee is a mortgage
Yes, a guarantee must always be made in a separate contract
Yes, the condition renders the sale void
No, the guarantee does not affect the original contract
explanation: Per 2/1/1, a guarantee is permissible in contracts of exchange and does not affect the permissibility of the original contract; it may be stipulated within it.

title: Payment Cards
q: Bank A gives its cardholders free air-miles and hotel booking discounts. The card's fees are not raised for these. What is the ruling?
options: Permitted, as Shari'ah compliant free benefits
Not permitted, as gifts to borrowers are riba
Not permitted due to gharar in the benefit
Permitted only on debit cards
explanation: Per 5/6/2, it is permitted to give cardholders Shari'ah-permissible benefits for free, e.g., gifts, discounts, air-miles and cash back.

title: Mortgage and its Contemporary Applications
q: A building mortgaged to Bank A increases in value and earns rental income. The contract is silent. What is the status of the increase and income?
options: They belong to the mortgagor free of the mortgage
They belong to Bank A as compensation for waiting
They are mortgaged along with the principal
Only the increase in value is mortgaged, not the income
explanation: Per 3/2/8, appreciation in value and income of the mortgaged asset are mortgaged along with the principal, unless the parties agree otherwise.

title: Islamic Insurance
q: Policyholders of Islamic Insurance Company T want a say in how insurance operations are run. What does the standard prefer?
options: Participation only after a deficit occurs
Their participation, e.g. through Board representation
Full control by the shareholders, without input from the policyholders
Participation only through the annual surplus
explanation: Per 5/7, preference should be given to policyholders participating in management, e.g. through representation in the Board of Directors.

title: Unilateral and Bilateral Promise
q: In an Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek, Bank A promises to gift the asset to the lessee if he pays all lease instalments. He pays them all, but Bank A hesitates. Is the promise binding?
options: Yes, but only if the gift was priced in the rent
No; promises of gifts are never legally binding, even when conditional on full payment
Yes; it is legally binding as a conditional gift promise
No; only the lessee's promises are legally binding
explanation: Per 5/2 with 3/6, the institution's promise in Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek to gift the asset conditional on payment of all instalments is legally binding.

title: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
q: Investors buying a conventional bank to convert it can negotiate to exclude interest receivables and leave impermissible liabilities with the seller. Must they?
options: Yes, Shari'ah requires them to do so
No, it is merely a recommendation
Only for receivables, not liabilities
No, they must take over all assets
explanation: Per 9/2, if the purchaser can exclude non-permissible receivables and leave the seller liable for non-permissible liabilities, Shari'ah requires it to do so.

title: Ju’alah
q: Bank A names Company Y as the worker in a Ju'alah to prepare a study. Company Y wants to hand the work to another firm. What does the standard require?
options: Only a notice to Bank A after the study has been completed
Nothing; any worker may get help from anyone he likes
It is never allowed; Company Y must do all the work itself
Express consent of Bank A, with the firm under Y's supervision
explanation: Per 5/1, a specified worker must do the work himself or, with the offeror's express consent, through someone under his supervision and control.

title: Zakah
q: Company X cannot tell which of its debts financed Zakatable assets. Zakatable assets are 40% of total assets and total debts are 10 million. What is deducted?
options: Nothing
10 million
4 million
6 million
explanation: Per 6/2/3, when it is difficult to know the debt from Zakatable assets, use their ratio to total assets; at 40%, 40% of total debts is deducted.

title: Online Financial Dealings
q: A client was deceived online by a forged identity of the seller. Per the basis, why may he terminate the contract?
options: It affects his consent, a fundamental prerequisite of contracting
The forgery is a contingent incident after signing
The forgery turns the contract into an adhesion contract subject to the State
The forgery makes the price unknown to the buyer
explanation: Per the basis, forgery or error about a party can influence the consent of the deceived party, and consent is the fundamental prerequisite of contracting.

title: Options to Revoke Contracts Due to Incomplete Performance
q: At contracting, Ahmad knew that part of a package of goods belonged to a third party and might be withheld. It is withheld. Does he have an option for deal fragmentation?
options: Yes, if the third party objects
Yes, but only to claim compensation
Yes, as the deal is now incomplete and he did not receive everything he bought
No; he must not have known the deal would fragment
explanation: Per 3/2, the option to revoke owing to deal fragmentation is subject to the buyer not knowing that the deal would become fragmented.

title: Hawalah
q: Per the Shari'ah basis, which school alone permits unrestricted Hawalah, and on what ground?
options: The Shafi'is, as it resembles a sale of debt
The Hanafis, as the order to accept did not require a debt
The Malikis, as market custom has always favoured this practice
The Hanbalis, as it is a kind of guarantee
explanation: Per the Basis, restricted Hawalah is agreed; unrestricted Hawalah is permitted by the Hanafis only, as the order to accept did not require the payer to be a debtor.

title: Sharikah (Musharakah) and Modern Corporations
q: A board member asks what the general basis of Sharikah is, since each partner acts for himself and for the others. What does the Shari'ah basis say?
options: Charitable donation
Mudarabah
Guarantee (Kafalah)
Agency (Wakalah)
explanation: Per the basis, the general basis of Sharikah is agency (Wakalah): each partner acts as principal and as agent for the others; Mufawadah also adds guarantee.

title: Waqf
q: An investment Waqf company seeks Shari'ah compliant financing to expand its commercial operations. What is the ruling?
options: Not permitted without the Waqif's stipulation
Permitted, if its revenues can settle the obligations
Permitted only for necessary maintenance of the existing assets
Not permitted unless the Waqf asset is in ruin or has no revenue
explanation: Per 5/2, investment Waqfs may incur debt for development under commercial practice, considering the Waqf's interest and adequacy of revenues.

title: Loan (Qard)
q: Bank A's actual direct cost of servicing a Qard is 50. It charges the borrower a service fee of 2% of the loan, which comes to 400. What is the ruling?
options: Permitted, as a percentage fee is common market practice for loans
Permitted, if disclosed before the loan is granted
Prohibited: charges above actual direct costs are not allowed
Permitted, if approved by the borrower
explanation: Per 9/1, a lending institution may charge only the actual amount directly spent on loan services; any charge in excess of that is prohibited.

title: Commercial Papers
q: A banker argues that discounting a bill is merely a trade in paper. Per the Shari'ah basis, what does discounting amount to in reality?
options: A loan with interest, varying with value and maturity
A sale of goods for a deferred price to the bank
A permitted reduction of the debt for early payment
A fee for collecting the bill's value as agent
explanation: Per the basis, discounting is in reality a loan with interest, as the charge varies with the paper's value and maturity date; loans with interest are prohibited.

title: Procrastinating Debtor
q: Late payers at Bank A customarily add 2% when finally settling, though no contract mentions it. May the Bank accept this extra under the standard?
options: Yes, as it counts as good settlement of debt
Yes, since nothing is written in any contract with the debtor
No, the custom on the extra makes it impermissible
Yes, if the debtor hands it over willingly
explanation: Per 2/5/2, an excess may be accepted only where there is no condition, whether written or verbal, or custom or mutual agreement relating to it.

title: Irrigation Partnership (Musaqat)
q: A Musaqat worker hires two helpers to assist him with the customary work, and asks that their wages be paid out of the overall crop. What is the ruling?
options: Their wages come from the crop before division
He may not hire anyone to assist him
The owner must pay their wages in full
He may hire them, but their wages are his alone
explanation: Per 6/2 and 8/3, the worker may employ others to assist, but if he hires others to do his work their wage is his sole responsibility, not taken from the crop.

title: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
q: Ahmad pledges his lost car as Rahn for a debt to Bank A. Later he defaults while the car is still missing. What is the position?
options: The Rahn is void, as a lost car cannot be pledged
The Rahn is valid, but the car cannot be sold until found
The Bank may sell the car's title at once
The Rahn is valid and the Bank may claim its estimated value
explanation: Per 6/1, Rahn may involve Gharar not allowed in sale, e.g. a lost car; but it cannot be sold to settle the debt unless the lost car is found.

title: Financial Paper (Shares and Bonds)
q: Bank A buys a controlling stake in a conventional bank, able to pass a resolution at the first general meeting to convert it to Shari'ah compliance. What is the ruling?
options: Permissible, as participation for purposes of conversion
Permissible only if Bank A takes no dividends at all from the bank
Not permissible, as the bank deals in Riba
Permissible only after conversion is complete
explanation: Per 3/3, participation or trading for conversion is permitted for one able to convert by a resolution at the first general meeting, or striving to do so.

title: Murabahah
q: Bank A takes the Murabahah asset itself as a mortgage to secure the customer's debt, without taking possession of it. Is this permissible?
options: No, the sold asset cannot secure its own price
Yes, as a fiduciary mortgage or registered charge
No, a mortgage requires taking possession
Yes, but only if a third party guarantees too
explanation: Per 5/2, the Institution may take the Murabahah subject matter as fiduciary mortgage (registered charge), with or without possession.

title: Financial Paper (Shares and Bonds)
q: Why can shares of a named corporation not be the subject-matter of Salam, per the Basis?
options: Shares cannot be described precisely enough to be the subject of Salam
Salam is valid only for food items and crops
Salam's subject is a debt; such shares are ascertained
Shares have no reliable market price for Salam
explanation: Per the Basis, the subject-matter of Salam is a debt, while shares of a named corporation are ascertained; Salam in them also sells what is not owned.

title: Credit Agreement
q: A client paid Hamish Jiddiyyah with his binding promise in a Murabahah, then retreated. Bank A suffered actual harm of 2,000 while the deposit is 5,000. What may the Bank do?
options: Return the whole 5,000 and claim nothing
Keep the whole deposit as part of the price
Keep the whole 5,000 as compensation
Deduct 2,000 of actual harm and return the rest
explanation: Per 5/3/1/6, if the client retreats from concluding the contract, the amount of actual harm caused to the Institution is deducted from the seriousness margin.

title: Istisna’a and Parallel Istisna’a
q: According to the Shari'ah basis, whose view supports Istisna'a being a binding contract, and why?
options: Abu Yusuf's: the maker spends money to produce to specs
Imam Ahmad's: 'Arboun makes contracts binding
Ibn Rushd's: all sales are binding by scholarly consensus
The Maliki view: a promise is always binding
explanation: The basis cites Abu Yusuf's view in the Mejelle: the manufacturer spends money to produce to specification and would suffer loss if the buyer could refuse.

title: Buyback
q: Why is leasing a purchased asset back to its seller under Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek not treated as 'Inah?
options: The lessee owns the usufruct and may sublease it to third parties
Rent is for usufruct, a different subject from the sale
The rent is fixed in advance and paid on spot at the contract
The lessor's possession is held in trust
explanation: Per the Basis, rent is paid for the renewable usufruct, a different subject matter from the first sale; also time passes and value changes.

title: Sharikah (Musharakah) and Modern Corporations
q: In a service partnership of two printers, one partner provides the printing machine required for the work. Which arrangement does the standard permit?
options: He provides it for a fee charged against the Sharikah as an expense
He must sell the machine to the partnership at its original purchase price
He receives a guaranteed fixed share of profit for it
The machine automatically becomes common capital of the Sharikah once he brings it
explanation: Per 3/3/4, a party may provide the capital goods for fees charged against the Sharikah as expenses; each may also provide and own his own goods.

title: Islamic Insurance
q: Company T manages an Islamic insurance fund and incurs costs for its own staff who invest the insurance assets. Who bears these costs?
options: The participants, through extra contributions
The fund and the company equally
The policyholders fund, as insurance expenses
The company, as expenses of its own operations
explanation: Per 3/1, the company bears all the expenses of its operations including those relating to its tasks for investing the insurance assets.

title: Buyback
q: In an investment deposit used for liquidity management, Bank A as investment agent wishes to tell the depositor bank about returns. Which statement is permitted?
options: A guaranteed minimum return only
A guarantee of the capital in full
An expected return, without obligation
A guaranteed specified return
explanation: Per 5/6/3/3(c), the manager may not guarantee a specified return; it may state an expected return without obligation to realize it.

title: ’Arboun (Earnest Money)
q: Ahmad pays 'Arboun for a car, but the contract is silent on the option period. There is an existing local custom that specifies the option period for such sales. How is the period set?
options: By the seller, unilaterally, after the contract
By the existing custom specifying the option period
It is left to Ahmad, who may revoke at any time
It stays open until Ahmad pays the remaining price
explanation: Per item 4, the option period must be specified by express stipulation of the parties or by custom where a custom specifies it.

title: Buyback
q: How does the standard justify characterizing a conventional repo as an interest-bearing loan rather than a sale?
options: The buyer bears the risk of loss of the assets
The assets are sold at a cash price
Contracts are judged by real intention, not form
The second price is set by an auction
explanation: Per the Basis, the essential consideration is real intention rather than form; the sale is fictitious and the assets are only security.

title: Irrigation Partnership (Musaqat)
q: An owner sets a Musaqat term ending before the produce normally materializes. Per the Shari'ah basis, why is this impermissible?
options: Short terms are prohibited in all contracts, as the parties cannot foresee the outcome
The worker must always receive a market wage
Harvest time must be fixed by a judge
Justice: the owner must not get the produce while the worker gets nothing
explanation: Per the basis, the term runs until produce materializes per the rules of justice, so the owner does not exclusively benefit and the worker is not deprived.

title: Sharikah (Musharakah) and Modern Corporations
q: Partners agree that only partner Bilal will manage their Sharikah. Later partner Ahmad signs a sale on behalf of the partnership. What does the standard say?
options: The other partners are bound by their consent not to act for the partnership
Restricting management to one partner is not permissible in Sharikah
Ahmad may act because he contributed part of the partnership capital
Every partner keeps an unrestricted right to act on the partnership's behalf
explanation: Per 3/1/3/2, partners may restrict management to one partner; the others are then bound to abide by their consent not to act on behalf of the partnership.

title: Murabahah
q: Bank A takes possession of goods ordered by Customer C and treats the Murabahah as automatically concluded with C at that moment. What is the ruling?
options: Permitted, if C was informed of the possession in advance
Permitted, if C paid Hamish Jiddiyyah
Not permitted; mere possession does not conclude it
Permitted, since C had given a binding promise to buy
explanation: Per 4/1, the Institution may not consider the Murabahah automatically concluded by its mere taking possession of the asset.

title: Waqf
q: A Waqf's beneficiaries are three named persons. With authority permission and a preferred interest, the overseer wants to redeploy some revenue in the Waqf asset. What else is needed?
options: The consent of the three beneficiaries
The Waqif's heirs' approval
Nothing further; the permission suffices
A court judgment for each redeployment
explanation: Per 9/6, if the Waqf beneficiaries are specific parties, their consent is required for redeploying revenue in the Waqf asset.

title: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
q: A jeweller sells an alloy of gold and silver containing 40 g of gold for 40 g of pure gold, exchanged on spot. Is the sale permissible?
options: Yes, as the gold weights are equal and it is spot
No, the pure gold must outweigh the gold in the alloy
No, such alloys may be sold only for currencies
Yes, provided the silver is valued separately
explanation: Per 3/3/1/1, a gold-silver alloy sold for pure gold needs spot exchange and the pure countervalue must weigh more; equal or lighter is not permissible.

title: Debit Card, Charge Card and Credit Card
q: Ahmad buys currency from a merchant with his debit card and signs the payment coupon. Per the Shari'ah basis, why is the possession condition satisfied?
options: Possession occurs when the statement is issued
Card purchases are exempt from possession rules
The signed coupon counts as actual delivery of the price
The accounting entry counts as constructive possession
explanation: Per the Basis (7), buying with a debit card is constructive possession, since an accounting entry is considered constructive possession (Fiqh Academy decision).

title: Guarantees
q: Bakr guaranteed Ahmad's 10,000 debt at Ahmad's request. Bakr obtains a discount and pays the creditor 8,000. How much may he recover from Ahmad?
options: 8,000, the amount he actually paid
10,000, the full original debt
9,000, sharing the discount equally
Nothing, as he chose to settle early
explanation: Per 3/3/2, a guarantor who secures a discount recovers only what he actually paid, not the full debt; this prevents a procedure potentially leading to Riba.

title: Online Financial Dealings
q: A call between Bank A and a client negotiating an Ijarah is cut off for a reasonably short while and then resumes. What is the effect on the contract session?
options: The session stops and the offer must be issued anew
The contract is deemed concluded at the time of disconnection
The session stops, but the offer stays binding for a day
The short disconnection does not stop the session
explanation: Per 4/1/1, disconnection stops the session unless the disconnection of the conversation is for a reasonably short while.

title: Waqf
q: Ahmad makes a three-year Waqf of specific Sukuk that mature in five years. What happens at the end of the three-year Waqf period?
options: The Sukuk become a perpetual Waqf
The Waqf continues until the Sukuk mature
Ahmad recovers the same number of Sukuk
The Sukuk are sold and Ahmad receives the price
explanation: Per 2/4/15/1(b)(2), if the Waqf period is shorter than the Sukuk term, the Waqif recovers the same number of Sukuk at the end of the Waqf period.

title: Possession (Qabd)
q: Bank A holds a customer's goods in trust (Amanah) as a depositary and then buys them, so its new possession entails liability for loss (Daman). How does its prior possession count?
options: It does not count, as possession in trust cannot become possession in liability
It stands in place of the new possession despite the difference
It counts only if the goods are first insured
It counts only if the customer re-delivers the goods
explanation: Per 3/6, prior possession substitutes subsequent possession whether the prior was Daman or Amanah and whether the later entails liability or trust.

title: Credit Agreement
q: In a sale, the buyer paid 'Arboun to Bank A, then used his right to terminate the contract. What happens to the 'Arboun?
options: It is returned in full to the buyer
It is held in trust until a new buyer is found
It is owned by the Bank as seller
It is returned after deducting actual harm
explanation: Per 5/3/2/2, 'Arboun is part of the price paid in advance; it is owned by the seller or landlord when the buyer or tenant uses his right of terminating the contract.

title: Payment Cards
q: Ahmad converts part of his prepaid card balance from the local currency into US dollars. Which rulings apply to this conversion?
options: The rulings of Hawalah (transfer of debt) only
The rulings of Qard (loan) given by the issuer
The rulings of Murabahah (sale with disclosed profit)
The rulings of ṣarf (currency exchange)
explanation: Per 4/2/2, rulings of ṣarf apply on conversion of the prepaid balance or part of it to currencies other than the local currency.

title: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
q: Paying all of Bank B's pre-conversion impermissible earnings to charity at once would lead to its collapse. What does the standard allow?
options: Returning them to former depositors as extra profit
Disposal may reasonably take place gradually
Keeping them permanently as part of its capital base
Using them to fund bonuses for the bank's staff
explanation: Per 10/1, impermissible earnings go to charity without delay unless that would cause collapse or bankruptcy; then implementation may be reasonably gradual.

title: Murabahah
q: Bank A buys a building. The seller vacates it, but Bank A is not able to have disposal of it. Has Bank A taken possession?
options: No, vacating without disposal is not possession
Yes, if the customer has already promised to buy
Yes, once the sale contract is signed
Yes, vacating real property always conveys possession
explanation: Per 3/2/3, real property is possessed by vacating it and placing it at the acquirer's disposal; if he cannot dispose of it, vacating is not possession.

title: Sharikah (Musharakah) and Modern Corporations
q: A stock company issues new shares to increase its capital. Its old shares' fair value is above their nominal value. At what price may the new shares be issued?
options: Only at a discount, to attract new subscribers
At any price the board sets, regardless of the value of the old shares
At the old shares' fair value, as assessed by experts
Only at nominal value, to treat all subscribers equally and avoid disputes
explanation: Per 4/1/2/3, new shares may be issued at the fair value of the old shares per expert valuation, i.e. at a premium, discount or market value.

title: Mudarabah
q: At liquidation, a Mudarabah shows a net loss and the Mudarib was neither negligent nor guilty of misconduct. How is the net loss treated?
options: Carried forward as a debt owed by the Mudarib
Shared 50:50 between the Mudarib and the provider
Recovered from the Mudarib's guarantee
Deducted from the capital; the Mudarib is not liable
explanation: Per 8/7, if losses exceed profits at liquidation, the net loss is deducted from capital; the Mudarib, a trustee, is not liable absent negligence or misconduct.

title: Liability of the Investment Manager
q: An investment agent's misconduct causes damage to a commodity held as an investment, and its value changes afterwards. Which date determines the extent of liability?
options: The date the loss or destruction occurred
The date the investment contract was concluded
The date Rab Al Maal files the claim
The date the liability is finally adjudicated
explanation: Per 7/4, for tangible assets, the date of the loss, shortage or destruction caused by the misconduct determines the extent of the liability.

title: Options to Revoke Contracts Due to Incomplete Performance
q: A buyer knew in advance that a package deal would be fragmented. Per the Shari'ah basis, why does this knowledge remove his option?
options: Knowledge transfers the risk of fragmentation to the third party who owns the goods
His knowledge evidences consent, and the defect is not hidden
Fragmentation is never a valid ground anyway
He should have bought from another seller
explanation: Per the basis, the buyer's prior knowledge is viewed as evidence of consent, and the defect is then not hidden or concealed.

title: Waqf
q: Why does the standard prevent pledging tangible Waqf assets?
options: A pledge allows sale to repay debt; Waqf assets can't be sold
Pledges are prohibited in all donation contracts, including Waqf
Waqf assets have no market value so cannot secure a debt
The overseer lacks any power to contract on behalf of the Waqf
explanation: Basis 6/1: a pledge secures debt with an asset that may be sold to discharge it, whereas sale of the Waqf asset is not permitted.

title: Rules for Calculating Profit in Financial Transactions
q: Bank A advertises "Home finance at only 4% profit!" without explaining how the profit is calculated. What does the standard require?
options: Nothing, as advertising is outside the contract and creates no obligation on the Bank
Disclosure only if a customer complains
Disclosure only once a contract is signed
Disclosure of the calculation method in its advertising
explanation: Per 9, the institution must disclose its method of profit calculation, including when mentioning profit in advertising and marketing, to prevent deception.

title: Islamic Reinsurance
