q: A participant company claims more compensation than the actual harm it suffered. Which principle in the basis limits reinsurance coverage?
options: Coverage includes expected profits of the insured
Coverage is for actual harm only, not for making wealth
Coverage equals the contribution paid in
Coverage is set by the reinsurer at its discretion
explanation: Per the basis, coverage rests on 'No harm and no reciprocal harm' and the rule that coverage is for actual harms and not for making wealth out of it.

title: Syndicated Financing
q: Bank A manages a syndicate as a paid agent for an agreed fee. The operation ends without any profit. Is Bank A entitled to its fee?
options: No, the fee is converted into a share of loss borne by Bank A
No, the fee is due only if profit is realized by the syndicate
Yes, the fee is due whether profit materializes or not
Only half of the fee, as no profit was made on the operation
explanation: Per 6/3, in paid agency the agent becomes entitled to remuneration whether profit is actually materialized or not.

title: Options to Revoke Contracts Due to Incomplete Performance
q: A buyer discovers a hidden defect in goods, but meanwhile the goods were damaged in his possession. The seller refuses to take them back. What is the buyer entitled to?
options: Return of the goods with a full refund
Nothing, since the goods are damaged
Return of the goods, less the damage
Compensation for the defect (Arsh) only
explanation: Per 2/6/2, if the item was damaged in the buyer's possession, he is entitled only to compensation for the defect, unless the seller accepts the damaged item back.

title: Al-Wakalah Bi Al-Istithmar (Investment Agency)
q: An investment agency expires with receivables still uncollected and no renewal. The principal demands that Bank A pay them from its own funds or via Tawarruq. Must it?
options: Yes; it must raise the amount through Tawarruq
No; it must collect them but need not pay from its own funds
No, and it has no duty to collect them either
Yes; it must pay them from its own funds and then recover the amounts from the debtors
explanation: Per 12/4, the agent must collect the receivables, but is not required to pay them from its own funds or to seek financing like Tawarruq.

title: Sale of Debt
q: Bank A sells a debt to Company Y, knowing that the debtor is insolvent, but does not tell Company Y. What right does Company Y have?
options: A claim against the debtor's guarantor
Recourse to Bank A for the full face value
The rescission option for misrepresentation
No right, as the risk passed upon sale
explanation: Per 5/7, the buyer has khayar al-taghrir if the seller knew of the debtor's insolvency or procrastination and did not inform him.

title: Liability of the Investment Manager
q: An investment agent managing a foreign-currency portfolio undertakes in the contract to bear any losses from exchange rate fluctuations. What is the ruling?
options: Prohibited, as a form of assuming the liability
Permitted, if limited to part of the capital
Permitted, if the agent charges no agency fee
Permitted, since currency risk is beyond his control
explanation: Per 3/5/2, an undertaking by the investment manager to assume losses from exchange rate fluctuations is a prohibited form of assuming liability.

title: Hawalah
q: Per the Shari'ah basis, why may a Hawalah not be concluded on a temporary basis or contingent on a future event?
options: The payer cannot know the debt in advance
The transferee may refuse a transfer that is set for the future
Contingent contracts are void in all cases
Its nature is the immediate transfer of the debt to the payer
explanation: Per the Basis, Hawalah has the character of an immediate exchange creating a new relationship at once; a temporary or contingent transfer conflicts with its nature.

title: Documentary Credit
q: A sale contract states its interpretation is subject to INCOTERMS. What condition does the standard attach to such a reference?
options: INCOTERMS prevail over the Shari'ah in international trade matters
The interpretation must not violate the rules of the Shari'ah
The reference is void in any Islamic transaction, whatever its content
It applies only if both parties are Institutions
explanation: Per 3/2/3, a contract's reference to INCOTERMS or similar rules is circumscribed with a condition that it must not violate the rules of the Shari'ah.

title: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
q: Bank A enters into a fixed-term Mudarabah with an investor. The outcome of the investment is uncertain. How does the standard treat the Gharar here?
options: It is permitted only because of a recognized need
It is excessive Gharar and nullifies the Mudarabah
It is medium Gharar and does not affect the contract
It is minor Gharar arising from the profit ratio
explanation: Per 4/2/3, medium Gharar may exist in contracts like Ju'alah, guardianship, companies and fixed-term Mudarabah, and it does not affect the contract.

title: Mortgage and its Contemporary Applications
q: A mortgaged warehouse burns down and the mortgagor receives compensation from a solidarity insurance scheme. What is the status of the mortgage?
options: It continues, with the compensation replacing the warehouse
It continues over the land only, but not over the insurance compensation
It ends, and the debt becomes due immediately
It ends, since the mortgaged asset has perished
explanation: Per 3/1/6 and 8, a mortgage ceases when the asset perishes unless compensation is obtained (e.g. solidarity insurance), which then replaces it.

title: Trading in Currencies
q: To hedge devaluation risk, Bank A and a customer each give a binding promise to exchange USD for EUR in three months. What is the ruling?
options: Permitted, since a promise is not a contract
Permitted, since hedging justifies the promises
Forbidden, even though the purpose is hedging
Permitted if the future rate is left open
explanation: Per 2/9/1, a binding bilateral promise to buy and sell currencies is forbidden, even for hedging against currency devaluation risk.

title: Commercial Papers
q: Ahmad owes Bilal 100,000 under a note due in six months. Ahmad, the debtor, offers Bilal, the first beneficiary, 95,000 now in full settlement. What is the ruling?
options: Permitted to pay the first beneficiary less before maturity
Not permitted: it is discounting of commercial paper at a lower amount
Permitted only if a bank is the intermediary
Not permitted: it is Riba al-Nasi'ah since the debt is paid early for less
explanation: Per 6/1, discounting is not permitted, but it is permitted to pay an amount less than the value of the paper to the first beneficiary prior to maturity.

title: Zakah
q: Bank A holds non-trading shares and makes an allocation for decline in their value. Can this allocation be deducted from Zakatable assets?
options: Yes, in full, as it is treated as a liability
Yes, if the decline in value is judged permanent
Yes, but only up to half of the decline in value
No allocation for such deterioration may be deducted
explanation: Per 4/2/4 and 7/3/2, for shares owned for non-trading purposes, no allocation for deterioration in value should be made from Zakatable assets.

title: Waqf
q: During the waiting period before distribution to beneficiaries, an overseer invests Waqf revenue. When is this permitted?
options: Only if the Waqif expressly stipulated it in the Waqf deed
When it does not affect distribution to beneficiaries
Never; revenue must be paid out to beneficiaries at once
Only in the overseer's own name
explanation: Per 8/1, Waqf revenue may be invested if the Waqif stipulates it or during the waiting period, where it does not affect distribution.

title: Options to Terminate Due to Breach of Trust (Trust-Based Options)
q: Ahmad paid 150,000 for equipment. Certified valuators' highest estimate is 110,000, which commercial custom deems excessive. Ahmad was unaware. What is his right?
options: None, since the price was agreed by mutual consent
To revoke only if the seller made a false statement
To keep the item and claim back the 40,000 excess
Khiyar al-Ghabn: to revoke the contract or accept it
explanation: Per 4/1 and 4/4/1, if the price exceeds the experts' highest estimate and is excessive by custom, the buyer may revoke or accept without refund.

title: Istisna’a and Parallel Istisna’a
q: Why is Parallel Istisna'a not 'two sales in one', according to the Shari'ah basis?
options: The same parties sign the two contracts together
They are two separate deals with no link between them
Only one single price is paid for the two deals together
The second contract is merely a promise
explanation: The basis: Parallel Istisna'a involves two separate Istisna'a deals with no link, so it is not two sales in one, and it is non-Riba-based financing.

title: Waqf
q: Ahmad wants to dedicate his house as Waqf for students for ten years, then take it back. Is this temporary Waqf permissible?
options: No; every Waqf must be eternal, so a time limit voids the whole Waqf
No; this is an 'Ariyah (lending), not a Waqf at all
Yes; temporary Waqf is permissible though eternity is the principle
Yes, but only when the Waqf is made for a mosque or a school
explanation: Per 3/1/4, Waqf in principle should be eternal, but temporary Waqf is also permissible when the donor wishes to get back his property after a specific period.

title: Combination of Contracts
q: Per the basis, what is the status of a loan stipulating that the borrower must give the lender a present?
options: Null and void, as the stipulated benefit is Riba
Valid, if the present is of small value
Disliked but valid, by agreement of the Fuqaha
Valid, but the present is not enforceable
explanation: The basis: Fuqaha unanimously agree such a loan becomes null and void; any loan with a prior condition of benefit to the lender is Riba.

title: Indices
q: Per the Shari'ah basis, why is developing indices permissible?
options: They replace the need for real transactions
They guarantee investors against losses in falling markets
They are a form of permissible trading in the market's overall value
They serve as a means of forecasting and observation
explanation: The basis: indices are a method of forecasting and observing circumstances (inferences), a recognized practice; Ibn Al-Qayyim gave proofs for it.

title: Combination of Contracts
q: Bank A designs a new set of combined contracts. Besides the rules on combination, what else must it observe?
options: Only the rulings on Muwata`ah
The general Shari'ah rules on structure, rulings and conditions
Only the parties' agreed commercial terms and the Bank's internal policies
Only the rules of the main contract in the set
explanation: Per 7/4 and 7/5, new combined sets must observe the general rules of Shari'ah on structure, rulings, requirements and conditions, and the rulings on combination.

title: Documentary Credit
q: On what basis does the standard make documentary credit permissible?
options: It is a Mudarabah between the bank and the importing client
It is a sale of the goods by the bank to the importing buyer
It includes agency for services and an institutional guarantee
It is a loan from the seller to the buyer for the goods' price
explanation: Per 3/1/1, documentary credit includes agency for procedural services (mainly document examination) and an institutional guarantee, both permissible.

title: Liability of the Investment Manager
q: In a Musharakah, the partners authorize Partner A to invest the partnership's funds. How does the standard classify Partner A's role?
options: He is an investment manager of those funds
He is a service agent with no investment role
He is a guarantor of the partners' capital
He is Rab Al Maal over the other partners' shares
explanation: Per 2/2/3, authorizing (tafwid) one of the partners to invest partnership funds is a form of investment management.

title: Irrigation Partnership (Musaqat)
q: Bank A does not own any orchards but wants to use Musaqat. Which structure does the standard recognise?
options: Lend money to tree owners in return for a share of their crop
Buy the future crop at a discount via Musaqat
Guarantee a fixed crop yield to tree owners
Contract Musaqat with tree owners, then hire workers
explanation: Per 15/1, an institution may enter into Musaqat contracts with owners of trees and then hire workers (irrigators) to carry out the work.

title: Ijarah and Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek
q: During the lease, the lessee's misconduct makes a leased machine unusable for two months. Who restores it, and what of the rent for those months?
options: The lessee repairs it, and the rent is waived
The lessor repairs it, and the rent stays due
The lessee repairs it, and the rent is not waived
The lessor repairs it, and the rent is waived
explanation: Per 5/1/6, if benefit is impaired by the lessee's misconduct, he must restore or repair the usufruct, and rent for the lost time is not waived.

title: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
q: Gold deposited with Bank A is damaged through the bank's negligence. How must Bank A indemnify the depositor?
options: It is not liable, as it holds the gold in trust
With equivalent gold of the same kind, if possible
With its value at the date of the deposit
With its value at the date of the claim
explanation: Per 5/4/3, the depository indemnifies with equivalent gold of the same kind if possible, otherwise its value at the time of the damage.

title: Mudarabah
q: A Mudarib has begun trading when the capital provider seeks to cancel. Per the Shari'ah basis, why is the contract now binding?
options: Ending it may frustrate profit and leave the Mudarib unpaid
The Mudarib has become the owner of the capital once he began trading with it
The capital provider has become a guarantor of the Mudarib's work
Starting work turns the Mudarabah into a loan owed by the Mudarib
explanation: Per the basis, unilateral termination after work starts might frustrate the aim of profit and damage the Mudarib, who might get no compensation for his work.

title: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
q: Converting Bank A needs funds to meet its liabilities. Which of these funding methods is listed as permissible in the standard?
options: Taking interbank loans with interest
Issuing bonds with a fixed coupon
Issuing preference shares carrying a fixed rate of return
Issuing Mudarabah, Musharakah or Ijarah certificates
explanation: Per 6/2, permissible funding includes capital increases, Islamic certificates (Mudarabah, Musharakah, Ijarah), Salam, Istisna'a, sale-and-leaseback and Tawarruq.

title: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
q: An investor wants to pay a fee to acquire the benefit of a binding promise to sell gold held by another customer of Bank A. What is the ruling?
options: Permissible, if Bank A consents to the transfer
Not permissible, as promises may not be traded
Permissible, since the promise is binding
Permissible, if the fee equals the Hamish Jiddiyyah
explanation: Per 8/4, trading in promises in any form is not permissible.

title: Competitions and Prizes
q: Bank A plans to organize a cultural competition and pay the reward out of the funds of its investment accounts. What does the standard require instead?
options: Costs are shared with investment account holders in proportion to their funds
Costs come only from investment account profits
Costs, including the reward, come from shareholders' funds
Costs may be charged to the charity account
explanation: Per 2/3/3/1, competition expenses including the reward must be covered from the Institution's own (shareholders') funds, not investment account funds.

title: Liability of the Investment Manager
q: A third party's commitment to cover Rab Al Maal's capital loss turns out to be void. What is the effect on the underlying Mudaraba contract?
options: It is not vitiated and remains in effect
It becomes vitiated (fasad) with the commitment
It turns into an investment guaranteed by the Mudarib
It is suspended until a new obligor is found
explanation: Per 4/2, default of the third party or voidness of its undertaking does not result in vitiation (fasad) of the investment contract.

title: Competitions and Prizes
q: Company X announces a reward for the winner of a cultural quiz it organizes. After the contest, it wants to withhold the reward. What is the ruling?
options: Payment is binding only if participants paid fees
Payment is binding on Company X, which committed to it
The reward is a voluntary gift it may withdraw
Payment is binding only once a court confirms it
explanation: Per 2/2, a reward-based competition makes payment of the reward binding upon the party committed to paying it.

title: Istisna’a and Parallel Istisna’a
q: Under an Istisna'a with stage payments, a contractor completes stage two in line with the specifications. What may he do?
options: Request payment for that completed stage
Request a bonus for early completion
Request the full remaining price
Wait for final delivery to be paid
explanation: Per 3/2/3, where work or payment is divided by stages, the manufacturer may request payment for each stage carried out according to specification.

title: Insolvency
q: Supplier S, unpaid, finds goods he sold to Company X among X's assets after its insolvency, but X had pledged them to Bank B as security. Can S reclaim them?
options: Yes, but only for the part exceeding Bank B's debt
Yes; the seller's right overrides any pledge
Yes, provided a judge approves the reclamation
No, unless Bank B renounces its right to the mortgage
explanation: Per the basis, reclamation requires that no right of another person relates to the asset, e.g. a pledge, except when the mortgagee renounces his right.

title: Payment Cards
q: Ahmad returns goods bought by card because of a defect that the seller knew about and concealed. Who bears the fees and exchange differences?
options: Ahmad bears them, with no recourse
The card network bears them
Ahmad may claim them from the seller
Bank A bears them as the issuer
explanation: Per 5/7, the holder may not revert to the acceptor for such fees or differences unless the acceptor knew about the defect and concealed it.

title: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
q: A plot is co-owned by A (50%), B (30%) and C (20%). C sells his share to an outsider, and A and B both claim Shuf'ah. How is the right shared?
options: In proportion to their shares in the property
Entirely to A, as the largest co-owner, who holds the greatest share
To whichever of them claims first
In equal shares to the two claimants
explanation: Per 7/2/2, where a jointly owned property has more than one preemptor, each has the right of Shuf'ah proportionate to his share in the property.

title: Sale of Debt
q: Bank A and a customer collude: the Bank pays cash now for oil to be delivered later, and on delivery the oil is replaced by a larger cash sum. What is the ruling?
options: Permitted, if the oil's value equals the cash
Permitted, as a Salam followed by substitution
Permitted, if replaced only after maturity
Prohibited, as a legal artifice (hila) for riba
explanation: Per 4/1/2, the transaction must not be a hila for riba, e.g., colluding to pay cash for deferred delivery then substituting more currency.

title: Zakah
q: Company X owes 3 million for trade goods bought on credit and 5 million for a factory machine bought on credit. Which debt is deducted from the Zakah base?
options: Neither debt
The two debts in full
The 3 million for trade goods
The 5 million for the machine
explanation: Per 6/2/1 and 6/2/2, debts for Zakatable trade assets are deducted from the Zakah base, while debts for non-Zakatable fixed assets are not.

title: Investment Sukuk
q: Holders of Sukuk of ownership of usufructs of a tangible asset have subleased the asset to a second lessee. How is trading in these Sukuk now treated?
options: As fully prohibited at all times, like Salam certificates
As trading in debt, under the rules for disposal of debts
As currency exchange, under the rules of Sarf only
As trading in tangible assets, freely permissible
explanation: Per 5/2/6, after sub-leasing the certificate represents rent receivables, i.e. a debt, so its trading is subject to the rules for disposal of debts.

title: Zakah
q: Ahmad's only Zakatable wealth is trade goods. Which Nisab is widely recognized as applicable to articles of trade?
options: 40 units, as for goats
The Nisab of silver: 595 grams of pure silver
The Nisab of gold: 85 grams of pure gold
653 kilograms, as for produce
explanation: Per 3/2/2, the gold Nisab is 85 grams of pure gold; the Nisab widely recognized as applicable to articles of trade is that of gold.

title: Online Financial Dealings
q: Bank A provides internet access service to subscribers against a specific fee. How is this contract characterised?
options: A shared-hiring contract (Ijarah Mushtarakah) with the beneficiary
A Wakalah contract with the subscriber against a fee
A sale of the network's usufruct outright to each individual subscriber
A Ju'alah contract payable only when the service succeeds
explanation: Per 3/2, the online access contract is a shared-hiring contract (Ijarah Mushtarakah), subject to the rulings on hiring of persons and hiring a shared employee.

title: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
q: Per the Shari'ah basis, why must a converting bank still repay the principal of its pre-conversion interest-based loans?
options: Repaying principal avoids court penalties
The loan is valid; only the interest condition is void
The lender may waive interest, not principal
Principal and interest form one indivisible debt in the contract
explanation: Per the Basis, following the Hanafi view, the loan contract itself is valid and the interest condition void; acts of Muslims are deemed valid as far as possible.

title: Documentary Credit
q: Per the Shari'ah basis, why may the bank's guarantee in an irrevocable credit be conditioned on the documents conforming to the stipulations?
options: Agency contracts may never be made conditional, so the guarantee cannot be either
The documents are themselves the subject of a loan to the buyer
The credit is a sale subject to an option to cancel if documents are rejected
Kafalah accepts qualification through a stipulated condition
explanation: Per the basis, the jurists ruled that Kafalah (guarantee) accepts qualification through a stipulated condition, so execution may depend on conforming documents.

title: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
q: Midway through a lease, the owner offers the tenant a payment to vacate and waive his right to the remaining period. What is the ruling?
options: Permitted only if the tenant pays a matching fee
Permitted only after the lease has expired
Permitted, as compensation for the waived usufruct
Not permitted, as it is payment for vacating
explanation: Per 8/2, the owner may pay the tenant during the lease for waiving his right to the usufruct for the remaining period; after expiry without renewal, no payment is allowed.

title: Options to Terminate Due to Breach of Trust (Trust-Based Options)
q: Ahmad knew, when buying, that the price was far above the market level, but bought anyway. He later seeks Khiyar al-Ghabn. Is he entitled to it?
options: Yes, but limited to partial compensation
Yes, if he returns the item within a week
Yes; an excessive price alone gives the option, whether or not the buyer knew of it
No; he must have been unaware of the gouging at inception
explanation: Per 4/2, a prerequisite of Khiyar al-Ghabn is that the buyer was unaware of the price gouging at the inception of the contract.

title: Hiring of Persons
q: A hiring contract is executed as planned after the employee received 'Arboun at signing. How is the 'Arboun treated?
options: As a seriousness margin held until expiry
As a prepaid part of the employee's pay
As a gift on top of the full pay
As a deposit returned to the employer
explanation: Per 4/11, if the hiring contract is implemented, the earnest money ('Arboun) becomes a prepaid part of the employee's pay.

title: Loan (Qard)
q: A loan agreement uses the word 'Salaf' rather than 'Qard', and the parties clearly intend a loan. Is the Qard concluded?
options: Yes; any word or act conveying the meaning of Qard suffices
Yes, but only if it is registered in writing
No; a loan must be concluded by an act of delivery, not by words
No; the word 'Qard' must be expressly used
explanation: Per 3/1, Qard is concluded through offer and acceptance using the words Qard and Salaf or any other word or act that conveys the meaning of Qard.

title: Stipulations and Ethics of Fatwa in the Institutional Framework
q: An officer of Bank A asks its Shari'ah board for a ruling on a purely hypothetical deal that has not occurred and is not expected to occur. Is the answer a Fatwa as defined?
options: Yes, if the answer is recorded in writing
No, Fatwa concerns only matters of worship
Yes, any Shari'ah opinion given by the board is a Fatwa, real or not
No, Fatwa concerns incidences that occurred or may occur
explanation: Per 2/1, Fatwa is a Shari'ah opinion on an incidence that has occurred or is expected to occur; it does not refer to answering hypothetical queries.

title: Waqf
q: An overseer manages two Waqfs whose revenues go to the same avenue of disposal. May he commingle their incomes?
options: Yes, if both Waqifs are still alive
No, incomes of different Waqfs may never be mixed in one account
Yes, though each Waqf remains independent financially
Yes, and the two Waqfs then become a single Waqf in law
explanation: Per 9/9, incomes of Waqfs with the same avenue may be intermingled; each Waqf remains independent in financial status, overseer fees, etc.

title: Procrastinating Debtor
q: In an Istisna'a contract, the manufacturer agrees to pay a fixed amount for each day of late delivery. Is this penalty clause valid?
options: Yes, penalty clauses are allowed in Istisna'a
No, unless the buyer proves actual loss
Yes, but only in construction contracts, not manufacturing
No, it is Riba, just like a penalty imposed on a debt
explanation: Per 2/3, penalty clauses may be included in construction, Istisna'a and supply contracts.

title: Arbitration
q: A government employee officially designated to perform arbitration asks the parties to pay him a fee for an arbitration. May he receive fees?
options: Yes, if the fee is a percentage of the claim
No; the fee entitlement excludes such a designated employee
Yes, if the fee is fixed in the arbitration document by the parties
Yes, as any arbitrator may receive fees
explanation: Per 14/1, the arbitrator may receive fees if he is not a volunteer or a government employee designated for arbitration.

title: Stipulations and Ethics of Fatwa in the Institutional Framework
q: Bank A wants to appoint a scholar to its Shari'ah board who is highly competent in financial transactions but not in all areas of Fiqh. Can he issue Fatwa to the Bank?
options: Yes, competence in institutional financial dealings suffices
No, unless he is also a qualified judge
No, a Mufti must be competent in all areas of Fiqh and its sources
Yes, but only with a second scholar co-signing
explanation: Per 5/2, issuing Fatwa to Institutions does not require competence in all areas of Fiqh; competence in their financial transactions suffices.

title: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
q: An agent wishes to sell the principal's property to his own wife. What is required under the standard?
options: Nothing, as long as the price is the market price
The agent should obtain the principal's consent
Nothing, unless the deal involves favoritism
The deal is prohibited even with consent
explanation: Per 6/1/1, in deals that involve the agent's spouse or relatives under his guardianship, the agent should obtain the consent of the principal.

title: Payment Cards
q: For its covered card, Bank A requires Ahmad to keep the liquidity cover in a current account. What does the standard require?
options: The cover must be kept in a current account, as it is a guarantee
The cover must be in an investment account earning profit
Ahmad may choose a current or investment-based account
No cover account may be opened
explanation: Per 6/2/2/1(a), the holder should not be required to deposit the cover in a current account but given the option of a current or investment account.

title: Sharikah (Musharakah) and Modern Corporations
q: Company X contributes a business whose assets include a negligible amount of receivables. On which principle does the Shari'ah basis accept this?
options: Custom as a source of rulings
Necessity making the prohibited permissible
Maslahah for the public good
Taba'iyyah: things that follow another thing
explanation: Per the basis, receivables combined with other assets at a negligible ratio may be contributed under the principle of Taba'iyyah (dependent things follow the principal).

title: Murabahah
q: Bank A requires post-dated cheques from a customer before executing a Murabahah, in a country where cheques can be presented before their due date. What is the ruling?
options: Permissible if the cheques are post-dated
Permissible if the customer agrees
Not permissible in such a country
Permissible with a written undertaking
explanation: Per 5/3, requiring cheques as security is not permissible in countries where they could be presented for payment before their due date.

title: Hiring of Persons
q: Bank A hired a well-defined service for future delivery. The service delivered turns out useless. What is the status of the contract?
options: The employer must accept it as delivered and pay in full
It becomes null and void at once for lack of benefit
The employer may only terminate it, with no other remedy
It remains valid; the employee must deliver a similar service
explanation: Per 8/2/1, where the useless service pertains to future delivery of a well-defined service, the contract remains valid and the employee must deliver a similar service.

title: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
q: Account terms state that Bank A's financial statements are authoritative. An account holder disputes a figure in them. What is the position?
options: They are authoritative and cannot be challenged
They are authoritative unless the holder proves them wrong
The Bank must prove each figure if challenged
They are void, as clauses making the Bank's own statements authoritative are impermissible
explanation: Per 2/2/9-2/2/10, authoritative status of the Institution's statements may be stipulated unless proved wrong; the claimant holder bears the cost of proving the accusation.

title: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
q: Company X deliberately sets up a portfolio for the specific purpose of trading in gold, and sells units in it on deferred payment. What is the ruling?
options: Not permissible unless it complies with al-Sarf rulings
Permissible, as the gold is held within a portfolio
Permissible, as the gold is an accessory to the entity
Permissible, as the units are not gold themselves
explanation: Per 3/1/2, it is not permissible to deliberately establish a portfolio for trading in gold unless it complies with the rulings of al-Sarf.

title: Mortgage and its Contemporary Applications
q: Bank A holds a mortgaged asset as a notary for the benefit of two other parties. Does the standard on mortgage cover this case?
options: No; notary arrangements are governed only by agency rules
Yes; it also covers mortgages it keeps as notary or agent
No; it covers only mortgages requested by the Institution
No; it covers only mortgages the Institution presents to others
explanation: Per 1, the standard covers mortgages requested by the Institution, those it presents to others, and those it keeps as notary or agent for others.

title: Islamic Insurance
q: Islamic Insurance Company T is being liquidated. Its insurance account holds accumulated reserves and provisions. How should these be disposed of?
options: Kept by the liquidator for future claims
Returned to the company as Mudarib
Spent on charitable purposes
Paid to the company's shareholders
explanation: Per 5/6 and 10/5, on liquidation all provisions and accumulated reserves pertaining to insurance should be spent on charitable purposes.

title: Documentary Credit
q: Bank A pays the full value of a credit that was totally uncovered by its client. Per the Shari'ah basis, which element of the irrevocable credit comes into operation?
options: The partnership (Musharakah) element
The mortgage (Rahn) element
The agency (Wakalah) element only
The loan (Qard) element
explanation: Per the basis, the loan element comes into operation when the Institution pays on behalf of the client in a credit that is totally or partially uncovered.

title: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
q: Before deciding to convert, Bank A issued preference shares and interest-based certificates on which it pays interest. What must it do?
options: Liquidate them as traces of conventional transactions
Keep them until their maturity dates
Keep them outstanding but cap the interest rate paid on them
Keep them if held by central banks
explanation: Per 6/1, all traces of conventional transactions on which the bank pays interest, including deposits, preference shares, bonds and certificates, must be liquidated.

title: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
q: A shop sells wooden boxes decorated with a small amount of gold gilding, on deferred payment for currency. Do the rulings for sale of gold apply?
options: Yes, the gold must be weighed and priced separately
Yes, spot exchange is needed for any gold content
No, such items are not subject to those rulings
Yes, if the gilding exceeds the box's value
explanation: Per 3/3/1/3, items with an insignificant amount of gold not intended per se, such as gilding and decoration, are not subject to gold sale rulings.

title: Hiring of Persons
q: Company X hires a contractor to translate a book within one month. He translates half; the half is useful, and Company X refuses to extend the period. What is he owed?
options: The pay normally paid for similar work (Ajr al-Mithl)
The whole agreed pay for the translation, as half was useful
Nothing, since the agreed work is incomplete
Half the agreed pay automatically by default
explanation: Per 5/1/2, if the partial work is useful and the employer will not extend the period, the employee is entitled to Ajr al-Mithl; if useless, to no pay.

title: Commercial Papers
q: A holder sells a 100,000 promissory note not yet due to Company Y for 100,000 in cash today. How does the standard classify this sale?
options: Riba al-Fadl only
Riba al-Nasi'ah
A permitted sale at par
A valid Hawalah
explanation: Per 6/2, selling commercial paper not yet due for an amount similar to its value is Riba al-Nasi'ah; for more than its value, it is Riba al-Nasi'ah plus Riba al-Fadl.

title: Rules for Calculating Profit in Financial Transactions
q: In a competitive market with no monopoly or extraordinary circumstances, a regulator proposes capping profit rates on all Murabahah sales. What is the ruling?
options: Permissible only if all the licensed banks agree to it beforehand
Obligatory, in order to protect customers from excessive prices
Permissible at all times, as part of the regulator's normal powers to protect customers
Impermissible in principle, save monopoly, extraordinary circumstances or public interest
explanation: Per 4/2, a regulator may not in principle cap profits; fixing the rate is allowed in monopoly, extraordinary circumstances or clear public interest, if not prejudicial.

title: Irrigation Partnership (Musaqat)
q: A Musaqat worker negligently fails to control pests, and part of the crop is lost. What is his position?
options: He indemnifies the actual loss but keeps his crop share
He indemnifies the loss and forfeits his share
He is not liable, as he acts as a fiduciary and a fiduciary bears no loss
He loses his entire share of the crop
explanation: Per 6/3, the worker is a fiduciary; for misconduct, negligence or breach he indemnifies the owner's actual loss but remains entitled to his share of the crop.

title: Loan (Qard)
q: Bank A and Company X sign a Qard contract today, but the funds will be handed over next week. When does Company X come to own the loaned funds?
options: When the first instalment is repaid
Immediately on signing the contract
On the maturity date of the loan
When it takes possession of the funds
explanation: Per 3/4/1, the borrower comes to own the subject-matter of Qard through possession, and becomes liable for repayment of a similar amount.

title: Options to Terminate Due to Breach of Trust (Trust-Based Options)
q: Ahmad validly exercises Khiyar al-Taghrir and must transport the item back to the place of sale. Who bears the expenses of the return?
options: Whoever is nearer to the place of sale
The seller
Both parties, equally
Ahmad, as the party revoking
explanation: Per 2/4/3, the seller is liable for expenses relating to the return of the item to the place of sale.

title: Mudarabah
q: Company X, acting as Mudarib for Bank A, is liquidated during the Mudarabah term. What is the effect on the Mudarabah?
options: It passes automatically to Company X's creditors to complete the term
It continues until the agreed maturity date regardless
It is liquidated, as the institution acting as Mudarib ended
It continues with Company X's shareholders taking over as Mudarib
explanation: Per 10/1/5, a Mudarabah is liquidated on the death of the Mudarib or the liquidation of the institution that acts as Mudarib.

title: Buyback
q: Ahmad sells his car to Company X for 100 cash and, by prior collusion, buys it back for 110 payable in six months. What is the ruling?
options: Permitted, since the first sale was for cash
Prohibited, as it constitutes 'Inah
Permitted, if the car was delivered in between
Permitted, since the same asset is returned
explanation: Per 3/5/1/2, selling an asset for cash and buying it back at a higher deferred price, with collusion or custom, is 'Inah.

title: Mudarabah
q: Why, according to the Shari'ah basis, is Mudarabah needed instead of handing money to an investor for a periodic pre-agreed payment?
options: A pre-agreed payment would make the contract binding
Mudarabah avoids the need for any profit ratio
A pre-agreed periodic payment would make it a debt with Riba
Investors may not deal with capital belonging to others
explanation: Per the basis, money cannot increase without work, and giving money for a periodic pre-agreed payment (rent) to an investor would be a debt with Riba.

title: Istisna’a and Parallel Istisna’a
q: Why does the Shari'ah basis allow a penalty for late delivery in Istisna'a, though not for late payment of debts?
options: Penalties are paid to charity in Istisna'a
Istisna'a is not a binding contract
The manufacturer is always the wealthier of the parties
It concerns items to be produced, not a monetary debt
explanation: The basis: the penalty clause serves the contract and relates to an obligation to produce and deliver items in the future, not to a monetary debt.

title: Debit Card, Charge Card and Credit Card
q: Bank A asks whether it may issue a credit card that is free from Riba and any other Shari'ah prohibition. Per the Shari'ah basis, what is the answer?
options: Yes, such a credit card is permissible
No, only debit cards may be issued
No, every credit card is prohibited
Yes, if interest applies to cash withdrawals only
explanation: Per the Basis (3), credit cards are prohibited where they rest on interest-bearing revolving credit; issuing credit cards free of Riba or other prohibition is permissible.

title: Waqf
q: A Waqf is for four specific persons with defined shares. Revenue this year falls short. How is the shortfall borne?
options: By the overseer from his remuneration
Equally among them, regardless of their defined shares
By the last-named beneficiary only, as the others rank ahead
By all beneficiaries in proportion to their shares
explanation: Per 9/10/3, if the Waqf is for specific persons and revenue falls short, the shortfall applies to all in proportion to their shares.

title: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
q: A trader buys a commodity with a cooling-off option, intending to revoke if the market price falls during the period. Is this use permissible?
options: Yes, if the period is under 3 days
Yes; protecting the buyer from price falls is the purpose of the option
No; options may not be used to avoid price fluctuations
No, unless the seller holds the option too
explanation: Per 2/8/5, it is not permissible to use cooling-off options to avoid price fluctuations during the option period.

title: Options to Revoke Contracts Due to Incomplete Performance
q: Ahmad bought land and built a house on it. He then discovers a hidden material defect in the land. What is his remedy?
options: Compensation for the defect, as return is prevented
Return of the land and recovery of the building cost
No remedy, as he has altered the land
Return of the land with the house to the seller
explanation: Per 2/6/3-2/6/4, an attached addition not growing out of the item, like a building on land, prevents return; the buyer is entitled to compensation (Arsh).

title: Sale of Debt
q: Some debts in Bank A's securitized entity are settled, and the entity extends a new Murabaha to the same debtor. Does this count as turnover bringing it under 8/1?
options: Yes, any new Murabaha counts as turnover
No; it is not turnover, and 8/2 still applies
Yes, as the debtor remains the same
No, and the sale of the entity becomes void
explanation: Per 8/2/4, substituting part of the assets or extending a new Murabaha to the same debtor is not turnover; 8/2 applies, not 8/1.

title: Sharikah (Musharakah) and Modern Corporations
q: Which of the following arrangements falls within the scope of the Sharikah (Musharakah) and Modern Corporations standard?
options: A diminishing Musharakah between an Institution and customer
Regulatory market procedures and listing rules for modern companies
An agricultural sharecropping or irrigation partnership (Muzara'ah)
A Mudarabah between a Rabb al-Mal and a Mudarib
explanation: Clause 1 applies the standard to modern partnerships including diminishing Musharakah, but excludes Mudarabah, sharecropping and market regulatory procedures.

title: Impact of Contingent Incidents on Commitments
q: A sudden frost, not caused by any human act and unavoidable even if foreseen, destroys part of fruits sold to Bank A. What is the effect under the rules on Jawa'ih?
options: The seller must replace the fruits with produce from another farm
The Bank pays the full price because the fruits were already sold to it
The whole sale is cancelled and the full price is refunded
The price is discounted in proportion to the damage in the produce
explanation: Per 5/5, Jawa'ih are non-human incidents that cannot be avoided even if known; in sale of fruits they lead to discounting the price in proportion to the damage.

title: Istisna’a and Parallel Istisna’a
q: Bank A agrees to sell to a customer 'the factory located at Plot 12', which already exists, on an Istisna'a basis. What is the ruling?
options: Valid, if the price is paid in stages
Valid, if the factory is described in detail
Invalid, as it is an existing identified asset
Valid, if the Bank owns the factory
explanation: Per 3/1/3, the subject of Istisna'a may not be an existing identified capital asset, e.g. a designated car or factory; Istisna'a is for items identified by specification.

title: Al-Wakalah Bi Al-Istithmar (Investment Agency)
q: Bank A, as agent, receives all profit above the expected profit in addition to its fee. How does the Shari'ah basis characterise this excess?
options: A share of profit as in Mudarabah
A type of conditional gift and an incentive
Compensation for the agent's cost of funds
A form of agency fee fixed in advance
explanation: Per the basis, allocating to the agent any profit in excess of the expected profit is a type of conditional gift and an incentive.

title: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
q: A sale contract grants the buyer a cooling-off option that ends "when the commodity index reaches 500 points". Is this option valid?
options: Yes, if the index is reached within a year
No, because options may not exceed 3 days
Yes, since the index is publicly known
No; its time limit is indeterminate
explanation: Per 2/2/2, the option must have a stipulated time limit; it is invalid if the limit is indeterminate, such as ending when an index reaches a particular value.

title: Commercial Papers
q: A holder of a note buys goods for delivery on the note's maturity date and, once the debt is established, transfers his creditor's claim to his debtor through the note. What is this transaction?
options: A Salam contract
A Hawalah
A discounting of the note
A sale of debt for a lesser sum
explanation: Per 6/4, after the debt is established, the holder transfers his creditor's claim to his debtor through the paper; such a transaction amounts to Hawalah.

title: Options to Revoke Contracts Due to Incomplete Performance
q: After discovering a hidden defect in a delivery van, Ahmad keeps using it for his business for months without any excuse. What happens to his option to revoke?
options: It ceases, as his conduct implies acceptance
It converts into a right to a new van
It continues, but the price is reduced
It continues until he formally waives it
explanation: Per 2/8/4, the option ceases if the buyer's conduct implies acceptance, such as continuing to use the item or delaying return beyond custom without excuse.

title: Waqf
q: On what analogy does the Shari'ah basis base the view that a Waqf donation should not exceed one third of the donor's wealth?
options: The analogy with Hibah (gift) in illness
The analogy with Zakah on wealth, a fixed share of the wealth
The analogy with Wasiyyah (will), leaving a share for heirs
The analogy with 'Ariyah (lent thing)
explanation: The basis grounds the one-third limit on the analogy between Waqf and Wasiyyah, where part of the wealth should be left to the heirs.

title: Mudarabah
q: A Mudarib argues he may lend Mudarabah funds interest-free to a friend. Per the Shari'ah basis, why are loans, gifts and donations from the fund barred?
options: They would make the Mudarib a partner in the capital of the Mudarabah itself
They would require a guarantee from the capital provider for the borrower
They would turn the Mudarabah into a binding contract on the capital provider
They do not benefit the Mudarabah and risk loss to the provider
explanation: Per the basis, loans, gifts and donations do not benefit the Mudarabah operation; rather, they involve potential loss to the capital provider.

title: Insolvency
q: In the second stage of insolvency, creditors fear that Ahmad will admit a debt owed to his first cousin to divert assets. What may they ask the competent authorities to do?
options: Nothing, since only admissions to his own children can be restricted, not those to other relatives
Prevent admissions of liability to relatives up to four vertical steps
Annul all contracts he has ever concluded with his relatives, whenever they were made
Have the cousin declared insolvent jointly with Ahmad
explanation: Per 4/2/4, creditors may seek to prevent the debtor admitting liability to those who may be preferred, e.g. blood relatives up to four vertical steps such as a first cousin.

title: Obtaining and Deploying Liquidity
q: Bank A securitises some of its assets by selling them to Sukuk subscribers and remains manager of those assets. At what price may it promise to repurchase them?
options: At the market price or at a price to be agreed
At face value, since it manages the assets
At book value as on the date of issuance
At original cost plus a fixed periodic return
explanation: Per 4/2/5, an institution managing securitised assets may promise to purchase them at the market price or at a price to be agreed.

title: Murabahah
q: A Murabahah debtor is insolvent. Bank A agrees to reschedule the debt to a later date in return for an additional amount. What is the ruling?
options: Permissible if the extra amount is less than the mark-up
Permissible, since the debtor is insolvent and needs time
Not permissible for a solvent or insolvent debtor
Permissible if the extra goes to charity
explanation: Per 5/7, it is not permissible to extend the payment date in exchange for an additional payment on rescheduling, whether the debtor is solvent or insolvent.

title: Hawalah
q: Ahmad, Bakr and Zaid conclude a Hawalah through clear offer and acceptance showing intent to shift the debt, but never use the word transfer. Is it valid?
options: Yes, the word transfer need not be used
No, the word Hawalah must be stated
Yes, but only between Institutions
No, it must be written and witnessed
explanation: Per 4/1, Hawalah is concluded by offer and acceptance clearly indicating the intention to transfer the debt; it is not necessary that the word transfer be used.

title: Liability of the Investment Manager
q: A Mudarib invests Rab Al Maal's funds as agreed, without misconduct or negligence, but the market falls and 20% of the capital is lost. Who bears the loss?
options: The Mudarib, as he made the investment decisions
Rab Al Maal, as the Mudarib's possession is fiduciary
The Mudarib, up to the profit share he expected
Both of them equally, as partners in the venture
explanation: Per 3/1, the investment manager's possession is fiduciary (yadd amana); he is not liable unless there is misconduct, negligence or breach of conditions.

title: Mortgage and its Contemporary Applications
q: A client mortgages his units in an Islamic investment fund to Bank A. What may the Bank do with respect to his redemption rights?
options: Nothing; redemption rights cannot be restricted
Sell the units immediately on signing
Take ownership of the units until repayment
Suspend them absolutely or in proportion to the debt
explanation: Per 6/1, the Institution as mortgagee can suspend the client's right to get back or draw, absolutely or in proportion to the debt, whichever is more suitable.

title: Al-Wakalah Bi Al-Istithmar (Investment Agency)
q: A principal argues that agency is by nature non-binding, so he can exit a fixed-term investment agency at will. Per the Shari'ah basis, why is it binding?
options: Any contract signed by a licensed institution is binding
The agent's fee for the whole term has already been paid in advance
It is for a specific period that neither party may dissolve unilaterally
The agent has invested some of its own funds alongside the principal
explanation: Per the basis, investment agency is binding because it is entered into for a specific period, the parties agreeing neither can unilaterally dissolve it except as specified.

title: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
q: Ahmad appoints two agents in the same contract to sell his land. One of them sells it alone without the other. Ahmad never authorized sole action. What is the ruling?
options: Neither may act as sole decision-maker without authority
Each agent may act independently of the other, since both are appointed
Sole action is allowed if the price obtained is fair and the principal benefits
The first agent to act binds the principal and the second agent
explanation: Per 6/5, where several agents are appointed in the same contract, none should become the sole decision-maker unless authorized by the principal.

title: Hiring of Persons
q: Per the Shari'ah basis, why can the pay for future periods be adjusted by consent while past unpaid pay cannot be increased?
options: Past pay remains owned by the employer until it is paid to the employee
Only increases in pay, not decreases, amount to Riba
Adjusting future pay renews it; increasing past pay is Riba
Future pay is already a debt, while past pay is not
explanation: The basis: adjusting future pay is a renewal for a coming period; increasing unsettled past pay against more time is Riba.

title: Stipulations and Ethics of Fatwa in the Institutional Framework
q: Bank A finds a Fatwa from another bank's Shari'ah board permitting a product. Its own board has not addressed it. May Bank A rely on that Fatwa?
options: Yes, any Shari'ah board's Fatwa may be used
Only with the permission of its own board
Yes, if the other bank is larger
No, never, even with its board's permission
explanation: Per 6/3, the Institution should not follow the Fatwas of other Shari'ah Advisory Boards except with permission of its own Board.

title: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
q: Per the IIFA resolution cited in the basis, how are current accounts in Islamic banks characterised?
options: As trusts that the bank must not use
As Mudarabah funds sharing in the profit and loss of the bank
As loans only if the bank is insolvent
As loans held under guarantee and repayable on demand
explanation: Per the basis (IIFA 86 (9/3)), current accounts are loans; the bank holds them under guarantee and repays on demand; its solvency does not affect the ruling.

title: Concession Contracts
q: The State breaches a material condition of a utilization concession, causing Company X actual losses. What are Company X's rights?
options: Revoke the contract and claim compensation for actual damages
Only revoke; no compensation is due
Neither, as the State may amend at will
Only claim compensation for its losses; it may not revoke the contract
explanation: Per 5/8, each party may revoke the contract when the other breaches a condition or commitment, and the breaching party compensates actual damages.

title: Mudarabah
q: A Mudarabah contract gives the capital provider 6% of the capital each year as profit, and the rest to the Mudarib. What is the ruling?
options: Allowed if the Mudarib also gives a guarantee for the capital provider's share
Not allowed: profit must be an agreed percentage of profit
Allowed if the 6% is paid only when profit exists
Allowed, as the ratio is known at the outset and the Mudarib agreed to it
explanation: Per 8/1, profit must be distributed by an agreed percentage of profit, not a lump sum or a percentage of the capital.

title: Guarantees
q: Bank A takes cheques from Ahmad as security for his Murabahah instalments. Ahmad pays every instalment on time. What happens to the cheques?
options: The Bank may present them for an added amount
The Bank keeps them as its own property
They are kept and a holding fee is charged
They are returned to him
explanation: Per 6/3, cheques or promissory notes may be taken to ensure timely payment; if the debtor pays on time they are returned, and on default they may be presented.

title: Arbitration
q: An arbitrator issues a verdict on an issue that, under the standard, may not be resolved through arbitration. What is the status of that verdict?
options: It is binding until revoked by a court
It is valid if both parties accept it
It is null and void
It is valid but not enforceable in court
explanation: Per 7/3, when the arbitrator issues a verdict on an issue that should not be resolved through arbitration, his verdict is null and void.

title: Monetization (Tawarruq)
q: In a Monetization structure drafted by Bank A, both the Bank and the customer sign binding promises: the Bank to sell and the customer to buy the commodity on deferred payment. Is this acceptable?
options: No; a binding promise, if used, shall be from only one party
Yes, provided the deferred price is fixed in the promise
Yes; mutual binding promises protect both parties from loss
No; Monetization may not involve any promise at all
explanation: Per 4/1, if the Monetization process involves a binding promise, it shall be from only one party.

title: Commercial Papers
q: A drawee bank accepts a bill and later seeks to avoid paying. Which hadith does the Shari'ah basis cite on the binding nature of such an undertaking?
options: The Prophet's order to Banu Al-Nadir to reduce debts and hasten payment
Al-Sa'ib's partnership with the Prophet in trade
Abu Qatadah's taking on the two dinars of a deceased man
Ibn Abbas's taking silver at Mecca for notes payable at Kufa
explanation: The basis cites Jabir's hadith: Abu Qatadah undertook a deceased man's two dinars, the Prophet accepted it, and the deceased was absolved by that undertaking.

title: Concession Contracts
q: Why does exploration, unlike survey, give the licensee exclusive status, per the Basis?
options: Surveys are done only by the State itself, never by private persons
Exploration licenses cost more than surveys and so confer more rights
Survey is a Ju'alah and exploration a sale of the minerals in advance
Exploration is like Tahjir; survey is mere expectation
explanation: Per the Basis, survey rests on mere expectation, while exploration is like Tahjir (retention) in wasteland development, which precedes utilization.

title: Waqf
q: Ahmad makes a Waqf for his future grandchildren, none of whom has been born yet. What is the status of the Waqf?
options: Void, as the beneficiary does not exist when the Waqf is declared
Valid; the beneficiary need not be present at declaration
Valid only if a current beneficiary is added
Suspended until the first grandchild is born
explanation: Per 3/3/3, the Waqf beneficiary need not be present at the time of declaring the Waqf.

title: Istisna’a and Parallel Istisna’a
q: Bank A acts as a mere financier of a deal already concluded between a supplier and a customer, calling it Istisna'a. Why does the Shari'ah basis reject this?
options: It is a Riba deal, with Istisna'a as a cover-up
The supplier's role is not specified in the contract
The price is not known at signing
The Bank cannot own manufactured goods in Istisna'a
explanation: The basis: a mere financier role leads to a Riba transaction, making the Istisna'a a mere cover-up and not a real Istisna'a.

title: Commercial Papers
q: Which evidence does the Shari'ah basis cite for allowing a creditor to accept less for early payment (Da' Wa Ta'ajjal)?
options: The verse commanding the writing of debts for a specified term
The Prophet's words to Banu Al-Nadir: 'Reduce and hasten'
Ibn Abbas's taking silver at Mecca against notes payable at Kufa
Abu Qatadah's taking on the debt of the dead man at the Prophet's request
explanation: The basis cites the hadith of Ibn Abbas: when Banu Al-Nadir had debts not yet due, the Prophet said 'Reduce the amounts to hasten payments'.

title: Debit Card, Charge Card and Credit Card
q: Ahmad holds a debit card issued by Bank A. In which case would he normally pay a charge for using the card?
options: When his balance falls below a minimum amount
When paying a merchant for goods out of his own credit balance
When withdrawing cash through Bank B, a different Institution
When withdrawing cash at Bank A's own machines
explanation: Per 2/1/3, no charges normally apply, except when the card is used to withdraw cash or buy another currency through an Institution other than the issuer.

title: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
q: Bank A buys specialised equipment and stipulates that its outside technical consultant may confirm or revoke the purchase within 10 days. Is giving the option to a third party valid?
options: No; only the two contracting parties may hold it
Yes, but only if the seller also holds the option for the same period
No; only the buyer may hold a cooling-off option, never an outside consultant
Yes; the option may be given to a third party
explanation: Per 2/1, cooling-off options give one or both parties or a third party the right to continue with or revoke the contract within a stipulated period.

title: Salam and Parallel Salam
q: On the due date, only part of the dates sold by Salam are available to the seller. What options does Bank A, the buyer, have?
options: Claim compensation from the seller for its lost profit
Wait for availability, or cancel and recover capital
Force the seller to buy dates at any price from others
Take the dates' market value in cash
explanation: Per 5/8, the buyer may wait until al-Muslam Fihi is available or cancel and recover the capital; the parties may also agree to replacement under 4/2.

title: Online Financial Dealings
q: Bank A concludes an online contract with someone who forged the identity of a well-known company. What right does Bank A have?
options: No right, as the contract was validly accepted
Only a right to claim a reduction in price
Only a right to require a new electronic signature
The right to terminate the contract
explanation: Per 8/2/3, when forgery or error occurs regarding the personality or characteristics of a party, the other party has the right to terminate the contract.

title: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
q: Bank A buys shares with a cooling-off option held by Bank A. During the option period, the company pays a dividend on the shares. Who is entitled to the dividend?
options: The seller
Bank A, if it confirms the purchase
Bank A, in all cases
Both parties, equally
explanation: Per 2/6/3, an increase that is separate but grows out of the original, such as dividends on shares and rent from leased assets, belongs to the seller.

title: Guarantees
q: Per the Shari'ah basis, what is the core justification for stipulating guarantees in contracts?
options: They are needed only for non-Muslim parties
They replace the need for written contracts
They protect property, an objective of Shari'ah
They allow a return to be earned on debts
explanation: Per the Basis, stipulating guarantees is permissible because it protects property, which is one of the objectives of Shari'ah.

title: Zakah
q: Company X owns goats that are mostly fed with purchased fodder for most of the year, kept for milk, not trade. Does the livestock Zakah rate apply?
options: No; livestock rates apply only to free-grazing animals
No; only animals for trade are Zakatable
Yes, as goats are a Zakatable kind of livestock, whatever the way they are fed
Yes, because they reach the Nisab
explanation: Per 5/6, livestock are subject to the Zakah rate on livestock only if fed through free grazing most of the year.

title: Trading in Currencies
q: Bank A and Bank B agree today to exchange USD for EUR in three months at today's rate, settled through deferred transfers of debt. What is the ruling?
options: Permitted, because the rate is fixed at contracting
Permitted, if settlement is netted on maturity
Prohibited, as a forward currency contract
Permitted, if the two banks are Islamic Institutions
explanation: Per 2/2, forward currency contracts are prohibited, whether effected by exchanging deferred transfers of debt or by a deferred contract without concurrent possession.

title: Sharikah (Musharakah) and Modern Corporations
q: Partners in a Sharikah agree to set aside 2% of the profit as a charitable donation to a hospital that is not a partner. What is the ruling?
options: Not permissible, as profit belongs only to partners
Permissible only if the hospital becomes a partner
Permissible only from the capital, not the profit
Permissible
explanation: Per 3/1/5/14, it is permissible to agree on setting aside a proportion of profit for non-partners as a charitable donation.

title: Payment Cards
q: Bank A financed the cover of Ahmad's covered card and lowered one financing instalment because he used little of the cover. What should the agreement state?
options: Bank A must lower every future instalment
Bank A is not obliged to lower or repeat it
Bank A must lower it whenever cover is unused
Lowering instalments is never permitted
explanation: Per 6/2/2/1(b), it must be stated that the issuer is not obliged to lower instalments, and if it lowers one, it need not repeat that later.

title: Options to Revoke Contracts Due to Incomplete Performance
q: Part of a package deal turns out to belong to a third party. The buyer keeps the rest, which has no defect, at its share of the price, and claims extra compensation. Is he entitled?
options: No; compensation applies only if what remains is defective
Yes, equal to the third party's part
Yes, as a fixed percentage of the price
Yes, for the inconvenience and loss caused to him by the fragmentation of the deal
explanation: Per 3/4, the buyer may revoke or accept the remainder at its portion of the price; he is not entitled to compensation unless there is a defect in what remains.

title: Waqf
q: The utilities of a Waqf building have been permanently cut off, making it impossible to use. What does the standard permit?
options: Ending the Waqf and returning the asset to the Waqif or his heirs
Distributing the land among the beneficiaries in their shares
Keeping it idle as Waqf cannot be changed
Substituting it with a better asset of the same kind
explanation: Per 10/1/2/2, if utilities are suspended or usufruct is impossible, the Waqf asset may be substituted with a better asset of the same kind.

title: Insolvency
q: Company X, whose due debts exceed its assets, applies to the court to have itself declared insolvent. How does the standard treat this application?
options: It is not allowed; only creditors may make the application
It is allowed only if all creditors give written consent
It is a valid basis unless the court considers it fraudulent
It is allowed only for individuals, not for companies
explanation: Per 4/3/2, a declaration may be based on an application by the debtor himself, except where the competent judicial authority considers it fraudulent.

title: Sharikah (Musharakah) and Modern Corporations
q: A student asks which Sunnah evidence the standard cites for the permissibility of partnership. Which is cited?
options: The hadith of the co-owner of a slave who frees his part of him
Al-Sa'ib Al-Makhzumi was the Prophet's business partner
The hadith 'No harm and no reciprocal harm'
The Prophet's sale of camels at Al-Baqi' for dinars and dirhams
explanation: The basis cites Al-Sa'ib Ibn Abu Al-Sa'ib Al-Makhzumi, a partner of the Prophet in business, whom he welcomed as 'my brother and my partner'.

title: Waqf
q: Which evidence does the standard cite for the validity of a Waqf created by a non-Muslim?
options: Khālid keeping his armour and weapons for Allah's Cause
Umar's Waqf of his land in Khaybar, on the Prophet's advice to him
The Prophet called Ḥakīm b. Ḥizām's pre-Islam charity a virtue
The Waqf of Banū Najjār's orchard
explanation: Basis 2/4/3/5: the Prophet called Ḥakīm b. Ḥizām's charity in ignorance a virtue, showing a disbeliever's donation is valid.

title: Waqf
q: A Waqif requires that Waqf income always be distributed to beneficiaries first, even when the Waqf building needs urgent renovation. What is the status of this condition?
options: Valid unless the beneficiaries waive it
Invalid, as it hinders the interests of the Waqf
Valid, but only for family Waqf
Valid, as the Waqif's conditions are like Shari'ah texts
explanation: Per 4/1/3 and 8/1/1, a condition requiring income distribution first even when maintenance is needed is invalid as it hinders the interests of the Waqf.

title: Combination of Contracts
q: Bank A structures a Diminishing Musharakah as one agreement with successive parts and stages leading to the parties' goal. How does the standard describe such combined contracts?
options: A prohibited combination of sale and lending
Combined contracts for separate values only
A single lump sum combination of two separate contracts of sale
An exhaustive statement of successive parts and stages
explanation: Per 2/2/4, combined contracts may be an exhaustive statement of successive parts and stages, e.g. Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek, Murabahah and Diminishing Musharakah.

title: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
q: Bank A buys an existing, ascertained commodity in an organized market and takes delivery immediately, agreeing to pay the price in six months. What is the ruling?
options: Permitted, as only one counter-value (the price) is deferred
Permitted only if the seller is an Islamic bank
Not permitted, as it is a forward contract
Not permitted, as the price must always be paid on a spot basis
explanation: Per 3/2/4, there is no restriction in delaying one of the counter-values, such as the price, as in a deferred sale.

title: Hawalah
q: Zaid holds goods belonging to Ahmad. Ahmad's creditor Bakr is to be paid from the value of those goods held by Zaid. What type of Hawalah is this?
options: An unrestricted Hawalah
A restricted Hawalah
An agency for collection
A sale of the goods to Bakr
explanation: Per 5/1/1, restricted Hawalah limits the payer to settling from a financial or tangible asset of the transferor in his possession.

title: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
q: Converting Bank A keeps accounts with conventional correspondent banks. What does the standard require regarding these relationships?
options: Close all of them on the very day of the decision to convert
Keep them unchanged until their maturity
Convert them into interest-bearing deposits
Revamp them and limit dealings to the extent of need
explanation: Per 3/6, the bank opens accounts with Islamic banks and revamps conventional bank accounts; dealings with conventional banks are limited to the magnitude of need.

title: Murabahah
q: Bank A and a customer have not agreed who will bear the expenses of preparing their Murabahah contract documents. Who bears them?
options: The Bank and the customer, evenly
Each party in proportion to its benefit
The Bank alone, as the seller
The customer alone, as the purchase orderer
explanation: Per 2/4/3, document preparation expenses are borne evenly by the two parties unless they agree that one party bears them wholly.

title: Mortgage and its Contemporary Applications
q: In a spot sale, the commodity is still in the seller's hands, and the buyer wants a mortgage from the seller to secure its delivery. Is this valid?
options: Yes; any obligation of the seller, including delivery of the sold commodity, may be secured
No, unless the price has been deferred
No; a spot sale commodity in the seller's hands is not a debt
Yes, if the commodity is a fungible asset
explanation: Per 3/3/1, a mortgage may not be for a non-debt deal, such as a specific price, usufruct of a specific asset, or a spot sale commodity still with the seller.

title: Istisna’a and Parallel Istisna’a
q: A contractor building on the purchaser's land under Istisna'a halts work. The contract has a clause for this case. What may the purchaser do?
options: Nothing until a court ends the contract
Charge the contractor interest on the delay
Take the structure without paying anything
Complete the work at the contractor's expense
explanation: Per 4/2/3, on the purchaser's land it may be stipulated that he may perform the contract at the manufacturer's expense from the date work halted.

title: Ijarah and Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek
q: Bank A plans to issue Sukuk al-Ijarah and asks whether the Ijarah and Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek standard governs this issuance. What is the answer?
options: No, they fall under the standard on Investment Sukuk
Only if the Sukuk end with transfer of ownership
Yes, it covers every instrument based on Ijarah
Yes, if the Sukuk are backed by leased property
explanation: Per clause 1, the standard does not cover Sukuk al-Ijarah, which are covered by the Shari'ah Standard on Investment Sukuk, nor labour contracts.
